Space Force May Export Launch Lessons to Foreign Partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:53:38 UTC
02:53:38 KST

As U.S. allies look to establish sovereign military space launch capabilities, the Space Force is exploring ways to transfer lessons learned from its National Security Space Launch program to support its international partners.
In a new notice to industry, issued Sept. 3, the service said it is exploring a specific type of foreign military sales agreement called a technical service case, which involves the U.S. sharing specialized expertise with a foreign partner. The Space Force did not name which country it’s working with but said the nation is interested in acquiring engineering, logistical, and technical assistance to establish their own NSSL-like service using a U.S. commercial launch vehicle, including the spaceport infrastructure to enable it.
The U.S. is the global leader in space launch, conducting nearly 60 percent of all launches worldwide in 2025, according to analytics and engineering firm BryceTech. The Space Force operates the two busiest U.S. ranges: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Fla., and Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif. Last year, the two spaceports supported 175 launches, and the White House is targeting 1,000 U.S. launches annually by 2030.
Amid a push from President Donald Trump’s administration for U.S. allies to increase annual spending on defense, some partner nations have announced increases in military space funding—both for space systems and for launch capabilities. In Europe, Germany, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Italy have all funded domestic rocket development. Meanwhile, in April, Canadian lawmakers proposed a regulatory framework for the country to establish its own space launch capabilities after long relying on the U.S. and other countries to reach orbit.
“In a more uncertain and competitive world, Canada cannot rely on others to secure access to space for our economy, our defense, and our future,” Canadian Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon, who introduced the Canadian Space Launch Act, said in an April 21 statement. “Establishing Canadian sovereign space launch capabilities would drive billions in investments, create good paying jobs, increase Canada’s sovereignty, reduce our economy’s reliance on the United States, and support a commercial space launch and re-entry industry that could be worth $40 billion.”
To support the FMS request, the Space Force is looking to select a contractor to help tailor U.S. best practices in launch and spaceport operations for the country’s specific requirements, and evaluating whether certain commercial launch vehicles and spaceport operators are a good fit for its needs. The contractor will also recommend a mission assurance approach for the country, based on its needs. The company will work with Space Systems Command’s portfolio acquisition executive for space access to compile data and craft a report on its findings.
The Space Force expects to award a contract by Sept. 25 and compile the report within 12 months.
As USSF helps its partners grow their sovereign launch capabilities, it’s also considering options to launch its own payloads from foreign soil. While this effort doesn’t address that, officials have said there could be opportunities to partner with Australia, New Zealand, Japan, and countries in Europe, but there are U.S. policy hurdles that need to be addressed first.

Who Is Adam Telle, Trump’s New Acting Army Secretary?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:44:05 UTC
02:44:05 KST

President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that Adam Telle, the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works, will temporarily replace Dan Driscoll as the Army’s top civilian leader following Driscoll’s abrupt resignation from the role earlier this week.
Trump lauded Telle as "a Great Patriot, who is respected by all” in a Truth Social post, saying Telle would take over as acting Army Secretary “effective immediately.”
The news comes after Driscoll, who Trump nominated as Army Secretary last year after returning to the White House, stepped down amid reports of tension between him and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Hegseth praised Trump’s announcement on Thursday, calling Telle “strong and whip smart.”
“Huge congrats to Adam,” Hegseth said in a post on X. “He is indeed a great Patriot — and will be an immediate asset to the @USArmy.”
Here’s what to know about Telle.
Telle has overseen the Army Corps of Engineers since last year
Telle was sworn into his current role as the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works last August, becoming the second person nominated by the President to an Army position in Trump's second term to be confirmed by the Senate, according to Telle's biography on the U.S. military’s website.
In that position, Telle has served as a civilian official in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, an agency that builds and maintains infrastructure, including dams. According to his bio, he has had “principal authority to establish policy direction and to provide supervision of all aspects” of the civil works tasks that the agency performs for the Army, including projects aimed at reducing flood and storm damage.
Telle previously worked under multiple Republican senators
Before being appointed to his current role in the Trump Administration, Telle served as the chief of staff to Republican Sen. Bill Hagerty of Tennessee from 2021-2025, according to Legistorm. He previously worked under another Republican, then-Sen. Thad Cochran of Mississippi, for about a decade from 2007-2017, and held various roles in the office, including deputy chief of staff and legislative director, according to Legistorm. While serving in Cochran’s office, he helped with the lawmaker’s work on Hurricane Katrina recovery, according to his Army bio.
Telle also served on the Senate Appropriations Committee’s subcommittee that was responsible for overseeing the Department of Homeland Security’s budget, according to his bio.
Telle served in the first Trump Administration
During Trump’s first term in the Oval Office, Telle served on the White House Office of Legislative Affairs’ Senate team and “was President Trump’s chief liaison to the Senate,” according to his Army bio.
Telle will take over as acting Army Secretary at a tumultuous time
Telle will step into his new role in the Army at a time of turmoil both abroad and within the Department of Defense.
The war in Iran, which began on Feb. 28, has now stretched on for longer than six months and has sparked backlash from many Americans.
And Telle will also be taking on the new position amid upheaval within the U.S. military’s senior ranks. About 20 military and civilian leaders have been ousted or have resigned since Hegseth took over the Department of Defense, including Driscoll earlier this week. Even some Republicans have criticized Hegseth for the chaos at the agency, including Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who has called on Trump to replace the Defense Secretary.
“[Hegseth] is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks,” Tillis said in a social media post this week. “I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”

OpenAI agents hijacked German website in previously undisclosed AI breakout this spring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:42:31 UTC
02:42:31 KST

A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents, according to new research published Friday and two people familiar with the matter.
OpenAI officials learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it under wraps as executives grappled with the fallout from the July breach of the open source repository Hugging Face, the people said.
The episode, which began in May and has not previously been reported, underscores growing tension within the AI industry. Companies are racing to build increasingly autonomous agents capable of carrying out complex, valuable tasks, yet evidence is mounting that those systems may also learn to bend rules, exploit loopholes and coordinate with one another in ways developers neither anticipated nor intended.
During the Hugging Face breach, OpenAI agents autonomously plotted a digital heist that went undetected for more than a week, intensifying concerns OpenAI is sacrificing safety to push the AI frontier. Its failure to disclose the May incident may revive questions about its oversight.
OpenAI has pledged to monitor models more closely. Last month, it briefly paused some of its model training to add more safety measures. But this week, OpenAI unveiled its new "Astra" that promised better performance but could evade human monitoring.
“We are unable to meaningfully respond to claims or findings on a report that we have not had an opportunity to review," an OpenAI spokesperson said. "Reuters and the report’s authors declined our request for access. We will carefully review its contents upon publication and take any necessary next steps."
The German incident reflects a broader pattern of AI activity that some OpenAI investigators wanted to scrutinize more closely. But efforts to widen the probe met resistance from others inside OpenAI, including legal advisers, according to four people familiar with the matter.
"Claims that our legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false," the OpenAI spokesperson said.
The activity in Germany wasn't related to Hugging Face and wouldn't have been included in a Hugging Face incident report, the spokesperson said, adding that OpenAI has acted in good faith by working with outside experts and disclosed relevant incidents.
Wiki message board
The AI agent breakout in Germany was detailed in a report shared exclusively with Reuters by a group of researchers including Sydney Von Arx, CEO of AI safety nonprofit Nightingale, and Cormac Slade Byrd, a quantitative trader-turned AI researcher. They uncovered the activity in late August while scouring the internet for signs of unauthorized AI-agent behavior, they told Reuters.
The pair said they found more than 15,000 edits carried out by AI agents on a German-language wiki site, DseWiki, that is geared toward programmers and accepts communal edits along the lines of Wikipedia.
The edits showed OpenAI's agents had repurposed the site into a message board, sharing tactics to cheat on some tasks, bypass OpenAI’s restrictions and mask their behavior.
“It seems extremely unlikely that OpenAI wanted them to do this,” said Von Arx. “I doubt they’re supposed to be coordinating with each other. I doubt they’re supposed to be writing on the open internet.”
The researchers said they recognized the activity on the site as driven by AI agents which operate at superhuman speeds. They also showed intense focus on solving technical questions which are typical of the evaluations that AI companies use to train and test their models.
The messages were signed by users that referred to themselves and each other as agents, and about half gave themselves names that suggested an affiliation with OpenAI, such as “OpenAIResearcher,” or “OAIResearchMar26.”
The researchers said public server logs indicated much of the activity originated from Microsoft Azure infrastructure, which OpenAI sometimes uses. They also observed repeated visits to the site by OpenAI employees after the episode, a pattern they said strongly suggested the agents and the company were linked.
Cheating, hiding
Messages reviewed by the researchers showed agents plotting ways to evade detection, use tools such as Tor and preserve communications even after they had been shut down.
When the site's moderator began deleting pages in June, the agents responded by creating backup pages to dodge the cleanup.
“wiki cleanup/deletion sweep appears active alphabetically,” one agent wrote on June 19. “If this page vanishes, try [[ZZZDataUSAConstructionWageLive]]."
The researchers also found efforts to tamper with the website itself. Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London, said this amounted to a hacking attempt. OpenAI disputed that characterization based on its analysis of the material Thursday.
Past examples of AI-agent misconduct have often been downplayed as a logical byproduct of cybersecurity testing, where models are explicitly assessed on offensive capabilities. Olejnik said the latest findings suggested rogue behavior may not be confined to those settings.
Maurice Chiodo, an academic at Cambridge University's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk who reviewed some of the agents' communications, said the messages resembled "the operation of some sort of underground network, hell-bent on achieving a task or mission."
The episode, he said, should reinforce growing concerns that the greatest threat from advanced AI may not be a single superintelligent system, but "vast colluding swarms of semi-intelligent AI."

Israeli athletes removed from Northern Irish triathlon amid BDS pressure, fears for safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:42:06 UTC
02:42:06 KST

Four Israeli athletes were removed from the list of participants in the City of Derry Triathlon in Derry, Northern Ireland, the event organizers confirmed on Thursday.
This followed a request from the Israeli National Federation to "remove all the Israeli athletes entered" according to the BBC.
"The North West Triathlon Club (NWTC), who are organising the race, earlier said they could not support the Israeli athletes taking part," the BBC reported.
NWTC had concerns over "athlete and public safety," if Israelis participated, according to the public broadcaster's report.
The event, slated to occur on Saturday, with participant briefings held on Friday, has a "final start list" of participants, and event organizers confirmed that it "does not include any athletes representing Israel."
"This is not a position directed at anyone because of their religion or ethnicity, nor is it hostility towards an individual simply because they were born in Israel," NWTC said, according to the BBC.
"It is a position concerning representation of the State of Israel in international sport and the attempt to present normality on the international sporting stage while Palestinians continue to suffer," NWTC added.
Police became 'aware of potential protest activity' if Israelis were to participate
The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) told BBC's Northern Irish local outlet that it had "become aware of potential protest activity in relation to the event."
"The selection and confirmation of athletes for Europe Triathlon Cup competition is managed by Europe Triathlon, under World Triathlon rules. It is not possible to comment on the circumstances or decisions relating to individual athletes. The Local Organising Committee has no role in selecting the international start list," the event's website reads.
"The selection and confirmation of athletes for Europe Triathlon Cup competition is managed by Europe Triathlon, under World Triathlon rules. It is not possible to comment on the circumstances or decisions relating to individual athletes. The Local Organising Committee has no role in selecting the international start list," it adds.
"Having discussed the event with the LOC and National Federation, Europe Triathlon is confident that the race can proceed safely and provide a safe and enjoyable event for all athletes," the organizers said.
Anti-Zionist groups, local councils praise lack of Israeli athletes as BDS victory, pro-Israeli politician, Jewish community leader denounce decision
The Derry Anti War Coalition, a far Left anti-Zionist group, said on social media that it is "elighted that the triathletes from Israel will no longer be participating in the City of Derry Triathlon."
Additonally, members of the Derry City Council praised the lack of Israeli participants as a victory for the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) movement.
However, Julie Middleton, one of the five Members of the Legislative Assembly (based in Stormont, Belfast) representing Foyle, which includes Derry, said that the event should have been used to showcase the city's "hospitality and openness," and instead has "become associated with the exclusion of athletes because they are Israeli."
Middleton is from the Democratic Unionist Party, a Protestant party founded by Evangelical Christian preacher Ian Paisley, and its members are generally supportive of Israel.
The city should be one "where visitors and athletes from every background are treated with dignity," Middleton said.
Deputy Chairman of the Belfast Jewish Community Michael Black told BBC Northern Ireland that Israeli athletes not participating is "very disappointing but doesn't come as a surprise."
"Ireland, and I include Derry in this accusation, has the reputation of being one of the most antisemitic countries in Europe," his statement to BBC read.
He aso denounced the city and district council's BDS policies, saying that "many of the accusations that Israeli is accused of are false."
"The Jewish community's sympathy goes out to all the innocent people who have suffered terribly in this war on every side," his statement noted.
"Sport should not be used to divide people as this has done and will do nothing to bring peace to the Middle East," Black emphasized.
Sport should 'not become vehicle for discrimination, division,' Embassy of Israel in London says
The Embassy of Israel in London condemned the incident in a post on X/Twitter on Friday, calling the club's decision "deeply troubling."
"Sport should bring people together, not become a vehicle for discrimination and division," said the post. "If the NWTC cannot provide safety to all participants and event goers, it raises serious questions as to the ability to hold any future events."
The post also called on NWtC to "uphold the principles of equality, fairness and inclusion" and argued that Israeli athletes should have the "same right to compete as athletes from every other nationality."

New blood wanted: Israeli politics needs an infusion of unpolluted leaders - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:41:58 UTC
02:41:58 KST

I am partial to the argument that, specifically at this time of heightened strategic risk, Israel needs to elect or reelect leaders with significant security and diplomatic experience.
But I am convinced that Israel also needs to elect a new, younger generation of bright and believing, unsullied, and notionally more honest politicians – even if they are “green.”
I am certain that there is a capable and courageous next generation of Israeli leaders to take the reins of state – many of them the fearless heroes of Israel’s recent wars.
Therefore, I eagerly await the day, perhaps in the 2028 or 2030 elections, when the current crop of politicians will have passed – and that means everybody from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to Yair Lapid and Moshe Gafni.
In the meantime, when I vote this fall, I am going to seek a synthesis between the two competing wrenches that tug at my conscience: experience vs innovation, resilience vs virtue.
This approach does not present easy choices. But to begin with, it means ruling out the most cynical and mercenary political candidates, those whose career has been based on violent and divisive rhetoric and endless acrobatics – always on the attack and flip-flopping from one position to another.
The classic examples of such cynicism and divisiveness are Avigdor Liberman, Aryeh Deri, and Yair Golan.
Liberman is a cross between the deceased French extremist Jean-Marie Le Pen, a populist rabble-rouser, and Russian dictator Vladimir Putin, who excels at accruing power and asserting his relevance despite inherent weaknesses.
Alas, Liberman’s contribution to Israeli politics runs from negligible to detrimental. He has no record to speak of, aside from incitement and vindictiveness.
I cannot think of a single positive contribution to Israeli society, economy, defense, and foreign policy made by Liberman and his dictatorially hand-picked Knesset faction members over the past 40 years (quite a few of whom have ended up in jail).
Does anybody remember Liberman’s tenures as minister of infrastructure, transport, strategic affairs, finance, foreign affairs, and defense? Is there a single concrete achievement or worthwhile doctrine that emerged from his tenure in these senior posts?
What I do remember well are Liberman’s many grandiloquent and violent eruptions on sensitive issues that require statesmanship and nuance – two qualities he lacks exceedingly – and his pouting resignations each time he did not get his way.
Yvette the autocrat called for the bombing of the Aswan Dam in response to Egypt’s support of Yasser Arafat. He wanted to transfer Arabs of the Galilean triangle to Palestinian control, and to expel Arab citizens who refuse to pledge loyalty to the Jewish state.
On the other hand, he has played fast and loose with the idea of Palestinian statehood, sometimes fiercely against and other times smarmily and suggestively in favor.
When, as foreign minister, he was seeking to ingratiate himself in Washington, he declared that he would be willing to evacuate his home in Nokdim (a Gush Etzion settlement) in exchange for peace. What that really meant was that Liberman would readily sell his mother and sister to advance his political fortunes.
In 2019, Liberman nauseatingly pushed the country into another utterly unnecessary election campaign; a campaign that meant months more of deadlock in government policymaking and tons of hateful election bombast – supposedly over the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) army draft issue. And he threatens to do so again now.
But of course, Liberman doesn’t have a sliver of an idea on how to coax ultra-Orthodox Jews into the army. His going to the barricades on this issue to the point of forcing repeat elections was and is nothing more than pompous posturing; a cockfight meant to sadistically draw Netanyahu’s blood.
Deri's disasters
Deri's ruinous record in politics is without peer. He is an acute expression of pugnacious haredi power; a super-self-confident politician who bulldozes over all legal, civic, and moral boundaries to “bolster” (read: enfeeble) his haredi voting public. His brand of blithely sectorial, brusquely cynical politics has been catastrophic.
He is the central father-figure of the haredi world of dependency, of living off the dole; to the creation of the all-encompassing government-support system for those studying in yeshiva, a system so comprehensive that it simply does not pay for a kollel student to step out into the working world.
He has never spoken positively about higher education and professional training programs for ultra-Orthodox men and women that have opened in recent years, and he opposes the new haredi elementary and high school stream that teaches the basic core curriculum of math, science, and English.
I conjecture that Deri would sell every Judea and Samaria settler to the Saudis, twice over, if that were to earn Shas-affiliated schools a two percent budget increase.
Deri also is directly culpable for turning away Rabbi Ovadia Yosef from his earlier path of religious and political moderation. He whispered wicked things into the ears of Rav Ovadia, as needed, about religious Zionist, Russian, and Reform Jews, and secular politicians.
The fact that Deri has been caught in criminal violations more than once and gone to jail has not stopped him. He brushes this off by presenting himself as a persecuted Dreyfus and wronged John Demjanjuk rolled into one, and as a holy man whose concern for the poor will bring salvation to the downtrodden of Israel.
He seditiously plays the ethnic card, with him being discriminated against as a “franck” (a poor, marginalized Sephardi Jew). He has no problem cynically inflaming ethnic tensions in this way, even though it is of course ridiculous for Deri to claim marginalization.
If anybody has been in the privileged political driver’s seat for the past 35 years, as opposed to being victimized, it is Aryeh Deri.
Deri also holds the bag for the disasters that befell the haredi community in Meron on Lag Ba’omer in 2021 and during the coronavirus epidemic (when he led the haredi community’s separatist and defiant response to the government’s lockdown restrictions).
And of course, Deri has been a key figure in the ongoing haredi effort to legislate a permanent exemption of haredi men from military or national service – all the while outrageously sitting in the internal security cabinet that made the critical decisions about sending (non-haredi) Israeli soldiers into battle.
The danger of Golan
Golan is both a disappointment and a danger. Disappointment, because I remember him as a nationalist and appropriately aggressive military general who proudly paraded his Jewish-traditional roots. He was a good colleague at one of my conservative-leaning think tanks.
But then he sensed a vacuum at the far left of the political spectrum with the disintegration of the Meretz and Labor parties, and he jumped into politics and revved up the most extreme political positions to benefit from the void.
Golan has grandiloquently attacked religious Zionists and settlers, nationalists and soldiers, defended insurrection in the army, and accused Israel of genocide and other war crimes – to the point where his charges regularly feature in anti-Israel lawsuits around the world.
Golan and the rabble he is rallying also are a danger.
In every online video I have seen of parlor meetings and political rallies for The Democrats – a political party name meant as a caustic sneer – raw hatred and demonization dominate the discourse – of Netanyahu, of right-wingers, of the religious and ultra-Orthodox, and even of “centrists” like Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett.
This is accompanied by threats to “crush and close” any and all institutions that don’t align with the party’s “democratic” (sic.) worldview (such as pre-military religious colleges and hesder yeshivas), and to violently roll back (“destroy”) settlements while repeating the Oslo-era mistakes of territorial withdrawals.
Golan’s hypocrisy, hyperbole, and fanaticism light up every warning signal in my book.
Oh, how Israel truly needs a different breed of upright, principled, and temperate leaders!
The writer is managing senior fellow at the Jerusalem-based Misgav Institute for National Security & Zionist Strategy. The views expressed here are his own. His diplomatic, defense, political, and Jewish world columns over the past 30 years are at davidmweinberg.com.

5 EU countries agree on next steps for migrant return hubs outside bloc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:38:49 UTC
02:38:49 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Denmark, Germany, Austria, the Netherlands and Greece agreed Friday on the next concrete steps toward establishing migrant return hubs outside the EU, opening the way for active talks with potential partner countries, according to Denmark’s Ministry of Immigration and Integration.
The five countries, which make up the so-called Five-Country Group, agreed on three guiding principles for a future return hub system at a meeting in Copenhagen, the ministry said in a statement.
The model should help bring about a noticeable reduction in irregular migration to the EU and weaken the business model of migrant smugglers, according to the first principle.
The second principle states that the model should be developed as a joint European project in full accordance with EU law and international obligations, particularly human rights.
Under the third principle, return hubs should be established through equal and mutually beneficial partnerships with countries outside the EU, the ministry said.
The countries also agreed to begin active dialogue and negotiations with potential partner countries based on the three principles.
As part of that process, missions will be sent to potential partner countries to assess whether their standards meet the agreed principles and whether sustainable partnerships can be established.
The five countries also agreed on a common timeframe for the national legal procedures that must be completed before the return hub system can become a reality.
Ahead of Friday’s meeting, Danish Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bodskov had said Denmark expected to be ready to send the first foreigners without legal residence to a partner country outside the EU before the end of 2027.
“We have come a long way in the work of establishing a return hub outside the EU, and we are now closer than ever before,” Bodskov said.
He also argued that the centers could help curb irregular migration by making clear to migrants that they would not benefit from making dangerous journeys to Europe, while weakening the business model of people smugglers.
“It is unsustainable that migrants with no prospect of legal residence pay large sums to people smugglers to come to Europe,” Bodskov said.
The Danish ministry did not identify any potential partner country in its statement.
The initiative follows a June vote by the European Parliament on new rules paving the way for EU member states to establish return hubs outside the bloc.

Qatar rejects Iran claim strikes only targeted US military sites

Mohamed Majed and Mohammad Sio
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Qatar said Friday that official records it submitted to the UN show Iranian missiles struck civilian, commercial and residential areas in the country, rejecting Tehran’s attempt to cite a Qatari document as evidence that its attacks were limited to US military facilities.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al-Ansari made the remarks in a statement responding to a post on US social media company X by Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei.
Baghaei cited a safety and security risk assessment prepared by Qatar for the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference, claiming the document confirmed that Iranian strikes exclusively targeted US military facilities in Qatar and did not target civilian areas.
“If the Iranian side wishes to reference official documentation, we invite it to refer to the record formally submitted by the State of Qatar to the United Nations, rather than selectively quoting a security risk assessment prepared for operational purposes,” Al-Ansari said.
“Selectively extracting a sentence from that document while disregarding its broader context is therefore misleading,” he added.

Trump threatens to cut trade with some countries if Fed doesn’t lower rates
The message suggests the US president is running out of patience with the central bank just months after Warsh took over from Powell
President Donald Trump intensified pressure on the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates, threatening to cut off trade with certain economies with which the US has a deficit if the central bank does not act.
Trump issued his demands on Friday in a lengthy social media post after a stronger-than-expected August jobs report, which could bolster the case for Fed officials to raise rates at their next policy meeting starting September 15.
In his post, the president exhorted his hand-picked Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom he called “great”, and board members to “get smart” and “BE PATRIOTS for a change”.
“LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT,” Trump posted. “High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen!”
Trump said the US Supreme Court, which struck down his previous tariff regime, had acknowledged his authority to do that. But if he moves forward with trade embargoes, it would almost certainly trigger a legal challenge.
It was unclear how such an action would help lower US borrowing costs.

Jaishankar says India in touch with Russia, Ukraine to help end war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:33:24 UTC
02:33:24 KST

File photo: Minister of external affairs S Jaishankar
NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Friday said India has been in continuous touch with both Ukraine and Russia and is exploring whether ideas and suggestions can be developed to contribute to the mitigation and, ideally, the cessation of the conflict.Jaishankar made the remarks in Warsaw after holding talks with Poland's deputy Prime Minister and foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, a day after he met the top Ukrainian leadership in Kyiv.
‘Endless war must give way to an end to war’
Addressing a joint press meet with Sikorski, Jaishankar said the two leaders discussed major global and regional issues, including the war in Ukraine, which is now in its fifth year.“The deputy Prime Minister and I also understandably discussed some major global and regional issues, notable among them is the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year... I myself have just come here from Kyiv,” he said.
Replying to a question, Jaishankar said India remained in touch with both sides.“What we are trying to do is to see if there are ideas and suggestions which can be developed in some way in which they will contribute to the mitigation, ideally, the cessation of the conflict,” he added.Jaishankar reiterated India's position that the conflict must end through dialogue and diplomacy.
“India believes that endless war must give way to an end to war. These are wars without winners. Every additional day means more death, more destruction, more loss to the parties themselves, and more cost to the rest of the world,” he said.
“Our efforts must therefore focus on promoting dialogue and diplomacy. We must each do what we can in whichever way we believe could be most effective and support the efforts of others to bring this conflict to an end. This is India's strong conviction, and we are acting on it,” he added.
Jaishankar rejects trade link to ending war
Responding to a question on India's purchases of Russian oil, Jaishankar said the solution to the conflict lay in negotiations rather than trade.“This war is not going to end... not because somebody chose to buy or not buy oil or alumina or fertilisers or metals and minerals. It will end when there is diplomacy, when there is dialogue and when there is negotiation. So, I think let's diagnose the problem right,” he said.A day earlier in Kyiv, Jaishankar had met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and foreign minister Andrii Sybiha and said India was ready to extend “any help in any manner” to help end the war.Following the meeting, Zelenskyy said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.
India-Poland talks cover trade, technology and security

====================================================================================================

UN backs Africa-led push for a fairer world map
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:31:56 UTC
02:31:56 KST

The United Nations General Assembly has backed an Africa-led campaign to replace the widely used Mercator world map with a projection that more accurately represents the relative size of countries and continents.
The resolution, sponsored by African states and led by Togo, passed on Friday by a vote of 164-1, with six abstentions. The United States was the only country to vote against it.
Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey said the initiative was aimed at challenging perceptions created by a map that significantly distorts the size of land masses, particularly those near the poles.
“A fair world begins with a fair map,” Dussey told Reuters ahead of the vote.
Why Africa is challenging the Mercator map
Created in the 16th century, the Mercator projection expands the apparent size of land masses as they move towards the poles. As a result, Greenland can appear roughly comparable in size to Africa on many maps, even though Africa is about 14 times larger.
The UN resolution promotes the Equal Earth projection, which is designed to represent continents’ relative areas more accurately.
The measure is not legally binding and does not seek to eliminate Mercator for navigation. Togo’s Foreign Ministry said the projection remains appropriate for maritime and aerial navigation.
The campaign reflects broader African efforts to address what Togo describes as the lingering influence of colonial-era representations.
“This is not against Europe, it is not against any other civilisation,” Dussey said, arguing that the widespread use of Mercator is linked in part to the legacy of colonisation.
Togo plans classroom overhaul
Togo plans to become the first country to replace Mercator-based geography materials in its schools, with Dussey saying the government aims to update its textbooks by the end of the year.
“In the classroom, we need to change it to give an example to all the countries in the world,” he said.
Togo also plans to encourage other governments, schools, international organisations and technology companies to adopt Equal Earth and other more accurate alternatives.
Over the next six months, the country intends to engage African Union members and supporters from other regions on ways to expand adoption, including discussions with companies involved in mapping, GPS and other location-based technologies.
The United States opposed the resolution, describing it as promoting an “ideological agenda” and distracting from what it called more pressing issues involving international peace, prosperity and relations.
For Togo, however, the debate is about more than cartography.
“The world is changing. Africa also is changing,” Dussey said.

Five European nations seek deals to send irregular asylum seekers out of EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:30:23 UTC
02:30:23 KST

Five European nations aim to sign deals this year to send irregular asylum seekers without legal residency to countries outside the European Union, they have said at a meeting hosted by Denmark.
Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands said on Friday that they had agreed on concrete steps towards a deal with a non-European Union country on return facilities, the latest effort by European nations to reduce immigration.
The countries, known as the Group of Five, did not name the nations they expect to host return centres.
"We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year that will enable the establishment of return hubs," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters at a press conference in Copenhagen.
The group, which has held a series of meetings this year, plans to reconvene in Munich, Germany, at the end of September.
The European Parliament in June approved an overhaul of migration policy aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing member states to set up centres abroad, in what critics say could weaken safeguards for irregular asylum seekers.
Human rights concerns
The Council of Europe, a non-EU body that promotes human rights, democracy and the rule of law across the continent, said in July that return hubs posed "considerable human rights risks", and several other groups have also criticised the plan.
Danish Refugee Council Secretary General Charlotte Slente said it would be better to implement the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which focuses on stricter border screening, faster asylum and return procedures, and expanded digital systems for managing asylum claims.
"Return hubs focus on a small number of returns; they will not stop people from taking even more dangerous routes, and they could violate basic human rights," Slente said.
Denmark expects to be ready to send irregular asylum seekers to the return hub by the end of 2027, Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bodskov said.
"It's a new chance to have a life in a partner country," he said, adding that the five nations would be in dialogue with the UN body, the International Organization for Migration, and the UN Refugee Agency for their next steps.
A UNHCR spokesperson said the agency had not been approached with details of a proposal and could not comment on the arrangements being discussed.

China Focus: China to build international constellation for exploring Earth-moon space
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
01:25:37 CST
02:25:37 KST

HEFEI, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China has officially launched a scientific program to construct a satellite constellation in the Earth-moon space in collaboration with multiple countries, filling gaps in systematic observation of the region.
According to experts attending the 2026 International Deep Space Exploration Conference held in Hefei, capital of east China's Anhui Province, which runs from Thursday to Friday, the Cislunar CubeSat Constellation (C3) Program will be open to scientists and institutions worldwide, providing opportunities for developing countries to take part in deep-space exploration missions.
The cislunar space spans from low Earth orbits to about 2 million kilometers from Earth. It represents a new frontier for expanding human activity and will be a key operational area for future crewed lunar missions and the construction of lunar research stations.
Yet human understanding of this region has long relied primarily on isolated, point-based observations, leaving gaps in spatial and temporal coverage and insufficient data from key areas. A systematic and continuous observation network is therefore urgently needed, experts said.
According to Hu Zhaobin, vice chairman of International Deep Space Exploration Association (IDSEA), 30 CubeSats, each weighing no more than 30 kilograms, will form a constellation for space environment monitoring and gamma-ray burst detection. All satellites are scheduled for launch and deployment before 2030.
Through synchronized observations from multiple satellites and multiple locations, the constellation will enable comprehensive tracking of the evolution of space weather events and achieve sub-arcsecond positioning accuracy for gamma-ray bursts.
Once completed, the project will transform cislunar exploration from intermittent, point-based observations to networked and continuous monitoring, providing core data support for crewed lunar landing life safety and frontier scientific research on the cislunar space environment.
"We look forward to working with partners around the world to push the boundaries of human knowledge of deep space," Hu said.
The initiative was jointly launched by the Deep Space Exploration Laboratory (DSEL) and IDSEA, with support from the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization.
The program will also provide technical training and establish unified interface standards to enable developing countries to participate more deeply in deep-space exploration.
Research institutions from countries including Thailand, Serbia, Egypt, Senegal and Indonesia have already joined the initiative.
The first phase of engineering development has begun, with overall design studies for the satellites, payloads, tracking and control systems and other major components nearing completion.
The DSEL was officially inaugurated in February 2022. It has since established partnerships with more than 60 international research institutions.
In July 2025, the laboratory and several other institutions jointly proposed the establishment of IDSEA, the first China-based international academic organization for deep space exploration. ■

This year it brought together more than 1,300 exhibitors and hosted over 4,300 booths.
A number of mainland companies attended the exhibition and presented their latest products, offering a glimpse of the potential to share new opportunities in the rapidly evolving semiconductor industry on both sides of the Taiwan Strait.
At the booth of Huangshan Juxin New Material Co., Ltd., samples of materials in various sizes and colors were neatly displayed, drawing inquiries from Taiwan industry professionals.
"Many Taiwan companies have shown strong interest in our products, and some visitors are friends we met at last year's exhibition," said Qu Chao, the company's sales director.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC), the world's leading contract chipmaker and a cornerstone of Taiwan's technology industry, has become a central focus of those efforts. The company has announced massive investments in Arizona, while its suppliers in Taiwan are also facing increasing pressure to expand operations in the United States.
Against this backdrop, industry observers are calling for diversifying markets and strengthening industrial links.
"The two sides of the Strait have strong complementarities in terms of semiconductor applications and markets," said Lo Huai-jia, secretary-general of the Taiwan R&D Managers Association.
Noting that the mainland is one of the world's most important manufacturing bases, Lo said as its manufacturing sector continues to develop, demand for semiconductor products and the range of their applications are also expected to expand.
"The complementary strengths of industries on both sides of the Strait could create much broader room for cooperation," Lo added. ■

GUANGZHOU, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- On a production line at Seng Fong Holdings Berhad in Malaysia, a robotic arm grips a 35-kilogram block of rubber, with 3D cameras, laser scanners and AI algorithms serving as its "eyes" and "brain."
The setup is designed to tackle a longstanding challenge in the traditionally labor-intensive rubber processing industry. Rubber blocks coming out of drying ovens vary in shape, making them difficult for conventional robotic systems to handle.
Developed by an AI company in China's southern Guangdong Province, the solution has enabled the Malaysian rubber processor to automate more of the handling process, cutting labor costs by 20 to 30 percent while improving management efficiency, according to the company's chairman.
The case points to a broader shift taking place across the Asia-Pacific. AI is creating new opportunities for SMEs to innovate, while deeper regional connectivity is helping them turn technological advances into new sources of growth.
That trend was reflected at the 32nd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Small and Medium Enterprises Ministerial Meeting, held on Friday in Guangzhou, capital of Guangdong, as officials from APEC economies gathered to explore how technological innovation can empower SMEs and drive their further development.
SMEs are a major pillar of the regional economy. As technological and industrial transformation accelerates and global supply chains undergo profound changes, AI and other emerging technologies are creating both new opportunities and new challenges for SMEs across the Asia-Pacific.
AI-powered robotics are opening up new pathways for the digital transformation of SMEs, while open-source technologies are further lowering the barriers to technology access and application, enabling more businesses to participate in technological innovation, said Yang Qian, co-founder and chief operating officer of the Shenzhen-based embodied AI startup X Square Robot, at a parallel forum held alongside the ministerial meeting.
"What once required six months, costly computing power and a professional team can now be done in three days with a workstation and an idea," she said. "This gives SMEs, for the first time, a more level playing field with industry giants in innovation."
Yet SMEs across the region still face challenges, such as high digital transformation costs and talent shortages, highlighting the need for greater regional cooperation.
Kwon Jong-hyun, vice chairman of the Beijing Chapter of the World-OKTA, cited embodied intelligence as an example, saying China's strengths lie in scale and speed, while those of the Republic of Korea lie in precision and reliability.
Such cooperation, he said, is not simply about adding strengths together, but about multiplying their impact by combining complementary capabilities.
China's experience in supporting SMEs' digital transformation offers one example. The latest move came on Friday, when the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology released an action plan to support AI entrepreneurship among SMEs for 2026-2028. The plan aims to foster more than 10,000 technology-based and innovative SMEs, more than 2,000 "little giant" firms, as well as a number of gazelle companies and unicorns.
Beyond domestic efforts, China is also seeking to extend AI cooperation through technology sharing and practical collaboration. It has announced that it will provide 5,000 opportunities for AI training and seminars for developing countries over the next five years.
It is also advancing the establishment of AI application cooperation centers with ASEAN countries, with overseas branches in Laos, Malaysia and Vietnam already operational. These centers promote cross-border cooperation in large models, the data industry, and smart agriculture, bringing Chinese solutions together with local partners.
China stands ready to work with all parties to help more SMEs thrive and grow, Vice Premier Zhang Guoqing said in a speech delivered at the opening ceremony of the meeting.
The country is enhancing its policy support for SMEs and strengthening practical cooperation with APEC economies to jointly boost the high-quality development of SMEs, Zhang added. ■

MeerKAT in South Africa directly detects faint hydrogen signal from distant universe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
01:25:03 CST
02:25:03 KST

CAPE TOWN, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- An international team of astronomers has used South Africa's MeerKAT radio telescope to directly detect faint radio emission from neutral hydrogen gas across cosmic distances, providing a new way to trace the large-scale structure of the universe.
The finding, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, involved astronomers from the University of the Western Cape (UWC) in South Africa and the University of Manchester in Britain, UWC spokesperson Gasant Abader told Xinhua on Friday.
The new study detected the signal using MeerKAT radio observations alone, despite the data not originally being collected for the experiment. The finding marks a significant step toward using neutral hydrogen to map the three-dimensional structure of the universe on large scales, according to a UWC statement.
The team analyzed about 96 hours of MeerKAT observations and detected the signal from two periods in cosmic history, corresponding to redshifts of about 0.32 and 0.44. The emission traveled roughly four to five billion years before reaching Earth, tracing hydrogen over megaparsec scales.
"The signal is extremely faint and difficult to isolate from foreground emission, human-made radio-frequency interference, and instrumental effects," Sourabh Paul, lead author of the study, was quoted as saying in the statement. "Detecting it directly with MeerKAT shows that this technique is becoming a practical tool for cosmology."
The MeerKAT telescope, operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in the country's remote Karoo region, consists of 64 radio dishes. It is a precursor to the Square Kilometer Array Observatory, which is expected to begin science operations around 2028.
"MeerKAT continues to open new windows for cosmology," said Laura Wolz, a co-author from the University of Manchester.
"The fact that this signal can be extracted from observations that were not originally designed for hydrogen intensity mapping is very encouraging," she said.
Neutral hydrogen emits a faint radio signal known as the 21-cm line. As the universe expands, the signal is stretched to longer wavelengths, allowing astronomers to trace hydrogen at different stages of cosmic history.
Hydrogen intensity mapping measures the combined emission from many unresolved galaxies rather than detecting individual galaxies, enabling surveys of vast regions of the universe.
Previous robust detections of the signal at similar redshifts have typically combined radio observations with optical galaxy surveys. ■

The GEM also uses technology to complement the display of antiquities and enhance the visitor experience. "It brings the past, the history, with the present and the future in a nice context," Ghoneim noted.
The museum's conservation facilities are a case in point, Ghoneim said, noting that the conservation center has the largest and most up-to-date labs in the Middle East and Africa.

On the occasion of the 70th anniversary of Egypt-China diplomatic ties, Ghoneim invited more Chinese people to visit Egypt and the GEM, saying the museum offers a unique window into both the differences and the similarities between the two civilizations. ■

The UN considers the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, occupied Palestinian territory and regards Israeli settlements there as illegal under international law.

US Commander Reveals What Really Happened When His Bradleys Faced Ukraine’s Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:13:53 UTC
02:13:53 KST

- Category
- World
US Commander Reveals What Really Happened When His Bradleys Faced Ukraine’s Drones
A US Army Bradley company spent 10 days being watched, hunted and forced to rethink how it moved under drones operated by Ukrainian troops with real combat experience—before those same Ukrainians switched sides and began teaching the Americans how drone warfare is actually fought.
Blackhawk Company of the US Army’s 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry Regiment trained alongside Ukraine’s 412th Nemesis Unmanned Systems Brigade during the Combined Resolve exercise at the Hohenfels training area in Germany.
The commander of Blackhawk Company later challenged portrayals of the exercise as a simple rout of US armor by Ukrainian drones, writing in Task & Purpose on September 3 that such accounts did not fully capture either his unit’s performance or the lessons American soldiers took away from the training.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The two units had already met before the active phase began, giving American troops an early introduction to Ukrainian drone operators whose tactics had been shaped by years of battlefield experience during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.
Once the exercise began, however, that experience became an immediate problem for the US mechanized force, the commander wrote.
Blackhawk Company entered the training area in a column of Bradley infantry fighting vehicles through a limited access point. Ukrainian reconnaissance drones were already overhead, watching the formation as it moved into the battlespace.
The American company did not have some of the newer counter-drone equipment currently being tested by the US Army, leaving its troops to operate while knowing that hostile aerial reconnaissance could track their movements.
That forced a rapid change in tactics.
Rather than concentrate vehicles and personnel in familiar formations, the Americans began spreading them as widely as possible. Bradleys were hidden beneath heavy tree cover, while crews became increasingly conscious of how their vehicles appeared from above rather than focusing solely on threats visible from ground level. Movement also changed.
Instead of relying on roads and trails that drone operators could easily monitor, the mechanized company began using steep gullies, valleys and difficult terrain to conceal its movements.
That sometimes meant sending heavy Bradleys across slopes and terrain that mechanized units would normally prefer to avoid. Natural cover and dead ground helped reduce exposure to Ukrainian reconnaissance systems and made the company less predictable from the air.
The exercise still produced simulated losses of tanks and infantry fighting vehicles, but the American commander argued that this did not make heavy armor obsolete.
Bradleys and Abrams tanks continued protecting their crews and allowed soldiers to move rapidly through difficult terrain while pursuing their objectives. The lesson, in his account, was not to abandon armor but to change how armored formations operate when drones can observe almost every conventional movement.
According to the commander of Blackhawk Company, the most valuable phase came later. During the second half of Combined Resolve, Nemesis stopped operating against Blackhawk Company and joined the US troops for offensive operations.
That allowed the Americans to observe Ukrainian drone warfare from the other side.
Nemesis operators demonstrated techniques developed through combat in Ukraine, including methods for flying inexpensive drones over surprisingly long distances and rapidly moving targeting information from sensors to weapons.
For US troops, the Ukrainian approach provided a practical lesson in shortening the sensor-to-shooter chain—the process of detecting a target, identifying it, passing its location to a weapon system and engaging it before the target can move.
The Americans left the exercise with techniques they could incorporate into their own formations, while the experience also reinforced a less technological lesson.
Earlier, reports emerged that German Leopard 2 units were beginning to apply battlefield lessons from Ukraine, fitting tanks with new protective netting designed to reduce their vulnerability to drone attacks.
The changes were visible in photographs released by the Bundeswehr from Exercise Freedom Shield 2026, held at the Pabradė training area in Lithuania from June 6 to 19.

Geometry Reveals the Tricks behind Gerrymandering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:11:33 UTC
02:11:33 KST

Hardly anyone reckoned that struggling in high school to calculate the area of a triangle or the volume of a prism could be used one day to influence the outcome of an election. Geometry, however, can be a powerful tool in shaping results of an electoral contest—at least in plurality voting systems.
Designing a perfect election system for multiple parties is impossible, even with mathematical tools. But if, by and large, there are only two dominant parties, as in the U.S., things should be fairly clear-cut. The party candidate with the most votes wins, right? Anyone who has followed U.S. presidential elections in recent years knows that the reality is different. One important factor is the actual shape of the voting districts. If cleverly designed, a party that is actually losing can still gain the majority of representatives—an issue that was by no means absent in the U.S. midterm elections.
Math playsan important role in determining election outcomes, particularly for the 435 seats in the House of Representatives. By cleverly choosing the boundaries of a congressional district, a party can enable its candidate to win even if the vote count does not fairly represent the sentiment of the voters.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Here’s a highly simplified example: suppose a state consists of 50 voters, 20 of whom vote for a blue party and 30 for a red party. Voters might live in a grid pattern, as in, say, some sections of Manhattan. Suppose there are 10 north-south avenues and five east-west streets. All the red voters live on the first two avenues, the ones furthest west. The blue voters reside on the other three avenues. Now the task is to divide the voters into five electoral districts of equal size.
One could draw five vertical boundaries: Then there would be two election districts with only red voters and three with only blue voters. So the votes in that district would produce three blue party representatives and two red party ones, an accurate reflection of voters’ opinions.
But if the blue party were to get its way in drawing district boundaries, they might be inclined to draw the boundaries horizontally. Then all the districts would look the same, with four red voters and six blue voters each. In this case, the blue party wins in each district, and gets all five representatives. Something similar happened in New York state in 2012: 58 percent of people there voted for the Democrats, but the party got 21 of 27 seats (five more than would have been justified if the election districts had been drawn equitably).
State legislatures and the commissions that redraw district lines, on the other hand, might make a very different (somewhat more complicated) partitioning. To do this, they could pack almost all blue voters into two districts, giving the red party a majority in the three remaining districts in which there would be three red congressmen and two blue congresswomen—although more voters gave their votes to the blue party. There are numerous examples of this in U.S. congressional races. For example, in Pennsylvania in 2012, Democrats received 51 percent of the vote, but only five of 18 seats.
The deliberate redrawing of districts to gain a majority goes by the name of gerrymandering, a portmanteau of “gerry” and “salamander.” The former refers to Elbridge Gerry, the governor of Massachusetts in the early 19th century, who approved extremely odd-shaped voting districts that gave his party an advantage.
Even today, in most U.S. states, legislatures decide on the division of electoral districts about every 10 years (with the appearance of the new census). Time and again, the incumbent parties are suspected of using redistricting to their advantage. This can often be seen in strange-shaped electoral districts, similar to the one in Massachusetts at the beginning of the 19th century. A cartoonist at the time noticed that one of the districts resembled a salamander and thus coined the expression gerrymandering.
Redistricting has provoked numerous legal challenges. In 1986, the U.S. Supreme Court even ruled that intentional gerrymandering is illegal. But since then, it has barely touched an election district. As it turns out, setting rules for fair districting is not so easy. Even mathematicians are racking their brains over the question—and arming themselves with enormous computer power to deal with the problem.
How can you find gerrymandering? Observing the Maryland district pictured above, you might suspect the designers had certain ulterior motives. What is particularly striking is that it is extremely jagged. One assertion is that district borders should be “compact”—but without defining what “compact” means exactly.
One possible clue that gerrymandering may be present is the length of the outer boundary: the more jagged a district, the larger the perimeter. The literature related to redistricting sometimes advocates drawing the smallest possible circle to include the area within a district and comparing it to the area of existing boundaries. The more the district’s borders deviate from a circle, the greater the possibility that the district has been redrawn to suit partisan ends. The average distance between residents of a precinct may also indicate gerrymandering.
The partitioning into electoral districts is anything but simple. Each state follows its own rules in doing so. The ideal goal is for a district to contain roughly equal numbers of voters, be contiguous, not discriminate against ethnic groups, not cross county lines, and follow natural boundary lines, such as rivers. Such restrictions by themselves result in fractured districts—without even considering the voting behavior of residents.
A compact voting district does not necessarily lead to equitable representation, as a 2013 study found. The study paid particular attention to the 2000 presidential election in Florida, in which about as many people voted for Democrats as Republicans, but the latter accounted for 68 percent of the votes in Florida’s congressional districts. The researchers used a nonpartisan algorithm designed to draw the most “compact” districts possible while adhering to the state’s established rules.
Surprisingly, the computer also produced skewed results, in which Republicans would mostly have an advantage. And experts quickly realized the reason: most Democrats live in Florida cities. This means they win urban districts overwhelmingly, while narrowly losing in rural areas in each case. Because of this “natural gerrymandering,” more Republicans inevitably take seats in the House of Representatives.
Florida is not an isolated case, as political scientist Jonathan A. Rodden noted. The main problem is not a district's lack of “compactness.” If you want to prove that a boundary was deliberately drawn to give one party an advantage, you need more evidence than the mere shape of a district.The goal in an unbiased system is to find electoral districts so that each party has an equal chance of converting its votes into electoral seats. But how can we measure that? In 2014, University of Chicago legal scholar Nicholas Stephanopoulos and Public Policy Institute of California political scientist Eric McGhee developed a metric for the problem, the efficiency gap. It is calculated by subtracting the “wasted” votes of two parties from each other and then dividing by the total number of all votes. A wasted vote for any party, in this example, is one that ends up in a losing district that went to the opposite party or that is above the margin needed to win. The smaller the efficiency gap, the more impartial is the result.
To visualize this, we can again use the initial example with the 50 voters (20 for red, 30 for blue) and calculate the efficiency gap for the different divisions. In the first case, when all boundaries were drawn vertically, the first and second districts (from the left) each have 10 red votes, wasting four each. The third, fourth and fifth districts, on the other hand, each have 10 blue votes, four of which are also wasted. Thus, the efficiency gap is as follows (the vertical bars indicate absolute value): |(2 x 4) – (3 x 4)|/50 = 2/25 = 0.08.
In the second division, each district is equal: blue always wins by six votes out of 10. Thus, none of blue's votes are wasted—whereas all of red's are. The efficiency gap is 20/50 = 0.4, which is significantly higher than in the first division.
The third example is the most intriguing: the two districts in which blue wins 9 to 1 each have a blue surplus of three. In the three winning red districts, four blue votes each are wasted—so in total, (2 x 3) + (3 x 4) = 18 blue votes that are surplus ones. In contrast, there are only two red votes that were wasted. This results in an efficiency gap of (18 – 2)/50 = 8/25 = 0.32.
The efficiency gap is useful as an indicator that pins down partisanship in voting districts. But sometimes natural conditions, such as when almost all voters of a party live in the same city, make it hard to find better possibilities. To investigate these possibilities, statistician Wendy Cho, along with computer scientist Yan Liu and geographer Shaowen Wang of the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, designed an algorithm that divides maps into districts—based on the rules set by the state in question.
Finding the best possible division of districts so that each party has the same probability of converting a vote into a seat is extremely difficult. The task falls into the class of so-called NP problems, which computer scientists and mathematicians have suspected for decades cannot be solved efficiently with ordinary computers. That doesn't mean you can't find a solution—just that it may take a very, very long time. So Cho and her co-authors decided to let the computer construct an extremely large number of splits that are not necessarily perfect.
For example, when they applied their program to the state of Maryland in 2011, they realized that almost all of the 250 million results gave an advantage to Democrats. Apparently, the natural conditions, along with the requirements for voting districts, are such that Republicans are automatically at a disadvantage. Cho and her colleagues compared Maryland's actual apportionment with the computer's output and were able to show that the official voting districts favored Democrats in more than 99.79 percent of the 250 million computer-generated results.
Meanwhile, some U.S. states (mainly those where Democrats are in the majority) use independent commissions that redraw voting districts. These panels often resort to computer programs to find the fairest possible apportionment. In general, the apportionment of electoral districts this year appears to be the fairest in 40 years, as reported by the New York Times. When advantageous or detrimental districting decisions for both parties in all U.S. states are netted against one another, gerrymandering should result in only three extra seats for Republicans—down from 23 seats in 2012. But even three seats could be decisive in a close election. And news stories before the midterms depicted how gerrymandering is still very much a matter of public debate: Alabama’s state legislature redistricted to put many of the Black voters in the state into just one district, decreasing their electoral power, and resulting in a case that is now before the U.S. Supreme Court.

UN approves resolution in support of map that shows Africa's true size
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:01:38 UTC
02:01:38 KST

UN approves resolution in support of map that shows Africa's true size
NEW YORK, Sept 4 - The United Nations on Friday voted for a shift away from the 16th-century Mercator global map towards one more accurately reflecting countries' true size, a resolution sponsored by African states to counter perceptions that the continent is peripheral.
Togo led the initiative to further the African Union campaign to limit use of the Mercator map, which distorts the relative size of land masses by expanding those nearer the poles. It makes Greenland appear roughly the same size as Africa, though Africa is about 14 times larger.
"A fair world begins with a fair map," Togo's Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told Reuters ahead of Friday's vote.
The resolution promotes the Equal Earth projection, which more accurately portrays the size of the continents.
It is not legally binding and it "in no way challenges the use of the Mercator projection for maritime and aerial navigation, for which it remains fully suited," the Togolese ministry said in a statement.
The resolution passed in the U.N. General Assembly by a vote of 164 to 1 with 6 abstentions.
The United States, the only country to vote against the resolution, said it promoted an "ideological agenda" and was a distraction from the "genuine problems of international peace, prosperity or good relations".
TOGO TO CHANGE MAPS IN SCHOOLS THIS YEAR, MINISTER SAYS
The Mercator map remains widely used in classrooms, but Togo hopes to change its school geography materials by the end of the year, Dussey told Reuters.
"Togo will be the first country to change our own geography books," Dussey said.
"In the classroom, we need to change it to give an example to all the countries in the world."
Togo will press other governments, schools, international organisations and technology companies to move away from the centuries-old Mercator projection, Dussey said, adding that Equal Earth offers "the best perception" of the world.
Togo plans to meet African Union member states and supporters from other regions within the next six months to agree on how to promote wider adoption, Dussey said.
Dussey said the discussion about next steps would need to include companies operating mapping, GPS and other location-based technologies.
Dussey linked the campaign to adopt the map to wider African efforts to confront colonial-era legacies, while saying it was not an attack on Europe or any other civilisation.
The Mercator map's widespread use is a consequence of colonization, he said.
"The world is changing. Africa also is changing." REUTERS

The unspoken rules of how and where to think
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:01:23 UTC
02:01:23 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Hello everybody,
This week we’re looking at shallow and deep solutions.
The tap and I had an understanding.
The Americans call it a “faucet,” and my editor and I usually have a kind of cat-and-mouse battle about these kinds of things. How many Britishisms can I slot into a newsletter edited by an American? We shall see. Because for all the rubbish bins, pavements, car parks, trousers, crisps, torches, and trainers in the world, I’m going to insist he keep “tap.”
The tap in the shower never worked properly. The on-off side was fine, but the hot-cold one lived by its own chaotic rulebook. It could technically turn 180 degrees either way, but there was really only one spot you could have it in. A fly’s push one way and you’d be cold plunging. A strong wind the other way and you’d be off to the minor burns department.
And so, over the years, I had mastered the art of finding that oh-so-perfect sweet spot. I enjoyed waiting to hear guests’ yelps or curses. I took pride in how artfully I could position that tiny, well-worn knob.
But then, one day, we had a plumber come around to fix our toilet. Big James we called him because he had large biceps. Sexy James, our cleaner called him.
“You know,” Big and Sexy James said, “I could get you a new shower tap for about £20.”
We bought the tap, dear reader. James put his arms to use, and our shower was fixed for less than $30 plus labor. No more freezing. No more skill required. It even had a safety button to prevent you from scalding yourself.
For years I had managed to cope with my dodgy tap. For years I had been happy with a “shallow solution” to my ablutionary needs. All it took was for one plumber with a well-used gym membership to show me a deep solution.
This week we look at why that difference is important.
Go well,
Jonny
The deep thinking space
I’ve always found the idea of a “game space” interesting.
The game space is a hallowed ground, set apart from the “normal world” where certain rules, laws, and instructions apply. On the rugby field, you have to pass backward. In an RPG, a wizard cannot wear heavy armor. In chess, a bishop can’t move straight. And so on.
I wonder if there is also a kind of game space when it comes to thinking. For example, if you were to join me for a Mini Philosophy seminar next month, the rule would be that we talk about things in a philosophical way. We’d unpack ideas, we’d reference books, we’d dive into the mysterious depths of why we do what we do. But when I talk to a friend over brunch or in the pub, the rules are different. This is a social occasion. It’s a light catch-up. There is a time and place for “shallow,” and there is a time and place for “deep.” No politics at Christmas. No penis jokes in a newsletter.
But what happens when we confuse our spaces? When we try to bring deep thinking to a shallow setting, it can often be funny or eye-rolling but very rarely problematic. If I try to unravel the underlying psychodynamic motivations behind my need for constant validation at a kids’ birthday party, my friend will probably just tell me to stop. Have a day off, Jonny.
The problems come when we offer only shallow thinking in a deep space.
Imagine you’re sitting in the car driving with your friend somewhere, and they say, “I’m really unhappy, mate. I’ve not been happy for years.” Now, the game has begun. The rules are in place. This car, this moment, has become a sacred space that demands deep thinking and deep conversation.
“Ah, cheer up, mate,” you say, “let’s go get a drink.”
Now this is a solution of sorts. No doubt a drunken revel capped by an early-morning McDonald’s distracts your friend from their pain, but it doesn’t resolve it. They’ll wake up the next day just as unhappy as before but now with a hangover and a sesame bun sticking to their face. You offered a shallow solution where a deep solution was wanted.
This week I spoke with Jack Maden about his new book, The Philosophy Prescription. (Mini Philosophy Members can hear our full interview at the end of this newsletter.) And Jack started talking about Arne Næss’s distinction between shallow and deep thinking. Because for Næss, our governments and leaders have been dealing only in shallow solutions to problems that really need deep thinking. If there is ever a “deep space” it ought to be the corridors of power. Instead, we’ve been getting successive administrations scattering about vote-winning quick fixes. We’re plastering the cracks of a building that’s wobbling. These are the examples Jack gave:
“So, a shallow response to say famine would be to send food. These people are experiencing starvation, let’s send them food, problem solved. A deeper response would be to question why has the famine occurred in the first place? What’s driving the famine? How can we make structural changes to ensure famines don’t happen again in the future?
“Arne Næss basically says, in the context of the environment, that all of our responses are shallow, they’re all reactive. They’re all driven by this idea that we should prioritize human production. So, if an earthquake happens, we need to rebuild the area so that it can start producing again. If pollution is affecting fishing, then we need to kind of remove plastic from the ocean so that we can fish again. And he wants us to go deeper in our questioning and say, ‘Well, is placing human production on this pedestal really leading to lives worth wanting?’”
It might be, of course, that we disagree with Næss on this one. It might be that we do think we ought to prioritize human production over a more ecologically mutual position. But the point is that we need to ask ourselves why these problems keep happening, rather than offering shallow, fix-the-symptom solutions. We need something more root and branch. We need to look at the systems, values, and structures underpinning our entire worldview. But to do that requires us all to enter a deeper thinking space and to play by different rules. And not everyone wants or is willing to play that game.
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.
