The Tainan branch of the High Prosecutors’ Office has indicted a retired navy sergeant surnamed Ma (馬) on charges of contravening the National Security Act (國家安全法) for allegedly attempting to develop an intelligence gathering organization for China.
Ma was also indicted for allegedly soliciting bribes from officials and contravening the Anti-Corruption Act (貪污治罪條例).
Ma allegedly began taking instructions from China as early as 2008 and was directed to develop an organization in Taiwan to collect intelligence on military, maritime and coast Guard Administration affairs, prosecutors said.
Photo: Taipei Times
In early 2021, Ma allegedly approached a retired major general surnamed Wang (王) and introduced him to Chinese officials, they said.
Ma allegedly gave Wang NT$42,100 and attempted to recruit him to collect intelligence related to the Ministry of National Defense, as well as information on cooperation agreements between the Ocean Affairs Council and the US, the indictment said.
Wang refused to cooperate, it added.
From 2023, Ma allegedly used a junior-high school alumni group on a messaging app to contact a Coast Guard Administration division chief surnamed Yu (于), it said.
Ma allegedly offered Yu up to US$100,000 per information and promised to pay him a monthly amount equivalent to his salary if he agreed to continue working on a long-term basis, the indictment said.
Ma allegedly gave Yu NT$50,000 and a cellphone to be used for intelligence gathering and instructed him to collect information on Taiwan’s maritime affairs exchanges with the US and Japan, it said.
Yu refused to cooperate, it added.

Housing market shows no sign of recovery: source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:22 UTC
01:38:22 KST

Taiwan’s housing market showed little sign of emerging from a prolonged downturn last month, as developers held back new projects and buyers remained on the sidelines amid high prices, tight credit and a seasonal slowdown.
The new housing indicator in northern Taiwan fell to 33.9 points last month, remaining in the “yellow-blue” range that signals a contracting market, according to My Housing Monthly (住展雜誌).
“Demand has yet to show any meaningful recovery,” My Housing Monthly research director and spokesman Chen Ping-chen (陳炳辰) said.
Photo: CNA
Ghost Month, heavy rains and summer travel all weighed on buyer activity, while developers largely waited for this month, a traditional sales season, he said.
Two of the indicator’s six components — presale launches and completed-home units — deteriorated, while buyer visits, transactions, bargaining rates and unsold projects were unchanged.
The value of presale projects launched last month fell by nearly NT$9 billion (US$284.54 million) from the previous month, with only a few projects carrying sales values of more than NT$2 billion, My Housing Monthly said.
Completed-home launches were even weaker, with about 60 units unveiled, compared with a typical monthly level of more than 100. Completed new homes generally command higher prices than other properties, while inflexible payment terms for presale projects have made them harder to sell in a weak market, Chen said.
Weekly visits to development sites averaged fewer than 10 groups, while transactions averaged less than one.
Some newly launched projects attracted potential buyers because of their developer brands or popular locations, but older projects in less-preferred areas have struggled to generate sales.
The weakness is also putting pressure on sales agencies, with some projects changing agents and smaller firms exiting after failing to generate sufficient transactions.
Developers’ restraint has helped prevent inventories from rising further. The number of unsold projects fell 2.6 percent to 1,559 last month from about 1,600 in July. However, that remains above the fewer than 1,000 projects seen during stronger market conditions, highlighting the scale of the inventory overhang.
Taipei and Taoyuan could face difficulty clearing inventory because of high prices and large stockpiles, Chen said.
A further deterioration could also increase the risk of contract cancellations, he added.
However, developers have largely resisted cutting prices. Bargaining rates have remained below 10 percent, with transactions concentrated in established brands and top-tier locations.
A broad recovery appears unlikely with only one quarter left in the year, Chen said.
Policymakers are also likely to remain cautious ahead of local elections for mayors and councilors in November, he said.
The earliest potential catalyst might instead come from the central bank’s December meeting, after the election, Chen said.

Minister wants all Palestinians out of Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:18 UTC
01:38:18 KST

Israeli Minister of National Security Itamar Ben Gvir on Thursday unveiled a plan to remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip and send them abroad.
Speaking in the run-up to close-fought Israeli elections, he said the plan aimed to see the departure of 250,000 Palestinians from Gaza in the first year, 2 million residents over the following six years.
“It’s realistic,” Ben Gvir said, claiming that some countries were “ready” to take in Gazans, without naming them.
Photo: Reuters
“We must encourage the emigration of Gaza’s inhabitants,” he said, adding that he believed the plan did not mean forcing Palestinians to leave their land.
Forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva Conventions.
For Palestinians, any effort to force them off their land would recall the Nakba, or catastrophe — their mass displacement during Israel’s creation in 1948.
Inflammatory comments from Ben Gvir, who is a key minister in the right-wing coalition of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, regularly draw international condemnation.
Ben Gvir said his right-wing populist Jewish Power party would demand “a ministry in charge of emigration” during the formation of the next government, adding that his plan was “the result of a year and a half of work and ... is concrete.”
In a 20-page document titled “National Work Plan for Voluntary Emigration from the Gaza Strip,” Ben Gvir further says his plan offers a solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Although members of the ruling right-wing coalition have made multiple statements about transferring Palestinians out of Gaza, it is unclear to what extent their remarks will be followed by action.
The Oct. 27 vote is expected to be close, and there is no guarantee that the parties currently in power will remain so after then.
Israeli Minister of Defense Israel Katz on Wednesday said his country was ready with plans to remove Palestinians from Gaza if the US gave its approval.
Katz has for several months been advocating such a measure, presented as the voluntary emigration of Gaza’s population.
Israeli Minister of Finance Bezalel Smotrich has even proposed extending the measure to Palestinians in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967.
US President Donald Trump, at the start of his second term, stunned much of the world by calling for all Palestinians to leave the Gaza Strip.
Trump spoke of developing the Mediterranean territory, devastated by Israeli bombardment since the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas, into a luxury resort destination.
He then walked back the idea following strong pushback, including from Egypt, the only country other than Israel to border Gaza.
Israeli attacks have already internally displaced the vast majority of Gaza’s people following the unprecedented Hamas attack on Israel, which killed 1,221 people, according to official Israeli figures.
Israel’s offensive has since claimed at least 73,470 lives in Gaza, with more than 1,330 since the ceasefire, according to the Gaza health ministry, which operates under Hamas.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:18 UTC
01:38:18 KST

Rescuers in Nepal yesterday pulled two workers alive from a tunnel at a hydropower plant, raising hopes of reaching dozens of others believed to be trapped nine days after deadly floods swept away villages and submerged the Himalayan region in mud and debris.
Search teams first heard voices from inside the tunnel in the morning, allowing them to locate the two men, Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane said.
Images showed a rescuer carrying one of the workers, covered in mud, on his back, while soldiers on either side helped.
Photo: AFP
One of those rescued said more people are alive inside the tunnel, Nepalese army spokesperson Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet said, and the search is ongoing.
“I can’t explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to god,” said Amir Maharjan, the brother of one of those rescued.
Basnet confirmed the first trapped worker’s rescue, and Neupane posted about the second on Facebook shortly after.
Both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu, and Maharjan said his family was on its way there. One of the survivors was in critical condition, a statement from the prime minister’s office said.
Officials identified the men as a mechanical foreman and a mechanical supervisor. They were rescued from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A plant.
About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said.
About 115 are believed trapped in the tunnel at Trishuli 3A alone, the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal said.
Nepalese Minister of Information and Communication Bikram Timilsina wrote on Facebook that officials “are waiting for the rescue of more and more people.”
At least 1,287 people were killed in the Aug. 26 floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 people remain missing, Nepal’s disaster management agency said.
Chinese official news agency Xinhua yesterday reported that 31 people were killed and 531 were missing on the Tibet side of the border.
Nepal’s disaster agency yesterday estimated that flooding caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees (US$2.57 billion) in damage to infrastructure and property.

Nvidia to buy AI start-up Hugging Face for US$13bn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:16 UTC
01:38:16 KST

Nvidia Corp agreed to acquire artificial intelligence (AI) start-up Hugging Face in a transaction valued at about US$13 billion, adding a popular software platform to the chip giant’s AI empire.
The price includes an equity-based retention program of as much as US$1 billion for Hugging Face employees who join Nvidia, according to a statement on Thursday.
Nvidia touted the deal as a way to protect open-source AI developers, who rely on Hugging Face to share software and data that can be freely used by anyone. Chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) has emerged as a strong advocate for open-source AI models as a means of keeping the technology broadly available and preventing it from becoming concentrated in the hands of a few massive players.
Photo: EPA
OpenAI, Anthropic PBC and other big AI developers mostly rely on closed models that are proprietary. In buying Hugging Face, Nvidia vowed to keep the platform open.
“Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” Huang said on X. “Nvidia is going to be a great home for Hugging Face, its community and the future of open models.”
Still, Nvidia’s move raises its own questions about the concentration of power in AI. It is already the biggest company in the industry, and acquiring Hugging Face would only add to its influence. A previous attempt to buy chip designer Arm was opposed by regulators because of the sway it would give Nvidia.
“The company now sits closer to the entire AI supply chain: compute, models, datasets and developer workflows,” Forrester Research Inc analyst Jeff Pollard said.
“That creates an opportunity to improve AI security,” he said, adding that “it also concentrates influence over a critical piece of the open AI ecosystem.”
Buying Hugging Face is one of the biggest moves yet in Huang’s push to broaden the uptake of AI and extend his customer list.
“Under this commitment, Hugging Face would continue to permit model makers, developers, and users to upload and download models and datasets of their choosing and to support other silicon vendors,” the statement said.
Nvidia was already a backer of Hugging Face, alongside Alphabet Inc’s Google, Amazon.com Inc, Intel Corp and Salesforce Inc, among others.
Founded in 2016, Hugging Face was valued at US$4.5 billion in a funding round three years ago. Nvidia’s talks with the company were reported earlier by Business Insider.
Hugging Face’s founders Thomas Wolf, Clement “Clem” Delangue and Julien Chaumond, initially began business in Paris, naming the company after the “hugging face” emoji. They joined billionaire Xavier Niel’s start-up campus Station F, located in a redeveloped, century-old freight station in Paris.
The dealmaking spree has some observers raising antitrust concerns about the Hugging Face purchase.
“I think it’s a process and we’ll see — we are confident,” Wolf, chief science officer of Hugging Face, said in an interview.
Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, is the leading maker of AI accelerators, the chips that help train and operate models. It has gradually added a variety of other technologies, including software and networking equipment, with the goal of expanding the AI economy.

Lin considered ‘graceful exit’ after Olympic gold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:15 UTC
01:38:15 KST

Taiwanese boxer Lin Yu-ting said that she considered retiring after winning gold at the Paris Olympics, but wanted to carry on fighting in part to defy those who questioned her eligibility.
Lin and Imane Khelif of Algeria found themselves in the middle of a major gender row at the 2024 Games, with US President Donald Trump, Elon Musk and author J.K. Rowling among those wading in.
The two boxers had been disqualified from the 2023 world championships by the International Boxing Association (IBA) after the organization said they failed unspecified gender eligibility tests.
Photo: AF
However, the International Olympic Committee allowed them to compete in Paris, saying they were victims of “a sudden and arbitrary decision” by the widely discredited IBA. Both went on to win gold.
Hailed as a hero in Taiwan, Lin wondered at the time whether it was the right moment to bow out of the sport she loves.
“I achieved everything I had worked for. It seemed like a good moment to make a graceful exit,” the 30-year-old said in a rare interview.
Initially the choice was taken out of her hands and her career forced on hold.
Then in March this year World Boxing — which has taken over the running of the sport — cleared her to return after 19 months in limbo following a one-off sex test.
Lin, a two-time world champion who is to compete at the Asian Games in Japan starting on Sept. 19, said quitting would have let down the people close to her.
“I couldn’t leave the people on my team behind,” Lin said.
“And I also wanted to see how far my own abilities could go,” she added.
Lin is keen to put the darker moments of Paris and its aftermath behind her.
Dwelling on negatives would get her trapped in a “pessimistic mindset,” she said.
“I’m able to continue competing now, in a way that’s a rebuttal to many of the things people were saying before,” she added.
Lin has stepped up a weight class as she pursues a second Asian Games gold in a row.
She won last time at 57kg, the same weight as her Paris triumph, but would box in the 60kg category in Nagoya-Aichi this month.
“Right now I feel like things are gradually falling into place for me,” she said.
“This year I started competing again and I’ve gradually regained my reactions and form. It really does feel like I’m getting back into my rhythm.”
On her return to international competition Lin won bronze at 60kg at the Asian Elite Championships in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, then silver at the World Boxing Cup in China.
“Moving up a weight class means everything is new for me,” Lin said.
“It’s a new goal, a new challenge and a new milestone,” she added.
Lin was 13 when she first pulled on a pair of boxing gloves at her junior-high school gym in Yingge District near Taipei. She was “a small-stature student without an obvious physical edge,” said her coach Tseng Tzu-chiang, who has been her trainer ever since.
Lin worked hard and captured a string of titles including world crowns in 2018 and 2022.
“Once she set her eyes on something, she would commit to it wholeheartedly,” Tseng said.
She meets setbacks head-on, resetting her goals and achieving them with “absolute clarity and determination,” he said.
Lin admits to “very high standards” and a “rigorous attitude” towards training, but there is a fun side too, unwinding from the physically taxing sessions with Tseng by playing Pokemon Go.
“I manage risk very strictly,” Lin said, likening trading stocks to throwing punches.
“The best risk management in the ring is making sure I’ve done my own part well. That’s something I can control,” she added.
Winning Paris gold was the culmination of years of devotion.
She failed to secure a spot at the 2016 Rio Games and was eliminated in the early stages in Tokyo in 2021.
Two years after her Paris win, Lin’s gold medal remains carefully wrapped and stored in her bedroom, rarely making public appearances.
“I haven’t displayed it yet because I haven’t found a good way,” Lin said, adding she might one day show it alongside her other medals.
“I’m worried about damaging it, getting it dirty, or accidentally scratching it,” she said.

Instead, injuries have foreclosed the possibility of a clash between the two champions in three of the four Grand Slams, with the Spaniard missing the French Open and Wimbledon due to a wrist injury and the Italian absent from New York because of a knee injury. US-China meeting likely to focus on each country’s domestic needs: expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:14 UTC
01:38:14 KST

Domestic political considerations in the US and China are likely to drive the agenda of the next meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), a Taiwanese academic said yesterday.
National Chengchi University Institute of International Relations Director Wang Hsin-hsien (王信賢) said during a book launch in Taipei.
Both leaders sought “strategic stability” during their meeting in Beijing in May, but the outcome was closer to “tactical stability,” he said.
Photo: CNA
“It is like two boxers agreeing to take a break,” Wang said. “The break does not end the fight; it is preparation for the next round.”
The anticipated second meeting, expected to take place on Sept. 24 in Washington, should be viewed not only through the lens of bilateral relations, but also in terms of the two leaders’ domestic needs, he said.
Ahead of the US midterm elections on Nov. 3, Trump would likely seek commitments from China to purchase more US products, including Boeing aircraft, soybeans and beef, Wang said.
Meanwhile, Xi needs to demonstrate that he can manage relations with Washington as China prepares for major Chinese Communist Party meetings, he said.
Taiwan is likely to receive less attention than it did at the first meeting, when Beijing made the “threat” of Taiwanese independence a top priority, Wang said.
That would be partly because the US would have more influence over the agenda this time, given that the meeting would be held in Washington, he said.
A wider range of issues are also expected to be addressed at the summit, including trade, tariffs, technology, supply chains, and the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, Wang said.
Meanwhile, National Taiwan University political science professor Chang Teng-chi (張登及) said China was seeking to add Chinese elements to the international system and maximize its interests without completely replacing existing institutions.
The event marked the publication of the Chinese-language book, the title of which could be roughly translated to “An Introduction to Contemporary China’s Foreign Relations (當代中國對外關係概論).”
Chang and Wang were its coeditors.
The book, which combines major theories with contemporary case studies, examines China’s foreign policy decisionmaking, and its relations with major powers and neighboring countries.
It also covers head-of-state diplomacy, the Belt and Road Initiative, territorial disputes and the international order, and includes discussion questions intended to encourage reflection on China’s foreign policy.

Singapore’s air quality hit an unhealthy level yesterday, as haze from forest fires raging in Indonesia continued to spread across swathes of Southeast Asia.
The city-state is currently one of the 10 most-polluted major cities in the world, coming in at third in IQAir’s ranking. Kuching, in the Malaysian part of the island of Borneo, was No. 1.
A government taskforce has “activated haze response plans” for schools, workplaces and community centers, Singaporean Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu (傅海) said in a video message on Facebook.
Photo: EPA
Most people could continue essential daily activities, but the elderly or vulnerable should check advisories before going outdoors, she added.
If air quality continues to worsen, “selected air-conditioned community spaces may be used by those who need respite from the haze,” she said, adding that the polluted air “could be with us for a while.”
Singapore’s 24-hour Pollution Standards Index stood at 105 as of 12 noon yesterday, the National Environment Agency said.
A reading between 101 and 200 is deemed “unhealthy,” while above 300 is categorized as “hazardous.”
The fires and accompanying haze are an annual occurrence, often attributed to traditional and commercial land-clearing practices. But this year’s “super El Nino” weather pattern, which is expected to start peaking from next month, threatens to intensify and prolong adverse impacts on public health and commercial activity across the region.
The number of fire hotspots was rising again on the Indonesian part of Borneo after a small decline earlier, according to local media that cited the country’s forestry minister, highlighting the challenge authorities face in containing the blazes.
Air quality was also deteriorating in other parts of the region. Malaysia’s Sarawak recorded “hazardous” levels of air pollution, while Indonesian authorities urged residents in Kalimantan, where the hotspots are concentrated, to be on alert for worsening conditions.

Study shows benefits of hospital mattress project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:13 UTC
01:38:13 KST

Automated repositioning air mattresses for critically ill patients can improve pressure injury prevention and reduce the physical burden on nurses who manually reposition patients every few hours, National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH) told a news conference on Wednesday.
NTUH superintendent Yu Chung-jen (余忠仁) said that people in critical care or intensive care units (ICUs) are often severely ill, connected to medical devices and tubes, or are unconscious and unable to reposition on their own.
If they remain in the same position for too long, they become prone to pressure injuries that can lead to severe infections, Yu said.
Photo: CNA
ICU staff typically reposition patients every two hours, he said.
It is not an easy task, especially with tubes attached to patients’ bodies, he said, adding that it often requires two or three nurses to work together to complete the task.
To address the challenges, NTUH said that its nursing team launched a clinical research project on an automated repositioning air mattress.
The project involved codevelopment, clinical testing and improvements to the devices, it said.
A study conducted in the ICUs of the hospital’s internal medicine and neurosurgical departments garnered data from use of the devices with 424 critically ill patients, it said.
Following the introduction of automated repositioning air mattresses, reports of pressure injuries fell from 4.7 percent to 2.9 percent; nurses’ workload associated with repositioning patients was reduced by 69 percent; while time spent on repositioning was shortened by 53 percent, NTUH said.
The proportion of repositioning procedures that could be completed by a single nurse increased to 91.8 percent from 36.7 percent, it added.
NTUH nursing supervisor Hsiao Wei-ling (蕭偉伶) said that manually repositioning patients can sometimes cause occupational injuries, such as lower back, shoulder and neck strains.
It is essential that medical lines and tubes connected to patients remain unaffected during the process, Hsiao said.
Introduction of the mattresses, with collaborative feedback from the hospital based on clinical needs, has allowed low-risk patients to be automatically repositioned every two to three hours without requiring any human intervention, she said.
For patients with higher risk of pressure injuries, a nurse needs to first adjust the patient’s position before using the automated machine to help perform the turn, but it only requires one nurse to complete the task, she said.
NTUH’s Department of Nursing said the mattresses are not intended to replace professional nursing care or all manual repositioning, but rather serve as an important assistant to nurses, helping them reduce the time and physical effort required to reposition patients, which gives them more time to attend to other patient care needs.
The hospital thanked Wellell Inc for donating 20 automated repositioning air mattresses to the hospital’s 3C and 4A ICUs.
Minister Without Portfolio Chen Shih-chung (陳時中) told the news conference that compared with pharmaceutical clinical research, medical devices are often overlooked because Taiwan’s medical device market is smaller and has high entry barriers for implementation in clinical settings.
The collaboration between NTUH and Wellell Inc serves as a model for industry-academia cooperation, Chen said.
Clinical-based empirical studies are crucial for developing Taiwan’s smart medical devices and promoting them globally, so the government would help open hospital clinical settings to promising and innovative smart medical devices, he added.

Power site work on schedule: premier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:10 UTC
01:38:10 KST

Work at Taichung Power Plant is on schedule to dismantle two coal-fired units amid its transition from coal to natural gas by 2034, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said yesterday during an inspection of the site.
Cho said that when he visited the power plant in 2024, everyone was hoping for clearer skies and better air quality.
Air pollution has improved in the past few years, so the visit was to express his deepest gratitude to Taiwan Power Co (Taipower) personnel, he said during an inspection of work on the gas-fired units — the first phase of a two-phase expansion — and to dismantle the No. 1 and No. 2 coal-fired units.
Photo courtesy of the Taichung City Government
The plant’s first gas-fired unit is expected to begin commercial operations soon, while the second is expected to begin accepting dispatch next month, with March next year the target for commercial operations, he said.
Taiwan is working toward net zero carbon emissions by 2050, but replacing coal with gas takes time, engineering expertise and patience from the central and local governments, he said.
The Taichung plant would complete the transition from coal to gas by 2034, he said.
The plant’s six coal-fired emergency reserve units would be tightly regulated and used only for limited periods in the event of major contingencies such as national security concerns or natural disasters, he said.
They would only be used for maintenance and testing, and would not typically be generating power, he said.
The central government aims to push for a review of the Taichung plant’s emergency reserve units to begin in 2030, with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Taipower to carefully assess and improve the transition plan, he said.
Taipower later said in a statement that a formal reassessment of the plans for emergency reserve units is scheduled for 2032.
Fulfilling the commitments depends on completing both phases of the gas-fired units on schedule, Cho said.
The four gas units planned under the plant’s second-phase expansion have passed an environmental impact assessment, Cho said, adding that they are scheduled to go online in stages from 2031 to 2034, with four of the 10 coal-fired units to be dismantled and six kept as reserve units.
Meanwhile, the Taichung City Government said that Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) is scheduled to visit the Taichung Power Plant next week to inspect the first-phase gas-fired units.
The city government hopes that the central government would promptly present a coal-reduction plan for the plant through 2030, it said.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Taipower have proposed reducing coal consumption to 10.5 million tonnes this year, but the next phase of reductions would not take place until after 2031 it said, calling on the central government to quickly make a commitment and set out concrete measures for further reducing coal use.

Addressing the shortage in STEM educators
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:09 UTC
01:38:09 KST

The shortage of natural science, physics and chemistry teachers in elementary and secondary schools has become a serious issue. Difficulties in recruiting teachers were once largely seen as a problem confined to rural areas, but today, even teacher recruitment exams in urban areas are attracting too few applicants to fill available positions.
If the trend continues, the impact would extend beyond class schedules and teaching quality — it could potentially undermine students’ scientific foundations and the development of talent in Taiwan’s technology industry.
The social responsibility of caring for and supporting local education has become an issue of growing importance for many universities. Faced with a short-term lack of teachers, universities could consider fulfilling their social responsibility by assisting elementary and secondary schools in addressing their needs.
For example, in situations where there is a shortage of certified teachers, a system could be established allowing doctoral students in science and engineering to teach on a short-term, part-time basis. Doctoral students who have received teaching or teaching-assistant training and possess the necessary professional expertise could be selected to teach natural science, physics or chemistry at elementary and secondary schools under predetermined teaching guidelines and school supervision.
Although doctoral students might not hold teaching certification, their professional training would make them an important source of supplementary faculty.
Doctoral students in chemistry, life sciences, physics, electrical engineering, computer science and other similar fields could provide support in their respective subjects. The system should be designed to supplement — rather than replace — certified teachers, and establish training, compensation and mentoring mechanisms to ensure teaching quality.
Furthermore, Taiwan’s thriving tech industry has created abundant career opportunities and relatively generous salaries for science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) graduates, diminishing the incentive for talented STEM professionals to enter the fields of elementary and secondary-school education.
In addition to increasing public investment in education, the government could encourage companies and foundations that recognize the importance of education and talent development to contribute resources by establishing a science education support program.
Many foundations already promote STEM education initiatives. They could further those efforts by providing salary supplements or other rewards to attract science and engineering talent into elementary and secondary science education.
Taiwan must not wait to address childhood science education until the teacher shortage becomes even more severe. The government should combine the expertise and professionalism of universities with resources from the private sector to establish a flexible system that can supplement the teaching workforce and maintain high educational quality.
By building a collaborative network among the government, universities, schools, industries and civil society, the nation can make better use of its abundant pool of higher-education and STEM talent resources, establishing more stable support for mathematics and science education and elementary and secondary schools, and laying a more solid foundation for the next generation of tech talent.
Chen Sinn-wen is a chair professor at National Tsing Hua University (NTHU) and chairperson of the NTHU Teachers’ Union.

US feminist icon Gloria Steinem dies at age of 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:06 UTC
01:38:06 KST

Gloria Steinem, the US journalist, author and activist who was one of the most recognizable and enduring faces of the feminist movement, has died at age 92, her foundation announced on Thursday.
“Yesterday, Gloria Steinem passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her,” Gloria’s Foundation said in a statement.
It did not specify the cause of death.
Photo: AP
The announcement sparked an outpouring of tributes honoring her decades of boundary-pushing activism.
Steinem “pushed open doors not just for herself, but for literally millions of women behind her,” said Hillary Rodham Clinton, the first woman to serve as US secretary of state and the country’s first female presidential nominee of a major political party.
Nancy Pelosi, the first female US House of Representatives speaker, called Steinem “a fearless trailblazer who transformed the fight for equality in America and inspired generations of women to know their power.”
“She lit a torch many years ago. It is now our responsibility to keep it lifted into the future,” said tennis legend Billie Jean King, winner of the famed 1973 “Battle of the Sexes” match and a prominent advocate of gender equality.
Before becoming a leading figure in the women’s rights movement, Steinem cut her teeth in journalism in the 1960s, denouncing the inequalities American women endured at a time when many needed their husband’s approval to open a bank account.
She came to prominence in 1963 with an expose about the pervasive sexism faced by cocktail waitresses at New York’s Playboy Club.
But she credited her awakening to activism to a 1969 meeting where women described the ordeal of having an abortion.
“It made some sense of my own experience. I had had an abortion and had never told anyone,” she later recounted in New York magazine.
The London doctor who gave her an abortion in 1957, when it was still illegal, made her promise two things: “First, you will not tell anyone my name. Second, you will do what you want to do with your life.”
In the 1970s, she founded Ms. magazine and the National Women’s Political Caucus and organized the first National Women’s Conference in Houston.
Donning her trademark aviator glasses, Steinem headlined conferences and protests in the United States and around the world for decades. She remained an outspoken defender of women’s rights well into her later years.
When in 2022 the US Supreme Court overturned the Roe v Wade decision of 1973, which had enshrined the constitutional right to abortion, she pointed out: “Banning abortions does not stop the need for them. It just bans their safety.
“Don’t agonize. Organize,” she urged.
After a lifetime battling injustice, she said in 2019: “I think the role of older people like me is to have hope, because we remember when it was worse.”
Born in Ohio on March 25, 1934, Steinem had a nomadic early life with a traveling salesman father. Her parents divorced when she was 10, forcing her to care for her mother who had mental health issues.
As a frontline feminist, she came under intense scrutiny from across the political spectrum. Her good looks, miniskirts and brief experience as a Playboy Bunny were used against her in attempts to undermine her credibility.
The fact that she remained single and childless was also weaponized. At 66, she married businessman David Bale, the father of actor Christian Bale.
Asked by a reporter why she had changed her position on single life, she said: “I didn’t change. Marriage changed.”
Bale died three years later of brain cancer, aged 62. Steinem herself underwent surgery for breast cancer in the 1980s.
Some younger activists saw Steinem as representing an outdated type of feminism.
She was criticized for defending Bill Clinton in 1989 when the then-governor of Arkansas was accused of sexual harassment.
In 2016, when Hillary Clinton was running for president but struggling to garner support among women, Steinem suggested young women preferred her rival Bernie Sanders because young men liked him.
“When you’re young, you’re thinking: ‘Where are the boys? The boys are with Bernie,’” she told talk show host Bill Maher. She later apologized.
Steinem was given numerous awards and honors, including the US Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013 by then-US president Barack Obama.
On Thursday, Obama praised Steinem as a “larger-than-life” figure who “helped awaken us to problems like domestic violence” and discriminatory hiring practices.
“Today, generations of women are walking a little taller and aiming a little higher because of what she fought for and achieved,” the former president posted on X.
Supporters stopped outside Steinem’s Manhattan apartment to pay respects.
“I’m just feeling very inspired and grateful for the life that she led,” said Makenna Lorange, 31, visiting from Boston.
“We’ve lost a little bit of light in the world.”

Lite-On Tech to invest in liquid cooling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:05 UTC
01:38:05 KST

Lite-On Technology Corp (光寶) yesterday said it would invest about US$176 million for a 25-percent stake in liquid-cooling solutions provider DCX Liquid Cooling Systems, as it seeks to pair its power-management products with in-row cooling systems for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.
Lite-On plans to combine its power-management expertise in AI servers, rack-level power systems and 800-volt DC architectures with DCX’s advanced liquid-cooling technologies, leveraging the Polish company’s capabilities, Lite-On said in a statement on Thursday.
“Through this partnership, we look forward to advancing innovation and creating new possibilities in the rapidly expanding AI market,” Lite-On chairman Tom Soong (宋明峰) said in a statement.
Photo: CNA
“Lite-On will continue to engage with global partners that possess deep technological expertise and strong strategic synergies, strengthening cross-domain technology integration through strategic investments and long-term collaboration,” Soong said.
The companies aim to develop integrated power and cooling solutions for AI infrastructure and next-generation high-density computing, LiteOn said.
DCX’s product portfolio includes enterprise-level coolant distribution units (CDU) ranging from 600 kilowatts to 2.6 megawatts, hyperscale-class facility coolant distribution units (FDU) of up to 16MW, as well as cold plates, rack manifolds and modular data center systems, Lite-On said.
The accelerating adoption of AI applications is driving unprecedented rack power densities, making liquid cooling a critical enabling technology for future data centers and high-performance computing, the company said.
Founded in 2019 and headquartered in Warsaw, DCX specializes in direct-to-chip and immersion liquid cooling, with design and integration capabilities for data center cooling infrastructure, Lite-On said.
Its products have been deployed by three of the world’s top 10 AI data center operators and shipped to 75 countries, Lite-On said.
In the early phase of the partnership, Lite-On and DCX would focus on in-row CDUs, already widely deployed at large AI data centers, and introduce them to customers, a Lite-On official told the Taipei Times by telephone on Thursday.
In the long term, Lite-On aims to expand its large FDU business as AI server rack power consumption rises and cooling architectures extend to facility-level systems, the official said.
It plans to combine DCX’s expertise with Lite-On’s customer relationships, manufacturing and supply chain capabilities to serve hyperscalers’ next-generation cooling needs going forward, the official said.

A UK clinical trial known as “Sentinel” is testing whether a small patch of skin from an organ donor can help detect lung transplant rejection at an earlier stage. The patch is grafted onto the patient’s forearm, making it possible to monitor visible changes such as rashes that may signal rejection before standard tests do. Scientists believe the skin may show signs of rejection earlier than other organs and is easier to observe directly.
In one case, a patient who received a lung transplant in 2024 noticed a purple rash on the patch, which led doctors to detect mild rejection early and begin steroid treatment promptly. The research team hopes the trial will improve understanding of transplantation and help patients live longer and healthier lives.
一項名為「Sentinel」的英國臨床試驗正在測試，來自器官捐贈者的一小片皮膚是否能幫助在較早階段偵測出肺臟移植排斥。這片皮膚會被移植到病患的前臂上，以監測像是皮疹等可能會比標準檢查更早顯示排斥反應的可見變化。科學家認為，皮膚可能會比其他器官更早出現排斥跡象，也更容易直接觀察。
Photo: Ivy English I 照片: 常春藤解析英語

Words in Use

The patient showed only mild symptoms after the procedure.

The doctor began treatment promptly after the diagnosis.
醫生在診斷後立即開始治療。

Bilingual 2030: time’s up for opinions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:03 UTC
01:38:03 KST

The irony of writing an opinion piece with this title is not lost on me. While Bilingual 2030 has generated substantial debate through recent opinion pieces and letters to the editor published in the Taipei Times, the time has come to shift from opinion to rigorous academic analysis.
Jye Smallwood’s piece, “Basic Misunderstanding of EMI” (page 8, Aug. 9), demonstrates sound academic grounding, and I largely agree with his points. However, his rigid definition of English-medium instruction (EMI) as purely an “end state” without language support creates a false binary where any real-world application is deemed incorrect by default. This risks ignoring essential teaching strategies, such as translanguaging (using a student’s full language repertoire to support learning; for example, planning or discussing in their language and then sharing in English), code-switching (alternating between English and Mandarin for clarity) and scaffolding (providing temporary learning support to help students grasp complex concepts).
While his critique of applied EMI methodology is valid, his example of the economics professor highlights a pedagogical flaw — the problem would exist even in the professor’s first language — rather than pedagogical regression (the temporary drop in a professor’s teaching effectiveness when forced to instruct in a second language).
Smallwood’s cited Saudi and Japanese models also faced massive challenges, high attrition and steep costs, proving that successful EMI relies on factors far beyond methodology, training and funding.
From a policy management perspective, Smallwood’s recommendation to “tie every dollar to measurable language outcomes” contradicts his premise that EMI is a content-learning context rather than a language-learning one.
Additionally, attributing policy failures merely to “basic misunderstandings” is overly polite. In reality, failure stems from perverse institutional incentives, such as universities rushing to label courses “EMI” simply to secure a slice of government funding.
In his letter “Bilingual Education” (page 8, Aug. 24), Paul Garrelfs relies on intuitive notions that fail under academic scrutiny. His claim that children absorb language like “sponges” is unsupported; beyond acquiring better pronunciation, children learn significantly slower than teenagers or adults. The Critical Period Hypothesis is overhyped, and expert-led language instruction at the university level remains far more effective for language gains than un-scaffolded EMI or “starting young.”
Garrelfs also confuses Basic Interpersonal Communication Skills with the Cognitive Academic Language Proficiency (CALP) required for EMI. His comparison to Ontario’s French immersion program is moot due to fundamental differences in writing systems (Chinese versus French), target language exposure and the documented limitations of the Canadian model highlighted by Merrill Swain.
Finally, Garrelfs’ assertion that Taiwan possesses a surplus of qualified English teachers is inaccurate. A 120-hour online Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages certificate is inadequate for institutional teaching, and I would be surprised if the percentage of teachers on ARCs with a Teaching English as a Foreign Language qualification exceeds 20 percent. Lowering entry barriers contradicts successful models in Finland and Singapore; instead, Taiwan should raise standards by requiring globally recognized credentials such as the Cambridge Certificate in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages or Trinity Certificate in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages. Regulations paradoxically prohibit world-renowned experts — such as Common European Framework of Reference for Languages coauthor John de Jong — from teaching in Taiwan simply based on country of origin.
CenYing English Studies Director Daniel Eyrich’s comparison of macro-level policy to classroom error correction in his article “The Challenges of Bilingual 2030” (page 8, Aug. 23) involves a severe scale fallacy. Applying a 10 to 15-minute micro-pedagogical speaking tactic to a multimillion-dollar national strategy overlooks the fact that teachers operate from a shared linguistic knowledge base, whereas policy execution lacks such standardized reference points. Moreover, adjusting communicative techniques in classrooms where students lack CALP fails to produce content mastery and perpetuates confusion between language acquisition and content delivery.
Eyrich’s suggestion to adopt a passive “wait-and-see” approach to gather evidence leads directly to institutional inertia, public waste and stakeholder burnout. Organizational change requires rapid feedback loops and immediate mid-course realignments to fix the supply chain mismatch in teacher training.
Eyrich’s second piece (“Bilingual Education Can Learn from Asia,” page 8, Sept. 1) is far more academically robust. Connecting school-level proficiency to university readiness correctly identifies the structural disconnect between teaching, testing and teacher training as a primary root cause of failure. Utilizing established frameworks (Cambridge, Trinity or International House) and localized, data-driven research (such as the Teaching Knowledge Test study) offers a far better pathway than unvetted training programs.
However, locking Taiwan into a single publisher or provider poses vendor lock-in risks, unlike the multi-supplier approaches used in Vietnam and Indonesia. Furthermore, standard advanced credentials such as the Cambridge Diploma in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages (DELTA) or Trinity Diploma in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages do not automatically prepare trainers for tertiary EMI contexts.
Taiwan must establish clear, scaffolded language proficiency goals across primary and secondary education to prepare students for university-level academic demands. The Ministry of Education must also overhaul its funding metrics and teacher-training models. Structural reform requires tough decisions, but continuing to observe failure is no longer an option.
Gerhard Erasmus is the course and academic director at Inspired CPD, a certified Cambridge DELTA and Trinity course director and tutor, an ex-trustee of the International Association of Teachers of English as a Foreign Language (IATEFL), and ex-coordinator of the IATEFL Leadership and Management Special Interest Group. He has more than two decades of experience in ELT management, teacher training and assessment.

Donovan’s Deep Dives: Democracy changed how Taiwan moves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:38:02 UTC
01:38:02 KST

No matter where one sits on the political spectrum and who one blames for the ongoing struggles between the executive and legislative branches or the latest food scandal, there has been noticeable frustration with the way democratic institutions are functioning.
Attempts to circumvent political opposition and institutional checks can begin a slide toward authoritarianism, even when presented as short-term solutions to gridlock. While that might solve problems in the short term, it inevitably evolves into a system that serves the rulers and the powerfully connected at the expense of the rights of regular folks.
One interesting lens to examine the differences between the Martial Law era and today is through traffic safety.
Photo: Lin Cheng-kung, Taipei Times
Democratization created institutions through which the public could demand change. A number of gruesome traffic deaths helped produce stronger rules, while open debate contributed to changing social expectations.
BEHAVIOR IN A DEMOCRATIC SOCIETY
CNN caused a stir in December 2022 when it ran an article entitled “Taiwan’s ‘living hell’ traffic is a tourism problem, say critics.” It was an alarmist piece that was not entirely fair. Taiwan’s official 2019 road-death rate of 12.1 per 100,000 was below the contemporary global average, but extremely high compared with several similarly wealthy countries, particularly for pedestrians and motorcyclists. Not great and still alarming, but by no means a “living hell.”
Photo courtesy of Penghu Traffic
Just a few weeks later, in a heart-wrenching story, a bus in Taichung ran over and killed a woman and her one-year-old son and injured the father, an Iraqi national. Several more incidents — especially here in Taichung — of pedestrians being run down throughout 2023 raised public awareness of pedestrian safety.
Authorities tightened oversight of bus operators, while the central government increased penalties and licence sanctions for drivers who failed to yield to pedestrians.
But what I observed next was more remarkable: as public awareness rose, vehicles began to stop, even when a pedestrian was not particularly near, and patiently wait until they had safely passed — even when no police or surveillance cameras were present. Now this is standard behavior here in Taichung.
People did this voluntarily, not out of fear of reprisal, but out of a sense of personal responsibility and civic duty. Authoritarian systems, on the other hand, weaken accountability and can encourage people to rely on status, connections and informal power rather than impartial rules.
This is a night-and-day difference in how people interact with the world. Citizens in a democracy broadly trust that their rights are protected and understand that with freedom comes responsibilities.
BEHAVIOR IN AUTHORITARIAN SOCIETY
Authoritarian Taiwan was very different. Might made right. Political connections, wealth and status often carried far greater weight than formal rights, leaving ordinary people with limited confidence that institutions would treat them fairly.
Everyone was out for themselves, and if you could get away with something, you often did. Corruption affected officialdom, law enforcement and parts of the judiciary, while political influence frequently distorted ostensibly neutral institutions. Gangsters ran a parallel system in some communities and industries, demanding protection money from even the smallest of businesses and administering justice for a price.
In traffic, one had to gauge the relative power of others and one’s relative place in the pecking order. At the top were the cars of officials, police and expensive black sedans. Below them were people in expensive cars who were likely well-connected and gravel truck drivers, who were often ex-convicts hired by the gangster-run construction companies.
On motorcycles, one had to beware of anyone riding anything bigger than 150cc, because those were illegal, and if one had the money and connections to get one, nobody messed around with them. Below them were the young gangsters, who often rode wangpai (王牌) — white, yellow and blue Honda racing-style motorcycles — at terrifying speeds. Inexplicably, for a while the fashion among those young gangsters was to wear a jacket with “sissy boy” emblazoned on the back.
For regular people, the rule was the bigger vehicle had right of way over smaller ones in traffic, with pedestrians at the bottom of the pecking order. People understood this might means right rule, including the police.
Once, in a rainstorm, I had to slam on my brakes as a Mercedes barreled down on me at high speed on a narrow road with no escape. My motorcycle went into a slide, and his car literally came to a stop on top of my bike. The obviously wealthy driver got out of his car to yell at me as if it was my fault, which was manifestly not the case. The neighbors came out to see what had happened, but when I looked at them, they put their eyes down and scurried back into their homes.
This attitude extended to all accidents. I noticed on several occasions that when someone was injured or even died no one would go to help. In a system where right and wrong are irrelevant, there was significant risk that by going to someone’s aid, the blame would be pinned on the good samaritan because they could be identified, not the actual perpetrator.
By the time the Mercedes had parked atop my motorcycle, I understood the rules and my lowly place in them.
I once saw a motorcyclist on the ground, screaming horribly in pain, his leg at an unnatural angle and blood everywhere. I immediately raced to a nearby police station to get help. They looked at me incredulously, then increasingly with irritation and hostility.
Finally, it became clear I was not going to go away, and someone called an ambulance — but only after the officers had argued among themselves. The cop who made the call was the only one who looked at me with some sympathy.
Even getting on the city bus was hazardous; there was no working-class solidarity or dignity there, either. Forget lining up; no matter how close I was to the door, people would push me aside and even elbow me in the ribs to get on first.
People today have substantially greater reason to expect legal accountability and to challenge unfair treatment, even if confidence in the system remains far from universal.
Contrast the way it was to today’s democratic Taiwan. Doesn’t look so bad, does it?

A sika deer was spotted wandering the streets of Kaohsiung’s Cianjhen District (前鎮) early yesterday morning before being safely captured and returned to its owner, police said, adding that it was “lucky” there were no traffic incidents.
A video posted on Threads showed the deer walking on a road. Police received a report at about 3:20am that it was near the intersection of Heping Road and Yingde Street.
The owner, surnamed Kuo (郭), said in a reply to the Threads message that the deer “sneaked out of the house to play on the slide at a nearby park, but got lost on the way back.”
Photo: CNA
The owner urged anybody who spotted the deer to contact them immediately.
Following the posts, the Cianjhen Precinct of the Kaohsiung City Police Department dispatched officers to the scene and contacted the Kaohsiung Animal Protection Office for assistance.
However, the deer had fled by the time officers arrived, the precinct said.
Concerned that the animal might run into traffic, endangering itself and drivers, police expanded their search to nearby roads.
The deer was spotted near the intersection of Ersheng Road and Kaisyuan Road, but it again eluded police.
Police said they searched the area while monitoring traffic to prevent possible accidents.
At about 8:20am, the precinct received another report that the deer was on a patch of grass near the Ersheng-Kaisyuan intersection.
Police rushed to the scene and kept traffic under control to avoid frightening the deer into darting onto a road, while working with the owner and animal protection officials to guide and capture the animal, the precinct said.
The deer was captured at about 9:45am. No accidents involving people or vehicles were reported, the precinct said.
The owner could face a fine of NT$300 to NT$600 under the Road Traffic Management and Penalty Act (道路交通管理處罰條例) for allowing the deer to escape supervision and wander on a road, police said.
The owner could also face up to three days in detention or a fine of up to NT$12,000 under provisions of the Social Order Maintenance Act (社會秩序維護法), police said.
The precinct said the owner would be notified to report to the police station for questioning as police investigate why the deer escaped and the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Agency warns of Chinese scams targeting the youth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:37:59 UTC
01:37:59 KST

Straits Exchange Foundation (SEF) Secretary-General Luo Wen-jia (羅文嘉) on Thursday warned about youth-targeted Chinese scams.
Luo made the comments in an interview with the Chinese-language Liberty Times (sister paper of the Taipei Times) published yesterday.
Whether it is a job scam or an employment opportunity linked to Beijing’s “united front” efforts, both carry significant risks, Luo said.
Photo: Chen Yi-ling, Taipei Times
Beijing has expanded its influence campaign targeting Taiwanese youths through tourism and cultural exchange programs, and economic incentives, he said.
Chinese organizers of the tour gorup or program typically insert “united front” activities aimed at indoctrinating participants, Luo said.
Some influence campaigns lure the youth with promises of employment, which are likely fake, as the unemployment rate for Chinese urban youths was 17.9 percent in July, he said.
Young Taiwanese who travel to China to look for work often find themselves jobless and unhoused, Luo said.
Chinese organized crime, especially scam groups posing as legitimate enterprises, is known to lure Taiwanese youths with promises of lucrative short-term work, then disappear once the victims arrive in the country, he said.
Those groups move agents to Taiwan by using Hong Kong or Macao papers, then set up shell corporations to get to potential victims, he said, adding that blood relations had also been utilized.
Additionally, Beijing’s new national security laws could be used to detain visiting Taiwanese for social media comments or being an employee of an entity that has been accused of breaching China’s technology export controls, Luo said.
About 160 Taiwanese have disappeared and more than 200 have been detained or incarcerated in China, marking increasing risks for Taiwanese traveling or working in the country, he said.
The SEF and the Mainland Affairs Council in 2023 jointly recorded 588 requests for assistance concerning Taiwanese who visited China and vanished or were in danger, he said, adding that the number surged to 1,027 last year.
Between Jan. 1, 2024, and Thursday last week, the organizations’ data showed that 462 Taiwanese had gone missing in China, including 160 who vanished without a trace, he said.
“The dangers for Taiwanese in China is on the rise, and the government has a responsibility to tell the people that we should not take these risks lightly,” Luo said. “We should not think that just because the vast majority of tourists in China were safe, we, too, would be safe.”

Safavid tilework: From architectural ornament to pictorial art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:37:09 UTC
01:37:09 KST

Safavid tilework: From architectural ornament to pictorial art
TEHRAN - Tilework during Iran’s Safavid era was not confined to geometric patterns, arabesques and inscriptions used to decorate religious buildings.
In 17th-century Isfahan, the Safavid capital, square tiles increasingly became a medium for pictorial compositions depicting people, gardens and scenes of courtly life. Examples of this distinctive form of tilework are now preserved in major museums, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the Louvre and the Victoria and Albert Museum.
One of the notable examples is a large tile panel in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Dating to the first quarter of the 17th century and attributed to Iran, probably Isfahan, the panel measures approximately 115.6 by 138.7 centimeters. It consists of square tiles, each about 22.5 centimetres across, assembled to form a single continuous scene depicting a woman and three men in a garden setting, ISNA reported on Friday.
The significance of such works lies not only in their imagery but also in the technique used to produce them. The tiles were made using a method known as cuerda seca, or dry cord, in which lines of a glaze-resistant material separated areas of different colours. During firing, the separating material burned away, leaving dark, dry lines between the coloured sections. This allowed several coloured glazes to be applied next to one another without running together.
The technique was particularly useful during the Safavid period because it enabled artists to produce richly coloured compositions more efficiently and at a lower cost than some more elaborate mosaic-tile techniques. Research by the Metropolitan Museum indicates that Isfahan and Nain were important centers of fine tile production during the Safavid period. While geometric and vegetal designs continued to dominate mosques, religious schools and other monuments, a different approach developed in secular architecture, where individual square tiles became components of larger pictorial scenes.
This approach required artists to think beyond the decoration of individual tiles. A large composition had to be divided into numerous small sections, with each tile functioning as a piece of an overall visual puzzle. Preliminary design, color coordination, the proportions of human figures and the continuity of landscape elements across adjoining tiles were therefore crucial to the finished work. The wall itself became the ultimate canvas—one made not of paper or cloth, but of glazed ceramic tiles.
The subjects of these compositions were closely connected with the Safavid tradition of miniature painting. The Metropolitan Museum notes that garden scenes featuring groups of men and women were among the subjects popular with Safavid painters. The depiction of figures in gardens, together with details of clothing, social interaction and leisure, brought aspects of courtly and everyday life into architectural spaces.
This distinction between religious and secular tilework is important for understanding the development of Safavid pictorial ceramics. In mosques and other religious buildings, vegetal, geometric and calligraphic decoration remained central. In royal residences, garden pavilions and other secular settings, however, representations of people and narrative scenes had greater scope to appear. Tilework consequently evolved from a primarily decorative architectural element into a visual medium capable of conveying aspects of courtly culture, gardens, clothing and social life.
Recent art-historical research has also provided clues about the original architectural settings of some surviving panels. Farshid Emami, a researcher in Islamic art and architecture, has examined groups of Safavid pictorial tiles in research published by the Metropolitan Museum. His work suggests that examples now dispersed among the collections of the Metropolitan Museum, the Louvre and the Victoria and Albert Museum may have originally been associated with a now-lost Safavid building.
Safavid pictorial tiles represent an important intersection of several Iranian artistic traditions: ceramics, tilemaking, painting, miniature art and architecture. Their production required both technical knowledge of ceramic materials and glazing and the artistic ability to design figures and complex scenes. Viewed up close, the works appear as collections of individual ceramic pieces; from an appropriate distance, they come together as unified and carefully composed paintings.
The enduring importance of these works lies in this close relationship between image and architecture. During the Safavid period, tiles could serve not merely as a surface covering but as a medium for depicting stories and scenes from the social and cultural world of their time. Although many examples are now dispersed in museums around the world, each surviving panel provides a valuable record of the artistic, architectural and visual culture of Safavid Iran.

Sangak bread added to Iran’s national intangible cultural heritage list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:33:22 UTC
01:33:22 KST

Sangak bread added to Iran’s national intangible cultural heritage list
TEHRAN — The way of preparing, Sangak, a traditional Iranian flatbread baked on heated pebbles, has been inscribed on Iran’s national list of intangible cultural heritage following a review by the country’s National Council for Intangible Heritage Registration, an official said.
Alireza Izadi, director general of national and world heritage registration at Iran’s Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts, said the registration recognizes Sangak as one of Iran’s traditional breads and an enduring part of the country’s food culture.
“Its registration is a step toward safeguarding part of the historical memory, everyday culture, indigenous knowledge and food identity of Iranians,” Izadi said, according to the ministry.
The name Sangak is derived from the Persian word for “pebble,” referring to the small river stones on which the bread is baked. The bread is typically made from whole-wheat, high-hydration dough and shaped into a rough triangle before being stretched over heated stones in a large oven. Sesame or poppy seeds are among the traditional toppings.
Izadi said the oldest known written reference to Sangak appears in the Borhan-e Qate (aka Burhan-i Qati), a Persian dictionary compiled by Muhammad Husayn ibn Khalaf Tabrizi in 1062 AH. The entry describes Sangak as a type of bread baked on heated pebbles.
He added that oral traditions and historical accounts have linked the bread’s origins to the Sasanian era and even earlier periods, while emphasizing that such accounts require further historical assessment.
Archaeological evidence has also been cited in support of the continuity of the baking tradition. According to Izadi, the remains of a Sangak bakery, including an intact oven and specialized baking pebbles, were discovered at a ruined fortress in Varamin, south of Tehran.
A popular account attributes the design of the Sangak oven to Sheikh Baha’i during the Safavid period, following a request from Shah Abbas to devise a method for supplying bread to soldiers during military journeys. Izadi said the story was recorded in a 1947 calendar published by Tehran’s bakers’ committee, but its historical accuracy remains uncertain.
He said national registration is intended not merely to preserve the appearance of Sangak, but also the knowledge and skills associated with preparing the dough, baking the bread, using traditional tools and maintaining related customs.
Izadi said the ministry would pursue efforts to document and study Sangak further with a view to seeking its inscription on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
He added that such an effort would require cooperation among researchers, historians, traditional bakers, heritage practitioners and other relevant institutions.

GYIRONG, Xizang, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Nepalese border residents stranded by a deadly mudslide in Gyirong Town in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region have received assistance and arrangements from the Chinese side for orderly return home or continued stay.
Caused by an ice-rock avalanche in Nepal on Aug. 26, the mudslide swept through Gyirong Port in Xizang, leaving 31 people dead and 531 others missing there as of Friday afternoon. It also disrupted roads leading to the port as well as communications and power supplies on the Chinese side, leaving some Nepalese border residents stranded in the town.
Following the disaster, the Chinese government quickly activated an emergency response mechanism for the resettlement and support of foreign nationals and coordinated efforts to provide daily necessities for stranded Nepalese border residents, address their concerns and facilitate their orderly departure.
At the time of the disaster, Gyaldup Tamang, a stranded Nepalese border resident in Gyirong Town in Gyirong County, was working in a village there, and four of his relatives remained out of contact.
"I was eager to return home, but the damaged roads made it impossible to travel, and I did not know what to do for a while," he said. "Fortunately, the Chinese government offered assistance, helping with exit procedures and arranging transportation. I heard that some Nepalese compatriots have already left through Zhangmu Port."
"We can now complete exit formalities free of charge, and I plan to go through the procedures this afternoon," Gyaldup Tamang told Xinhua on Thursday.
At the Gyirong Port Branch of the Xigaze Municipal Public Security Bureau, many Nepalese border residents were seen queuing to complete exit procedures.
A staff member at the branch said those wishing to leave could complete the formalities by presenting their Nepalese identity cards and China-Nepal border crossing permits. After completing the procedures, they can take government-arranged buses to leave through alternative ports.
For those choosing to stay, local authorities have also made arrangements to meet their basic needs.
A dedicated service site for Nepalese border residents has been established along a street in Gyirong Town, providing free supplies such as instant noodles, milk, beverages and medicines.
According to authorities in Gyirong Town, more than 2,000 items of daily necessities have been distributed to hundreds of Nepalese border residents in the town.
Another Nepalese border resident, who works at a hotel in Gyirong, does not currently plan to return home. "I have worked in Gyirong for two years. My income here supports my family of five, so I will continue working here," he said. ■

Feature: Afghan entrepreneur takes bus ticket booking online
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
00:32:39 CST
01:32:39 KST

KABUL, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Every morning, Sadaf Afghan arrives at her office in Kabul to receive orders from customers and book bus tickets online, hoping her fledgling business can make travel easier for passengers in Afghanistan.
Her online platform, qasid.af, allows customers to book bus tickets to different destinations without having to visit a bus terminal and pay for them in cash.
"We book tickets for our customers online, make the payment and then deliver the tickets to their doorsteps," Afghan told Xinhua.
The young entrepreneur developed qasid.af about a year ago and launched its online ticket booking and purchasing services five months later with a three-member team.
The business has since expanded to eight employees, including four women, who provide booking and ticket delivery services to customers.
Afghan hopes to further expand the business and open branches in other provinces, creating more job opportunities for Afghans, particularly women.
"Our main goal is to further develop our business and open more offices in the provinces so that we can create job opportunities for both men and women," she said.
Starting a business has not been easy, particularly in a society where many services are still conducted through traditional, face-to-face transactions. But Afghan said the response from customers has been encouraging.
"Launching any business is difficult in the beginning, but we should not give up. In general, people support us," she said.
Afghanistan's transport system remains largely reliant on road travel. With no extensive railway network or metro system, buses are an important means of intercity transportation. Many passengers still have to travel to bus terminals and pay cash for tickets before setting out on often lengthy journeys.
A journey of about 450 km between Afghan cities, for example, can take at least 10 hours, depending on road and traffic conditions.
Afghan believes digital services can make at least part of that experience more convenient.
"We need government support to improve the transport system, provide necessary services and support companies that provide services to travelers," she said.
She also plans to expand qasid.af into air travel, allowing customers to book airline tickets online and have them delivered to their homes.
The company's ambitions are also creating unconventional jobs for young Afghan women.
Mohammadi, 20, is one of the company's female employees. Every day, she rides a motorbike through Kabul to deliver tickets to customers.
"I feel happy to deliver bus tickets to the doorsteps of our clients," she told Xinhua.
Mohammadi said she hopes the company will continue to expand and provide jobs for more people, particularly women.
"It is very good to serve people, and I hope to see more job opportunities created and more people employed," she said.
Having completed the 10th grade, Mohammadi said riding a motorbike and working outside the home have given her a sense of encouragement.
"Riding a motorbike and serving people is encouraging, and I am pleased to see women being encouraged," she said. ■
