British warship fires gun near Falklands in deterrence drill
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:22:23 BST
22:22:23 KST

HMS Medway recently carried out live machine gun firings at the edge of the Falkland Islands Conservation Zone during a four-day patrol at the end of July, British Forces South Atlantic Islands stated.
The patrol, designated Operation Southern Vigilance, ran from 26 to 29 July. The ship’s company fired mounted machine guns and worked through a man overboard exercise alongside an RAF A400M Atlas transport aircraft, work the command describes as maintaining operational readiness. According to BFSAI, the deployment demonstrated the UK’s enduring commitment to the Falkland Islands by maintaining a visible presence and a capable force, helping to deter potential adversaries.
The Falkland Islands Conservation Zone extends 150 nautical miles from the centre of the archipelago and was established in 1990 to manage fish stocks, principally squid, which underpin a large share of the islands’ economy. Licensing and enforcement within it fall to the Falkland Islands Government, with the Royal Navy providing the deterrent presence and the fisheries patrol vessel Lilibet carrying out routine inspection work.
HMS Medway is a River-class offshore patrol vessel commissioned in 2019 and took over the South Atlantic Patrol Task from HMS Forth, which held the role for several years after replacing HMS Clyde. The class displaces around 2,000 tonnes and carries a 30mm gun, machine guns and a flight deck able to take a Merlin, with an endurance suited to long independent patrols in remote waters.
The ship is the only Royal Navy vessel permanently assigned to the region. British Forces South Atlantic Islands also operates Typhoon fighters and A400M and Voyager aircraft from RAF Mount Pleasant on East Falkland, alongside an infantry company, Rapier’s successor Sky Sabre air defence and a radar station on Mount Byron.
HMS Medway has remained active around the Falkland Islands since the exercise. Last month, members of the ship’s Senior Rates were ashore in Port Stanley, where they helped the Lighthouse Seafarers Mission prepare for renovations.
This is not the first British deterrence and sovereignty operation in the South Atlantic in recent times, with HMS Forth and RAF aircraft previously taking part in Operation Southern Sovereignty earlier this year to demonstrate the ability to project force across the region and deter aggression.
Argentina continues to claim the islands, which it calls the Malvinas, and raises the question annually at the United Nations Special Committee on Decolonisation. The British position rests on the 2013 referendum in which islanders voted by 1,513 votes to three to remain a British Overseas Territory.
Editor’s note: BFSAI puts the live firing under training serials and applies the deterrence line to Operation Southern Vigilance as a whole. It is my view that the gunnery was highlighted precisely as part of the overall presence and deterrence point. Nobody publicises machine gun drills for the sake of it.
A patrol vessel deters by being present and visibly able to do something about it, and a crew that has not fired its weapons in months is neither. Leaving that out would report the operation less accurately than the command described it. On Argentina, BFSAI says “potential adversaries” and stops. There is one country with a standing claim to the islands. Writing around that would be coy.

Türkiye’s southwestern Antalya city will host the 31st iteration of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in late November will extend the tourism season well into the month, while the event will help showcase the country’s efforts in sustainable tourism ahead of COP31, Antalya will also be home to the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) on Oct. 5-9.

“Hotels in the Kundu region in particular are seeing high occupancy rates due to the conference, as we normally would’ve already reached the end of the season by then,” he said.

‘Arvand Martyrs Bridge is just beginning of a larger development path’
TEHRAN- The Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free Trade and Special Economic Zones, emphasizing the need to continue the development process in the Arvand Free Zone, stated that the inauguration of the Arvand Martyrs Bridge is not the end of a construction project, but rather the beginning of a larger path for implementing infrastructural, economic, and developmental projects in Abadan, Khorramshahr, and the Arvand Free Zone.
Hossein Forouzan, speaking at the official inauguration ceremony of the Arvand Martyrs Bridge mega-project, said: "The people of Abadan, Khorramshahr, and the Arvand region paid a heavy price during the eight years of the Sacred Defense [Iran-Iraq War] in defending the country. Today, it is the duty of officials to use all their capacity to compensate for part of this sacrifice and to strive for the development and prosperity of this region."
Forouzan, referring to his history of presence in Khuzestan and Khorramshahr, added: "My first presence in this region dates back to 1982, and being in a land where the sacred bodies of great martyrs such as Mehdi and Hamid Bakeri rest has always been an honor for me and a reminder of the heavy responsibility I bear toward the people and the martyrs."
Referring to the importance of inaugurating the Arvand Martyrs Bridge, he emphasized: "This project can resolve some of the problems faced by the people of the region, but it should not be seen as the end point of development efforts. Rather, this bridge should serve as a precursor to the implementation of a series of major infrastructural, economic, and developmental projects in Abadan, Khorramshahr, and the Arvand Free Zone."
The Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free Trade and Special Economic Zones continued: "The right of the people of this land upon officials goes far beyond the implementation of a single construction project. We must strive to make maximum use of the region's existing capacities to create welfare, employment, economic prosperity, and sustainable development."
Forouzan, referring to the meetings and reviews conducted in recent days in the Arvand Free Zone, said: "During my recent multi-day visit, a series of important priority projects for Abadan and Khorramshahr were identified, and plans have been made for their implementation. It is expected that a significant portion of these projects will reach the operational stage in the coming year."
Expressing appreciation for the performance of Mostafa Khanzadi, the CEO of the Arvand Free Zone Organization, he stated: "In recent days, numerous meetings have been held with the CEO and the management team of the organization. The prevailing approach of this team is a serious move toward development and gaining the satisfaction of the people."
The Secretary of the Supreme Council added: "Serving the people and striving to solve their problems must be the top priority of the region's management. We believe that the people's satisfaction paves the way for God's satisfaction."
Forouzan also pointed to the industrial capacities of the Arvand Free Zone and said: "Significant actions are also underway in the industrial sector. Some industrial projects currently being implemented could have considerable impacts on the region's economy and even the national economy in the future."
He emphasized: "Activating the region's industrial, economic, and investment capacities requires continued support and coordination among various agencies. All available capacities must be used to accelerate the development process."
The Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free and Special Economic Zones noted: "The success of the Arvand Free Zone Organization in implementing development programs requires the cooperation and support of the Governor of Khuzestan, representatives in the Islamic Consultative Assembly, and other executive bodies."
Forouzan added: "Coordination among various entities can speed up the implementation of infrastructural and economic projects and pave the way for achieving the region's development goals."
He also referred to the message from the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance and the President for the people of the region, saying: "I conveyed the greetings and message of the President and the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance to the noble people of Abadan, Khorramshahr, and the Arvand Free Zone, and emphasized their special attention to this region and their support for its development process."
The Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free and Special Economic Zones, emphasizing the historical standing of Abadan and Khorramshahr in contemporary Iranian history, said: "The people of this region deserve to enjoy the best infrastructure, facilities, and development opportunities."
Forouzan concluded: "The Secretariat of the Supreme Council of Free Zones will stand alongside the Arvand Free Zone Organization with all its capacity to ensure that the path of development and prosperity for Abadan, Khorramshahr, and this region is pursued with greater speed and seriousness."
The Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free Trade and Special Economic Zones, during his visit to the Arvand Free Zone, toured the Shalamcheh commercial terminal and its infrastructure.
Hossein Forouzan, leading a delegation from the Secretariat, visited various sections of the Shalamcheh commercial terminal, including its cargo yard and commercial and logistical infrastructure. He closely examined the capacities, issues, and operational processes of this terminal.
During the visit, the existing capacities of the Shalamcheh commercial terminal, cargo loading and unloading processes, support infrastructure for export activities, and the provision of services to economic activists and traders were reviewed.
The Shalamcheh commercial terminal, as one of the key commercial infrastructures of the Arvand Free Zone, plays an effective role in Iran-Iraq economic exchanges. Developing its infrastructure could increase export capacity, facilitate the movement of transport fleets, and improve logistical services at this international border crossing.
The 100-hectare cargo loading and unloading yard in Shalamcheh is also among the infrastructures established in this area, providing suitable capacity to support commercial and logistical activities at the Shalamcheh border.
Additionally, given Shalamcheh's commercial capacities and its position in developing trade with Iraq, removing implementation obstacles, strengthening logistical infrastructure, and increasing the terminal's productivity are among the key priorities in the path of developing economic activities in the Arvand Free Zone. Previously, the allocation of import codes to Shalamcheh port had also made it possible to import and clear goods through this route.
During the visit, Forouzan conducted a field review of the capacities and existing issues and was briefed on the latest status of the Shalamcheh commercial terminal's infrastructure and the progress of economic activities at this border crossing.
The CEO and a number of managers from the Arvand Free Zone Organization, along with officials related to the Shalamcheh commercial terminal, were also present during this visit.
The Arvand Free Trade-Industrial Zone is one of Iran's most strategically significant economic hubs, located in the southwestern Khuzestan province at the confluence of the Karun and Arvand rivers. Spanning over 37,000 hectares, it encompasses the cities of Abadan, Khorramshahr, and Minoo Island, sharing borders with Iraq and Kuwait.
The zone serves as a vital gateway for international trade, offering multi-modal transport advantages through the Abadan International Airport, Khorramshahr's second-largest container port, and the Shalamcheh border terminal – a key crossing for commercial activities with Iraq. Its logistics capacities are being further developed with a 700-hectare "Logistics Park" project.

Why did Xi choose to visit Egypt amid the US-Iran tensions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:21:59 UTC
22:21:59 KST

Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in Cairo as China and Egypt marked 70 years of diplomatic ties, shortly before a possible meeting with US President Donald Trump in late September.
The visit came amid renewed regional tensions, with US forces attacking IRGC targets and Tehran retaliating by attacking American bases across the Middle East.
Egypt, which has been largely silent on US-Iran tensions, condemned recent Iran attacks on Arab states.
During the visit, Xi and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called for a “comprehensive agreement” to end the war with Iran and signed more than 20 agreements. They included a deal allowing Beijing to complete the third phase of a joint industrial zone at the Suez Canal, expanding China’s economic presence along one of the world’s most important trade routes.
Cairo and Beijing have a significant economic relationship, with bilateral trade reaching close to $21 billion, as the two countries have linked Egypt’s Vision 2030 with China’s Belt and Road Initiative.
“There is a clear economic interest on both sides, especially given the current circumstances in the region,” Altay Atli, an expert on Chinese politics and a senior scholar at Sabanci University’s Istanbul Policy Center, tells TRT World.
He highlighted both states’ growing concerns that the war in Iran has stalled global trade because of tensions in the Bab el-Mandeb and Hormuz straits.
Egypt, whose economy depends heavily on Suez Canal trade, has been concerned that pro-Iranian Houthi attacks in the Bab el-Mandeb have disrupted shipping across the Red Sea, reducing revenues.
Burdened by deep structural debt, the Egyptian economy has long been vulnerable to regional conflicts like the current Iran-US war.
China, a major consumer of Gulf oil, has also been concerned about the Iran conflict, as blockades across the region’s two key straits have disrupted global energy shipments.
“While the anniversary provided the occasion for the visit, the deeper issue is a shared interest in regional stability,” Atli tells TRT World, referring to possible Egyptian-Chinese cooperation to ensure regional stability across the Middle East.
Why Egypt matters
Despite Houthi attacks in the Red Sea, Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has pushed more oil tanker traffic towards the Suez Canal, making the waterway even more strategically important at a time when China is increasing its investment there, according to Atli.
Egypt could also help China deepen its engagement not only with Arab states but also across Africa, given Cairo’s involvement in several regional conflicts, including those in Palestine, Sudan and Libya.
“In that sense, Egypt offers China geography, markets, and political legitimacy at precisely the moment Beijing wants a larger Middle Eastern role,” Dania Thafer, the executive director of Gulf International Forum, a Washington, DC-based research institute, tells TRT World.
Atli also highlights Egypt, the most populous Arab state with good relations with both China and the US, as “a potential point of convergence” between Washington and Beijing.
“Egypt is continuing to diversify its partnerships, bringing in Chinese investment and cooperation without giving up its relationship with the United States. And China, for its part, seems quite comfortable being one partner, but a very important one, among several, rather than trying to pull Egypt exclusively into its camp,” says Atli.
While Egypt has substantial economic ties with China, it remains the second-largest recipient of US military aid, receiving roughly $1.3 billion annually, while pursuing a foreign policy of “strategic balance.”
“For Xi, engaging such a close US partner allows China to demonstrate that deeper relations with Beijing do not require governments to formally abandon Washington,” says Thafer.
This balancing act between the two great powers may also be one reason for Xi’s visit to Cairo ahead of his possible late September meeting with Trump.
China wants to guide Cairo “to lead from the center” because Beijing supports “an architecture that develops in concentric circles,” says Dan Steinbock, a geopolitical analyst and international economist.
“Egypt could serve as the maritime anchor of this new architecture, preempting interference in regional choke points,” Steinbock tells TRT World.
That potential role also carries a message for Washington.
Kadir Temiz, director of ORSAM, an Ankara-based Turkish think tank, believes that “Xi’s Egypt visit might also be a coded message to the Trump administration that if the US can not secure regional stability, China and its Middle Eastern partners can offer an alternative order based on regional autonomy.”
‘Regional autonomy’
The meeting also came at a time of what Atli describes as “a broader regional trend”, with several Middle Eastern countries exploring a shift away from reliance on the US security umbrella toward a more regional security architecture, as reflected in the recent Mecca Agreement between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
“Xi’s four-point proposal with its emphasis on greater regional ‘strategic autonomy’ fits into that trend. Notably, China did not name either Iran or the United States in this proposal,” says Atli.
He refers to the Chinese leader’s call for Middle Eastern countries to be “the masters of their own affairs”, oppose external interference and pursue regional dialogue on peace and security.
“Xi’s proposal is based on the idea of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security. That echoes the basic thinking behind the Mecca Agreement, which is that countries in the region should rely less on outside security guarantees and do more among themselves,” Atli says.
But Atli also stresses that the Mecca Agreement and Xi’s Cairo proposal are “very different things”, noting that the former is a defence pact with concrete commitments, while the latter rests on a much broader diplomatic and economic framework.
“China is trying to position itself as a complementary player in this emerging regional environment, rather than trying to create or join an arrangement like Mecca.”
Cairo was also part of a quadrilateral format developed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Pakistan in the wake of US-Iran tensions, which sought a third way to address regional conflicts.
While Egypt did not join the Mecca Agreement, Ankara expects Cairo could eventually join the defence pact.
“During his visit, Xi explicitly called for Middle Eastern nations to explore a new, independent security architecture and oppose external interference. By echoing the philosophy of the new Mecca alliance, China actively backs indigenous security arrangements run by regional leaders rather than external powers,” Steinbock says.
Thafer also sees parallels between the two approaches, saying that “Xi's Cairo message fits remarkably well with the political logic behind Mecca”.
But she notes that China is not “offering to become the region’s new security guarantor” by endorsing greater regional security autonomy.
“The Egypt-China communiqué does not mention the Mecca Pact or commit China to collective defence,” she says.
“Put differently, China appears interested in helping legitimise a new regional security architecture without underwriting it in the way the US historically has. That distinction is crucial.”
The Mecca Agreement signatories have publicly said the pact is not directed against any particular country and instead aims to develop a regional security arrangement. Most recently, the foreign ministers of the three countries announced the establishment of a Strategic Political and Defence Committee, signalling the agreement's growing institutionalisation.
“It is significant that, prior to his visit to the US, Xi articulated an approach emphasising the importance of regional powers taking ownership of their situation,” Temiz tells TRT World.
“His argument—that countries should take their own initiatives rather than relying on external forces to define the Middle East's security architecture—aligns interestingly with the rhetoric developed by the Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani trio.”
Hongda Fan, a Chinese professor and director of the China–Middle East Center at Shaoxing University, also believes Beijing is closely following the heightened tensions in the oil-rich region, adding further significance to Xi's Cairo visit.
“Beijing is certainly paying close attention to cooperation among the major Middle Eastern powers,” Fan tells TRT World.
Beijing has repeatedly expressed support for Middle Eastern countries to “determine their own destiny” and deepen cooperation among themselves, Fan says.
In particular, Beijing encourages “the formation of a security framework by major regional powers that can bring stability and peace to the region,” he adds.
“This aligns with China's interests. A more stable Middle East is more beneficial to China. After all, the realisation of China's strategic goals in the Middle East depends on the cooperation, support, and coordination of the region's major powers.”

What a Record Hunting and Fishing Expansion Means for America’s Wildlife Refuges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:20:00 UTC
22:20:00 KST

The Department of the Interior implemented a massive expansion of fishing and hunting access in the United States, opening 1,488 opportunities across 32 states. With the rule in effect as of Monday, more than 92 million acres, or 95% of National Wildlife Refuge System land, are now available for the practices.
Expanded hunting and fishing are now allowed in areas where the practices were never before legal, including Rocky Flats National Wildlife Refuge in Colorado and Stewart Lake National Wildlife Refuge in North Dakota.
The rule also permits hunting and fishing for additional species and expands some seasons at locations where those activities were already allowed.
“America’s hunters and anglers now have something significant to look forward to in the fall,” said Interior Secretary Doug Burgum in the press release announcing the rule Aug. 13. “We are also promoting good government by reducing the regulatory burden and working with states to facilitate these outdoor activities.”
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) oversees more than 570 national wildlife refuges that were “established to serve a statutory purpose that targets the conservation of native species dependent on its lands and water,” according to the agency’s website.
Christopher Williams, a professor of wildlife ecology at the University of Delaware, says the refuges were initially created to protect wildlife and then later helped to combat “extreme market hunting,” or unregulated hunting of animals. They became safe habitats and breeding sanctuaries for endangered species under the 1966 Endangered Species Preservation Act.
Now, hunting and other forms of recreation are permitted across a majority of those refuges when “compatible with each station’s purpose and mission under federal law,” per FWS.
The very definition of a refuge seems to have “slowly morphed into an entity that was meant to provide an opportunity for hunting access,” Williams says.
The new rule raises a question of compatibility: How can the refuges fulfill their conservation mandate amid the nation’s largest-ever expansion of hunting and fishing?
Does hunting undermine the purpose of a wildlife refuge?
The FWS said this week’s expansion is about “maximizing access where compatible with conservation goals.”
It also said that the new rule will help revitalize rural economies, as hunters and anglers contribute more than $144 billion annually to the U.S. economy.
“These activities support jobs, fund conservation efforts, and sustain outdoor traditions that connect communities to the land and to each other,” the August announcement read.
Sporting groups touted the “historic expansion” and its potential ability to help retain hunters and fishers at these refuges, which may rely on them for curbing overabundant and invasive species.
Williams says it makes sense that conservation groups support the expansion, since hunters and anglers play an “enormously important role in American wildlife conservation.”
“And with long-term concerns about declining hunting participation, providing meaningful access remains an important part of recruitment, retention, and reactivation efforts,” he says.
“BHA applauds all efforts to responsibly expand and improve public access for hunters and anglers and appreciates the Administration’s recognition of the important role sportsmen and women play in the conservation and stewardship of public lands and waters,” Backcountry Hunters & Anglers said in a statement when the expansion was proposed in May.
This was not the first time the Trump Administration proposed such an expansion. A version of the rule from 2020 opened some 859 opportunities across 2.3 million acres. The increase in scope from his first term is about 73%.
The new rule also makes more than 1,000 modifications to existing federal regulations that previously guided access to the refuges, including simplifications and deletions. The Trump Administration has said the sweeping revisions aim to make it easier to understand and enforce guidelines from state to state. But some conservationists have concerns about how the abrupt elimination of that many regulatory mandates, all at once, will affect the refuges.
Robert Fischman, professor of environmental law at Indiana University Maurer School of Law, says that such a dramatic overhaul is worth noting. “I mean, 1,000 rules sounds pretty important,” he tells TIME.
The new rule reverses restrictions on lead ammunition
One significant change that comes with the new rule is a reversal on lead ammunition and tackle.
Following a lawsuit in 2021, the government said it would phase out the potentially harmful materials and require hunters and anglers to switch to non-toxic alternatives.
The Center for Biological Diversity sued FWS after it proposed an expansion on hunting opportunities during Trump’s first term. The lawsuit argued that the expansion could jeopardize protected species, which are susceptible to ingesting the lead ammunition and tackle. It also claimed that there would be residual harm to the greater ecosystem, as lead ammunition and tackle can contaminate fields and waterways.
The lawsuit was settled under the Biden Administration in 2022, with FWS saying it would phase out the use of lead ammunition and tackle at several refuges across the country.
Aaron Bloom, a senior attorney with nonprofit Earthjustice's Biodiversity Defense Program, said the phase-out was supposed to go into effect across eight refuges in September 2026. But with the new rule, the phase-outs will no longer take effect.
In response to the reversal, Bloom says Earthjustice will be looking at litigation—as will other environmentalist groups.
These phase-outs would have “protected both wildlife and human health, hunters and their families, from the adverse impacts of lead poisoning,” Bloom tells TIME. “There's absolutely no reason we should be allowing them in our wildlife refuges.”
Recent staffing cuts raise concerns about oversight
FWS staffing decreased by approximately 18% between April 2024 and May 2025, according to agency records obtained by the Center for Biological Diversity. The decline can be attributed in part to the “workforce optimization initiative” implemented by the Department of Government Efficiency at the beginning of 2025.
Fischman and Williams both express concern about the staffing cuts and how they will impact oversight amid expanded hunting and fishing access.
“What I'm hearing from people who are on the ground is you have whole national wildlife refuges that no longer have any staff there full-time,” Fischman says. “You have a refuge manager running around from one refuge to another, riding circuit to try to keep things together.”
Fischman questions whether there are enough staff left to “really understand” and document the impacts of the new rule. He says that streamlining refuge-specific regulations makes enforcement easier and may partially compensate for staffing reductions; however, he is skeptical that states have enough staff to patrol the affected refuges and ensure that hunters and anglers are complying with the regulations that do still apply.
“It’s dependent on there being people there to maintain trails, to monitor impacts on species, to enforce the law,” he says. “It could be that the rulemaking seems pretty logical [to the Administration], but on the ground can't be practically implemented in a way that is consistent with public safety and compatible with both the system mission and the refuge purposes.”
According to Williams, it's all a balancing act. He points out the need to preserve conservation efforts while boosting the economies of rural communities and reversing a long-term decline in hunting participation in the U.S.
“On one hand, are you reaching a point where you might be doing some harm of not having adequate sanctuary for wildlife? Or maybe you are making a net improvement to increase retention and recruitment of hunters, which provides a financial benefit?” he wonders. “The answer is probably yes on both sides of the house.”

Canada’s labor market is losing momentum — how much did employment decline, and did the “dispute” with the US have an impact?

2026-09-04
16:09:44 EEST
22:09:44 KST

Canada’s labor market is losing momentum — how much did employment decline, and did the “dispute” with the US have an impact?
Kyiv • UNN
In August, Canada lost 41,700 jobs, while unemployment remained at 6.4%. New US tariffs threaten further slowdown.
In August, Canada's economy lost 41,700 jobs, signaling a sharp slowdown in hiring after an exceptionally active summer period; meanwhile, the unemployment rate remained unchanged at 6.4%, reports UNN, citing Reuters.
Details
The August report provides one of the last "clean" pictures of the state of Canada's labor market before the effects of new 50% tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump begin to affect the economy.
These tariffs affect a relatively small share of Canadian exports, but they target vulnerable industries — including wood product manufacturing — increasing the risk that the recent growth in labor-market activity could practically evaporate.
Analysts surveyed by Reuters had forecast an increase of approximately 15,000 jobs (following a significant increase of 75,100 in July). The forecast for the unemployment rate matched the actual figure.
The Canadian dollar fell 0.51% to 1.3860 Canadian dollars per U.S. dollar (or 72.15 U.S. cents). The yield on two-year government bonds rose after the labor-market data were published, increasing by 1.3 basis points to 2.469%.
According to Statistics Canada, the main reduction in employment occurred in the full-time sector (down 35,900 positions), while the number of part-time jobs decreased by 5,800.
Recent hiring figures were inflated by temporary factors, such as hiring staff to conduct the census and work related to the FIFA World Cup; together, these factors generated an increase of 181,000 jobs from April to July.
The growth in recent months was also explained by the fact that the economy as a whole demonstrated considerable resilience to U.S. trade restrictions that have been in effect for more than 18 months, and mass layoffs have so far been avoided.
However, the entry into force of the new U.S. tariffs and Canada's retaliatory measures (starting early next week) is expected to slow this growth somewhat. Four out of five members of the labor force are employed in the services sector, including health care, education, transportation, and finance; this sector bore the brunt of the employment decline in August.
According to Statistics Canada (StatsCan), 51,500 jobs were eliminated in this sector in August; the greatest losses occurred in industries such as business and support services (including building services), as well as wholesale and retail trade.
The unemployment rate remained at its lowest level in two years, despite the economy facing a wave of tariffs imposed by the Trump administration.
Slower labor-force growth, caused by stricter immigration rules and an aging workforce, also contributed to improved unemployment figures in recent months.
The labor force, which stood at 22.632 million people, declined for the first time since February.
The youth unemployment rate rose by 0.3 percentage points in August, reaching 12.9%, interrupting the downward trend observed from April through July.
Average hourly wages for permanent employees — an important indicator of inflationary pressures — fell to 2% in August (from 3% a month earlier), reaching their lowest level in more than seven years (excluding the pandemic period).

A Philippine court on Friday ordered the arrest of Vice President Sara Duterte over alleged grave threats to her former ally, President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr., his wife, and a former House Speaker.
The warrant against Duterte, 48, set the bail at 120,000 pesos ($1,900) for each of the three counts against her.
“Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” Duterte’s lawyer said in a statement.
Duterte has been charged with threatening the lives of Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and his cousin, former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
The case stems from a November 2024 virtual press conference where the Vice President revealed an apparent assassination plot against Marcos, his wife, and Romualdez.
“I already talked to someone—I told him, If I’m killed, kill [Marcos], Liza Araneta, and Martin Romualdez,” she said in Filipino, “No joke, no joke. I already gave orders. If I die, I told them, ‘Don’t stop until they’re dead.’ And then he said, ‘Yes.’”
The threat is also one of the allegations included in the impeachment complaint against Duterte, on top of alleged misuse of public funds as Vice President and during her stint as Education Secretary. Duterte has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.
The Vice President is currently standing trial at the Philippine Senate, serving as an impeachment court, following her second impeachment in May. If convicted in the impeachment court, she could be removed from office and barred from running in the 2028 national elections, where she said she plans to contest the presidency.
Philippine law typically allows candidates to run for public office even if they face pending criminal charges.
Duterte controversies and public standing
Duterte is the daughter of former President Rodrigo Duterte, who is awaiting trial before the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, for the thousands of deaths attributed to his violent anti-drug campaign.
The Duterte family still enjoys broad public support in the Philippines, despite the controversies. Recent surveys show Sara Duterte herself is the top preferred candidate by Filipinos to succeed Marcos, whom she had a falling out with. Marcos, who took office in 2022, is limited to a lone six-year term.
The presidential office said in a statement that it “respects the decision of the court” to issue an arrest warrant.
Jean Encinas-Franco, a political science professor at the University of the Philippines, tells TIME that “the law has finally caught up with the Vice President,” but questioned the timing of the arrest warrant’s release. Franco said Duterte’s arrest warrant could successfully repel criticisms that Marcos is a “weak” leader as the impeachment proceedings have dragged on.
However, Franco says it remains unclear which political camp—if any—will benefit from the latest political development. “We don't know what will happen because it's still 1-½ years [until the elections] and that's a lifetime in Philippine politics.”

From naval blockade to land corridors: Iran's strategic pivot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:07:45 UTC
22:07:45 KST

From naval blockade to land corridors: Iran's strategic pivot
TEHRAN- Iran's maritime trade has faced serious disruption due to geopolitical tensions and sanctions, but this challenge has unexpectedly accelerated the development of land-based transit routes. What initially appeared as a strategic vulnerability—over-reliance on the Strait of Hormuz—is now forcing a fundamental shift in the country's trade infrastructure. The result could transform Iran from a sea-dependent economy into a regional transit hub connecting East, West, North, and South.
The recent naval pressures, intensified after failed military confrontations, have exposed a long-standing weakness: Iran's trade was disproportionately channeled through a single maritime choke point. Rather than simply imposing costs, however, this constraint has made the diversification of trade routes an urgent necessity. In response, Iran is actively developing four major land corridors that could redefine its economic geography.
First, the East-West Railway Corridor links China to Iran via Central Asia, passing through Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. This 10,400-kilometer route can cut shipping times from 30 days by sea to just 15 days by rail, significantly reducing costs and risks. Second, the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), through Pakistan's Gwadar port and Iran's Rimdan border, offers an eastern bypass of the Strait of Hormuz. Third, the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) connects Iran to Russia and India, providing access to northern and southern markets. Fourth, the Shalamcheh-Basra railway—only 32 kilometers short of completion—can open Iran to Iraq, Turkey, and the Mediterranean.
According to Ahmad Bakhshayesh, a member of Iran's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, the government has actively expanded trade cooperation with neighbors like Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkey, Pakistan, and Oman. He emphasized that these corridors have prevented shortages of essential goods during the crisis, ensuring price hikes rather than outright scarcity.
The activation of the Iran-Pakistan transit corridor is particularly significant. With instability on Pakistan-Afghanistan border routes, Islamabad now looks to Iran for access to Central Asian markets. Iran's Mirjaveh and Rimdan terminals are central to this exchange, with a bilateral trade target of $10 billion. Rimdan has been developed since 2020, with passenger facilities and infrastructure upgrades underway.
These corridors must not remain temporary fixes. If completed and sustained, they can offer lasting competitive advantages, attract investment from China, India, and Russia, and reduce Iran's vulnerability to maritime disruptions. What began as a forced response to containment can become a permanent pillar of Iran's economic strategy. The lesson is clear: a country with Iran's geography cannot be blockaded when it turns its land borders into bridges rather than barriers.

Germany has begun mass production of more than 5,000 medium- and long-range strike drones for Ukraine, defense company Auterion and its Ukrainian joint-venture partner Airlogix said.
The first units have already been manufactured in the greater Munich area under a German government order that industry sources estimate at about €300 million ($348 million).

Production is underway at an undisclosed site near Munich and is also planned at a second plant in eastern Germany, German news agency dpa reported.
Two models are being manufactured, according to company sources.
One has a medium range, while the other can fly up to 1,500 kilometers (about 930 miles), the sources said.
Auterion supplies the software and operating system, while Airlogix provides the hardware.
The one-way strike drones carry explosives and are designed to hit and destroy their targets rather than return.
Artificial intelligence is intended to keep the drones on course even when electronic warfare systems attempt to jam them.

Psychiatrists detail mother’s sudden descent into severe psychosis and delirious mania following childbirth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:00:38 UTC
22:00:38 KST

A recent case report published in Frontiers in Psychiatry details the experience of a 27-year-old woman who developed a rare and severe condition known as delirious mania shortly after giving birth. The case highlights how women with bipolar disorder may face an increased risk of complex manic episodes following multiple pregnancies and deliveries. The findings suggest that electroconvulsive therapy can be an effective and rapid treatment for this life-threatening psychiatric emergency.
Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition characterized by extreme mood swings, including emotional highs known as mania and lows known as depression. Following childbirth, women with bipolar disorder experience a heightened risk of recurrent psychiatric episodes. These postpartum episodes typically present as depression or standard mania. Postpartum psychosis is another related condition where mothers experience an abrupt onset of psychotic symptoms shortly following childbirth.
Delirious mania is an unusually severe neuropsychiatric condition that is rarely documented. It combines the hyperactive and erratic behaviors of mania with delirium, which is a state of profound confusion and disorientation. Patients may also experience psychosis, meaning they lose touch with reality through hallucinations or delusions.
Diagnosing delirious mania is challenging because doctors must first rule out a variety of physical illnesses that can cause similar symptoms. Infections, drug toxicity, and severe metabolic imbalances can all produce a state of delirium. Medical teams typically conduct extensive blood tests, brain imaging, and neurological exams to ensure the symptoms are not caused by an underlying physical disease.
Because delirious mania is poorly understood and infrequently documented, it often goes unrecognized in clinical settings. Lead author Bowen Song, a researcher at Sichuan University’s Mental Health Center in China, and a team of scientists documented this specific case to build a medical literature base that helps other doctors recognize the condition. By detailing the patient’s symptoms and treatment, the authors aim to provide evidence on how to identify and manage postpartum delirious mania before it escalates into a life-threatening situation.
The patient in this report was a 27-year-old Chinese woman with a documented history of bipolar disorder type I. She had previously experienced manic episodes characterized by excessive talking, a decreased need for sleep, and impulsive behavior. During her first pregnancy in 2020, she experienced a manic episode with psychotic symptoms following a routine amniocentesis. An amniocentesis is a medical procedure used to test amniotic fluid, and the physical stress of the event appeared to trigger her symptoms.
She was treated with medication and later delivered her first child via a cesarean section without further postpartum psychiatric issues. In 2024, she became pregnant again and delivered her second child, also via a cesarean section. Her mood had remained stable throughout the pregnancy on a low dose of an antipsychotic medication called quetiapine.
On the first day after her second surgery, her behavior changed drastically. She became highly excitable, talked excessively, and showed uncharacteristic aggression toward her family members. Over the next three days, she did not sleep and began experiencing auditory hallucinations, hearing voices mocking her. She also developed paranoid delusions, believing her husband had been unfaithful.
Her condition quickly deteriorated into a state of severe confusion and physical restlessness. She exhibited inappropriate behaviors, such as bedwetting, and became completely disoriented. She claimed to have lived for hundreds of years and could no longer recognize familiar people, places, or the current time.
Her family brought her to the emergency department, where doctors initially attempted to calm her using various medications. These initial treatments included sodium valproate, a mood stabilizer, and propofol, a strong sedative. These medications did not improve her symptoms. Her extreme agitation posed a risk to herself and the medical staff, requiring continuous sedation and physical restraints.
Given the severe and life-threatening nature of her symptoms, the medical team recommended electroconvulsive therapy, commonly known as ECT, on her seventh day of hospitalization. ECT is a medical procedure that involves passing small electric currents through the brain to intentionally trigger a brief seizure. This process appears to alter brain chemistry in a way that can quickly reverse symptoms of certain severe mental health conditions.
The patient received daily ECT sessions for the first three days, followed by treatments every other day. After the third session, her mood began to stabilize, and her consciousness returned to normal. She was once again able to recognize her surroundings and interact amicably with her family members.
Following the eighth ECT session, her emotional state stabilized entirely. Her hallucinations, delusions, and severe agitation resolved. She was discharged on the 19th day of her hospital stay and prescribed maintenance doses of oral psychiatric medications.
During a follow-up visit four weeks later, the patient remained alert and emotionally stable. She reported complete amnesia regarding the acute phase of her illness. She remembered nothing from the delivery until her third ECT treatment.
This single account cannot establish that multiple pregnancies or cesarean sections directly cause delirious mania in women with bipolar disorder. Biological changes during childbirth are complex, and individual medical events do not indicate a direct cause-and-effect relationship. The onset of psychiatric symptoms after delivery likely involves a combination of hormonal fluctuations, physical stress from surgery, and underlying genetic vulnerabilities.
These findings also do not imply that standard psychiatric medications are ineffective for postpartum psychiatric emergencies. For this specific patient, standard drugs did not stabilize her condition quickly enough, necessitating electroconvulsive therapy. Different individuals respond uniquely to treatments, and medications remain the standard initial approach for managing acute mania.
During the diagnostic process, the patient’s family declined a lumbar puncture, a routine procedure used to test the fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord. This meant doctors could not definitively test for autoimmune encephalitis, a condition where the immune system attacks the brain and produces similar psychiatric symptoms. The patient’s rapid recovery following ECT indicates an underlying psychiatric condition rather than an autoimmune disease, but the absence of this test leaves a small degree of diagnostic uncertainty.
Case reports describe the unique experiences of individual patients. They cannot be used to determine how common a condition is within the broader population or to create universal treatment guidelines. They are highly useful in medicine because they document rare clinical presentations, helping other doctors recognize unusual symptoms and consider alternative treatment options when standard therapies fail.
The report, “Postpartum delirious mania in a patient with diagnosis of bipolar disorder after cesarean delivery: a case report,” was authored by Bowen Song, Yiwen Yuan, Zhixiong Li, Zhongrui Ma, Xiufang Yang, and Zhe Li.

Why are fuel and petrochemical prices outpacing crude – and how long will it last?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:00:08 UTC
22:00:08 KST

Why are fuel and petrochemical prices outpacing crude – and how long will it last?
Global refined-product exports were down 25 per cent year on year in August, with losses concentrated in Russia and the Persian Gulf, analysts say
This summer, David Chen, a Chinese national living in Japan, got an unexpected lesson in global industrial supply chains – delivered through a bag of potato chips.
When popular Japanese snack brand Calbee replaced its signature colourful packaging with monochrome designs, Chen initially assumed it was a marketing gimmick. “Then news reports explained the switch stemmed from a naphtha supply crunch. I even looked up the word,” Chen said.
Naphtha, a flammable liquid processed from crude oil, might not be a household name, yet it serves as a foundational input in polyester fibres, packaging and industrial solvents. The squeeze has prompted Japanese media to coin a new term: “naphtha bankruptcies”, reflecting mounting anxiety among some companies over securing vital oil-derived inputs.
A June survey by corporate research firm Tokyo Shoko Research underscored the widespread impact, finding that about 80 per cent of more than 7,000 responding firms had difficulty procuring oil-derived products.
However, behind Japan’s localised squeeze lies a wider strain on global supply. According to late-August estimates by Goldman Sachs analysts led by Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby, global refinery outages – which take refining capacity offline or force facilities to reduce output – stood 60 per cent above seasonal norms.
Market and industry analysts attributed the tight conditions to two main pressures: mounting geopolitical conflict and fuel export controls from China, which has the world’s largest oil-refining capacity.

New island emerges in Norway’s Svalbard as glacier retreats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:59:45 UTC
21:59:45 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
A new island has emerged in Norway’s Svalbard archipelago after the Austfonna glacier retreated, Norwegian public broadcaster NRK reported Friday.
The island, covering roughly 0.45 square kilometers (0.17 square miles), was first identified in satellite images taken this summer, according to Geir Moholdt, a glaciologist at the Norwegian Polar Institute.
Radar images indicate that the landmass became separated from the glacier in late autumn last year. It now lies about 400 meters (1,312 feet) from the glacier front.
Austfonna, Norway’s largest glacier, has been melting at a record rate. Its glacier front stretches for more than 180 kilometers (112 miles), making it the longest in the Northern Hemisphere, according to the institute.
“In recent years, glaciers in Svalbard have lost more than one meter of ice on the surface on average per year,” Moholdt said, adding that the rate was far higher than previously observed.
He said Svalbard’s glaciers are retreating further onto land, causing fjords to lengthen while the ice becomes thinner because of warmer summers and extensive melting.
The rapidly changing terrain also makes updated maps increasingly important for researchers, local authorities, police, aircraft operators, and people traveling outdoors, said Anne Urset, a geodesist at the institute.
Moholdt warned that other landmasses could emerge as warming and glacial retreat continue.
“There are several candidates for new islands that could emerge with rapid warming and melting,” he said, adding that some glaciers could eventually disappear entirely.

WINDHOEK, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The United States will begin reducing financial assistance for Namibia's HIV response as the southern African country assumes greater responsibility for sustaining its epidemic-control programs, the two governments announced in a joint statement released Friday.
The reduction will be implemented in phases over the next year, with U.S. support shifting from financial assistance to technical cooperation as HIV programs are integrated into Namibia's national health system, according to the statement.
The transition marks a winding down of more than two decades of substantial U.S. financial support provided mainly through the U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR.
The two governments attributed the shift to Namibia's progress in controlling the epidemic, noting that the country has achieved a 96-98-98 rate for HIV testing, treatment and viral suppression, exceeding the UNAIDS targets of 95-95-95.
The planned phase-down follows earlier disruptions to U.S. funding that affected parts of Namibia's HIV response.
UNAIDS previously reported that the disruptions affected community-based prevention services, services for key populations and community health worker programs.
UNAIDS also reported intermittent condom shortages, reduced access to some pre-exposure prophylaxis services and the termination of some staff contracts among U.S.-funded implementing partners.
Namibia launched a sustainability roadmap for HIV, viral hepatitis, tuberculosis and malaria control in November 2024, according to the joint statement. The roadmap is intended to strengthen the country's health systems and prepare them for a shift in international donor support toward technical assistance. ■

2026-09-04

ROME, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Food Price Index averaged 133.3 points in August, up 1.9 percent from July and 2.5 percent from a year earlier, reaching its highest level since the end of 2022, the FAO said Friday.
The increase was broad-based, with all five commodity group indices rising. The FAO Sugar Price Index recorded the biggest increase, surging 11.9 percent month-on-month to its highest level since June 2025, amid growing concerns over global sugar supplies in the 2026/27 season. Hot and dry weather in the European Union and parts of Asia, lower sugar production in Brazil, and India's decision to allow duty-free raw sugar imports contributed to the rise.
The FAO Cereal Price Index rose 2.2 percent in August to its highest level since May 2024. Wheat prices increased 2.6 percent, supported by continued disruptions to Black Sea export logistics, lower production prospects in parts of Europe due to hot and dry weather, and a weaker U.S. dollar. Maize prices climbed 2.5 percent amid concerns over crop yields in parts of the United States and the European Union, strong demand from the ethanol and feed sectors, and disruptions to Ukrainian exports.
The Vegetable Oil Price Index rose 0.6 percent to its highest level since June 2022, marking its third consecutive monthly increase. The Meat Price Index increased 1.0 percent, driven by higher poultry, pig and ovine meat prices, while the Dairy Price Index rose 2.3 percent, its first increase in four months.
Despite the August rise, the FAO Food Price Index remained 16.8 percent below its record high reached in March 2022, the FAO said. ■

South Korea’s military turns to AI as low birth rate shrinks pool of recruits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:57:44 UTC
21:57:44 KST

As South Korea's population rapidly ages and the pool of military recruits shrinks, Seoul is increasingly looking to artificial intelligence, robots and autonomous systems to help defend one of the world's most heavily militarized borders with fewer soldiers.
Earlier this month, President Lee Jae Myung called for selective conscription and a shift toward a smaller, technology-driven force, describing his goal as a “smart, elite and strong military centered on advanced equipment and technologies.”
The push is already moving beyond plans and policy.
In July, South Korea conducted its first test of a humanoid robot performing a ship's helmsman duties, with the robot successfully executing steering commands under simulated conditions including narrow waterways, bad weather and nighttime operations.
The Navy also carried out its first minesweeping trial using AI technology and unmanned vessels earlier this month.
The Army, meanwhile, has commissioned a study into automating key maintenance operations, including through AI-powered predictive maintenance, automated information management, maintenance robots and wearable strength-assist suits.
The push is part of South Korea's broader embrace of AI. In June, Lee unveiled investment plans worth more than $1 trillion for projects including semiconductors, physical AI and data centers.
But for the military, the technology is intended to address a particularly pressing problem – South Korea is running out of people to fill its ranks.
South Korean men are required to complete at least 18 months of military service, with some exempted or assigned alternative service.
But decades of falling birth rates are rapidly shrinking the population from which the military can draw its conscripts.
South Korea's total fertility rate stood at 0.8 in 2025, far below the 2.1 children per woman generally considered necessary to maintain a stable population without migration.
Around 1 million babies were born annually in South Korea in the early 1970s. By 2022, that number had fallen to just 249,000 and the fertility rate had dropped to 0.78, a level the government described as “unprecedented in world history.”
South Korea's population is projected to fall from around 52 million in 2024 to 36 million by 2072. Within the same time frame, the proportion of people aged 65 and older is projected to surge from 19.2% to 47.7% – meaning nearly half the population could be elderly.
“The demographic rationale is explicit and quantifiable,” Dongyoun Cho, a senior fellow for advanced technologies, national security and defense at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS-Europe), told Anadolu. “The active force has fallen to around 450,000, at just over 90% of required manning.”
But AI cannot simply replace every soldier who disappears from the ranks, she cautioned.
“AI substitutes selectively, not one-for-one – it is most credible in persistent surveillance, logistics and other manpower-intensive tasks,” Cho said. “The force will shrink regardless of AI. The question is what a smaller force can still do.”
South Korea is pursuing several programs aimed at building autonomous and AI capabilities across its armed forces, with the Future National Defense Strategy Committee putting AI and unmanned forces on the agenda, she said.
The Army aims to introduce more than 50,000 training drones by 2029, enough to provide one drone per squad, the Korea Herald reported in April, enabling service members to acquire basic drone operating skills and practical experience.
The Army's TIGER Plus program also envisions integrating AI, drones and other advanced technologies across the force by 2040.
In the air, South Korea is developing the LOWUS unmanned combat aircraft, envisioned as a “loyal wingman” that could operate alongside crewed fighters such as the country's KF-21.
At sea, the Navy's Sea Ghost concept is aimed at creating a force in which crewed warships operate alongside unmanned systems using AI.
But Cho argued that Seoul's technological ambitions are moving faster than its ability to put them into practice.
“Political will is running ahead of the ecosystem that has to deliver it,” she said, pointing to the reorganization of the Drone Operations Command after its initial creation was acknowledged as hasty.
And the biggest obstacles may not be the AI models themselves.
“The practical obstacles are less about algorithms than about integration – interoperability across platforms and services, test and certification bottlenecks, communications resilience under jamming, safety assurance and operator training,” Cho said.
Those challenges are compounded, she added, by military acquisition systems designed to purchase hardware rather than software that is continuously updated.
The gap between South Korea's ambitions and its ability to implement them will be “the defining feature of the next several years,” she said.
South Korea is hardly alone in racing to integrate AI and autonomous systems into its armed forces.
But Cho said Seoul differs from Washington and Beijing “less in scale than in motivation and structure.”
The US and China are investing in military AI on a much larger scale and across a wider range of applications.
South Korea, however, has an “unusually explicit demographic rationale,” Cho said, alongside an export-oriented defense industry and the need to ensure its systems remain interoperable with those of its US ally.
Japan has historically taken a more incremental approach, though that may now be changing, she added.
Tokyo is moving to revise its three major national security documents, with AI-enabled decision-making and unmanned systems reportedly among the issues under consideration.
According to media reports, Japan is also considering utilizing cutting-edge AI systems under its preemptive cyber defense policy such as US company Anthropic's Claude Mythos.
Rather than seeing the developments as a single race for AI military supremacy, Cho said each country is responding to its own strategic pressures.
“Rather than a race with a single scoreboard, these are programs shaped by quite different drivers and constraints – and (South) Korea's may prove one of the more instructive cases of adoption under demographic pressure,” she said.
Putting increasingly autonomous technology into military operations brings a different set of problems.
For Cho, three are particularly concerning: AI systems could misidentify targets or make errors in chaotic environments; human operators could place too much trust in machine-generated recommendations; and faster automated decision-making could increase the risk of military escalation.
All three carry particular weight on the Korean Peninsula.
Real-world conditions, Cho said, are “far harder than those in which systems are trained and tested.”
Under intense pressure, operators could also defer to recommendations generated by AI, weakening meaningful human control even when formal “human-in-the-loop” requirements remain in place.
Speed is another issue.
AI can process information and recommend action far more quickly than conventional military decision-making systems. While that can provide an advantage, it could also leave humans with less time to question what a system is telling them, Cho said.
That, Cho said, is “particularly consequential on a peninsula where warning times are already measured in minutes.”
Cho expects AI to move from an experimental capability to a structural part of South Korea's defense posture, shaping how the country designs its military rather than simply being added to existing forces.
The Army's TIGER Plus blueprint, which targets force-wide application by 2040, already points in that direction.
AI could help accelerate the process from detecting a potential target to deciding how to respond, including by integrating information from reconnaissance satellites. It could also support military command decisions and use predictive logistics to identify equipment problems before they occur, she said.
“The trajectory points toward a smaller but more automated force, and toward autonomy becoming a component of Korea's defense-export offer as well,” Cho added.
But whether that transformation succeeds, she argued, will depend on more than technological capability.
“The decisive variable will be whether governance keeps pace with adoption – assurance and safety cases, doctrine and interoperability with the United States and other partners.”
Countries that deploy military AI “responsibly and demonstrably will also be the ones trusted as suppliers and allies,” she predicted.

EU says Brazilian animal-product exports can resume once safety requirements met
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:56:46 UTC
21:56:46 KST

Melike Pala
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Brazilian exports of meat and other animal products to the European Union have been suspended following the introduction of updated EU animal health and food safety requirements, but shipments can resume once Brazilian authorities demonstrate compliance with the new rules, the European Commission said Friday.
"Once they can show compliance, exports to the European Union of these products from Brazil will be able to resume," European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill told reporters in Brussels.
The EU suspended imports of Brazilian animals and animal-origin products intended for human consumption on Thursday, pending assurances that the country's exports comply with EU rules.
The measures affect products including beef, poultry, eggs, honey and animal casings.
EU rules require imports of animal-origin products for human consumption to meet the bloc's animal and public health standards, including requirements concerning residues from veterinary medicines.
Gill said the EU's rules on antimicrobial resistance apply equally and without discrimination to European producers and those from third countries seeking access to the bloc's single market.
He said the EU had engaged with its trading partners and provided support to help them meet the new requirements.

Netanyahu partners renew calls for removal of Gazans as Israeli election nears
Unknown

2026-09-04

Netanyahu partners renew calls for removal of Gazans as Israeli election nears
JERUSALEM, Sept 4 - Two Israeli ministers floated proposals this week for the mass removal of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, resurfacing an idea voiced repeatedly by right-wing politicians over the past three years as they seek to rally supporters ahead of an election.
The calls by two of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political allies have revived Palestinian fears that Israel ultimately aims to forcibly expel them from Gaza despite U.S.-led diplomatic efforts to end the conflict there.
Far-right security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir laid out a seven-year plan for removing Gaza's population through "voluntary emigration" during a press conference on Thursday night. He said he would seek the creation of a "ministry in charge of emigration" in the next government.
"Instead of illusions of peace now, we need actions of emigration now," he said. "Instead of (them) digging tunnels, it’s time to pack suitcases," referring to tunnels dug under Gaza by Hamas before the war.
Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party said in a statement on Thursday that Turkey, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo were being considered as potential destinations.
Ismail Al-Thawabta, director of the Hamas government media office, said: "The Palestinian people are deeply rooted in their land and will not be intimidated by such threats."
Israel is due to hold a general election on October 27. It will be the first since Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, triggered an Israeli military campaign that laid waste to Gaza, which has a population of more than two million.
An October 2025, U.S.-backed, ceasefire halted large-scale fighting, but it has not ended Israeli strikes or produced progress on a plan for permanent peace.
FEARS OF A NEW 'NAKBA'
Ben-Gvir's comments followed those of Defence Minister Israel Katz, from Netanyahu's Likud party, who said on Wednesday there was "no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration".
“We are fully prepared to move them out if it becomes possible — by sea, by air, by every way possible. Egypt is not willing, so it won’t be through them," he said during an online conference hosted by Israel’s Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper.
Netanyahu's office did not immediately provide comment.
Polls suggest Netanyahu, who has led the most right-wing coalition in Israeli history, could lose power next month, his security credentials still shaken by the 2023 attack — though analysts say he can't be written off.
Israel's defence ministry in 2025 established an office tasked with overseeing “voluntary emigration” from Gaza, after comments by U.S. President Donald Trump suggesting Gazans could be permanently displaced.
Trump later backed away from the idea, which faced strong resistance from Arab states and was widely rejected internationally. Israel reportedly sounded out several African countries as potential resettlement sites.
Netanyahu has said he supports what his government has described as "voluntary emigration" from Gaza, but that far-right ministers' goals of re-establishing Jewish settlements in the territory are unrealistic. Israeli officials have denied intending to transfer Gaza's population out by force.
Calls for resettlement of Gazans have prompted fears among Palestinians of a new "Nakba" (catastrophe), the name given to the displacement of hundreds of thousands of Palestinians who fled or were driven from their homes in the wake of the 1948 war that accompanied the founding of the state of Israel.
The Gaza Strip is central to Palestinian hopes of statehood in territory captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
GENOCIDE ACCUSATIONS
The 2023 Hamas-led attacks killed 1,200 people in Israel while another 251 were taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies.
More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's military campaign, according to Gaza health authorities.
A U.N. inquiry determined that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, arguing that its killings, siege and destruction were carried out with the intent to destroy Palestinian life in the enclave.
Israel, which is fighting a genocide case at the International Court of Justice, rejects genocide allegations as politically motivated and says that its military campaign targets Hamas, not Gaza’s civilian population.
This week, Ben-Gvir posted an AI-generated video depicting dozens of Palestinian prisoners on a conveyor belt, entering a prison facility. They emerge from the other side emaciated, distressed and in tears.
Ben-Gvir later deleted the video, after it had amassed millions of views on X. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In a crowded Gaza City displacement camp, some Palestinians said that they believed the latest Israeli calls were an election ploy.
They also said Gaza was their land and they would never leave it.
"We will die on the land of Gaza," said one resident, 52-year-old Mohammed Abu Al-Qumbuz. "We were born on it, our children grew up on it, so it is very difficult to think of leaving." REUTERS

Kyiv schools are gradually returning to in-person learning — 11 institutions will remain online
Kyiv • UNN
In Kyiv, most schools are gradually transitioning to in-person learning with safety considerations in mind. Eleven institutions will remain online due to the lack of shelters.
After the first week of the school year, schools in Kyiv are gradually returning students to in-person learning, taking the security situation into account. The Kyiv City State Administration reported this, UNN writes.
In total, more than 248,000 students study at 412 schools in the capital. This week, more than 45% of schoolchildren studied in person in shelters—mostly primary school students; nearly 30% studied in a blended format, more than 17% remotely, and another 7% according to an individual learning format. Now, students in grades 5–11 are also returning to in-person learning in most schools
At the same time, 11 Kyiv schools will continue studying remotely for now. These are primarily institutions that do not have their own shelters and, for various reasons, are unable to set them up on their premises.
Previously, during air raid alerts, students at such schools could move to the nearest shelters at metro stations. However, due to the changing nature of military threats, this model is no longer a safe option for organizing the educational process.
Valentyn Mondryivskyi, Deputy Head of the Kyiv City State Administration, emphasized that the format of schooling may continue to change. At the same time, the safety of children and employees of educational institutions remains the main criterion.

How the Chinese Government Has Controlled the Narrative on the Tibet Floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

As rescue efforts have continued on both sides of the border following the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, a fight over how the disaster is being reported has been growing in intensity on social media. The dispute centers on the claims and counterclaims following a story by the BBC’s China correspondent, Laura Bicker, about how China is censoring videos of the floods.
Bicker said videos of the landslide and flood surge sweeping through Gyirong Port on the border was scrubbed from the internet, in part, because Beijing fears instability in the politically sensitive region of Tibet.
Some social media users, however, have posted screenshots of the footage used by the BBC, pointing out it had actually been shown in the Chinese media. One Chinese journalist put it bluntly: “Never seen the BBC spread rumors so blatantly.” Another X user said the “middle ground often gets lost” in heated debates like this over Chinese censorship.
The Chinese government has long complained about what it sees as Western media “bias” in reporting on Tibet. Its supporters seem to have doubled down on this narrative this week on social media, zeroing in on the BBC.
But Chinese social media users, both inside and outside China, have long dealt with the authorities exercising control over information. This has certainly been the case in the aftermath of the floods, too.
As Bicker noted in her report, the most concrete example is the deletion of videos showing the massive wave of mud and water swallowing Gyirong Port. The footage was initially circulated on the platforms Weixin and RedNote, but users later could not access it.
Another form of control has been the restricted access for independent and foreign journalists. Allyson Horn of the Australian Broadcasting Corporation said she had made repeated requests to travel to Tibet, but was denied. Other foreign journalists have similarly been blocked. This makes it difficult, if not impossible, for foreign media to independently verify the Chinese government’s account of what happened there.
The absence of independent reporting, combined with the removal of footage from social media, has allowed the Chinese state media to dominate the narrative. This reflects a longstanding tendency in Chinese media to avoid material that could cause social instability or public panic.
Coverage of the Tibet floods by the state-controlled media has focused heavily on the People’s Liberation Army rescue operations, President Xi Jinping’s leadership during the crisis, and Premier Li Qiang’s visit to the disaster zone. There has also been some coverage of efforts to reopen roads and the delivery of disaster-relief supplies to affected residents.
But as the Guardian has noted, there has been much less reporting about how the disaster has affected local villagers, their homes, and communities. On the Nepali side of the border, meanwhile, foreign journalists have been able to interview survivors without restrictions.
Critics also say the Chinese government is hiding the true number of casualties. The problem with these contested claims is that no outsiders – whether they be critics or not – have been able to verify the death toll due to the restricted access to the disaster site.
China’s media environment has, at times, been less controlled than it is today.
On May 12, 2008, an earthquake measuring 8.0 on the Richter scale struck Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people and leaving millions homeless. Chinese state media provided extensive live coverage almost as soon as the quake struck. This continued for weeks, with China Central Television regularly updating the death toll and reporting extensively on rescue efforts.
Foreign media did raise questions about whether lives had been unnecessarily lost due to the collapse of poorly constructed school buildings. Foreign journalists also questioned whether justice would be served for the families of the victims. Chinese media reported on some of these controversies, including questioning whether the local government had done the proper quality control checks on school construction.
At the beginning, the coverage represented a major breakthrough in Chinese media reporting of emergencies and natural disasters. Its “unprecedented openness” was widely observed by Western media. But within weeks, the government had begun to clamp down on information about the schools for fear the issue could drive anti-government sentiment.
As a general practice, China’s state media outlets are instructed to emphasize “positive reporting” during times of crisis, while censors remove criticisms of government responses or culpability online.
The media coverage of a fatal train accident in the city of Wenzhou in 2011 was a good example.
Research shows that, unlike the Sichuan earthquake, the government kept a tight control on what was permissible in the media. The authorities ordered media outlets not to send reporters to the scene, limited the frequency of their reporting, and instructed them not to link the story to high-speed rail development. Journalists were also told not to investigate the accident’s causes or impact, or circulate personal microblogs on the incident.
Instead, they were urged to seek “moving” stories of bravery and sacrifice, such as local blood donations. The aim was to evoke love and compassion in the wake of the disaster.
When Xi came to power in 2012, the government’s concerns over potential challenges to its rule led to even more tightening on Chinese media and social media. The media’s handling of the Tibet floods is now following this pattern of restricted coverage and emphasizing positive news.
The disaster has also occurred at a time of growing distrust between China and the West. This seems to be adding to the perceptions of biased coverage. None of this is helped by the logistical difficulties in accessing both the disaster site and first-hand sources of information.
Chinese restrictions are making it harder for Western journalists to independently verify what is happening. The resulting information gap is raising suspicions in the West and criticism of censorship and biased coverage in Chinese media.
And that criticism, in turn, may reinforce Beijing’s belief that Western reporting on Tibet is inherently biased, giving it another reason to restrict information.

Details
We have seen this initiative and closely followed the visit of the President of Ukraine to Moldova—it was a very interesting meeting. This initiative is officially called the Odesa Triangle. What is this Odesa Triangle? It means developing and further expanding logistics through Moldova—so, we have the Odesa region, Moldova, and the ports of Constanța
She noted that over the past seven months, 1.5 million tonnes of cargo have already been transported through Moldova, which is 35% more than during the same period last year. As part of the "Odesa Triangle," these volumes are planned to increase by at least 10%. In addition, the development of the route is of long-term significance.
So, the Moldovan route will not be shut down. If it is developed, it will remain in place for the future

Such projects should be scaled up not only to include Moldova, Romania, and Turkey, but also to involve all the countries of the Black Sea region as much as possible, as well as everything that follows the logistics routes we need—not only to Europe, but also to the Middle East and the countries of the South Caucasus, among others
