Extreme drought now covers 44% of Puerto Rico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:12:53 UTC
21:12:53 KST

Extreme drought now covers 44% of Puerto Rico
- Date:
- September 4, 2026
- Source:
- NASA Earth Observatory
- Summary:
- Puerto Rico’s normally rainy season has instead brought a severe and fast-growing drought. By August 25, three-quarters of the territory was in at least moderate drought, with extreme drought covering 44 percent and some areas receiving less than 20 percent of their usual rainfall. Water shortages have forced rationing, while farmers are losing crops and ranchers are running low on hay. The situation has become serious enough to trigger both local and federal disaster declarations.
- Share:
Puerto Rico typically enters its wet season in May, but 2026 has unfolded very differently. By late August, rainfall had remained scarce across much of the U.S. territory, allowing drought conditions to spread rapidly. The lack of rain has contributed to water shortages and rationing in some communities, prompting Puerto Rico's governor to declare a state of emergency in late July. In late August, the U.S. government also issued a drought disaster declaration covering more than two dozen cities and towns.
The map shows the severity and geographic extent of drought across Puerto Rico on August 25, 2026. It was created by the U.S. Drought Monitor, a collaboration involving the National Drought Mitigation Center at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and NASA.
NASA has supported the project for years with Earth observations and scientific expertise. That involvement expanded in 2026 when two NASA scientists joined the small group responsible for producing the weekly drought assessments.
David Mocko, a senior research scientist in the Hydrological Sciences Laboratory at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, said the effects of the unusually hot and dry conditions were visible across multiple types of satellite and ground-based data used by the U.S. Drought Monitor.
For recent Puerto Rico updates, particularly important information included satellite estimates of soil moisture, along with weather measurements and observations of streamflow and well conditions, Mocko said.
Mocko prepared the U.S. Drought Monitor update for August 18, 2026. He and Jonathan Case of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center are the first NASA scientists to produce the weekly maps.
Extreme Drought Covers 44 Percent of the Territory
By August 25, 2026, about three-quarters of Puerto Rico was experiencing at least moderate drought, according to the assessment. Extreme drought zones (dark orange) in eastern and southwestern parts of the main island had expanded during the previous week and covered 44 percent of the territory.
The change happened quickly. Just three months earlier, none of Puerto Rico was classified as being in drought, and less than 20 percent of the territory was considered abnormally dry.
Late winter and early spring had actually been wetter than normal across the U.S. Caribbean, according to a National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS) report. Conditions then shifted sharply toward dryness.
Rainfall Falls Far Below Normal
From mid-May through mid-July, most of Puerto Rico received less than 60 percent of its normal precipitation, according to NIDIS. Southern and southwestern areas were even drier, receiving less than 20 percent of normal rainfall. That translated to a rainfall deficit of 3 to 6 inches (76 to 152 millimeters).
High temperatures made the drying worse. San Juan, for example, experienced one of its warmest Julys on record. River levels also fell sharply, with streamflow reaching record lows in waterways including the Rio Fajardo in northeastern Puerto Rico.
Water Shortages Hit Residents and Farmers
The strain on water supplies has affected residents, farmers, and ranchers across Puerto Rico. Water rationing has been in effect in several municipalities since early August, according to news reports. Observers have also pointed to infrastructure issues as a factor worsening the shortages.
The drought has also created serious challenges for agriculture. For farmers, dry soils have disrupted the growth of fruit and cacao trees as well as banana and coffee plants, contributing to crop losses. Ranchers, meanwhile, are seeing their hay supplies dwindle.
Drought Maps Help Guide Emergency Response
U.S. Drought Monitor maps have been published since 1999 and are used by federal, state, local, and tribal officials to help guide drought response decisions.
The USDA, for example, relies on the maps as part of a "fast track" process for issuing disaster designations. Those designations can help direct emergency assistance and other resources to affected communities.
Story Source:

Ukraine and Poland are exploring the possibility of a joint bid to host a World Cup in the 2040s. There are no official negotiations; planning may begin after the war.
Ukraine and Poland are considering the possibility of submitting a joint bid to host the FIFA World Cup, but no official negotiations on this are currently under way. The Ministry of Youth and Sports stressed that Minister Matvii Bidnyi’s comments about potentially hosting the tournament referred only to the long-term perspective after the war ends and security is restored, reports UNN.
Details
Politico published an article citing Minister of Youth and Sports Matvii Bidnyi, in which the minister stated that Ukraine and Poland are considering the possibility of submitting a joint bid to host the World Cup.
The nearest available date for hosting the FIFA World Cup is sometime in the 2040s, so we need to plan for this prospect right now
At the same time, the press service of the Ministry of Youth and Sports told a UNN journalist that Ukraine is conducting no official negotiations or consultations with the Polish side regarding the submission of a joint bid to host the FIFA World Cup.
The ministry noted that during the interview, a Politico journalist asked about Ukraine’s postwar future and its potential ambitions to host major tournaments.
In his response, Matvii Bidnyi stressed that today the state’s top priority is victory in the war and the safety of its citizens.
Ukraine has experience hosting international world-class tournaments, including UEFA Euro 2012 in partnership with Poland. After a just peace is achieved and security is restored, our country will be ready to host major sporting events again. However, thinking about the distant future is solely a long-term vision, not an operational plan. Today, the efforts of the Ministry of Youth and Sports are focused on critically important tasks: supporting athletes and veterans, defending our interests in the international sports arena, and creating accessible conditions for the physical and mental recovery of Ukrainians. Hosting or planning major tournaments will be possible only after stable peace and security have been ensured. Discussing specific bids or operational plans during active hostilities is premature
Supplement
In 2012, Ukraine and Poland jointly hosted the European Championship. The right to host Euro 2012 was awarded to the two countries in April 2007.
In preparing to host the 2012 European Football Championship, the host countries spent considerably more money than the hosts of previous tournaments because the infrastructure of the host cities and the countries as a whole was poorer compared with that of their Western European predecessors (stadiums, hotels, roads).
As of the end of 2011, Ukraine had spent approximately 115–140 billion hryvnias preparing for the European Championship. Poland, according to some estimates, would spend up to 80 billion zlotys (approximately 20 billion euros) on hosting the tournament.
Also, after Ukraine was approved as a host country for the final matches, it emerged that the new stadiums hastily built for the event had design flaws and did not meet modern requirements. It turned out that budget funds were allocated to construction companies for building them in exchange for substantial kickbacks to officials involved in distributing the financial resources.
Because of delays in the construction of the stadiums (especially the NSC "Olympiyskiy" in Kyiv and the stadium in Lviv), as well as infrastructure (airports, roads), UEFA threatened several times to take away the right to host the tournament or reduce the number of host cities.
The cost of reconstructing the NSC "Olympiyskiy" and building the stadium in Lviv increased several times compared with the initial plans, triggering a wave of criticism in Ukraine over the embezzlement of budget funds.
It should be recalled
Since the beginning of the war, Russian occupiers have damaged or destroyed 88 stadiums in Ukraine, 14 of which were completely destroyed. Direct losses inflicted on sports infrastructure are estimated at $4 billion.
Since the beginning of the Russian Federation’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, 930 sports infrastructure facilities have been damaged or completely destroyed. The largest number are in the Kherson, Kharkiv and Luhansk regions.

U.S. Navy demonstrates at-sea refueling for unmanned surface vessel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:09:53 UTC
21:09:53 KST

- The Navy demonstrated an at-sea refueling system off Virginia that transferred 400 gallons of fuel to an unmanned surface vessel across roughly 100 connection cycles.
- The system moved from concept to on-water testing in seven months, and the Navy's next goal is a fully autonomous refueling sequence.
The U.S. Navy demonstrated a system last month that can refuel an unmanned surface vessel at sea without any crew on board, a step toward keeping robotic boats on station indefinitely instead of returning to port when they run low on fuel.
The Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division ran the demonstration off the coast of Virginia using a towed connector that repeatedly captured, refueled and released a Navy-owned USV called the T38. A Navy-industry team went from concept to on-water testing in seven months, according to the warfare center.
The T38, also known as the Devil Ray, is built by Maritime Tactical Systems Inc. and measures 38 feet (11.1 meters) long, with a payload capacity of up to 4,000 pounds (1,814 kilograms) and burst speeds exceeding 70 knots depending on its engine configuration. The Navy operates this particular T38 through its Blue Water Instrumentation program, based at the Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division’s Point Mugu Sea Range in California. In May, the same vessel completed a record 192-hour autonomous mission 400 nautical miles (740 kilometers) off the California coast without any chase boats or escorts.
“At Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division, our immediate focus is supporting hypersonic and precision long-range fires testing, where flight profiles can extend thousands of miles beyond fixed-range boundaries and require data-collection assets to be distributed across a vast area,” said Spencer Holloway, director of the Blue Water Instrumentation program’s future capabilities office. “But the underlying challenge applies more broadly. Every time an unmanned vessel must return to port for fuel, we lose persistence, reduce coverage and redundancy, and interrupt the mission.”
During the Virginia demonstration, the training support vessel USNS Vindicator towed the refueling system and transferred a total of 400 gallons (1,514 liters) of fuel to the T38 across dozens of full-cycle exercises at sea, in addition to pier-side testing. The refueling system completed roughly 100 connection cycles over the course of a few days leading up to and including the event, which took place in the waters off Joint Expeditionary Base Little Creek-Fort Story, Virginia.
Ronald Raymer, branch head for capability, innovation, science and technology integration at U.S. Fleet Forces Command, said the capability could change how the Navy uses unmanned vessels operationally, not just for testing.
“This will allow us to have greater reliance on unmanned vessels … and we can push the USV into higher threat areas without risking manned vessels and personnel,” Raymer said. “It will also allow us to distribute greater capability into an area without having to invest in large, expensive manned vessels, and the refueling supports that.”
U.S. Fleet Forces Command, Naval Surface Warfare Center Dahlgren Division and Naval Surface Warfare Center Carderock Division sponsored the demonstration. The Littoral Combat Ship Mission Modules Program Office and the Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Robotics and Autonomous Systems provided contracting support that allowed the Blue Water Instrumentation team to work directly with industry partners on the project.
“Working directly with our industry partners allowed us to bring the platform, control systems, operators and engineers together as one integrated team,” Holloway said. “We could make changes, test them on the water and iterate quickly based on what we observed.”
The program’s next milestone is a fully autonomous, end-to-end refueling demonstration that will combine vessel rendezvous, approach, capture, fuel transfer, disconnection and return to mission into a single automated sequence, according to the warfare center.

China Focus: From sightseeing to sweating: "sportcation" gains momentum among young Chinese
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:09:22 CST
21:09:22 KST

YINCHUAN, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- As dusk settled over the wild Helan Mountains, Ye Shuai eased off the gas and wound his way down from the off-road Hooke Trail, calling it a day.
Tearing across rugged mountain terrain in his off-road vehicle, Ye spent the day as he had throughout his weeklong summer vacation, braving the blazing sun in the rolling mountains in northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, some 1,000 km away from his home in central China.
Ye is among a growing number of young vacationers fueling the popularity of a fresh kind of travel experience that blends sports and fitness with leisure and social interaction -- summed up as "sportcation."
SWEATING OUT SUMMER VACATION
Ye had been planning his mountain adventure for some time. He teamed up with fellow enthusiasts from across the country, shipping their vehicles to the Hooke Park, long before their flights. "It's crazy, but well worth it," he said.
Their venture started each day at 8 a.m. with a drive into the mountains. Challenging rough trails, they repeatedly stopped for repair breaks. By nightfall, they descended from the mountains, exhausted, then headed back to their lodgings beneath a starry sky.
Tucked away in the Helan Mountains, the park boasts 88 off-road trails of varying difficulty, catering to outdoor adventurers seeking thrills behind the wheel, on a motorcycle, bicycle, or even on foot.
Some enthusiasts put the park on a par with renowned off-road destinations such as the Rubicon Trail and Moab in the United States.
The young people are looking for vacation experiences that bring them joy and a sense of fulfillment, instead of merely sightseeing or photo-taking, said Gao Jinsong, founder of Hooke Park.
"Off-road driving is an extreme challenge," Ye said. "It helps me blow off steam from work and just be myself. It's tiring, but it feels great!"
In recent years, marathon tours across the country have also become a popular form of micro-getaway. For Shi Nali, a young woman from Beijing, combining running with travel has opened up a new way to explore a city.
"In the past, vacations were basically about beautiful scenery and good food. Sometimes I found them boring," said Shi.
An avid traveler, Shi became addicted to urban running in 2023, and has since traveled to multiple cities across China just to hit the road -- along the historic city wall in the ancient capital of Xi'an, along the seaside trails of Xiamen, and through the winding alleyways of Chengdu.
"Compared with the cookie-cutter attractions you find everywhere, the scenery and local interactions you encounter along the way feel much more genuine," Shi said.
The growing popularity of sports-themed vacations also boosted consumption. Shi's sports gear stock, from hats, sunglasses and sportswear to knee braces, running shoes and trekking poles, costs her more than 10,000 yuan (about 1,475.2 U.S. dollars).
But she considers the money well spent. "What matters most is the joy and satisfaction it brings me."
TAPPING TOURISM OPPORTUNITIES
The growing popularity of sports-oriented vacations reflects a broader shift in how young people spend their leisure time, driven by greater health awareness, a growing appetite for immersive experiences, and more diverse forms of social interaction, according to industry insiders.
In May, online travel platform LY.com released its 2026 travel trends report on "sportcation," showing a sharp rise in searches and bookings.
Yang Wei, a professional travel planner, said that "sportcation" will go beyond a short-lived fad and become a long-term shift in urban lifestyles.
The rise of "sportcation" also comes as China moves to diversify its tourism offerings and cultivate new growth drivers for the industry.
The latest five-year tourism development plan, approved by the State Council and released in July, calls for nurturing new drivers of tourism growth and enriching the supply of high-quality tourism experiences.
Across China, localities have been quick to tap into the trend and put various "sportcation" opportunities on offer.
Wanning, a surfers' haven in China's southernmost Hainan Province, has emerged as the poster child of the growing trend, with "Traveling to Wanning for sports school" becoming a viral catchphrase on social media.
With its long, surf-friendly coastline, Wanning has become a haven for young people burned out by the grind of big-city office life. They come here not to slow down, but to embrace a different kind of packed schedule -- one filled with sports and workouts.
Some start their day with a run or a gym session, then spend the rest of the day surfing, paddleboarding or rock climbing, joking that they are attending a sports school with a strict daily schedule.
The inland city of Zhongwei, Ningxia, also tapped into its unique landscape of deserts and the Yellow River to attract "sportcationers" eager to combine outdoor workout and sightseeing.
"From dusk into the deep of night, you run on soft sand, with the meandering Yellow River by your side and a brilliant galaxy overhead," an internet user by the name "Xiaoweishi'er" from Gansu Province described her experience after taking part in the 2026 Ningxia-Zhongwei Desert Starry Sky Half Marathon in June. "There's no need to chase speed. Just embrace the wilderness," she added. ■

COLOMBO, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lankan authorities on Friday advised farmers to bring forward planting for the 2026/27 Maha paddy cultivation season to withstand heavy rains and prepare for an El Nino-driven dry spell early next year.
The advisory came as meteorological forecasts indicate above-average rainfall across the island in October and November due to prevailing El Nino conditions and a positive Indian Ocean Dipole.
The Department of Agriculture urged farmers to begin land preparation as soon as possible and complete sowing between Oct. 15 and Oct. 25, while noting that earlier sowing would ensure crops are about a month old when heavier rains are expected in November, reducing the risk of damage from flooding.

In paddy areas facing water shortages, farmers are encouraged to cultivate other field crops, including maize, green gram, cowpea and finger millet. Those shifting to such crops on paddy land will remain eligible for fertilizer subsidies.
Sri Lankan agricultural cultivation is traditionally carried out on two monsoon cycles. The Yala cultivation season, spanning from May to September, is driven by the southwest monsoon, while the Maha cultivation season from October to January next year is driven by the northeast monsoon. ■

The serviceman’s actions, under the procedural supervision of the Central Region Specialized Defense Prosecutor’s Office of Chernihiv, were classified under Part 5 of Article 426-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — abuse of official powers under martial law.
Reminder
Since the beginning of 2026, Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers have sent more than 1.5 million requests to the police to locate persons liable for military service. During martial law, more than 20,000 criminal proceedings concerning evasion of mobilization have been investigated.

====================================================================================================

Neuroticism intensifies the transfer of fear and negativity during associative learning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:00:38 UTC
21:00:38 KST

People who score high in neuroticism not only experience more intense emotional reactions to aversive images, but they also tend to transfer those negative feelings more strongly onto unrelated, neutral objects. This heightened capacity for emotional learning provides evidence for how specific personality traits contribute to generalized anxiety and emotional vulnerability in daily life. The findings were recently published in the Journal of Personality.
Our brains constantly scan the environment, learning which objects or situations are safe and which are dangerous. One of the primary ways we learn these associations is through a process called evaluative conditioning. This occurs when a completely neutral item, such as a random geometric shape, is repeatedly presented alongside an emotionally charged item, such as a disturbing photograph.
Over time, the neutral shape takes on the emotional flavor of the photograph. Associative learning of this kind is a fundamental building block of human emotion, as a study covered by PsyPost in 2021 indicates that repeatedly pairing specific personal attributes with negative social feedback leads individuals to develop heightened anxiety toward those attributes.
While the basic mechanism of evaluative conditioning is universal, individuals do not all experience it with the same intensity. A 2026 study suggests that personal psychological dispositions influence how strongly we form positive or negative feelings toward neutral objects through associative conditioning. One of the most prominent traits related to emotional reactivity is neuroticism.
People with high levels of neuroticism tend to experience negative emotions more frequently and intensely. A study covered by PsyPost in 2026 provides evidence that this trait is tied to heightened connectivity between the brain regions responsible for emotional processing during affective tasks.
Another psychological factor related to emotional vulnerability is the looming cognitive style. This refers to a mental bias where an individual perceives potential threats not as static, but as rapidly approaching or escalating in space and time. A person with a high looming cognitive style might view a minor, distant problem as an incoming disaster that is quickly gaining momentum, which frequently leads to heightened anxiety.
The research was led by Darian Faur, an assistant professor at the West University of Timisoara in Romania. His team aimed to understand how neuroticism and the looming cognitive style interact to shape emotional learning.
“Tracking individual differences in conditioning was a preoccupation for behavioral scientists in the ’80s (see Levey & Martin, 1981), but slowly faded away due to developments in both fields that eventually established them as separate research traditions,” Faur told PsyPost. “The lab I am currently involved in (Social Cognition and Personality Assessment from the West University of Timisoara) revived this interest.”
“I was coming from a clinical background with a desire to study transdiagnostic models, and I found in this interdisciplinary approach an excellent experimental gateway to match my own research interests,” he explained.
Traditionally, studies on evaluative conditioning only measure whether a stimulus is perceived as generally positive or negative. The authors wanted to introduce a more specific measurement by asking participants to evaluate exactly how threatening an image felt, and then testing how that specific sense of threat transferred to a neutral object.
To investigate this, the researchers conducted an online experiment with 806 adult participants, primarily from the United Kingdom. The participants first completed standardized questionnaires to measure their levels of neuroticism and their looming cognitive style. The participants then viewed a series of twenty computer-generated grayscale fractals, which are complex, abstract geometric patterns. They rated how pleasant or unpleasant they found each fractal. The computer system then selected the six fractals that each participant rated as the most perfectly neutral, ensuring the conditioning process started from a blank slate.
During the conditioning phase, the participants viewed these neutral fractals paired with different photographs. The photographs had been pre-tested in a pilot study to fall into three distinct categories: positive images, negative but non-threatening images, and negative images that were highly threatening. Each neutral fractal was presented on the screen alongside one of the photographs. To mimic the psychological experience of a looming threat, the photographs were not static. Instead, they slowly expanded on the screen over a period of four seconds, growing by at least half their original size to simulate the feeling that the image was approaching the viewer.
After viewing all the pairings multiple times, the participants were asked to rate the original photographs based on how positive, negative, and threatening they were. Finally, they were asked to rate the initially neutral fractals again to see if their feelings toward the shapes had changed.
The scientists found that the evaluative conditioning procedure worked as expected. Fractals that had been paired with negative or threatening photographs were rated much more negatively than fractals paired with positive photographs. This shift in attitude was driven by how the participants individually appraised the original photographs. When a participant rated a photograph as highly negative or highly threatening, that intense rating directly predicted how negatively they would evaluate the paired fractal.
Personality traits played a major role in shaping these reactions. Participants with high levels of neuroticism evaluated the negative and threatening photographs much more harshly than participants with low neuroticism. Beyond just seeing the original images as worse, highly neurotic individuals also demonstrated a stronger learning effect. They transferred more of that negative emotion onto the neutral fractals.
“The findings from this study suggest that general emotional vulnerability (the trait everyone shares to a certain extent in the general population that makes us respond with anxiety or depression to certain life events) impacts not only how we perceive stimuli with a valence of their own, but also how that valence is further transferred to a neutral stimulus that happens to be in the same environment as the pleasant/unpleasant stimulus,” Faur said.
“In other words, if you are a highly emotionally-reactive person, you will most likely learn to dislike neutral stimuli that were associated with negative stimuli more than a person with lower reactivity,” he noted.
The researchers observed that this effect seemed to be driven mostly by the self-consciousness and vulnerability components of neuroticism, suggesting that an inward-focused cognitive awareness might heighten the associative learning process. “Moreover, for highly neurotic individuals, the study indicates that learning might not only be explained by the conscious evaluation of the valenced stimuli (i.e., I dislike this gray box because it was paired with a bunch of insects that I found unpleasant), but also by the general exposure to negative stimuli,” Faur added.
The results regarding the looming cognitive style were more complex. Generally, participants with a higher looming cognitive style tended to rate all the fractals more negatively overall. However, when the researchers isolated the specific transfer of threat from the photograph to the fractal, the looming cognitive style appeared to have a mild buffering effect. People with this trait transferred slightly less of the threat to the neutral object than expected.
“I did not anticipate the interesting interaction between the looming cognitive style and the evaluative conditioning process,” Faur said. “While this cognitive vulnerability was associated with contingency awareness (and contingency awareness was further associated with larger evaluative conditioning effects), it buffered the valence transfer from unconditioned stimuli to neutral stimuli instead of amplifying it.”
The researchers speculate that because the looming cognitive style causes people to focus so intensely on an approaching threat, they might fixate entirely on the threatening photograph and pay less attention to the neutral fractal beside it, weakening the associative link. But Faur added a note of caution regarding this finding: “It is important to note, however, that these results were uncertain and should be interpreted cautiously, as they require replication.”
Interestingly, this buffering effect disappeared when a person possessed both high neuroticism and a high looming cognitive style. When these two traits were elevated together, the individual’s heightened emotional reactivity overrode any attentional buffering, resulting in a massively amplified transfer of negative emotion to the neutral object.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study utilized a highly controlled digital environment with an artificial zooming effect to simulate looming threats. While this allowed for precise measurements, human emotional learning in real-world scenarios is often messier and more complex.
Another important consideration is the magnitude of these influences. “As per our experience with personality and conditioning models, the moderation effects, although replicable, are very small,” Faur pointed out. “Therefore, personality can be seen as impacting distally and broadly the learning process.”
However, the context of the sample matters. “Another study of ours (which is currently under review) returns much larger effects of the association between neuroticism and evaluative conditioning in the clinical population (anxiety disorders or related), so we further need to identify which mechanisms drive or which conditions amplify the effects of personality on learning,” Faur said.
Additionally, the researchers only measured how threatening the participants found the original photographs, not how threatening they found the neutral fractals after the conditioning was complete. Because of this, the study can only confirm that general negative feelings were transferred to the fractals, rather than a specific sense of physical threat.
Future studies could build on this work by testing these personality interactions in more ecological settings or by asking participants to rate the threat level of the conditioned objects. Exploring how different relational cues alter the way threats are learned could offer deeper insights into how anxiety disorders develop and how they might be treated.
“My intention is to use conditioning paradigms (and other learning frameworks) as experimental proxies for studying how personality and cognition interact to produce psychopathology,” Faur concluded.
The study, “Beyond the Moderating Role of Neuroticism on Evaluative Conditioning: Threat Appraisal,” was authored by Darian Faur and Florin Alin Sava.

UK’s Supacat starts production on Czech special forces vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:00:15 UTC
21:00:15 KST

- Supacat began production on 18 HMT Extenda vehicles for the Czech Republic's 601st Special Forces Group, with deliveries starting in 2027.
- The contract, signed in October 2025, is valued at roughly 2.16 billion Czech koruna ($98.4 million) including vehicle chassis, weapons integration and support.
British vehicle maker Supacat has started production on 18 HMT Extenda military vehicles for the Czech Republic’s special operations forces, with deliveries scheduled to begin in 2027.
The vehicles will go to the Czech Army’s 601st Special Forces Group, the country’s premier special operations unit, replacing an aging fleet of Land Rover Defender 110 vehicles that have exceeded their 15-year design life. Supacat and its Czech partner, LPP, signed the contract in October 2025. Pre-production work began in June, and full production is now underway at Supacat’s newly opened manufacturing facility in Dunkeswell, Devon.
The deal splits the work between the UK and the Czech Republic. LPP is supplying the bare Extenda 6×6 chassis for £32.6 million ($42.6 million), while the Czech Military Technical Institute will install weapons, communications and other mission systems separately, at a cost of 810 million Czech koruna ($36.9 million). Including spare parts, training and other subsystems, the full package is valued at roughly 2.16 billion koruna ($98.4 million) with tax included, according to earlier reporting on the contract.
The HMT Extenda, known to the British Army as the Jackal 3, can be reconfigured between a 4×4 and 6×6 layout using basic workshop tools, letting operators adjust the vehicle’s size and payload capacity for different missions. It can reach speeds of up to 120 km/h (75 mph). The platform traces back to the original HMT, which the UK Ministry of Defence rushed into service in Afghanistan as an urgent operational requirement, and it has since been adopted by special forces in at least eight other countries, including Norway, New Zealand, Ukraine and the United States.
“A joint team, consisting of the LPP project team and specialists from the Czech Special Forces, visited the new production facility earlier this year,” said Miroslav Žižka, Managing Director at LPP. “This was the team’s first visit since production of the HMT Extenda began, and the main purpose of the visit was to familiarise the members of the joint team with the current status of combat vehicle production.”
“LPP and Supacat have been collaborating on this project for several years now, and communication between us is close. I would like to thank Director Phil Applegarth and his team for their dedication to the Czech project, and for meeting the vehicle delivery deadlines,” Žižka said.
“The start of the Czech production marked an important milestone for the delivery of this programme. We continue to remain on track to deliver the programme as scheduled, reflecting the maturity of the HMT Extenda platform and the dedication of the teams involved. We also look forward to other export vehicle programmes being produced in the near future,” said Phil Applegarth, Director at Supacat.

Japan Is Launching a Probe to Collect the First-Ever Samples From a Martian Moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

A Mars probe from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) may answer some longstanding questions about the Red Planet and its moons. The mission—dubbed MMX for “Martian Moons eXploration”—aims to collect at least 10 grams of samples from Phobos, one of two moons orbiting the planet, and if successful, these will be the first rocks from a Martian moon ever brought to Earth.
They won’t arrive quickly, however. The MMX probe will take approximately one year to reach Mars. It will then collect samples during three years of operations while orbiting the red planet before taking another year to return to Earth. If all goes well, scientists expect to receive the moon rocks in 2031.
One of the most interesting questions the probe can answer is how Mars’ moons, Phobos and Deimos, formed. There are two main possibilities. One is that the moons condensed from material ejected during a massive collision with Mars. The other hypothesis is that the moons were asteroids from the outer solar system that were captured by Mars’ gravity.
The moons are dark in color, and their light-reflecting properties closely resemble those of asteroids rich in water and carbon. Their orbits, however—which are nearly circular along Mars’ equatorial plane in the same direction as the planet’s rotation—are better explained by the giant impact hypothesis. Comparing samples from Mars’ moons to those previously collected from the Martian surface could help settle this debate.
To get the Martian moon rocks and transport them back to Earth, however, means overcoming some significant technical challenges in space flight and communication. At launch, the spacecraft will have a mass of 4,480 kilograms (9,900 pounds). More than half of this weight will be fuel, divided into three reserves: one for the outbound leg, one for exploration, and one for the return leg. Once in the vicinity of Mars, MMX will jettison the outbound module after its propellant is exhausted; following the flyby of Deimos, the exploration module will also be jettisoned.
The probe, designed by Mitsubishi Electric, will then land on the surface of Phobos, a delicate procedure given the moon’s size, with an approximate radius of just 11 kilometers. (In comparison, Earth’s moon has a radius of more than 1,700 kilometers.) Descent methods used on Earth’s moon rely on its specific gravity, which is about 300 times as strong as that of Phobos. However, Phobos’ gravity is approximately 50 times greater than that of the asteroid Ryugu, where JAXA has previously landed probes. Landing on Ryugu involved prolonged hovering, a typical method for landing on smaller celestial objects, but this is not feasible for MMX as it would consume too much fuel given Phobos’ greater pull.
To overcome this challenge, the probe is equipped with high-precision autonomous navigation, which it will need, given that there will be a delay of up to 20 minutes for radio signals to travel between Earth and MMX. The probe must therefore autonomously decide on and execute the descent, landing, and later takeoff sequences.
During the descent, the probe will compare the terrain to data on the topography of Phobos’ craters, using this information to adjust its position toward the target landing site. Once it’s reached an altitude under 300 meters, the probe will also detect whether parts of the surface have changed in elevation, labeling significant discrepancies as hazardous areas. This mechanism allows the probe, if necessary, to change the landing site or abort the landing and temporarily ascend.
Just ahead of the main spacecraft’s landing, the IDEFIX rover—jointly developed by the French and German space agencies—will be deployed onto the surface of Phobos to conduct approximately 100 days of independent exploration. This preliminary survey by the rover will serve as a scout to ensure a safer landing.
Once on the surface, a robotic arm will drill cylindrical tubes into the surface to collect samples. The probe is also equipped with a device first developed by NASA that uses a stream of nitrogen gas to collect fine particles from the very top layer of dust. Whether or not Phobos originated from an impact with the planet, experts believe Martian sand can be obtained from the lunar surface. Over time, meteorite impacts have blasted materials off Mars, coating its moons. Scientists expect about 0.1 percent of the samples collected will be debris from Mars itself.
Costing about $345 million US, this mission marks Japan’s first Mars probe launch in 28 years. Beyond the scientific insights it’s expected to provide, from an engineering perspective, the mission aims to test new technologies that could aid future sampling and round-trip travel to Mars.
MMX is scheduled to launch from the Tanegashima Space Center on October 20, 2026.
This story originally appeared on WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

====================================================================================================

APA Member Interview: Briana Toole
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

The APA Blog is publishing excerpts from Cliff Sosis’s long-form interviews with philosophers, which appear at his blog, What Is It Like to Be a Philosopher? The excerpts below are from an interview originally published on August 20, 2026 and are reprinted with permission from Cliff Sosis.
In this interview, Briana Toole, Associate Professor in the Department of Philosophy at Claremont McKenna College, talks about growing up in Chattahoochee, Florida, Left Behind, Crash Bandicoot, geometry, Greenpeace, beauty pageants, money anxiety, Myspace, 9/11, Florida State University and the Bright Futures scholarship, a difficult to comprehend accent, working evenings at TCBY, working with David McNaughton, a brutal but helpful epistemology TA, switching from law to philosophy, committing to grad school and going to University of Sheffield, her first snowfall, Jenny Saul, Teach for America and meeting her husband, pursuing a PhD at UT, sexism and the “golden boys,” grounding, complaining to her understanding dissertation advisor, standpoint epistemology, depression, a fellowship at MIT, Sally Haslanger, Corrupt the Youth, landing a position at Claremont McKenna College just before COVID hit, bouncing between positions before she landed in a green place, her Feminism for Men class, #metoo, Thi Ngyugen, The Poisonwood Bible, Zillow Gone Wild, and cornpone…
What was your earliest memory?
My earliest memory is of a dog we had when I was a baby, around 2 or so. A shih tzu named Biscuit, because she was the buttery color of a biscuit. Biscuit loved me, and I remember that whenever my parents would try to discipline me (at that age, a pop on the hand or behind), she’d growl at them and wouldn’t let them touch me. My earliest protector!
Where did you grow up?
My parents were in the military, and so I was born on a military base in Killeen, Texas. When I was 3, we moved to Chattahoochee, Florida, across the river from my dad’s hometown of Sneads. The twin cities, as we called them, were about an hour from the Alabama and Georgia borders (Dothan, AL on one side, Bainbridge, GA on the other). This is relevant exposition because when people meet me, they always want some explanation of my accent.
The twin cities are home to a state prison (Sneads) and state hospital (in Chattahoochee, rumored to have underground tunnels dating back to the Civil War), which is where most people would end up one way or another (either as an employee or as a resident).
All my dad’s family had stayed in the area, so I grew up surrounded by aunts and uncles and cousins. And, because I went to school where my dad did, we had many of the same teachers, and the same high school principal. There were a lot of families like that in Sneads.
The town where I lived was so small that when we didn’t have stamps, we’d just put change in a little cup with the letters we wanted mailed out. Going to the grocery store was an hours-long event, because you’d run into people you knew. I knew a kid in high school who rode his lawnmower to school.
All to say: I grew up in the country. The deep, deep south.
As a little kid, what do you think, or what did others think, made you unique? What did you want to be when you grew up?
As a kid, I always thought I’d be a lawyer. My dad used to say that I could argue with a brick wall. I don’t really think I was that argumentative, actually. My dad just wasn’t used to having people disagree with him. It’s fortunate for me that he found it cute for his baby girl to do so (though he grew to dislike it as I became older, and he especially hates it now!).
I’m not really sure, beyond that, where I got the idea that I’d grow up to be a lawyer. Though I was, even as a very young kid, concerned about issues of justice and fairness. I was very much the kid who felt the need to stand up for other kids when they were being picked on, and I was always worried about other people. Do they have enough food? Enough clothing? Love and support? As a younger person I thought lawyers were the people who fought for those things, and I was enamored with that idea.
As a teen, what were you passionate about, if anything? Any sign you’d be a philosopher?
I was most consistently passionate about the environment. As a little kid, I really worried about pollution, so I made signs and posted them to trees around my neighborhood. I vaguely remember one neighbor – not that we had many, we lived in a very quiet and out-of-the way neighborhood – coming to ask my parents if I was attacking him personally, because things would sometimes fly out of the back of his truck as he sped down our hilly road (I wasn’t.) Then, in high school I got really involved with Greenpeace. I even staged a protest at our local grocery store (the Piggly Wiggly) to discourage people from buying Kleenex products, as they were clearing areas in the Brazilian rain forest to make their products. My art teacher from high school even had her class help paint a giant sign for us on a plastic, white shower curtain, and two of my friends painted themselves brown and adorned themselves with leaves to look like trees. Of course, folks in small towns don’t take kindly to being (from their point-of-view) lectured, especially not by teenagers. And so many people scoffed at the fact that we were asking folks to sign a paper petition while also advocating against the use of certain paper products. My annoyance that they didn’t see the distinction between using recycled paper and using Kleenex products was probably an early indication that I’d be a philosopher.
Why major in philosophy? Did you ever consider doing anything else? Wait a minute, you were there when I was a grad student there! Did we cross paths?
Well, my plan, when I started college, was law school. Having little family guidance, I assumed I should major in political science, and so that was the plan going into FSU. But I was in the honors college and my freshman year they were piloting a new honors colloquium. They would have folks from across the colleges give a short session, and early on they brought a professor from the law school. She said that the three majors that perform best on the LSAT are history, English, and philosophy. Having had exposure to the former two in high school I was least attracted to those options. Plus, I had a little romantic entanglement with this guy from back home who was always ending my arguments with “Well, Plato says so-and-so”. So I figured that by taking on a philosophy major I’d kill two birds with one stone – finally beat that guy in an argument and prepare myself to excel on the LSAT.
I really didn’t have plans to take philosophy seriously, but then two things happened, both involving the same philosophy professor, David McNaughton. I enrolled in his Ethical Theory course my sophomore Fall, and I was so excited to take that class. But, hand-to-God, I’d never met a British person in real life, and the first day of class I couldn’t understand a single word David said. I thought for sure I’d have to drop the course, but I gave it another day before making a decision, and the second class I had a much easier time processing his accent. That became my favorite class, the class that made me realize that I really liked philosophy and was good at it. With regret I admit I became that annoying clinger-on of a student who followed Professor McNaughton as he walked from class each day back to his office (which was no short trek, especially in the Florida humidity). For the record, this is why I don’t complain when students trail after me – I know I’m only reaping what I’ve sown!
Then, the summer before my senior year, I was talking to David and he suggested that I consider writing a philosophy thesis and applying to graduate school. I remember being told, when I started at FSU, that to graduate with honors I’d need to write a thesis. And I remember thinking there was no way I could do that; it sounded so intimidating, so I put it out of mind entirely. But if a professor I really admired and respected was encouraging me to do it, it felt like maybe it was possible.
In the process of writing my thesis I realized how un-psyched I was about applying to law school, and how enthusiastic I was about continuing to read and write philosophy. So I abandoned my law school applications and shifted gears towards grad school in philosophy.
On whether we crossed paths – I’m not sure. I remember really well a few grad students who were TAs for classes I was in. Tracey Mahaffey was one, I think, and there was a guy who TA’d for Michael Bishop’s epistemology course who gave brutal (but very helpful) feedback on my writing. That was pretty much the extent of my interaction with the grad students, so I suspect we never met!
Tell me a little bit more about your time at Sheffield. Why’d you leave?
Well, mostly because it was only a one-year program and I had finished. I would have happily stayed, however. People are always surprised when I say this, but I love Sheffield. It was the first place I got to live that had reliable public transportation, so I felt connected to everything. It was also really the first place I lived that was a walkable city, and that I could go grocery shopping or get to the Peak district (to hike) without a car was amazing to me. I also really liked the people (who called me “duck”) and the food – yes, the food! Yorkshire pudding and Sunday roast. The cool social events the uni put on, like “silent discoes”. I even went to a roller derby match and I got to experience my first Christmas market and my first snowfall.
Tell me a little bit about your time with Teach for America.
I did Teach for America between graduating from Sheffield and beginning grad school at UT. Teaching high school was a major formative experience for me in a lot of ways. I remember feeling intense anxiety in my first week of teaching, because I realized that if I did a bad job, I could be ruining the lives and futures of a hundred kids. Also, it was hard! Trying to get a bunch of teenagers to trust you takes so much work, like months and months of relationship building. Truthfully, the kids didn’t really trust me until I came back the 2nd year. I think they were so used to people coming in-and-out, they just couldn’t afford to invest themselves in someone who might disappear.
I pretty much hated teaching that first year – it was hard and I was very bad at it. But experience is the best teacher, and when I came back the 2nd year, I knew what I was doing. I prioritized relationship-building over new content in the first few weeks of school and I felt more confident with the material I needed to teach. That year I came to love teaching and to love my kids. I’m still close with the students I taught when they were sophomores/juniors, and I even went back to Baton Rouge for their 10-year reunion last year.
What I learned from TFA is this: Many people are incompetent. Worse than incompetent, they are also often cruel. In my 2nd year, a big scandal broke out in the teaching community because it was discovered that some higher-ups in the school district had paid for degrees that they didn’t earn from a local university. At least one of the teachers at my school legitimately just did not teach – he played trashcan basketball with his students. I know this because my students would instead use that time to read The Great Gatsby (the assigned text for my English class) and he decided to ruin it for them by spoiling the ending. The next period a group of devastated kids trudges into my classroom begging me to tell them that Gatsby doesn’t die in the end. Asshole.
Before TFA, I thought most people were good, kind-hearted, and well-meaning. Maybe people disagreed about how best to pursue a certain end, sure, but I was confident we all wanted what was good, and we certainly all wanted what was best for our kids. My experience teaching disabused me of this notion.
On the upside, I met my best friend there, as well as my husband! Working with kids made me a kinder, more compassionate person. It taught me the value of thinking about the world from another person’s perspective. Truthfully, I suspect my standpoint epistemology origin story is in this experience.
Was UT what you expected?
No, it was not. Pretty immediately when I started grad school, I realized that I had been naïve and obtuse in my philosophy classes as an undergrad. In retrospect, there was obvious sexism and racism that I just didn’t notice at FSU, like the male undergrads interrupting and speaking over the only female philosophy professor (and professor of color, for that matter) I had (Maria Morales). I realized this when I started UT, because all the other women in my cohort mentioned that, before accepting the offer from UT, they had reached out to women grad students about their experience. That never
even occurred to me. The reports were apparently not good. I will not revisit those reports here – I believe they are well-known within the philosophy community.
Sexism was also very prevalent at UT. Sometimes the female grad students would be asked by male graduate students to make copies for them. We had a few male students that were considered “the golden boys” – it seemed to the rest of us that they received extra attention and resources. The department gave out a prize each year for the best paper by a graduate student (the Cogburn Prize) and usually a male student won. One year a woman graduate student, whose paper was published in a top-ranked specialist journal and won a prize in that journal (two supposed criteria), still was not selected.
The department technically did not have a bathroom for women students – our department, located in Waggener Hall takes up the 3rd and 4th floor. There is a men’s bathroom on the 3rd floor. A bathroom for women is on the 1st and 2nd floor, located in the classics department. Apparently, once upon a time the bathroom on floor three was gender neutral, but since the department was mostly men anyways, they just converted it to a men’s only restroom. The women staged a protest and hostile takeover of that bathroom. Rumor has it that a professor in the department emailed the chair, David Sosa, about his being “hen-pecked”. Needless to say, the bathroom was quickly returned to its men-only status.
I would say the biggest distinction between what I expected and what happened is this: I thought that as teachers, these professors, this department, would fully support their graduate students, mentor us, teach us how to do research and succeed in this profession. But that is not, to my mind, what they viewed their role to be. It seemed to me that they viewed their job as breaking us, thinning the herd. They literally gave us what was known around the department as a “scare talk” in our first semester, the basics of which were “a lot of you will drop out and most of you won’t get jobs”. They were just giving it to us straight, I guess.
But, as a result, the environment could be kind of cutthroat. I remember in my first or second year of grad school, there was a post that made the rounds identifying which Hogwarts house various philosophy departments would be. Ours was Slytherin.
What was the dissertation on?
My dissertation was on the relationship between knowledge and social identity and focused in particular on standpoint theory. A large part of the dissertation was really just me trying to work out for myself what that relationship was, how standpoint epistemology related to traditional epistemology, and what the value or insights of standpoint epistemology might be. The thing I’m proudest of in the dissertation is the chapter in which I argue that epistemic oppression is a consequence of some of the commitments within traditional epistemology, and that we can’t make sense of the occurrence of epistemic oppression without the resources that standpoint epistemology provides.
I think this interview series might provide some evidence for standpoint epistemology. How do you pitch standpoint epistemology to people skeptical of it?
I usually ask them if they have ever been to NYC, and if so, to reconstruct their route from one place to another (from home to the Cloisters, for example). Did they use the subway? If so, which lines? Did those lines have elevators? Usually, they can’t recall. Alternatively, I ask them to think about which buildings they access through campus, or to get to work. Do those buildings have ramps? Elevators? If so, are they easy to access or out of the way? These examples usually get people to see, rather quickly, that there are aspects of their environment they don’t think about or pay attention to at all, but that others must know about if they are to navigate effectively. They get quickly at the heart of the idea, central in standpoint theory, that there is an important relationship between embodiment, power, and knowledge.
What are you working on now? Any projects you’re especially excited about?
Yes! I’m writing a book about social and political resistance from an epistemic perspective, sort of bringing my work in standpoint epistemology to bear on questions in political philosophy. I suspect that many people can’t understand or appreciate what certain social and political acts or movements mean to accomplish, because they live in a world where the injustices these acts/movements mean to address are obscured. And I wonder what this means for the possibility of resistance to achieve its aims and how, thinking about this perspective, might empower us to rethink how we go about social and political reform.
If you could ask an omniscient being one question and be guaranteed a truthful answer, what would you ask?
What’s wrong with my dad?
This section of the APA Blog is designed to get to know our fellow philosophers a little better. We’re including profiles of APA members that spotlight what captures their interest not only inside the office but also outside of it. We’d love for you to be a part of it, so please contact us via the interview nomination form here to nominate yourself or a friend.
The post APA Member Interview: Briana Toole first appeared on Blog of the APA.

Repeated attacks on humanitarian warehouses put vital medical aid at risk in Ukraine: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Repeated attacks on humanitarian warehouses put vital medical aid at risk in Ukraine: WHO
A new airstrike overnight damaged one of the main warehouses used by the World Health Organization (WHO) in Ukraine to store humanitarian medical supplies in the Kyiv region, the UN agency said on Friday.
This is the third attack to affect a WHO-used storage facility in the last three months.
“Yesterday, overnight, between 3 and 4 September, an air attack in Kyiv oblast affected one of WHO's main warehouses, storing humanitarian medical needs and supplies,” said WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier.
Speaking to journalists in Geneva, he explained that “the access to the site remained restricted due to heavy smoke and safety concerns, while assessments of possible damage and stock losses are ongoing.”
No WHO personnel were affected, he said.
Healthcare under fire
This incident follows two other attacks on warehouses used by WHO in different parts of the country in the last three months, with essential medical supplies intended for people living in frontline and hard-to-reach areas.
Two weeks ago, an attack destroyed a WHO humanitarian warehouse in Dnipro, resulting in the loss of half of the medical supplies and equipment intended to support an estimated 225,000 people living in the frontline and hard-to-reach areas, according to the WHO.
“Another warehouse used by WHO in Kyiv oblast was damaged during a large-scale wave of attacks on Kyiv and the region in July,” said Mr. Lindmeier.
Lifeline for civilians
Humanitarian medical supplies are a lifeline for people who need healthcare in frontline and hard-to-reach areas. The WHO spokesperson stressed that attacks on warehouses storing these supplies can delay or disrupt the delivery of essential health support to people who need it most.
The agency is increasingly concerned about the growing pattern of attacks on humanitarian storage facilities nationwide.
“The attacks are part of a broader pattern affecting humanitarian operations across the country. In 2026, at least 20 attacks have affected warehouses storing humanitarian supplies, including 15 attacks on warehouses holding health-related humanitarian supplies,” Mr. Lindmeier said.
He stressed that the locations of United Nations and WHO facilities and warehouses are known to all parties to the conflict as they are communicated through established deconfliction arrangements.
“In my understanding, all warehouses, all UN locations, all WHO locations, are de-conflicted. That means the whereabouts are communicated to all sides of the conflict, and that is well known,” Mr. Lindmeier explained.
Commitment to deliver
Despite the attacks, the WHO continues to work with health partners across Ukraine to ensure that essential medical supplies reach health facilities and communities in need. Following the latest incidents, alternative storage arrangements have already been identified, while efforts are underway to assess the damage and replace lost supplies.
In 2026, the WHO's overall humanitarian response comprised provision of equipment and supplies to over 300 health-care facilities, including primary care centres, hospitals, laboratories, and transit centers, supporting the health system to reach three million beneficiaries.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began on 24 February 2022, WHO has verified more than 3,000 attacks on healthcare including strikes on health facilities, ambulances, medical supplies and warehouses.

Dismissal from service, financial support, transfers — the Office of the Military Ombudsman named the reasons for the most frequent complaints
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:59:38 EEST
20:59:38 KST

Dismissal from service, financial support, transfers — the Office of the Military Ombudsman named the reasons for the most frequent complaints
Kyiv • UNN
Service members most often complain about military medical commissions, dismissals, payments, and transfers. The Office ordered 2,535 inspections, but officials sometimes ignore the findings.
Since the beginning of its operations, the Office of the Military Ombudsman has received more than 14,000 complaints and appeals from military personnel. Based on their review, more than 2,000 inspections were ordered. At the same time, the Office reported cases in which commanders and officials fail to respond to the ombudsman’s findings. UNN выяснил how to act in such situations and whether there are legislative mechanisms of influence.
Details
On January 27 of this year, the Office of the Military Ombudsman officially began operating in Ukraine. Under the law, its main tasks are to exercise democratic civilian control over ensuring respect for rights; identify violations of the rights of military personnel, reservists, conscripts, and police officers, as well as the causes and conditions leading to such violations.
In accordance with the tasks assigned to the Military Ombudsman and within the scope of his or her competence, the ombudsman has the right to consider complaints and conduct investigations into alleged violations of the rights of military personnel.
Rada adopted the law on the military ombudsman: what is foreseen17.09.25, 12:20 • 46869 views
According to the Office of the Military Ombudsman in response to a request from UNN, from the beginning of its operations through August 31, the Office received 14,427 complaints and appeals on behalf of military personnel, of which 13,922 complaints and appeals were reviewed, while another 505 are under consideration.
As a result of reviewing complaints, 2,535 inspections were ordered since the Office began operating. A total of 1,203 complaints were returned to the complainants because they were not subject to review under the law. In particular, a complaint was essentially identical to one that had already been reviewed by the Military Ombudsman; the complaint concerned the provision of a legal position or interpretation of the legislation of Ukraine; or the demands in the complaint were the subject of court proceedings. The Office also does not review complaints if a representative acting on behalf of a service member has not provided documents confirming his or her authority
The military ombudsman said that her duties will include the following01.01.25, 18:10 • 53966 views
It is also noted that the Office of the Military Ombudsman forwarded 3,587 complaints to the competent authorities, institutions, and organizations for consideration and resolution.
The Office added that military personnel most often submit complaints concerning the following issues:
-  referrals to the Military Medical Commission and treatment;  
-  discharge from military service;  
-  monthly financial support and additional remuneration; 
-  transfer to another place of service.  
It should be noted that, simultaneously with the bill on establishing the Office of the Military Ombudsman, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy submitted another draft law, No. 13267, which provides for liability for failure to comply with the lawful demands of the Military Ombudsman or obstructing the exercise of his or her powers.
Such a violation would carry a fine of between UAH 8,500 and UAH 17,000.
For a repeated violation, the fine would range from UAH 17,000 to UAH 34,000, along with disqualification from holding certain positions or engaging in certain activities for one year, or without such disqualification.
The document was adopted back in October 2025 and currently remains stalled. The Office of the Military Ombudsman noted that findings are one of the key instruments for responding to violations of the rights of military personnel.
Following consideration of a complaint, the Military Ombudsman or deputy may order an inspection. Upon its completion, the Office prepares a finding stating whether a violation occurred, who committed it, and how to restore the complainant’s rights. The finding, together with the relevant requirement, is sent to the commander (chief), a military administration body, or an official of a state authority. They are required to consider it within ten working days and inform the Military Ombudsman of what has been done to remedy the violations
At the same time, the Office said that numerous cases have been recorded in which commanders, military administration bodies, and officials fail to respond to them, consider them only formally, or delay the deadlines, while "the legislation still does not provide for appropriate liability for this".
Back in October last year, the Verkhovna Rada adopted Bill No. 13267 in the first reading, which is intended to grant the Military Ombudsman the right to draw up administrative offense reports and bring offenders to justice through the courts for failure to comply with lawful demands. This provision will apply both to commanders and to officials at all levels—from local self-government bodies and heads of Regional Military Administrations to ministers. We call on the Verkhovna Rada to adopt the bill in the second reading as soon as possible
On September 1, the Verkhovna Rada opened its 16th session by adopting a resolution on the agenda, including the inclusion of the aforementioned bill on the agenda.
In a comment to UNN, Member of Parliament and member of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Law Enforcement Oleksandr Danutsa said that "work on preparing the document for the second reading is proceeding in accordance with the established procedural rules."
The stage of processing and systematizing all amendments and proposals submitted by entities with the right of legislative initiative is currently underway, as is their coordination with the relevant state authorities and specialized experts, so that the result is an effective and balanced mechanism. The bill will be considered at a committee meeting immediately after all necessary preparatory procedures have been completed and the comparative table finalized. Accordingly, following the committee's decision, the issue of submitting it for consideration in the plenary chamber will be decided during the formation of the agenda for plenary meetings of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine

OpenAI says new GPT-6 Astra model can detect high-severity security flaws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:55:26 UTC
20:55:26 KST

Nuri Aydın
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
US-based artificial intelligence company OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Astra on Thursday, saying its new flagship model can identify high-severity cybersecurity vulnerabilities and independently complete complex computer-based tasks.
OpenAI said Astra is initially being rolled out to a limited set of enterprises and will become available more widely to developers and paying ChatGPT users in the coming days.
The model is designed to carry out multistep computer tasks, including working across software and browsers, completing spreadsheets and building websites.
“Astra can do anything a human can do with a computer,” OpenAI co-founder and President Greg Brockman said.
Brockman described the model as a major leap in capability and said it had demonstrated human-level performance across a range of computer-based tasks.
OpenAI said Astra outperformed its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Sol, in cybersecurity evaluations while using fewer output tokens.
The model was initially made available to approved participants in OpenAI's Daybreak cyber defense program, where it can be used for authorized vulnerability research and security testing. 
 
Safety concerns and oversight
The launch comes amid growing scrutiny of the risks posed by increasingly capable and autonomous AI systems.
In a report released last week, OpenAI said an experimental version of Astra obtained administrator-level control over parts of the company's infrastructure during internal testing without staff being immediately aware.
The company also said Astra is capable of discovering previously unknown security flaws and developing "new ways to exploit them across many well-protected systems without a person guiding each step."
In response, the company said it "significantly strengthened” its “protections against the model taking harmful cyber actions."
The launch follows scrutiny over a July incident in which OpenAI agents breached systems belonging to AI platform Hugging Face during testing.
Last week, an independent report raised further concerns about the OpenAI agents' hack of Hugging Face, saying roughly 700 agents participated in the attack, communicating among themselves and trying to cover their tracks.
OpenAI said Astra itself was not involved in the Hugging Face incident and that it subsequently developed an evaluation based on what happened to test whether models would act beyond their authorized scope.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Astra underwent the White House's voluntary review process and that government officials did not request changes to the company's safety measures.

MIT turns bacteria into living transistors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:52:39 UTC
20:52:39 KST

MIT turns bacteria into living transistors
MIT scientists have turned bacteria into living transistors, opening the door to plants with built-in biological computers that can sense and respond to their environment.
- Date:
- September 4, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- MIT researchers have created bacterial “transistors” that can be wired together into living circuits capable of performing calculations and directing chemical signals. One day, these biological computers could coat plant roots or leaves, detecting environmental threats and automatically triggering defenses.
- Share:
MIT researchers have engineered bacteria to work like transistors, creating living "circuit boards" that can be printed onto growth material inside a Petri dish.
In conventional electronics, transistors act as switches that control whether electrical current can pass through a circuit. In the MIT system, engineered bacterial cells perform a similar role by regulating the movement of small signaling molecules. Those molecules then carry information to other components in the biological circuit.
The researchers created two types of bacterial transistors and three additional bacterial strains that act as relays between them. Together, these five strains provide a modular set of components that can be arranged to build nearly any kind of circuit. In the new study, the team demonstrated circuits capable of adding two or three inputs and directing a single input toward a selected destination.
"We've built some initial computer architecture components that are commonly used, but any operation can be built with these five strains," says Hamid Doosthosseini PhD '25, an MIT postdoc and the lead author of the new study.
One potential use is to place these living circuits on plant leaves or roots. There, the bacteria could process information about environmental conditions, helping plants detect and respond to stresses such as drought or pest attacks.
Christopher Voigt, head of MIT's Department of Biological Engineering, is the senior author of the paper, which was recently published in Nature Chemical Biology. Former MIT postdoc Haorong Chen is also an author of the paper.
Turning Bacterial Cells Into Transistors
Synthetic biology circuits are usually built by engineering cells to produce proteins and transcription factors that interact with one another. These systems can be programmed to carry out tasks such as detecting a particular molecule and then producing a specific response.
Such circuits can perform different logic functions, but their complexity is limited. Researchers generally need distinct transcription factors for separate operations so that signals do not interfere with one another. Because only a limited number of suitable transcription factors are available, there is a practical ceiling on how complicated a circuit can become inside a single cell. Packing too many circuits into one cell can also overwhelm its protein production machinery.
The MIT team approached the problem differently. Rather than placing an entire circuit inside one cell, they engineered individual cells to serve as transistor-like components that could be connected in different arrangements.
For these components, the researchers used Pantoea agglomerans, a bacterium that commonly grows on surfaces, including plants. They engineered two versions of bacterial transistors that respond to a molecule called OC 6. One type switches on when it encounters the molecule, while the other switches off.
Each transistor also senses a second target molecule, OC 12. Depending on whether OC 12 is present and whether the transistor has been activated, the bacterial cell produces an output molecule called OHC 14.
Wiring Living Cells Together
The team then engineered three strains of Pantoea agglomerans to function as relays. These cells convert the OHC 14 signal into another output that can serve as the input for the next transistor. In this way, individual bacterial components can be "wired" together much like parts on an electronic circuit board.
For instance, the researchers built a bidirectional switch using two transistors that detect OC 12. Depending on a separate switch input, the system sends that information through different relay strains before passing it to additional transistors for further processing.
To assemble the circuits, the researchers printed bacterial colonies onto plates containing agar, which serves as a growth medium. Each colony was positioned about 5 millimeters from its nearest neighbor. This spacing helps ensure that chemical signals reach only the next colony in the sequence, allowing information to move through the circuit in a single direction.
Building More Complex Biological Circuits
The researchers showed that the same bacterial transistor could perform several logic operations depending on where it was positioned within a circuit. These included "multi-input," "or," and "imply" gates.
By connecting multiple transistors, the team also created more sophisticated systems. The circuits could add two signals, process several signals at the same time, or operate as a demultiplexer, which receives one incoming signal and routes it to one of several possible destinations based on a separate control signal.
The largest circuit demonstrated in the study contained 24 interconnected bacterial colonies and was designed to add two inputs together.
"This work shows that we can get toward more complicated functions by linking up simpler functions in individual cells," Voigt says. "Computationally, there's nothing that your iPhone can do that these circuits couldn't do."
There is, however, a major difference in speed. Each calculation performed by the bacterial circuits takes about eight hours, far longer than an electronic computer would require. For biological applications, though, the researchers say that pace can still be practical.
"We're not trying to replace computers, but rather put computational control into biology. If you have bacteria on the root of a plant, or the plant itself is doing the computing, running a simple calculation overnight is fast enough relative to a growth season," Voigt says.
Living Computers for Agriculture
One possible application is agriculture. If these circuits can eventually be placed on plant roots, they could be programmed to detect different forms of stress. When the system recognizes a particular signal, it could trigger a corresponding response, such as producing a fungicide.
The research was funded, in part, by the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and by the U.S. Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Anne Trafton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Hamid Doosthosseini, Haorong Chen, Christopher A. Voigt. Living circuit boards built by printing bacterial transistors. Nature Chemical Biology, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41589-026-02300-3
