From the Nile to the Red Sea, can Egypt and Ethiopia ever agree?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:36:07 UTC
19:36:07 KST

Breadcrumb
A new crisis is brewing over the Nile between Egypt and Ethiopia, unless mediators step in
Almost one year after Ethiopia inaugurated its Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Blue Nile, Addis Ababa is looking to advance plans for three additional hydropower projects, prompting renewed warnings from downstream Egypt.
Ethiopia underlined its increasingly assertive position on August 21, when Water and Energy Minister Habtamu Itefa Gelata said Addis Ababa required no permission to develop its water resources, defended its right to equitable use of the Nile and rejected calls for joint management of GERD.
That has intensified concern in Egypt, which derives more than 97 percent of its renewable freshwater resources from the Nile, and has voiced alarm about Addis Ababa’s dam building.
In August, Egyptian officials, including the foreign and irrigation ministers, warned that Cairo would not “allow” any further dams on the Nile and reaffirmed Egypt’s right to defend its water security.
Ethiopia announced plans in March 2026 for three further Blue Nile hydropower projects (Karadobi, Mandaya and Beko Abo) with a reported combined generating capacity of approximately 5,700 MW and an estimated total cost of $10.5 billion.
While these projects have alarmed Egypt, they remain in the planning and preconstruction stage, and their specifications could change. Furthermore, all three sites have featured in earlier Nile Basin studies, showing their current status is speculative.
The real change is Ethiopia is now confident enough to pursue further Blue Nile development, even as GERD remains unresolved with the downstream states Egypt and Sudan.
“For decades, Ethiopia had plans to develop its water and hydropower resources, but the combination of limited financing and Egypt’s opposition constrained those ambitions,” Tsedale Lemma, founder and editor-in-chief of the independent Ethiopian publication Addis Standard, told The New Arab.
After GERD, control or coordination?
GERD gave Ethiopia’s new dam plans greater political weight. Construction began in 2011 after Cairo was bogged down in the Egyptian revolution that year, while Ethiopia had pondered a dam for decades, although the threat of Egyptian military action had deterred it.
Its construction continued despite Egyptian and Sudanese objections and Ethiopia officially inaugurated the $5bn hydroelectric project on September 9, 2025, with 5,150 MW of installed capacity.
The latest plans point to a longer-term hydropower programme built around GERD, rather than just individual stand-alone dams.
Tsedale Lemma said the new proposals are likely to reinforce a view among many Ethiopians that the country “should be able to use its water resources for electricity, irrigation, food security and broader economic development, provided it does not deliberately cause significant harm to downstream states.”
This shift in outlook also shows up in the Cooperative Framework Agreement, which calls for a fairer sharing of the Nile’s water. While it entered into force in October 2024 it remains opposed by Egypt and Sudan, as Cairo demands a legally binding treaty.
However, concerns over how future downstream flows would be affected continue to fuel the political dispute.
Hydropower itself does not use up the water the way large irrigation projects do, since water simply passes through its turbines.
The problem lies with the reservoirs, which lose some water to evaporation, and their changing of the natural rhythm of the river can make downstream flows less predictable.
Yet like GERD, the three new dams do not have to be a zero-sum game if they are managed carefully.
“There was no harmful disruption of water to Egypt while filling the reservoir behind the GERD because of either normal or heavier than normal rainfall in the Nile Basin during this period,” David Shinn, former US ambassador to Ethiopia and adjunct professor at George Washington University, told The New Arab.
Yet he warned that “in the case of the three new dams, Ethiopia must manage with great care the reservoir filling process so as not to harm Egypt.”
In July, Sudan’s irrigation ministry recorded inflows to Roseires falling from 207 million to 129 million cubic metres per day between 7 and 9 July, attributing the temporary decline to reduced GERD discharges. Ethiopia did not confirm a cut.
This incident, along with the competing claims over flooding in late 2025, shows why advance notice, shared water data and agreed operating rules still matter after GERD.
A rivalry beyond the Nile
Cairo is determined not to give up its own long-standing dominance over the Nile, however. And with an agreement remaining elusive, it has sought to pressure Ethiopia elsewhere in the region.
As landlocked Ethiopia also seeks maritime access via the Red Sea, Cairo has cultivated regional partnerships intended to temper Addis Ababa’s ambitions, viewing the maritime and Nile disputes as mutually reinforcing.
Egypt expanded military cooperation with Somalia following Ethiopia’s January 2024 memorandum of understanding with Somaliland, which offered maritime access in exchange for eventual recognition of the breakaway region.
Although Turkey’s Ankara Declaration in December 2024 defused the immediate confrontation and helped restore ties between Addis Ababa and Mogadishu, Ethiopia’s pursuit of dependable maritime access remains unresolved.
Cairo has therefore expanded ties with Eritrea as relations between Asmara and Addis Ababa have again deteriorated. The neighbours fought a devastating border war from 1998 to 2000, five years after Eritrea’s independence which left Ethiopia without sea access.
In May, Egypt and Eritrea signed a maritime transport agreement and agreed to establish a shipping line connecting their Red Sea ports.
During a Cairo summit in June, Sisi and Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki pledged to intensify coordination over Red Sea security and affirmed that governance should remain the exclusive responsibility of littoral states, a position implicitly opposing any Ethiopian naval role in the waterway.
There is a risk of a vicious cycle in which Egyptian engagement with these countries fuels Ethiopian fears of encirclement, hardening Addis Ababa’s position and pushing a negotiated settlement over the Nile further out of reach.
Regional powers such as Saudi Arabia and Turkey are perhaps best to facilitate dialogue, given their ties with both Ethiopia and Egypt.
Riyadh offered to mediate in 2021, and Turkey’s recent Horn of Africa diplomacy has placed it in a stronger position to facilitate talks. However, neither state currently leads a formal process.
China’s growing diplomatic footprint in the region adds another possible mediator to the mix. President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Egypt on 1–3 September 2026, his first in a decade, produced a joint statement in which Beijing explicitly recognised the Nile as Egypt’s “lifeline” and affirmed Cairo’s “legitimate right” to protect its water and food security under international law, while calling on all Nile Basin countries to refrain from harming downstream states. Historically seen in Addis Ababa as relatively neutral—or even tilted toward Ethiopia, given Beijing’s role as a major infrastructure financier, this new, explicit backing for Egypt’s water-security claims could give China fresh leverage as a potential bridge between the two capitals, especially if it couples political support with technical offers such as desalination cooperation and remote-sensing assistance.
Beijing’s Belt and Road ties with both countries and its recent push to position itself as a neutral security broker in the Middle East could allow it to convene talks that address both Nile sharing and broader Horn of Africa issues, including Ethiopia’s maritime access and Red Sea security.
For talks to succeed, however, any mediator would need to win Addis Ababa’s confidence rather than appear simply to endorse Cairo’s position.
Tsedale Lemma said Addis Ababa sees the dispute as a clash between Cairo’s invocation of “established water rights” and Ethiopia’s demand for equitable, basin-wide use. Ethiopia also fears that rules governing GERD could become “a de facto permanent Nile-water allocation treaty” restricting future upstream projects.
During Donald Trump’s first Presidential term, Washington appeared to validate those fears.
In February 2020, after Ethiopia skipped the final talks and requested more time, the US Treasury went ahead with Egypt and Sudan, called the proposed deal balanced, and warned Ethiopia against filling GERD without an agreement. Washington later froze up to $100 million in aid when Ethiopia started filling the reservoir.
Trump’s subsequent suggestion that Egypt might “blow up” GERD certainly compounded that mistrust. From Ethiopia’s perspective, the facilitator had become an advocate for Cairo’s position.
In January 2026, Trump offered to restart US mediation over Nile water-sharing. Sisi and Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan welcomed the proposal, but it has yet to produce an announced negotiating process. So far, diplomacy remains frozen despite Ethiopia’s determination to pursue new projects on the Nile.
Still, with the Nile dispute becoming increasingly interlinked with broader Horn of Africa security, addressing Addis Ababa’s concerns over maritime access may need to form part of any broader settlement.
“One issue that would get Ethiopia’s attention on a Nile water compromise would be Egyptian engagement with Eritrea for negotiating permanent Ethiopian access to the Red Sea,” said David Shinn.
He cautioned, however, that it was difficult to see what Egypt would gain from such an arrangement, while Eritrea would also require substantial incentives.
Beyond such a bargain, Ashok Swain, professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University, argued that the dams themselves could create incentives for cooperation.
“Additional dams could also create interdependence: coordinated reservoirs can regulate flows, reduce floods, produce electricity and support regional power trade with Sudan and Egypt,” he told The New Arab. “Which path is taken will depend less on the dams themselves than on how they are planned and operated.”
“Transparency, advance consultation, shared data, agreed drought-time water-sharing rules and Egyptian access to Ethiopian electricity would encourage cooperation; unilateral construction, threats, domestic nationalism and competition over ports, Somalia and the Red Sea would deepen confrontation,” Swain added.
Jonathan Fenton-Harvey is a journalist and researcher who focuses on conflict, geopolitics and humanitarian issues in the Middle East and North Africa.

US military turns off ad trackers on devices amid reports data used to target forces in Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:31:46 UTC
19:31:46 KST

US military officials say they have disabled advertising trackers on a range of phones and computers, according to letters released on Friday by US Senator Ron Wyden and statements given to Reuters, a development that follows reports that commercially available location data had been used to target American forces in the Middle East.
The Air Force told Wyden it disabled the advertising identifiers on computers and mobile phones two months ago. US Special Operations Command said in a separate letter that it had "recently" disabled them on its Windows devices. The Army told Reuters that advertising IDs tied to mobile devices had been disabled since earlier this year.
Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, has pressed the Pentagon on the issue for months.
The disclosures highlight a growing national security concern: that location data collected by the advertising industry and sold by data brokers - companies that collate and resell personal data - can be used to track and target military personnel deployed to war zones.
The Air Force and Special Operations Command declined further comment. Similar letters from the Army and Navy to Wyden said they disabled advertising IDs on military devices but gave no indication of when the restrictions were imposed. The Army said in a statement that advertising IDs had been blocked on Windows computers "since before 2021" but that Android and Apple mobile devices had only had it disabled by default "since at least February 2026."
Messages seeking comment from the Navy went unreturned.
Military officials weighing restrictions on phone use
The effort to reduce the location data generated by smartphones comes as military officials weigh increasingly strict restrictions on phone use overall. In July, Reuters reported that some deployed personnel in the Middle East could be ordered to surrender their phones amid concerns that mobile videos they were posting to the internet were helping Iran target American bases in the region.
Wyden and US Representative Pat Harrigan, a North Carolina Republican, sent a letter to the Pentagon on Friday asking for an investigation into whether the military had properly countered the dangers of the location data trade. The letter included the updates from the various service branches on their efforts to disable advertising IDs on military devices.
Wyden said in a statement that it was clear that the military's efforts "have not been effective at neutralizing this threat." Harrigan said that US enemies "should not be able to pull out a credit card and buy information that helps them track American troops."
The Pentagon said in an email it would respond to the lawmakers directly.
Personnel could still be tracked via apps, privacy ad tech company head warns
Mobile advertising IDs, often abbreviated MAID, are unique identifiers tied to specific devices that can be used to track a person's activity across mobile apps and pinpoint their physical location.
Zach Edwards, co-founder of privacy ad tech company Decryptads, said that efforts to disable MAID on military-operated devices were "definitely a positive thing."
The restrictions "will essentially ensure their location isn't being included in bulk data sales being done by numerous vendors," although he cautioned that personnel might still be tracked through apps in other more complicated ways, for example by triangulating technical device details with network data or location information.

Why less visibility into how OpenAI’s new GPT-6 Astra ‘thinks’ is sparking safety concerns
The Hugging Face breach in July highlights the importance of being able to inspect what models are ‘thinking’, say analysts
When announcing Astra on Thursday, OpenAI said it was “the world’s most intelligent and aligned model,” with a “significant jump in cyber capabilities”.
OpenAI president Greg Brockman said at the end of a press call announcing Astra’s arrival that it likely represents AGI, or artificial general intelligence – AI that matches or outperforms human intelligence.
However, OpenAI also said the model’s written reasoning was “harder to monitor” compared with GPT-5.6 Sol, the previous generation released in July.
“We have found that GPT-6 Astra is more capable of controlling its own CoT (chain of thought) than GPT-5.6 Sol, and less likely to include incriminating information in its CoT,” OpenAI said, referring to the intermediate reasoning steps an AI generates while solving a task.
The shift in visibility stems from a technique known as recurrent depth, or looped transformers, which reuses parts of a neural network. As a result, it processes complex logic inside hidden mathematical loops rather than in step-by-step readable text, The Information reported on Tuesday ahead of the launch.

ICE Wants to Know Who Bought a Certain Green Beanie From REI in the Last 2 Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Did you buy a beanie from REI recently? The Department of Homeland Security might be looking for you.
New court filings allege that Homeland Security Investigations agents subpoenaed the outdoor retailer in March, requesting the transaction information for “all persons” in the greater Minneapolis–St. Paul area who had purchased a specific type of dark green beanie from the company since 2024. REI did not respond to questions about whether it had complied with the request and, if so, how many people are affected.
The filings are part of a broader lawsuit by the federal government against 39 people who attended an ICE protest at a church whose pastor also worked as an acting ICE field office director. Both protesters and journalists who were attempting to cover the event, including former CNN host Don Lemon, are now defendants.
The subpoena to REI was one of 92 sent as part of HSI’s investigation into the defendants, according to the court filings. Other recipients included social media companies, airlines, telecom providers, a car rental company, and a state employment agency. At least one subpoena sent to an unnamed airline, the filings allege, asked not only for information about a defendant’s past flights, but also requested that the airline give HSI a “lookout notification” about the defendant’s travel in the future. DHS declined to comment. The US Attorney’s Office in Minnesota, which is litigating the case on behalf of the government, did not respond questions about why it was necessary to identify everyone in Minnesota who purchased the beanie from REI, or why it specifically targeted REI customers, since the beanie is sold on other platforms as well.
The subpoenas sent by HSI agents are also known as 1509 customs summons, and are meant to be used to request information related to imports and exports. However, since the start of the Trump administration, WIRED and other news outlets have reported on DHS’s attempts to unmask online critics using the legal tool, which can be sent without the oversight of a judge or a jury.
“It’s flat-out absurd for DHS to demand REI search two years of customer data as part of Trump’s campaign against the people of Minneapolis,” US senator Ron Wyden of Oregon tells WIRED. “Customs summonses only allow DHS to request information directly related to compliance with customs laws, not to conduct unending fishing expeditions into the lives of people critical of Donald Trump.”
The total number of 1509 summonses that have been sent since the start of the Trump administration—and how many people have had their personal information guzzled up by DHS as a result—is unknown. Companies that receive these types of subpoenas are typically asked to keep their existence a secret. When the public has gotten a glimpse of them, it’s usually because the target has contested it in court, either because the recipient company ignored the request for silence and notified the target, or because the target discovered it after the fact.
According to a recent letter written by Wyden and Representative Pramila Jayapal, big tech companies will sometimes ignore the government’s request for silence when not legally required, but other companies in more heavily regulated sectors have told Congress that they’ve complied because of fear of regulatory retaliation.
Court filings, internal DHS documents, and companies’ own public statements show that companies have responded to recent customs summons in different ways.
Attorneys for Georgia Fort, a journalist and one of the defendants in the Minnesota case, wrote in a court filing that they were “stunned” when they realized that the government had obtained logs detailing six months’ of Fort’s calls and text messages from T-Mobile after the government sent a customs summons to the telecom provider. The attorneys allege that Fort was never notified by either T-Mobile nor the government.
“We take our responsibility to protect customers’ privacy and personal information very seriously,” says a T-Mobile spokesperson, who also said the company does not comment on specific legal requests. “Our team carefully reviews government demands for customer information and responds in accordance with the law.”
In the same filing, the attorneys said that Google refused to comply with a customs summons requesting information about Fort’s YouTube viewers and subscribers. A Google spokesperson says that the company reviews each government request for lawfulness and that Google will try to narrow requests or outright reject them when it believes the request is too broad.
Reddit recently announced that during the last half of 2025, it received DHS administrative subpoenas seeking information about 11 different Reddit accounts that made critical posts about ICE actions. After Reddit objected to them on First Amendment grounds, the company said, the agency withdrew them.
“Privacy is central to how Reddit operates, and we take our commitment to protecting it seriously,” says Ben Lee, Reddit’s outgoing chief legal officer. “We routinely push back on law enforcement requests and stand up for users who are exercising their First Amendment rights.”
Meta also pushed back against at least one customs summons, according to internal DHS correspondence obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Meta declined WIRED’s request to comment.
“I think DHS has proved time and time again that they can’t be trusted as the stewards of applying this law correctly,” says Mario Trujillo, a senior staff attorney at the EFF who has been tracking DHS subpoenas sent to tech companies. Congress could pass a law that would restrict how the agency used 1509 customs summons, or add penalties when they are misused, but until then companies and their customers are on their own.

Measles Outbreaks Are Forcing Immunocompromised Kids to Make Impossible Choices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

As students head back to school, parents have all the usual worries about their kids, like remembering to pack lunch and making it to the bus stop on time. But parents of immunocompromised kids have a new one: How to deal with the resurgence of measles.
Cases of the highly transmissible disease have reached a 35-year high in the US, with nearly 3,000 confirmed infections in 2026 so far. The first two measles-related deaths of the year were recorded in Pennsylvania, right as the school year is getting going. With vaccination rates dropping across the country, parents of kids who aren’t able to get vaccinated or don’t mount a strong enough immune response due to weakened immune systems are weighing whether it’s safe enough to go to school.
Victoria Schiano, national community engagement coordinator for Little Lobbyists, a nonprofit that advocates for children with complex medical needs and disabilities, says the return of measles is “absolutely terrifying.”
While it’s not known exactly how many US children have compromised immune systems, a study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated that 2.6 percent of children are immunocompromised. Immune deficiencies can have genetic causes or secondary reasons, such as chemotherapy for cancer treatment.
Schiano’s kid is among them. Her 10-year-old has mitochondrial disease. The family lives in Chester County, Pennsylvania, which has the second-highest number of measles cases in the state right now. Schiano has been closely monitoring the vaccination rates in her son’s school district, which have dipped below the 95 percent threshold needed for community protection against measles. Measles is breaking through in places where vaccination has dropped below that threshold. In neighboring Lancaster County, for example, just 87.6 percent of kindergartners are fully vaccinated against measles and 83.3 percent of seventh graders are.
Her son can’t be vaccinated, and he receives weekly infusions of immunoglobulin—concentrated antibodies from donated human blood plasma—to help his body fight infections.
“Measles is dangerous for anyone, but for him, this absolutely could be life or death,” she says.
The virus can cause severe, life-threatening complications such as pneumonia and brain swelling. Measles can also wipe out the body’s memory of past infections—a phenomenon known as immune amnesia—leaving people susceptible to other diseases.
Her son already wears a mask and uses a plexiglass screen at school, and the family is diligent about handwashing. Now, Schiano says they’ve had to make the difficult decision to limit her son’s time with friends and after-school activities like karate. She says it’s hard as a parent to balance his quality of life with his safety.
“He just wants to play and to do all the things that he sees other kids doing,” she says.
Her son did online school for a time during Covid-19, and she says she’s prepared to take him out of school if there’s even one confirmed measles case. That comes with a different set of risks, though. During the pandemic, remote learning was associated with an increase in social isolation and behavioral and mental health issues among students.
Amalia, a parent in South Carolina who asked to go by a pseudonym for privacy reasons, has already chosen to keep her 16-year-old son home this year and do online schooling due to concerns about measles. Her son has immunoglobulin A deficiency, in which the body doesn’t produce enough of an antibody found in mucous membranes, body fluids, and digestive tracts that help fend off germs.
“Even if there’s just a flu going around, he gets sicker than the average kid will,” she says.
Her son was able to get the measles vaccine, but doctors monitor his antibody levels regularly to check for waning immunity.
She lives in Spartanburg County, where measles broke out earlier this year and caused nearly 1,000 cases and 21 hospitalizations. About 91 percent of those cases were among children and teens, and most were among those who were not fully vaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status. Even though there was a 94 percent increase in the number of vaccines administered during the outbreak in Spartanburg County compared to the year before, she still wasn’t comfortable sending her son back to school.
“Covid happened, and then measles happened, and we just feel like it's not going to be the last time,” she says. “If it's not measles, it's going to be something else because rates for other vaccines have fallen, too.”
Before this year, her son shared a classroom with other students who have special accommodations. But outside of that setting, Amalia says it has been difficult for him to make friends because of his medical condition. She says it’s hard to talk to other parents about vaccination status because it can be such a hot-button issue. The family is thinking about moving because of what she views as an anti-vaccination sentiment in the community as well as “hostility” toward masking that she’s encountered.
“Some people don't want to take ownership of the responsibility of public health,” she says. “I think it's something we're supposed to share across humanity. It's not supposed to be carried by one person.”
Cortney, another South Carolina parent of an immunocompromised kid, says the state’s measles outbreak was highly concerning because the family needed to travel near the epicenter for medical appointments. Whereas before they might stop in town to eat lunch or do some shopping, they ended any unnecessary stops. “We planned to drive directly into that county, we go only to the doctor, and we leave,” Cortney says.
Her 17-year-old daughter Grace’s condition means that rhinovirus—the cause of the common cold—led to her getting hospitalized. During Covid, Grace and her brother were homeschooled, and that is something mother and daughter considered again for Grace’s senior year.
“At the end of the semester, we're going to reevaluate and see where things are,” Grace says.
Even though she is immunocompromised, Grace doesn’t wear a mask at school because of fear of being bullied. Cortney says her family’s preference would be to mask while in public, but she’s concerned about being ostracized. “You worry that your family could be targeted,” she says. “It’s unfortunate that we have to think about that.”

Death toll rises to 12 after ship sinks off Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:28:39 UTC
19:28:39 KST

The death toll from a ship that sank off Girne (Kyrenia) in the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) last week rose to 12 after two more bodies were recovered, Prime Minister Unal Ustel said Friday.
“As a result of the work carried out last night, we reached two more female bodies. Thus, the number of bodies recovered from a depth of 554 meters (1,818 feet) has risen to four. The number of people who have died is now 12,” Ustel said.
Ustel made the announcement at a news conference at Girne Port, where he provided an update on the search and rescue operation.
Search and rescue efforts remain underway as authorities work to locate 16 missing people.
The operation is being carried out with nine vessels and 11 aircraft deployed in the area, with Turkish Navy search and rescue vessels TCG Isin and TCG Alemdar leading the effort. Teams are working around the clock, including overnight, to locate those still missing and recover the vessel's black box.
The Filo Jet, a high-speed passenger vessel operating between Girne Port in the TRNC and Tasucu Port in Mersin, Türkiye, departed Girne at around noon Sunday, Aug. 30. Shortly after leaving port, the vessel began taking on water through its bow and sank as it attempted to return to Girne Port.
The wreck was subsequently located at a depth of 554 meters (1,818 feet) off the coast of Girne.
Following the sinking, Ustel said authorities had recovered the bodies of 12 people, while search and rescue teams continued efforts to locate 16 others.
Ustel said agencies in the TRNC and Türkiye have continued round-the-clock efforts to locate those aboard.
Turkish Navy search and rescue vessel TCG Isin arrived at the site and joined the operation, followed by TCG Alemdar.
The search is being conducted at a depth of 554 meters (1,818 feet), making the operation particularly difficult, Ustel said.
“The wreck is at a depth of 554 meters, and people cannot descend to that depth to conduct search operations. The work is being carried out entirely by robots,” he said.
Anadolu captured footage aboard TCG Alemdar showing rescue teams using remotely operated underwater vehicles, or ROVs, to search the wreck 554 meters (1,818 feet) below the surface. The robotic systems are being used both to search for missing people and to carry out operations on the wreck.
The TCG Isin's robotic system initially scanned the area where the ship sank to identify possible entry points into the wreck. The vessel has a crew of 60 personnel, including 15 highly specialized first-class divers involved in the operation.
The ROV used in the operation can descend to depths of up to 1,000 meters (3,281 feet), securely grasp and recover objects and wreckage, and lift loads weighing up to 135 kilograms (298 pounds). Equipped with thermal cameras, the system is also being used for imaging operations.
TCG Isin's Dynamic Positioning System allows the vessel to maintain a stable position in difficult sea conditions, supporting underwater operations. The vessel can also remain stationary using four-point anchoring at depths of up to 600 meters (1,969 feet).
Its side-scan sonar can locate objects at depths of up to 1,000 meters, while its multibeam echosounder, capable of operating at up to 3,000 meters (9,843 feet), provides detailed scans of the seabed.
TCG Alemdar arrived in the area Wednesday and has since been used to conduct robotic operations on the wreck and recover the bodies of missing people. The 4,200-ton submarine rescue vessel is equipped with an ambulance helicopter platform and continues to support the operation through its Dynamic Positioning System and sonar equipment.
Rear Adm. Baybars Kucukatay, commander of Türkiye's Southern Maritime Area Command, said about 800 Turkish naval personnel were participating in the operation aboard ships and naval aircraft.
Speaking to reporters aboard TCG Alemdar, Kucukatay said searches were continuing across the seabed, sea floor, underwater and surface areas, as well as along the coastline.
Kucukatay said the operation had become the deepest search and rescue effort carried out in the region to date.
“The most important aspect of the search and rescue operation we have conducted to date is that it has been recorded as the deepest underwater search and rescue operation carried out in this region,” he said.
He also said the vessel carrying out the operation had the capability to work at depths well beyond that of the wreck.
“The vessel we are on has the capability to operate at depths of up to 3,000 meters, and the wreck is currently at a depth of 554 meters. Operations are continuing,” he said.
Kucukatay offered condolences to the families of those who died, saying: “On this occasion, I wish God's mercy upon our citizens who lost their lives and patience to their grieving families.”
Ustel said Türkiye's Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz visited the island the previous day, conveyed his condolences and delivered a message of sympathy from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
He thanked personnel from the Turkish Naval Forces, Peace Forces Command and Security Forces Command, as well as military personnel aboard TCG Alemdar and other teams supporting the operation.
Rear Adm. Eren Gunay, commander of the Turkish Navy's Underwater Operations Command, said the search and rescue operation was being conducted under the operational control of the Southern Maritime Area Command.
Gunay said two search and rescue vessels, first-class divers, SAT special forces and SAS underwater defense teams were taking part in the operation, with 215 personnel involved.
He said the Turkish Naval Forces are among a small number of countries with the capability to conduct search and rescue operations in deep waters.
“The Turkish Naval Forces, with their superior technological capabilities and trained specialist personnel, are one of nine countries in the world capable of conducting operations with search capabilities in these deep waters,” Gunay said.
He said all available state resources and capabilities were being used in the operation.
“Using all the resources and capabilities of our state, we are carrying out search operations day and night to try to reach our citizens,” Gunay said.
Gunay also expressed condolences for those who lost their lives.
Ustel said he told families that difficult conditions at a depth of 554 meters meant the operation would take time and stressed that the search would continue until the last person was located.
He also said everyone responsible for the accident and resulting deaths, “from the lowest level to the highest level,” would be held accountable under the law.
The TRNC's parliament, known as the Republic Assembly, is scheduled to reconvene in the first week of October.
Ustel said the government had already taken steps to launch a parliamentary investigation into the accident.
“Before we begin the normal opening of the Republic Assembly, we, as the government, are submitting a motion to our Republic Assembly to investigate this accident.
“We have also submitted our application as of yesterday for an investigative committee to be established in the Republic Assembly and for the work to begin there,” he said.
Ustel said he would provide another update to the public and families later Friday.
Ustel stressed that hope remained and said Turkish naval forces were continuing their efforts around the clock.
“To turn hope into reality, our Naval Forces continue their work 24/7,” he said.
He said authorities could not provide a precise timetable for completing the search because of the technical difficulties.
“We are talking about work being carried out at a depth of 554 meters under extremely difficult conditions. I want you to know how difficult this work is,” Ustel said.
The two bodies recovered during the latest operation were taken to Burhan Nalbantoglu State Hospital in Lefkosa for identification.
“They will be announced to the families after identification is completed,” Ustel said.

Ig Nobel prizes go to scientists studying cockroach milk, nose-blowing, more

Ig Nobel prizes go to scientists studying cockroach milk, nose-blowing, buried underwear, more
Ten research teams were honored Thursday at a satirical science awards ceremony that was hosted outside the U.S. for the first time due to travel concerns.
Researchers who studied milk from cockroaches and analyzed soil health using underwear received Ig Nobel prizes celebrating unusual and imaginative contributions to science.
The awards, organized by a digital magazine called the Annals of Improbable Research, shifted to Europe after 35 years in the United States over concerns about attendees being able to get visas.
At a convention center in Zurich, Switzerland, research teams received a custom trophy resembling a cross between a mushroom and a human foot. Among them were Matilda Brindle and Stuart West from the University of Oxford and the Florida Institute of Technology's Catherine F. Talbot, who reconstructed the evolutionary history of kissing, and the late Dr. Tokuji Unno, who investigated the science of blowing one's nose.
Another research team buried 1,000 pairs of underwear in more than 25 countries to study how critters in the soil helped them decompose.
For future ceremonies, organizers plan to alternate between Zurich and other European countries. The 2027 ceremony will be held in the Belgian city of Antwerp. Previous iterations took place at Harvard University, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Boston University, but there are no immediate plans to return to the U.S.
"During the past year, it has become unsafe for our guests to visit the country," Marc Abrahams, master of ceremonies and editor of the magazine, told The Associated Press in an email in March.
The Nobel Prizes, which have no relation to their cheekily named counterpart, will be announced at the start of October.

NATO Status of Forces Agreement - identification of status
An explanation of the NATO Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) and identification of status.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) is the treaty that sets out the terms under which the armed forces of a NATO Member State are allowed to operate and live through arrangement within another NATO Member State.
While assigned to a NATO Member State, UK Ministry of Defence personnel are through arrangement entitled to the rights and privileges and subject to the obligations of the NATO Status of Forces Agreement, to which all NATO Member States are parties.
In accordance with Article 5.4.7 of EC C(2022) 7591 (Practical Handbook for Border Guards), the European Commission recognises in law those “documents issued pursuant to paragraph 2 of Article III of the NATO Status of Forces Agreement between the Parties to the North Atlantic Treaty regarding the Status of their forces”.
Germany
The issue of a NATO Status of Forces Agreement Identification Card to a member of the ‘force’, the ‘civilian component’ or their ‘dependents’ is pursuant to Article III of the NATO SOFA and Article 5 of the Supplementary Agreement to the NATO SOFA Germany, together with the inclusion of a NATO Status of Forces Agreement Status Certificate (sometimes referred to as a “Status Stamp”) within the passport of the bearer.
An example of the NATO Status of Forces Agreement Identification Card is shown below.
The bearer of these documents:
- is a member of the Force, the Civilian Component or a Dependant of the NATO Sending State (GBR) as defined by Article I of the NATO Status of Forces Agreement
- should be afforded the privileges accorded by Article III of the NATO Status of Forces Agreement in respect of passport and visa regulation and immigration inspection on entering or leaving a NATO Member State, and on the registration and control of Aliens
- pursuant to the NATO Status of Forces Agreement, and by virtue of their living in the NATO Member State, the bearer of these documents is not subject to the restrictions that may be placed on other Third Country Nationals in respect of the time period of their stay within the European Union, and should be treated accordingly
Both the ID card above and the NATO SOFA certificate held in passport are approved through the appropriate federal department in Berlin.
The use of the card outside of Germany is without formal endorsement from any other nation state but is proven useful evidence in supporting purpose of entering and exiting the EU.
UK Defence personnel serving in the territory of a receiving state under the NATO SOFA should seek further guidance from their supporting National Support Element (NSE).
Lost and found identification cards
If you have lost an identification card, please contact your issuing authority.
If you have found an identification card, please hand it in at your nearest police station or email CSOCIGDN-GEO-Residency@mod.gov.uk.

Latino voter backlash puts Texas governor's race on Democrats' midterm map
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Latino voter backlash puts Texas governor's race on Democrats' midterm map
BEEVILLE, Texas, Sept 4 - The makeup and toys on Valencia Macias' table are items people buy on impulse at discount stores. But on a sweltering summer day in South Texas, she is trying to sell them to turn them into gas money, grocery money, student loan money: any kind of money.
With three young children, a job as a medical assistant and nursing classes at night, the 26-year-old has little time for politics. But when Texas officials withdrew funding for the only after-school program available in her rural town of George West, politics became impossible to ignore.
Then, a TikTok video appeared: A Mexican American woman on the screen, Gina Hinojosa, talked about the high cost of living and badly needed investments in Texas public education. Macias stopped scrolling.
“With everything just getting so expensive and the gas and everything, it's really hard to just make do,” Macias said. Seeing a mother and a woman who looks like her, Macias made up her mind: “100%, she has my vote.”
Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative, is trying to end an electoral drought that has defined Texas politics for a generation: no Democrat has won statewide office in Texas since 1994.
Her strategy hinges on persuading Latino voters like Macias that rising costs and strained public schools matter more than the cultural and immigration issues that have pulled many Latino voters toward Republicans in recent years.
Hinojosa said that means resisting the tendency to treat Latino voters as a distinct political constituency with separate priorities. Instead, she argues they are motivated by the same concerns as other Texans, including housing costs, schools and day-to-day expenses. So, her campaign delivers that message in Spanish to Latino audiences.
"We are as Texan and American as anyone," she said in an interview in Austin. "Latinos are feeling the economic strain just like families all across this country and in Texas in a big way."
Her campaign tests whether Democrats can regain support among Latino voters by emphasizing pocketbook issues.
The test is whether it can overcome the political machine Republican Governor Greg Abbott has built over the last 12 years in office.
He has name recognition, President Donald Trump's endorsement and a vast support network that stretches beyond Texas. He has raised roughly $25.5 million between February and July, while Hinojosa raised about $6 million. Abbott holds more than a 22-to-1 cash-on-hand advantage, with $67.2 million to Hinojosa's $3 million, the latest campaign finance reports show.
Abbott spent years cultivating support in South Texas, regularly visiting heavily Latino border communities, building an extensive field operation in the Rio Grande Valley and making border security a centerpiece of his outreach.
Republican gains followed his sustained efforts to compete for Hispanic voters on issues including immigration, public safety and the economy.
Hinojosa’s betting that the sharp drop in support for Trump and the party he leads will lead her to victory. State polls have consistently shown she's within striking distance of Abbott all year.
FORMIDABLE INCUMBENT
Abbott is still favored to win in the Republican-leaning state. Hinojosa would have to break the three-decade Republican streak in the office. To stay in power, Abbott has turned to a Republican playbook portraying Hinojosa as out of step with his law-and-order agenda on the campaign trail.
“Governor Abbott is not taking the support of any voter — including Latino voters — for granted, which is why he is investing significant time and resources to earn votes in every community,” Abbott's campaign press secretary Eduardo Leal said in a statement to Reuters.
Recent polling suggests Latino voters favor Hinojosa over Abbott. An August 2026 Emerson College Polling/Nexstar survey found Hispanic voters favored Hinojosa over Abbott by 17 percentage points and that 57% disapproved of Abbott's job performance. That same statewide poll, which surveyed 1,000 likely voters, showed Abbott leading Hinojosa 49% to 45% overall, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points.
Abbott recently released an "affordability agenda" — including property tax cuts, housing reforms, lower electricity costs, expanded low-cost health insurance, a $25-a-month cap on certain prescription drugs, and more. His campaign says the measures will help Texans offset rising living expenses.
“Latino voters care about the same issues that are important to all Texans: overhauling the property tax system, securing the border, putting dangerous criminals behind bars, and keeping Texas affordable,” Leal said.
Samuel Aguero, 28, a Navy veteran, voted for Trump in 2024. But as a single father of two daughters, his top issue is education — he says Beeville's public schools need more state resources, and if Hinojosa offers specifics on improving them, he may back her instead.
"We have to have higher standards in school," he said. "Teachers should be paid a lot more, like, a heck of a lot more."
NUMBERS
Hinojosa may benefit from electoral tailwinds that eluded Beto O'Rourke and other statewide Democratic candidates before her.
Demographic trends have strengthened Democrats' long-held belief that Texas' growing Latino electorate could eventually reshape statewide politics. Texas now has about 6.5 million Latino eligible voters, roughly 1 million more than in the years leading up to Abbott's last reelection campaign.
But the key to Hinojosa’s campaign is how many people actually turn out to vote. Nearly 4.5 million Texans voted in the Democratic and Republican primary elections in March, a recent midterm record.
Record participation, fueled by the high-profile Senate primary battles involving Attorney General Ken Paxton and State Representative James Talarico, could offer Democrats a rare sign of momentum in a state where voter turnout has historically trailed the national average.
Still, voters like Dawn Barraza, 54, an eighth-grade schoolteacher in Victoria, Texas, want “change.” At a monthly outdoor market in Beeville, Barraza said her family fares okay financially, but there’s palpable frustration among Latinos in South Texas that Republicans are not addressing.
“They need to be standing up for our people here; it's high time everybody realizes that we're not going anywhere,” she said. REUTERS

Asia-Pacific Community: China's meteorological early warning system helps Pakistan protect lives, livelihoods from extreme weather
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:26:19 CST
19:26:19 KST

This photo taken on Aug. 17, 2026 shows the building of the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) in Islamabad, Pakistan. (Xinhua/Ahmad Kamal)
by Misbah Saba Malik
ISLAMABAD, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Riaz Hussain, a resident of a village in Talagang district in Pakistan's eastern Punjab province, had grown used to seeing rain damage his wheat crop year after year. But this harvest season, instead of relying on luck, he closely followed weather forecasts and advisories issued by the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD), adjusting his farming activities accordingly.
"I live in a rain-fed area, and after losing a lot of money during the last few years due to poor planning and getting caught by rain in the middle of reaping the crop, I saved a lot this year because I kept following the meteorological department's advisories right from the start," Hussain told Xinhua.
His good harvest has since made him a role model in the village. Other farmers are now following his example and seeking weather guidance from the meteorological department at different stages, from sowing to raising their soon-to-be-harvested peanut crop.
For Hussain, an accurate forecast meant more than just information, it helped protect his livelihood. A similar warning proved crucial for Rustom Baloch, who lives more than 1,000 miles away in Naseerabad district of southwestern Balochistan province.
Baloch received an early warning from the PMD that his home was in a flood-prone area. Acting on the alert, he evacuated his family and moved his valuable belongings to a safer place before the floodwaters arrived.
"A flash flood subsequently struck the area. Though I faced financial losses, the warning gave me valuable time to take precautionary measures and protect my family from the worsening situation," he told Xinhua.
The PMD's ability to provide timely weather alerts has been strengthened through cooperation with the China Meteorological Administration (CMA), including the use of MAZU, China's homegrown AI-powered meteorological early warning system.
"We were already doing a great job in forecasting weather, but the cooperation between the CMA and PMD has helped strengthen our forecasting and early-warning capabilities, with the MAZU system serving as an important component of this cooperation by providing an integrated platform for accessing and analyzing weather information," Furrukh Bashir, director of the Research and Development Division of the PMD, told Xinhua.
"With MAZU, observational data, numerical weather prediction models, satellite information and AI are brought together on a single platform, streamlining meteorologists' work and allowing them to produce faster, more informed forecasts and early warnings," he added.
MAZU is now helping communities in more than 40 countries, including Pakistan, one of its early recipients. Pakistani meteorologists received training at universities in China to operate the system, while Pakistani scientists also took part in its co-development. The system has been in use in Pakistan for about one and a half years.
"The MAZU system provides access to international forecasting models from different sources while also integrating information from the PMD. This gives Pakistani meteorologists a broader picture of developing weather conditions and helps them make more informed decisions regarding significant weather changes and early warnings," Bashir said.
The cooperation has also brought the two countries' meteorological communities closer through scientific exchanges, training and joint development of meteorological systems.
Talking to Xinhua about the system, Zaheer Ahmad Babar, acting director general of the PMD, said the CMA has been helping developing countries strengthen their meteorological knowledge and capabilities as part of a broader effort to improve early-warning systems.
"It is helping countries strengthen their meteorological capabilities and better understand weather patterns, enabling vulnerable communities to take preventive measures, protect lives and livelihoods, and build greater resilience against extreme weather events," Babar said.
The cooperation reflects China's efforts to share its meteorological expertise and technology with other countries and help ensure that early warnings reach communities in time, he added.
For Pakistan, where agriculture is highly dependent on weather and communities in flood-prone areas remain vulnerable to extreme events, such warnings are making a real difference. For local authorities, it can save precious time to prepare communities before conditions become dangerous. For a family living in a flood-prone area, it can mean having enough time to leave home and move to safety. For a farmer, a timely forecast can mean delaying harvest until dangerous weather passes. ■

The Military Court Service
The Military Court Service provides a criminal court for the Royal Navy, Army and Royal Air Force in the Court Martial, Summary Appeal and Service Civilian Court.
Introduction
The Military Court Service (MCS) works closely with, but is independent of: the Office of the Judge Advocate General; the Service Prosecuting Authority, which is equivalent to the Crown Prosecution Service; the Service chains of command, Service and MOD personnel branches; the National Probation Service; and the victim and witness services and military court advocates.
Service Court proceedings are publicised over a two-week assize period. Military court listings. All hearings are open to the public in exactly the same way as civilian courts, unless otherwise directed by the presiding judge.
Service Court results are now published on a monthly basis.
Further information on the Court Martial, Summary Appeal Court and the Service Civilian Court can be found in the Manual of Service Law JSP 830.
HM Crown Prosecution Service Inspectorate - Military Court Service Report - August 2026
This inspection was undertaken at the invitation of the Director of the Military Court Service. Such invitations reflect a commitment to transparency, continuous improvement and independent scrutiny. I welcome the willingness of the MCS to subject itself to external inspection and to seek assurance about the effectiveness and efficiency of the service it provides. This is reflective of a positive approach and demonstrates a mature organisation with a culture that is open to challenge and improvement.
Anthony Rogers HM Chief Inspector of the Crown Prosecution Service
HMCPSI - The Military Court Service, August 2026
Organisation
The MCS is independent of the Service chains of command and is staffed by civil servants employed by the Ministry of Defence (MOD) working from both court centres.
To ensure independence, the Director MCS is appointed by the Defence Council as the Court Administration Officer (CAO). The CAO has a legislated function to give notice of court proceedings and to specify lay members of the court (equivalent to jury selection).
The Court Martial Appeal Court recently clarified the respective roles of the Judge Advocate and the CAO in relation to the constitution of the Court Martial, concluding that the Judge Advocate’s role is to give direction on the composition category, while the CAO is responsible for specifying individual members. These duties are conducted in accordance with the Armed Forces Act 2006 and related Statutory Instruments.
The CAO is a permanent member of both the Service Justice Board (SJB) and the Service Justice Executive Group (SJEG).
The Director MCS operates from the Bulford Court Centre supported by a Senior Management Team and a Court Administration Unit. Each Court Centre has a dedicated Court Officer who is directly responsible for the management of court proceedings, liaison with the Judiciary and court listings.
The current Director of the Military Court Service is Mr Cleaven Faulkner JP:
Military Court Service Strategic Plan 2026-2030
The Strategic Plan, owned by the Director of the Military Court Service (MCS), sets the direction for MCS personnel and partners in delivering Military Court business.
The Service Justice System is a vital public service relied upon by hundreds of victims, witnesses, families, and defendants across the UK and overseas to deliver justice outcomes that matter.
Building on the achievements of the past four years, this plan provides a clear roadmap for delivering an operating model centred on timely, impartial, and efficient administration of Service court proceedings. It aims to strengthen confidence in a justice system that is fair, effective, and accessible to all who depend upon it.
The strategy drives a culture of continuous improvement and ongoing modernisation of our court processes. It recognises the value of embracing technology‑based systems that enhance efficiency, reduce duplication and bureaucracy, and improve integration with our partners and stakeholders. These reforms lay the groundwork for MCS to deliver a new fully integrated Military Court Listing System (MCLS), with its incumbent in‑court digital case management system, Case Center.
Following significant investment in recent years, the MCS is now well placed to consolidate progress, continue to adopt innovative technologies and ensure that the Services have a modern, effective court system that works in the interests of all Service personnel and their families. Looking ahead to 2030, the strategy identifies the areas in which the MCS will continue to modernise and transform, ensuring best value for money and delivering an increasingly efficient and effective criminal court service for the Royal Navy, the Army, and the Royal Air Force.
Through this modernisation, we aim to build greater confidence in and respect for the Service Justice System. We are committed to continue our work in building a leading‑edge service that is open, inclusive, and innovative. Success will be delivered through the professionalism, dedication, and integrity of our people, who work every day to uphold the principles of justice.
Military Court Centres
There are two permanent court centres in the UK. Bulford, Wiltshire and Catterick, North Yorkshire.
A view of the Bulford Military Court Centre
A view of the Catterick Court (BSL Version)
Military Court Centre information and images of our court rooms.
Due to the draw down of British Forces Germany, the permanent court centre at Sennelager has been converted for other use but has been retained as a Court Martial location should one be required. MCS have a permanent Court Martial capability at Episkopi, Cyprus.
The court system is entirely portable, with the ability for MCS to convene trials outside of the MCCs anywhere in the UK or elsewhere. The most recent examples have included Nightingale Courts at Tidworth and Catterick and overseas in Cyprus, Germany and Gibraltar.
MCS have invested in the latest Digital Audio Recording (DAR) technology to meet legal compliance for the recording of proceedings. The capability covers both the four fixed courts and two portable recording equipment sets. The Service Courts have the latest Digital Evidential Presentation System and now have the capability to support the pre-recording of evidence from victims of serious sexual assault (Section 28).
The Service Courts have a state-of-the-art case management system called Case Center. This product is the latest version of the Crown Court system, Caselines and has been operational since September 2023. MCS are moving towards completing the last element of its digital transformation program with Board members using laptops to view evidence, via the Case Center Jury Portal, during proceedings.
Procedure
The Deputy Director MCS oversees the delivery of the MCS assize programme. Cases are listed within ‘assize sessions’, held at the Military Court Centres run by MCS staff. However, a particularly lengthy or complex Court Martial or Service Civilian Court case may be listed as a ‘stand-alone’ outside the assize sessions. Where possible the volume of cases is equally split between both Court Centres.
At the listing phase of case management, the Court officer will work with the resident Judge Advocate to appoint a Judge Advocate to each case.
The MCS policy is to list a case for an initial hearing within 42 days after receipt of directional papers from the Service Prosecuting Authority.
How we select a Court Martial Board
Our Operating procedure for selecting Court Martial Boards
.
On 1 January 2023 legislation delivered changes to the constitution of a Court Martial board. The changes required the CAO to specify Court Martial boards with at least one man and one woman (so far as is reasonably practicable) and to specify an increase from five lay members to six, for proceedings of a prescribed description. Specification of the OR7 rank from the nominated pool of lay members may now also be permitted under the act.
‘OR7 rank’ means any of the following— chief petty officer, staff corporal, staff sergeant, colour sergeant, Royal Marines, flight sergeant, chief technician.

The Military Court Service case management system, Case Center (formerly Caselines)
The Military Court Service partners with Thomson Reuters using Case Center. The application streamlines the way the courts prepare, manage, and present digital cases within a centralised cloud-based solution.
The court will manage proceedings by sending and sharing case materials from any device, keeping all parties in sync as they prepare for a hearing. In a hearing, purpose-built presentation tools streamlines proceedings so parties can direct others to the right document in a timely manner.

Remote observation of Service Court proceedings
Open justice has been a fundamental principle for centuries. The principle is a broad one, but at its core has always been a right of access to a public hearing. Historically, this has meant access for reporters and other members of the public to the court or other room in which the hearing takes place.
The primary legislation is contained in section 85A of the Courts Act 2003 as inserted by section 198 of the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022. The regime is implemented by the Remote Observation and Recording (Courts and Tribunals) Regulations 2022. The power is to “direct that images or sounds of the proceedings be transmitted electronically”. It is to be exercised “for the purpose of enabling persons not taking part in the proceedings to watch or listen to” them. It is not designed for those taking part in the proceedings.
Any person wishing to make an application to the Military Court Service to request permission for the remote observation of a hearing can do so:
Applicants must ensure the court are given at least 3 clear working days to process applications.

Japan's FY2027 budget requests hit record 915 bln USD amid fiscal health worries
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:25:48 CST
19:25:48 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Budget requests from Japanese ministries and agencies for fiscal 2027 reached a record of about 143 trillion yen (around 915 billion U.S. dollars), marking the fourth consecutive year of record highs, the Finance Ministry said Friday.
The 143.07-trillion-yen request came in sharply above the more than 130 trillion yen projection reported by local media in late August, and marked a steep jump from the current fiscal year's initial budget of 122.31 trillion yen.
As many ministries also submitted "itemized requests" without specifying exact amounts, the final budget figure could climb even higher.
According to Kyodo News, the significant increase was driven partly by 12 trillion yen in requests under a new uncapped special investment category created to advance Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's so-called "responsible and proactive" fiscal policy agenda, even as financial markets grow increasingly wary of her government's expanding fiscal commitments.
With outstanding debt twice the size of its economy, Japan's fiscal health is the worst among advanced economies, and rising interest rates are putting further pressure on the country's debt-servicing costs.
Among the requests, the Defense Ministry sought a record of about 8.84 trillion yen. Previous media reports said key spending areas will include procuring large numbers of interceptor drones, introducing artificial intelligence (AI) into command-and-control systems, and further deploying long-range missiles to strengthen what Japan calls "counterstrike capabilities."
The Health, Labor and Welfare Ministry filed the largest request at 36.58 trillion yen, reflecting mounting pension, health care and nursing care costs as the country's population continues to age.
The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry requested 5.70 trillion yen, including 4.53 trillion yen under the investment category for AI, semiconductors and other sectors.
Debt-servicing costs are set at a record 36.64 trillion yen, with the assumed interest rate used to calculate payments raised to 3.8 percent for fiscal 2027 from 3 percent in the fiscal 2026 budget.
Earlier reports suggested that the Japanese government has forecast tax revenue of about 83 trillion yen for fiscal 2026. That means budget requests topping 143 trillion yen will likely lead to new debt issuance, further straining the debt-ridden country's fiscal health.
The draft budget is expected to be finalized by the cabinet by the end of the year. The government plans to submit the budget bill during next year's regular parliamentary session and aims to secure its passage by the end of March. ■

Feature: From subjects to storytellers: ordinary Chinese take the pen
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:25:24 CST
19:25:24 KST

Winners of the Lu Xun Literature Prize in poetry are pictured on stage at an awarding ceremony in east China's Shanghai, Aug. 28, 2026.(Xinhua/Wang Xiang)
by Xinhua writers Zhou Xinyi, Yu Junjie and Zhang Yunlong
SHANGHAI, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- For eight years, Wang Jibing threaded through streets and alleys on his electric scooter, delivering meals, breakfast, lunch or dinner. Last week, he took a very different path, stepping onto the stage at the ceremony for one of China's top literary honors.
There, Wang's poetry collection "Low Flight" won him the Lu Xun Literature Prize, making him the first takeout rider-turned-laureate. His works are now stocked at Beijing's prominent bookshops, and have appeared in The Baffler, a literary journal published in New York.
Beside him on stage was Zhang Ergun, a former geological driller whose poems draw on years spent working in remote mountains and mining regions.
The moment highlighted a broader shift: individuals whose lives have long been subjects of literary works are now picking up the pen, by and for themselves.
According to Yuewen Group, one of China's largest online literature platforms, more than 6,100 delivery riders and over 4,000 truck drivers and ride-hailing drivers are among its creators. Beyond those figures are security guards, cleaners, domestic helpers, farmers, rural teachers and others who write about their lives outside established literary institutions.
One of Wang's best-known poems sprang from a routine delivery stop. While collecting an order from an eatery one afternoon, he noticed the owner asleep on a sofa with her child in her arms.
The scene inspired his poem "Three O'Clock in the Afternoon," in which he wrote: "One dream was holding another dream inside a dream." Trying not to wake them, he quietly picked up the order and left, comparing himself in the poem to a "thief of time" who stole away, if only briefly, part of the hardships carried by the mother and child.
In plainspoken language, Wang captures the rhythms, challenges and moments of warmth that mark the lives of delivery riders: slippery roads during storms, brief exchanges between couriers and customers, and solitary journeys beneath streetlights late at night.
"An excellent writer should move from writing for oneself toward giving voice to others," Wang said at a recent public event in Shanghai. "Life gives you material, and you respond with your work."
Zhang's poetry, however, emerges from a different landscape. His verses portray windswept northern plains, mountain roads, stonemasons and travelers making their way through difficult terrain.
The success of Wang and Zhang offers two examples of the rising "new popular literature and art," a term used to describe creative work rooted in the lived experiences of ordinary people.
Earlier this year, 35 representatives of this literary trend gathered at the National Museum of Modern Chinese Literature in Beijing.
One participant, Li Wenli from northwest China's Gansu Province, worked in Beijing as a domestic helper before writing and publishing a memoir. "I am just an ordinary rural woman," she said. "I never imagined I would write a book."
In Xihaigu, a once-impoverished area of northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, some farmers tend crops by day and craft stories at night. As one local writer put it, "The crops grown from the soil sustain the body. The words grown from the pen sustain the soul."
Bai Ye, honorary president of the Chinese Association of Contemporary Literature, sees "new popular literature and art" as a vivid expression of the nation's creative vitality, saying the trend could encourage more literature lovers to take part in literary creation.
This year's Lu Xun prize for literary theory and criticism went to "Workers Sing of Their Lives: New Popular Literature & Art and the Reconstruction of Literary Spirit," a study examining how new forms of grassroots writing are reshaping literary expression in the digital era.
Its author, Zhuo Jin, poses a pointed question: When ordinary workers pick up the pen to express their own voices, should the boundaries of literature be reconsidered?
What began as individual acts of writing is drawing recognition from literary institutions and scholars alike.
Qiu Huadong, vice chairman of the China Writers Association, said these creators from all walks of life and their new literary and artistic practices are among the clearest signs of a new cultural landscape in China.
"Not every pair of wings can soar high," Wang said after receiving the award. "Flying close to the ground is still a kind of flight." ■

China Focus: Who will care for China's aging countryside?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
18:25:23 CST
19:25:23 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- For about 2,700 yuan (roughly 398 U.S. dollars) a month, Zheng Qiuping washes clothes, feeds the aged who can no longer eat on their own and takes night shifts at a rural home for the elderly in central China.
Most of the caregivers there are themselves in their 50s or 60s.
Zheng's work points to a broader challenge as China's population ages: providing care in rural areas, where caregivers can be hard to recruit and the dispersed population makes home-based services more costly to deliver.
By the end of 2025, China had 320 million people aged 60 or above, accounting for 23 percent of the population. In recent years, the country has expanded its rural eldercare network. As of June 2024, there were about 16,000 rural homes for the elderly with 1.68 million beds, along with roughly 145,000 mutual-aid eldercare facilities.
The physical network is taking shape, yet the harder task is keeping it staffed, financially sustainable and in regular use.
In Xinjin District of Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, 67-year-old Chen Qi has lived at the Huaqiao central home for the elderly for six years.
"Necessities of life are all taken care of, so I don't have much to worry about," Chen said. "I like drinking tea and playing chess with friends."
Over the past three years, Xinjin has allocated 66.94 million yuan in public funding for eldercare services, developing a three-tier network across the district, township and village levels. One district-level facility mainly serves elderly people in extreme difficulty and those with disabilities. At the township and subdistrict level, five eldercare service centers provide professional care and home visits, while 83 village and community sites offer day care, home visits, information and referrals.
The network now reaches more than 10,000 elderly residents, according to local authorities.
Yet building facilities is only part of the equation.
In neighboring Chongqing Municipality, a private eldercare company has taken over the operation of 11 publicly built homes in Banan District since 2023. It has invested nearly 20 million yuan in renovations and can serve 1,125 people.
Managing several facilities together helps lower fixed costs for procurement, staffing and operations. The homes also admit fee-paying residents alongside those covered by government safety-net programs, while offering additional services such as home bathing assistance and rehabilitation. The 11 facilities are now roughly breaking even.
Banan has begun extending the public-built, privately operated model to all 25 of its government-run eldercare homes, said Zhu Zongbo, deputy head of the district civil affairs bureau.
These experiments reflect a broader search for a sustainable way to run rural eldercare facilities.
Keeping operating costs manageable is one part of that effort. Local operators said spending on accessibility upgrades, fire safety, food safety and healthcare has increased in recent years, adding to the cost of running eldercare facilities.
A more persistent issue is finding and retaining enough caregivers. Care work is physically taxing and often poorly paid. Interviews in several regions found that many rural caregivers were in their 50s and 60s.
For Zheng, the pay remains a concern. "I hope the pay can go up in the future," she said.
Training is becoming increasingly important as care needs grow more specialized. Many caregivers can handle basic tasks such as cleaning, meal delivery and assistance with daily activities, but lack the skills needed for more specialized care, from tailored nursing for elderly people with underlying conditions to psychological support and dementia care.
Some local governments are trying to improve pay, training and career prospects for caregivers.
In Wanning, south China's Hainan Province, a publicly built but privately operated eldercare home in Damao Township has more than 120 residents and 31 staff members, including over 20 professional caregivers.
Local caregivers generally undergo training at least once every two years, combining classroom instruction with simulations and hands-on practice. Monthly pay typically ranges from 3,000 to 6,000 yuan, rising above 6,000 yuan for those with medical nursing skills or higher vocational qualifications.
The city also uses government-purchased services and operating subsidies to help institutions improve caregivers' pay, while encouraging career advancement, skills competitions and vocational skill assessments.
Even where facilities are in place, how effectively those facilities are used also matters.
At some rural eldercare sites, space is shared with village public-service centers, an arrangement intended to make better use of existing facilities and save construction costs. In one district in a central Chinese city, such shared sites accounted for about 80 percent of the total.
Local civil affairs officials said administrative work often takes priority, while many of the eldercare sites have no full-time staff. As a result, some offer only limited eldercare services despite having space set aside for that purpose.
The challenge extends beyond the facilities themselves. Providing home-based care can be more costly in rural areas, where older residents are more widely dispersed and transportation is less convenient.
Since Jan. 1, older people across China who are assessed as moderately, severely or fully unable to care for themselves have been eligible for monthly electronic vouchers worth up to 800 yuan to help pay for care services. Issued for 12 months under a nationwide program launched by the Ministry of Civil Affairs and the Ministry of Finance, the vouchers can be used to offset part of the cost of home-based, community-based and institutional care, including meal and bathing assistance, housekeeping, mobility support, rehabilitation nursing and daytime care.
Local officials say further refinement could help the program work better in rural areas, where home-based services are more costly to deliver, and out-of-pocket payments may affect voucher use.
For China's rural eldercare system, expanding the service network has laid an important foundation. The next task is to make that network work better by keeping facilities running, attracting and retaining qualified caregivers, and delivering services efficiently across widely dispersed communities as care needs continue to grow. ■

Flooding along the China-Nepal border has killed at least 1,308 people, with more than 5,600 others still missing, according to Nepalese authorities and Chinese state media.

Finance Minister Marchenko warned of Ukraine’s most difficult budget situation since the start of the war ahead of a &quot;very difficult winter&quot; - media
