13:25:18 EEST
19:25:18 KST

Finance Minister Marchenko warned of Ukraine’s most difficult budget situation since the start of the war ahead of a "very difficult winter" - media
Kyiv • UNN
The Finance Minister forecasts a budget deficit of up to $32.6 billion and a possible postponement of non-military payments. He called on the EU to use Russian assets.
Ukraine’s Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko warned of possible liquidity problems in the state budget and delays in some non-military payments due to rising defense spending. He also called on EU countries to consider a new Ukrainian plan for using frozen Russian assets. Marchenko made the statement in an interview with Euronews, UNN writes.
Details
Ukraine’s finance minister warned that the country may have to cut non-military spending if it is unable to secure funding from its allies. He urged European ministers to "think outside the box" as Kyiv prepares for another winter of Russian escalation.
Serhii Marchenko, who has been responsible for the country’s finances since 2020, told Euronews that Ukraine had not faced such a difficult budgetary situation since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Because of the focus on military spending and weapons procurement, other budget items may suffer, and payments may be delayed if a solution is not found.
We are already seeing some liquidity problems and anticipating a certain shortfall of funds in our budget. This means that due to the lack of liquidity, we may have to postpone some payments unrelated to the war. The consequences will be
Asked whether this could affect external creditors, Marchenko answered that it would not.
At the same time, he said, the consequences may be felt at the local level, particularly with regard to the construction of shelters and infrastructure, which he called "still important," as the country prepares for another winter of Russian attacks.
"We have not faced such a situation since 2022; back then, we really suffered greatly from a lack of liquidity. Now we are again dangerously approaching the same scenario we faced in 2022."
He also reported that the intensity of Russian attacks on Ukraine increased sharply in August. Marchenko said he was working on a new budget based on the assumption that the war would continue into 2027. In his assessment, a funding gap of $32.6 billion would need to be covered. According to him, the IMF, whose representatives visited Kyiv this week, cites similar figures.
The war has escalated very rapidly. We are fully aware of this ourselves. Compared with last month, it is a completely different reality, given the recent attacks on our logistics. We expect a very difficult winter. Escalation means that we need to find the resources to get through it
"Think outside the box"
Ukraine’s finance minister urged European ministers to take a creative approach to finding solutions and consider a new Ukrainian plan to use approximately $300 billion in frozen Russian assets.
Last December, the plan was rejected by EU ministers, who were unable to overcome differences among the member states. Instead, they decided on joint financing for a €90 billion loan.
Last week, a group of EU countries led by Sweden revived the proposal, arguing that the costs of the war effort should be fairly distributed among European taxpayers. Since President Donald Trump took office, the EU has largely been left alone to finance this support.
Marchenko welcomed the move and said he hoped more countries would join the initiative by the scheduled September meeting of eurozone finance ministers.
According to him, the new Ukrainian plan, which provides for the transfer of responsibility for the assets currently held in Belgium, contains "entirely new elements" intended to reduce the legal risks for the Belgian government and Euroclear, where the assets are held.
"We want to discuss this; the plan creates new conditions under which Belgium will not be responsible for legal disputes with Russia, but this will be the shared responsibility of all 27 countries."
However, Ukraine and its allies supporting the plan, including neighboring Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands, and Spain, are facing significant difficulties in trying to revive the idea.
Last December, amid serious concerns from the European Central Bank and strong resistance from key member states — Italy and France — the EU postponed lengthy negotiations on the use of frozen assets.
The reasons cited included concerns about possible retaliatory measures by Russia, reputational damage to the eurozone, and lengthy legal disputes related to possible lawsuits by Moscow over the confiscation of assets.

====================================================================================================

Mad king: how Sanders rebuffs Trump over Hormuz renaming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:22:27 UTC
19:22:27 KST

Senator Bernie Sanders has recently slammed Donald Trump over his reported suggestion to rename the Strait of Hormuz after himself, saying Americans want the president to focus on ending the war in Iran instead. Sanders argued that the conflict has pushed diesel and petrol prices higher, adding that the economic toll of the war matters more than renaming a strategically important waterway.
“You’re the President, not a mad king. Act like it,” Sanders said in a post on X, directly rebuking Trump’s proposal amid the worsening US-Israel-Iran conflict.
The “mad king” in American history clearly refers to King George III of Great Britain, the same king who in the 18th century stood up to the rebellion of the American colonies and eventually accepted American independence in one of the most significant defeats in the history of the British Empire.
The thirteen American colonies entered into conflict with Britain in protest at London’s policies. George III was not willing to simply back down. He was concerned that American independence would not be limited to the secession of these colonies and that other parts of the British Empire would follow suit. Therefore, preserving the authority of the empire was of great importance to him.
But the outcome of the war was exactly the opposite of what London had expected. The Eight Years’ War eventually ended with the defeat of Britain and the recognition of American independence in 1783. This part of history is where Sanders’ quip about Trump makes sense. He is, in effect, trying to connect two historical images: a king who believed he could control rebellion by relying on military might and royal authority, and a president whose critics now accuse him of relying too much on threats, pressure, and displays of power.
Of course, George III cannot be simply summed up as a “mad king.” He did indeed experience periods of severe illness, and at times displayed unusual behavior and extreme agitation. His condition deteriorated sharply in his final years, and he virtually withdrew from the public sphere. However, he spent much of his reign actively, interested in agriculture, art, science, and music; to the point where he was nicknamed “Farmer George.”
The comparison today is also noteworthy in another sense. American historian Rick Atkinson, comparing George III to Trump, said: “George III is Abraham Lincoln compared to Trump.”
This sentence practically shows the intensity of the criticism directed at Trump. Atkinson is not saying that George III was a perfect ruler; rather, he wants to say that even the figure known in American political culture as the “Mad King” can look like a very different person compared to Trump’s behavior and political style.
 
 From this perspective, the issue of the Strait of Hormuz also becomes more important. The Strait of Hormuz is one of the most important energy waterways in the world, and its name was established centuries before the formation of the United States and the current American political system. Therefore, the plan to rename it after a president, even if it is presented in the form of a symbolic or political position, is a sign of excessive personalization of power for Trump’s critics.
Sanders is aiming for exactly this point. He wants to say that in a situation where the war and crisis in Iran have affected regional security and the global economy, the US president should not be concerned with showing personal power or registering his name on a historical waterway.
From Sanders' perspective, the priority should be ending the war; not continuing threats, not expanding the scope of the conflict, and not turning an international crisis into a stage for the president to show off his power.
Of course, this criticism is not only directed at Trump's policy towards Iran. His critics believe that Trump's foreign policy model in many international crises has been based on maximum pressure, military threats, and the use of force to impose America's demands. The problem with such an approach is that showing power does not necessarily mean achieving a political result.
The history of George III provides a classic example of exactly this: military power can temporarily control a crisis, but if it fails to create a political solution, it can ultimately have the opposite effect.George III wanted to preserve the British Empire; he lost America. Now, Sanders says, Trump should also be mindful of the limitations of the presidency, rather than insisting on war and threats.
For that, the phrase “You are the president, not a mad king” should not be seen as a mere verbal attack on Trump. It is actually a reminder of one of the most fundamental political narratives of America: the narrative that the American Revolution was founded on the centralized power of a king and that the new republic was founded on the idea of limited power.
Now, 250 years later, a US senator is presenting the same historical image to his country’s president. Sanders' message is clear: No matter how much military and political power the American president has, he is not meant to be a king; and if war, threats, and displays of power replace politics and diplomacy, history has shown that even the greatest powers may end up achieving precisely the outcome they did not want.
MNA

Advisers to Reform UK’s Farage step down after allegations of electoral law breach
BIRMINGHAM, England - Britain's populist Reform UK said two senior advisers to leader Nigel Farage stepped down on Sept 4 after an undercover investigation alleged the party had broken electoral law by arranging for a foreign donor to pay for political polling.
Reform denied any wrongdoing and said it had been the victim of a hoax perpetrated by climate activists.
The governing Labour Party wrote to the police asking them to investigate possible criminal offences, including an alleged proposal to channel a larger overseas donation through a UK intermediary.
The investigation, broadcast by Channel 4 just as Reform's annual conference opened to the public, said two senior figures in Reform had arranged for a US company to pay more than £30,000 (S$51,450) for three opinion polls commissioned by the party.
Such an arrangement could breach British laws on political funding, which ban foreign donations.
Posing as wealthy donors from the United States with British connections, the undercover team from an investigative group called Verbatim said it spent a year speaking to top officials in Reform about possible donations, culminating in a lunch with Farage.
Channel 4 said Verbatim was an independent organisation founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, but that it had verified their findings, which included covertly filmed footage of meetings.
Farage, a veteran Brexit campaigner who is under parliamentary investigation over earlier donations, told LBC radio: "The party has broken no laws. The party has not taken any dodgy money or anything like that whatsoever."
Poll lead faltered
Reform, which has seen its commanding lead in opinion polls falter over undeclared donor allegations, announced an internal investigation and said the two officials featured in the undercover filming — head of policy James Orr and Farage's right-hand man Dan Jukes — had stepped down pending its results.
Orr, a philosophy professor at the University of Cambridge and friend of US Vice-President J.D. Vance, said in a video on X that Reform had not been involved in commissioning the poll.
"There's absolutely no way this could amount to a benefit or donation in kind at all," he said.
"It wasn't internal party polling. It wasn't Reform UK's poll. It was a public poll arranged by an independent person paying an independent pollster, and those polls were published immediately for the general public."
The latest accusations over donations come on the first public day of the party’s annual conference, which Farage had hoped would offer him a chance of a reset after a difficult summer.
Farage, 62, is being investigated by a parliamentary watchdog over a £5 million donation from crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne in 2024. He denies any wrongdoing but has seen support for his party soften in recent weeks.
Further breaches
On Sept 4, Farage said both Jukes and Orr had "said things that shouldn't have been said" in relation to donations purportedly originating in the United States, but no such donation had been accepted by the party and that the two had been "entrapped".
In a letter to the Metropolitan Police, Labour said the documentary contained two further possible breaches: discussion of channelling a donation from a US-based donor through a UK-based son and the suggestion that similar methods have been used in the past.
A spokesperson for Reform said: "Reform UK has been the target of a hoax perpetrated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors. The party denies any wrongdoing.
"Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission."
The Metropolitan Police said it was aware of the allegations in the broadcast and would assess any information provided to them. This did not amount to the formal launch of an investigation.
The Electoral Commission, which oversees and regulates political finance in Britain, said:
"We are considering all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit, and we are in touch with the Met Police.
"The Electoral Commission has not approved the donor vetting process for Reform, or any other party. Parties are responsible for ensuring their internal processes and controls are fit for purpose." REUTERS

US military turns off ad trackers on devices amid Middle East targeting reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:21:26 UTC
19:21:26 KST

US military turns off ad trackers on devices amid Middle East targeting reports
WASHINGTON – US military officials say they have disabled advertising trackers on a range of phones and computers, according to letters released on Sept 4 by US Senator Ron Wyden and statements given to Reuters, a development that follows reports that commercially available location data had been used to target American forces in the Middle East.
The Air Force told Wyden that it disabled the advertising identifiers on computers and mobile phones two months ago.
US Special Operations Command said in a separate letter that it had “recently” disabled them on its Windows devices.
The Army told Reuters that advertising IDs tied to mobile devices had been disabled since earlier in 2026.
Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, has pressed the Pentagon on the issue for months.
The disclosures highlight a growing national security concern: that location data collected by the advertising industry and sold by data brokers – companies that collate and resell personal data – can be used to track and target military personnel deployed to war zones.
The Air Force and Special Operations Command declined further comment.
Similar letters from the Army and Navy to Wyden said they disabled advertising IDs on military devices but gave no indication of when the restrictions were imposed.
The Army said in a statement that advertising IDs had been blocked on Windows computers “since before 2021” but that Android and Apple mobile devices had only had it disabled by default “since at least February 2026”.
Messages seeking comment from the Navy went unreturned.
The effort to reduce the location data generated by smartphones comes as military officials weigh increasingly strict restrictions on phone use overall.
In July, Reuters reported that some deployed personnel in the Middle East could be ordered to surrender their phones amid concerns that mobile videos they were posting to the internet were helping Iran target American bases in the region.
Wyden and US Representative Pat Harrigan, a North Carolina Republican, sent a letter to the Pentagon on Sept 4 asking for an investigation into whether the military had properly countered the dangers of the location data trade.
The letter included the updates from the various service branches on their efforts to disable advertising IDs on military devices.
Wyden said in a statement that it was clear that the military’s efforts “have not been effective at neutralising this threat”. Harrigan said that US enemies “should not be able to pull out a credit card and buy information that helps them track American troops”.
The Pentagon said in an e-mail it would respond to the lawmakers directly.
Mobile advertising IDs, often abbreviated MAID, are unique identifiers tied to specific devices that can be used to track a person’s activity across mobile apps and pinpoint their physical location.
Zach Edwards, co-founder of privacy ad tech company Decryptads, said that efforts to disable MAID on military-operated devices were “definitely a positive thing”.
The restrictions “will essentially ensure their location isn’t being included in bulk data sales being done by numerous vendors”, although he cautioned that personnel might still be tracked through apps in other more complicated ways, for example by triangulating technical device details with network data or location information. How the war changed Ukrainian cinema - key takeaways from 2026 Odesa International Film Festival
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:20:54 EEST
19:20:54 KST

How the war changed Ukrainian cinema - key takeaways from 2026 Odesa International Film Festival
Kyiv • UNN
The 17th Odesa International Film Festival has concluded in Kyiv. Over the course of nine days, audiences were shown more than 80 films across ten programs, including 13 Ukrainian films in the National Competition. Professional discussions about how to develop Ukrainian cinema during the war and where to find resources for new projects were an important part of the festival.
The 17th Odesa International Film Festival has concluded in Kyiv; it ran from August 27 to September 4. This year, the festival screened more than 80 Ukrainian and foreign films in ten programmes. The National Competition featured 13 Ukrainian full-length films. In addition to film screenings, the OIFF hosted professional panels with directors, producers, actors, veterans and other industry representatives, UNN reports.
Cinema of the New Reality
The 17th OIFF was held in Kyiv for the third time. Due to the full-scale war and security risks, the festival was temporarily relocated from Odesa to the capital. This year, the main festival venues were the Zhovten and Oscar cinemas. In total, viewers had the opportunity to watch more than 80 films in ten programmes.
The National Competition programme was particularly notable this year. Only films whose production was completed in 2025 or 2026 were selected for it. In other words, these works were created during Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine.
One of the festival’s main premieres was Valentyn Vasyanovych’s dystopian film "For Victory!". The director does not show the war itself; he looks further ahead—to post-war Ukraine, where victory does not at all mean a return to normal life. According to the plot, the protagonist is a film director who remains in the country but can no longer work as he did before. His wife and daughter have lived in Vienna for several years and see no reason to return. Through this personal story, Vasyanovych addresses the contemporary problems of broken families, emigration and what awaits people in a country where the war has ended but pre-war life has not returned.
The National Competition also included Denys Kolesnikov’s "Kira’s Dream" and Serhii Storozhev’s "The Soloist".
Documentary films also stood out at the international film festival. Viewers were impressed by Yevhen Titarenko’s work—the film "Generation 2014". For ten years, the filmmaker filmed six volunteers from the Hospitallers medical battalion. The film shows how the war, which began for them in 2014, changed their lives and influenced their personal development.
"Peace for Nina" by Zhanna Dovhych tells the story of Nina Branovytska—the mother of Donetsk Airport defender Ihor Branovytskyi, who was captured in 2015, tortured and killed by Russians. In the film, the fallen soldier’s mother searches for witnesses, reconstructs the circumstances of her son’s death and seeks punishment for those responsible.
The subject of war also appeared in the International Competition. In the Bulgarian-Greek film "Dirty Money—White Nights" by Kristina Grozeva and Petar Valchanov, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine destroys the plans of a married couple who had been saving money for a trip to St. Petersburg. Through this story, the filmmakers portray people trying to remain "above politics", even when the war is already directly affecting their lives.
Gábor Holtai’s Hungarian film "Like Home" is structured as a surrealist thriller but in fact tells the story of the mechanisms of an authoritarian state—when lies gradually become the norm if society agrees to accept them.
The OIFF also presented the "Festival of Festivals" programme, featuring films that had already received awards at international film festivals. These included the winner of the Sundance-2026 Grand Jury Prize, "The Mischievous Bear" by Gabriela Osio Vanden and Jack Weisman, and "The Tin Castle" by Alexander Murphy, which was recognised in Cannes.
How has Russia’s war against Ukraine changed the film industry?
In addition to screenings, the Film Industry Office professional section operated at the OIFF. Here, film-industry representatives discussed not individual films but the problems facing the industry itself during the war.
Topics included financing new projects, international cooperation, the distribution of Ukrainian films, the work of television channels and streaming platforms, as well as how cinema should address the subjects of war, military personnel and veterans.
A separate block of discussions was devoted to veterans.
At the panel "Veterans, War and Cinema: New Heroes, New Professions", participants discussed the involvement of military personnel in the film and television sectors, not only as on-screen heroes but also as part of film crews and creative teams. The discussion was attended by Yegor Skalyha, founder of the BRIGHT POINT Skalyha Foundation; producer and veteran Volodymyr Yatsenko; director, actor and serviceman Akhtem Seitablaiev; Dmytro Khrypun, general producer of ICTV2's serial production; Maksym Sukhenko, host and producer at 2+2; and Lesia Prymakova, Work.ua's Director of Communications and Partnerships. The panel was moderated by television presenter Yuliia Zorii.
Producer and veteran Volodymyr Yatsenko pointed out that the Ukrainian situation differs from the classic idea of a veteran: thousands of people who worked in film, business, culture and other fields before the war went to the front. And after their service, far from all of them will be able simply to return to their former lives.
"We are civilians who went to war. The only thing to remember about trauma is that it is very important. Many people are waiting, it seems to me, for them to return the way they were. (...) They will be somewhat different from how they were," Yatsenko said.
Yegor Skalyha, who worked in cinema for around 20 years before the full-scale war, stressed that the industry itself has many professions in which military experience can become an advantage. These include the work of set constructors, lighting technicians, administrators, drivers and other members of a film crew.
"A person who is capable of building themselves a shelter in a dugout will certainly also be capable of building a set—a three-room apartment—in two days. So there are many points of entry," Skalyha noted.
He agreed with Yatsenko's view that employers will also have to take into account the consequences of war—health, memory or psychological problems. According to Skalyha, in such cases it is important not to reject a person, but to consider where they have returned from and help them adapt.
This is one of the fundamental changes that the war has brought to Ukrainian culture. For cinema, a veteran is no longer only a character. It is a future screenwriter, director or cinematographer.
Cinema is already shaping the image of the Ukrainian military with which the country will live for decades. That is why the Film Industry Office held a separate discussion about the ethics of working with women in the military, the boundary between artistic intent and the psychological safety of the heroes, as well as who has the right to tell someone else's combat experience at all.
Other discussions focused on how Ukraine will remember this war and where the boundary lies between art, documentation and propaganda.
"Culture is our space. And this space gives us the strength to be ourselves. By defending it, we are thus resisting," said Vadym Karpiak, spokesperson for the 8th Corps of the Ukrainian Air Assault Forces, during a panel on cultural resistance.
In fact, the point is that after 2022, culture in Ukraine lost the possibility of existing separately from the war. Even a film that is not about the war is created by people who live through war, lose loved ones, experience mass emigration and are already shaping the memory of events that will define the country for generations to come.
Not Waiting for the War to Become History
The symbolic guest of this year's festival was Bosnian director and screenwriter Danis Tanović. His feature-film debut, "No Man's Land," based on his own experience working as a documentarian during the Bosnian War, received an Oscar, a Golden Globe and the award for Best Screenplay at the Cannes Film Festival.
At the Odesa International Film Festival, Tanović was presented with the Lifetime Achievement Award for his contribution to world cinema. Presenting the award, festival president Viktoriia Tihipko called on Ukrainian directors not to wait until the war becomes history, but to talk about it now.
This thought aptly captures the mood of this year’s festival. Ukrainian cinema reflects on the war and speaks about loss and pain, veterans, emigration, and the country’s future. At the same time, filmmakers are seeking a way not to reduce all Ukrainian cinema solely to wartime themes and to leave room for other stories.

Top 5 recipes for preserving cucumbers for the winter that will turn out perfectly the first time
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:20:30 EEST
19:20:30 KST

Top 5 recipes for preserving cucumbers for the winter that will turn out perfectly the first time
Kyiv • UNN
UNN presents a selection of five recipes for homemade cucumber preserves: pickled, garlic, mustard, oil-based, and spicy with sesame.
Crisp, piquant, or spicy? UNN has put together a top 5 list of recipes for homemade cucumber preserves that can be prepared for the winter.
Which cucumbers are best for preserving
For homemade preserves, it is best to use young, slightly underripe cucumbers. They have a more delicate texture and are well suited for pickling. Cucumbers for preserving are classified by size: the smallest, 3–5 cm long, are called picules, fruits 5–9 cm long are gherkins, and cucumbers from 9 to 12 cm are considered pickling cucumbers. It is advisable to process harvested cucumbers as quickly as possible. Before preserving, they should be sorted, damaged or soft fruits removed, and the cucumbers arranged by size. It is better not to mix large and small cucumbers in the same jar. The first harvest from the plant can also be used for preserves, as such cucumbers are particularly well suited for home canning.
Top 5 best recipes for canned cucumbers
Classic pickled cucumbers
Ingredients:
-  water - 1 l; 
-  salt - 2 tbsp.; 
-  sugar - 2 tbsp.; 
-  6% vinegar - 2 tbsp. or approximately 1.5 tbsp. of 9% vinegar; 
-  cucumbers - the amount depends on the volume of the jars; 
-  dill - 1–2 umbrellas; 
-  garlic -  2-3 cloves; 
-  horseradish - a piece of root or 1 leaf; 
-  black peppercorns - several; 
-  currant or cherry leaves - optional. 
Preparation
Wash the cucumbers well and leave them in cold water for 3–4 hours.
Place some of the dill, garlic, horseradish, and pepper on the bottom of the prepared jars.
Fill the jars with cucumbers, arranging them as tightly as possible.
Pour boiling water over the cucumbers, cover with lids, and leave for approximately 10 minutes.
Pour the water into a saucepan, add the salt and sugar, and bring to a boil.
Finally, pour in the vinegar.
Pour the hot marinade over the cucumbers, filling the jars to the very top.
Close the jars with lids, leave them to cool, and then transfer them to a cool, dark place.
Cucumbers with garlic
Ingredients:
-  cucumbers - 1 kg; 
-  water - 500 ml; 
-  sugar - 100 g; 
-  salt - 1 tbsp.; 
-  9% vinegar - 100 ml; 
-  garlic -  3
cloves. 
Preparation
Pour the water into a saucepan and add the sugar, salt, and vinegar.
Bring the mixture to a boil, then leave it to cool.
Place the cucumbers and garlic in a sterilized jar.
Pour the cooled marinade over the contents and cover with a sterilized lid.
Place a towel on the bottom of a large saucepan, put the jar inside, and pour in water up to the jar’s shoulders.
Once the water boils, sterilize the jar for 10–15 minutes.
Remove the jar, screw on the lid, wrap it, and leave it until completely cool.
Cucumbers with mustard
Ingredients:
-  cucumbers -1.5–2 kg; 
-  water - 2 l; 
-  dill umbrellas - 1-2 pcs.; 
-  oak leaves - 1-2 pcs.; 
-  cherry leaves - 2 pcs.; 
-  horseradish leaves - 
1-2 pcs.; 
-  bay leaves - 2-3 pcs.; 
-  black peppercorns - 5-7 pcs.; 
-  garlic - 3 cloves; 
-  cloves - to taste; 
-  chili pepper - 1 pc.; 
-  salt - 4 tbsp.; 
-  mustard - 2 tbsp. 
Preparation
Place the dill, oak, cherry, and horseradish leaves, bay leaves, pepper, and cloves on the bottom of a three-liter jar.
Add the garlic and hot pepper, then fill the jar with cucumbers.
Pour the water into a saucepan, add the salt, and boil until completely dissolved.
Pour the hot brine over the cucumbers, cover the jar with a lid, and leave it to cool at room temperature.
After two days, add the mustard, close the jar, and shake it well. Leave it for another 6 hours.
Pour the brine into a saucepan and boil for approximately 5 minutes.
Pour it over the cucumbers again.
Screw the lids onto the jars.
Cucumbers with garlic in an oil marinade
Ingredients:
-  cucumbers - 4 kg; 
-  sugar - 1 cup; 
-  9% vinegar - 1 cup; 
-  oil - 1 cup; 
-  ground black pepper - 1 tbsp.; 
-  salt - 2 tbsp.; 
-  garlic - 3 heads. 
Preparation
Wash the cucumbers and cut off the ends.
Cut each cucumber lengthwise into four pieces.
Grate or finely chop the garlic.
Separately mix the sugar, vinegar, oil, salt, and pepper. The marinade does not need to be boiled.
Combine the cucumbers with the garlic and marinade.
Leave the mixture in a cold place for at least 7 hours, preferably overnight.
Arrange the cucumbers in jars and pour over the liquid that has formed.
Sterilize the jars for 10 minutes and seal them.
Spicy sweet-and-sour cucumbers with sesame
Ingredients:
-  cucumbers - 2.5 kg; 
-  non-iodized salt - 2.5 tbsp.; 
-  sugar - 3.5 tbsp.; 
-  sesame seeds - 70 g; 
-  garlic - 7 cloves; 
-  red hot peppers - 3 pcs.; 
-  sweet paprika - 2 tbsp.; 
-  odorless oil - 10 tbsp.; 
-  soy sauce - 2 tbsp.; 
-  essence of vinegar - 1 tsp. 
Preparation
Wash the cucumbers, pat them dry, cut off the ends, and cut them into sticks approximately 5 mm thick and up to 2.5 cm long.
Add salt, mix, and leave for 40 minutes–1 hour. Stir from time to time.
Squeeze the cucumbers well and transfer them to another container.
Toast the sesame seeds in a dry frying pan.
Chop the garlic and add it to the cucumbers.
Crush the hot pepper or cut it into thin rings.
Add the pepper, sesame seeds, paprika, soy sauce, and sugar to the cucumbers.
Pour in the vinegar essence and mix everything.
Heat the oil until very hot and immediately pour it over the cucumbers, then mix again.
Some can be set aside for consumption without sterilization—it should be kept in the refrigerator.
Distribute the rest among sterilized jars, cover with lids, and sterilize for 30 minutes after the water comes to a boil, for 0.5-liter jars.
Seal the jars and store them in a cellar or pantry.

Malaysia declares emergency in Sarawak town as haze pollution level hits 521

The Air Pollutant Index in Serian, a small agricultural town of just under 90,000 near the border of Indonesia’s Kalimantan province, surged to 521 on Friday, according to Malaysia’s environment department. Sarawak’s much larger capital, Kuching, also showed a hazardous reading of 311.

Haze is a recurring seasonal problem in Southeast Asia, where smoke from forest and peat fires in Indonesia can travel across national borders and affect neighbouring Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore.
Sarawak has been the worst-hit Malaysian state by the haze, with several areas having hazardous air levels in the past few days.
The haze this year has been particularly severe, with elevated fire activity in several provinces in Indonesia, including Kalimantan, and prolonged dry conditions contributing to worsening pollution across parts of Borneo.

UK moves to secure critical minerals for defence
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:14:26 BST
19:14:26 KST

The Ministry of Defence is working to reduce reliance on concentrated sources of critical minerals used by the defence sector, including through alternative suppliers, allied investment and domestic production, Defence Minister Luke Pollard has said.
Responding to a written parliamentary question, Pollard set out work under way to improve the resilience of critical raw material supply chains and reduce exposure to individual suppliers and higher-risk sources.
Pollard said: “The Department is addressing dependencies on concentrated sources of Critical Minerals likely to be affecting the defence sector by improving visibility and enhancing collaboration with industry and like-minded Allies (including NATO and Australia).”
He added: “Efforts focus on developing alternative sources of supply, investing in allied capacity, ensuring security of supply and promoting recycling and substitution to reduce reliance on single suppliers and high-risk geographies.”
The work forms part of the Government’s wider Vision 2035: UK Critical Mineral Strategy, with the MOD involved in implementing measures intended to strengthen access to materials required by defence and advanced industries.
Australia is one of the countries involved in that work, of course. Pollard said: “MOD is also playing an active role in implementing Vision 2035: UK Critical Mineral Strategy through this work, and on 10 June, signed a new Joint Statement of Intent with Australia on collaboration to secure critical minerals supply chains for Defence.”
The Government is also backing efforts to restore a domestic source of tungsten through the Hemerdon mine in Devon. Pollard said: “Furthermore, the UK Government is investing £71 million through the National Wealth Fund to restart Tungsten West’s Hemerdon mine in Devon, securing the ability to negotiate over the next 6 months for a domestic supply of tungsten, a strategically important mineral used in defence and advanced industries.”
Tungsten is used across a range of industrial and defence applications where high density, strength and resistance to heat are required. The Government’s investment in Hemerdon is intended to give the UK an opportunity to negotiate access to domestic production rather than relying entirely on overseas sources.
The MOD’s work also covers recycling and material substitution, alongside efforts to identify alternative suppliers and increase production capacity among allied countries. The department is working with NATO and Australia as part of that effort, while also seeking better visibility of where defence-related supply chains remain exposed to concentrated sources.
Pollard said the work reflected the growing importance of these materials to both the economy and national security, with early discussions identifying areas where countries face common supply risks.
He stated: “This recognises that critical minerals are essential to our modern economy and increasingly our national security, with initial exchanges identifying opportunities for closer collaboration on shared critical mineral supply risks.”

Zehut party chairman Moshe Feiglin said that he fully forgave Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich for the harsh comments made against him in the past, while discussing their parties' joint run in the upcoming election with 103FM on Thursday.
“I think what you do not understand is that it is possible to forgive as well,” Feiglin explained. “We are in the month of mercy and forgiveness. The fact that I truly forgive is not just lip service. You probably have not experienced the pressure of political campaigns, during which he said those things. I have experienced it, and I can understand how a person gets to that point. I forgot about it, and now you are reminding me.”
Feiglin went on to clarify the planned political arrangement, explaining that the Zehut party and the Religious Zionist Party were running as a technical bloc. “We are a completely separate party from the Religious Zionist Party. We respect it, but we will run a separate campaign and operate separately afterward. After the elections, each party will go its own way, without a doubt. I believe we are going to bring five Knesset seats in the upcoming elections, and the connection with Smotrich will bring a double digit number of mandates, ‘read my lips.’”
One of Feiglin’s demands is the Defense Ministry portfolio. When asked, “How can a person who is irresponsible and megalomaniacal be defense minister?” Feiglin chuckled and responded, “With all due respect, the person who has been fighting Oslo for 30 years and the processes that led to the massacre, I was your loyal servant. The line represented by the Zehut party is a line that knew how to predict this massacre better than all the generals.”
The discussion later turned to security issues and the Israel-Hamas War. Feiglin strongly criticized the handling of the campaign and explained why he opposed hostage release deals.
“I think this deal will lead to the next kidnappings. I did oppose it, and I still oppose it,” he said emphatically. “The hostages could have been brought back after two weeks simply by shutting off Gaza’s water supply, a real siege. The first decision should have been that Gaza must be defeated immediately, and that this problem must be eliminated rather than leaving future generations with another round of kidnappings and massacres.”
October 7 was fault of both right and left, Feiglin claims
Regarding responsibility for the October 7 failure, Feiglin refused to point a finger at the political leadership.
“Responsibility for the massacre is divided equally between both sides, between the left and the right,” he claimed. “Although the left, through Oslo, brought the terrorists to the doorstep of the kindergartens of Kibbutz Be’eri and directly caused the terrible massacre, the right, which came to power in 1996 and did not cancel Oslo, cannot avoid responsibility. But one thing I do know: shortly before October 7, there was a terrible betrayal here by those who did everything they could to openly dismantle the army, especially with foreign state money.”
Regarding the establishment of a state commission of inquiry, Feiglin expressed reservations about the involvement of the judiciary, saying that while he believed a commission of inquiry must be established, "at the same time, the High Court of Justice is a political party. Middle Israel: Why is Sara Netanyahu going to war against Yair Golan? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:12:05 UTC
19:12:05 KST

Having survived his ship’s bombardment and emerged bewildered from the Mediterranean into which he was thrown, Menachem Begin resolved to turn military defeat into moral victory.
The consequent twisting of the confrontation’s events, from who provoked the Altalena war to who waged it, was discussed here last week. Yet Begin twisted another fact, concerning the size and significance of the cargo on the arms ship he led to Tel Aviv in June 1948.
Emerging that evening on the Irgun’s radio station, Begin delivered his famous address in which he ordered his men not to join a prospective civil war. While at it, he claimed that his crippled vessel had carried “10,000 aerial bombs.” Had those bombs joined the Independence War along with the cargo’s rifles and machine guns, “we might have been standing today on the Jordan, and maybe even beyond it,” Begin asserted.
In fact, that number was far-fetched, and so was the strategic claim attached to it – a sequel to Begin’s earlier suggestion that “the ship of salvation” would “decide the fate of the war.” (Avi Shilon, Begin: 1913-1992, Am Oved 2007, pp. 127, 135).
In fact, Begin’s cargo was but a fraction of what David Ben-Gurion had already secured half a year earlier, through an extensive arms deal with Czechoslovakia that included 50,000 rifles, 6,000 machine guns, and 20 fighter planes. This was besides 14,000 submachine guns and mortars that the Hagana had obtained and manufactured before 1948.
Begin’s twisting of the facts came to mind this week as Sara Netanyahu – whom this column has generally refrained from discussing – made an even more preposterous quip about one of her husband’s rivals, the Democrats’s Yair Golan.
'I don't want to talk'
“YOU CLAIM you fought on October 7,” she said on Channel 14, referring to Golan, suggesting he did not fight. “Early in the morning,” she continued, “you were already there, dressed and ready at a very early hour, while others, like the prime minister, didn’t know.” Asked whether there was treason that day, she didn’t say “God forbid,” or “let’s not get carried away,” or “are you out of your mind?” Rather, “I don’t want to talk.”
Yet talk she did, and her insinuation was as transparent as it was flabbergasting. Golan, according to this “conspiracism,” had advance information of the enemy’s invasion, and was part of it.
Golan is no political genius. He made some outrageous statements and seems clueless about his party’s domestic agenda, as well as its history as the engine of Zionist pioneering. That is why most voters don’t consider him a suitable candidate for prime minister. But this does not mean he is a villain, let alone a traitor. In fact, Golan is a major-league patriot.
In contrast to Sara Netanyahu’s hallucination, Golan rushed to the western Negev once news of Hamas’s massacre broke out. There are testimonies of people he personally saved and of others who fought alongside him, like Oz Davidian of Moshav Patish, who said he and Golan jointly rescued people from the Supernova music festival’s bloodbath.
No one can rob Golan of these heroic credentials. And so, the question arises: why did Sara Netanyahu utter the libel that Golan did not deserve, and which the swing vote will not reward? And the answer is that she twisted the facts of 2023 for the same reason Menachem Begin twisted the facts of 1948.
 
LIBELS ARE invented when the facts are impossible to refute, and their results are impossible to bear. 
Begin could not justify his reckless refusal to unconditionally hand the Altalena’s arms to the sovereign Jewish state. He therefore tried to shift the blame from those who made the provocation to those who responded to it. Similarly, the lie that his unsolicited arms shipment could have changed the course of the war was meant to change the subject, from his reckless misjudgment, to the war’s results.
Now Sara Netanyahu and the rest of the October 7 conspiracists cannot bear Benjamin Netanyahu’s misjudgments en route to that catastrophe. That is why they, and the entire ruling party, twist the facts and invent libels.
Likud’s denialism did not start with Begin’s lies in 1948.
Disastrous moves or fateful mistakes?
BEGIN’S MENTOR, Ze’ev Jabotinsky, made two disastrous moves that his followers would never admit were fateful mistakes. First, in 1923, he resigned from the Zionist Organization’s executive; second, in 1935, he made his Revisionist party secede from the Zionist Organization to establish a competing outfit, the New Zionist Organization.
It was a separatist mindset that culminated in the creation of a separate militia that challenged the Jewish Agency and its military arm, the Hagana. Jabotinsky thus condemned himself and his followers to history’s margins, where they remained for 37 years after his death.
Admitting that their irrelevance was their leader’s fault was mentally impossible for his followers. He was infallible. Begin never admitted that his mentor’s legacy of going it alone was catastrophic to himself, his followers, and the Zionist cause. Now that same spirit of “we can’t be wrong” and “it’s us or them” is governing the Netanyahu couple’s treatment of the past three years’ events.
That is why Sara Netanyahu, her husband, and the ruling party refuse to assume responsibility for what happened on October 7: not Benjamin Netanyahu’s funding of Hamas, not his rejection of pleas to attack Hamas, and not his 2004 vote for the unilateral withdrawal from Gaza – an idea that was conceived and executed not by Golan or any other lefty, but by a government led by the Likud.
Repenting for any of this does not cross their minds. Like Begin before them, they will finger anyone but themselves. Yet Begin had a good excuse for his denialism and lies: his Jewish enemies had aimed a cannon at him, and fired. What’s your excuse, Sara?
The writer, a Hartman Institute fellow, is the author of the bestseller, The Jewish March of Folly (Yedioth Books 2026), now available in English on Amazon.

Israel cannot prevent another October 7 if Netanyahu keeps rewriting the first one - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:11:57 UTC
19:11:57 KST

“We are getting dangerously close to a violent, multifront confrontation. According to reports from the security establishment, the number of warnings in Judea and Samaria is unprecedented.
“The ones who will pay the price are our children, who will once again have to enter the Jenin refugee camp, once again go into Gaza, and perhaps once again into Lebanon. The ones who will pay the price are our parents, who will once again have to sit in their safe rooms.”
These words sound like something that could have been said yesterday. They were, however, spoken by Yair Lapid, the head of the opposition, three years ago this month, on September 20, 2023 – just a couple of weeks before the Hamas invasion on October 7.
Lapid later explained that he decided to go before the cameras with such a stark, dire warning after receiving one of the regular monthly security briefings given to the opposition leader by the prime minister and his military secretary. During that meeting, Lapid said, he was shown some of the most sensitive and classified intelligence collected by Israel’s security establishment.
The message, as he understood it, was clear: Israel’s enemies were watching the deep divisions tearing through Israeli society over the government’s judicial overhaul. They saw weakness and vulnerability. And they believed there might be an opportunity to strike.
That was why, on the eve of Yom Kippur in 2023, Lapid issued his warning. He could hardly have been more prophetic. Two-and-a-half weeks later, Hamas invaded Israel. Our children were sent to fight in Gaza, Jenin, and eventually Lebanon. Our parents – and the rest of us – were sent running to bomb shelters and safe rooms.
October 7 to play a role in next election
From the moment elections were called for the end of October, it was obvious that October 7 would play a central role in every political party’s campaign. What was less obvious was the extent to which the disaster would become the subject of manipulation, distortion, and outright fabrication, particularly by members of the governing coalition determined to deflect criticism and wash their hands of responsibility for the greatest catastrophe to befall the Jewish people since the Holocaust, a catastrophe that happened on their watch.
That is how we need to look at the interview that Sara Netanyahu gave this week to Channel 14 in which she attempted to tarnish the reputation of Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats Party, who famously put on his uniform on the morning of October 7, drove south, and helped rescue Israelis from the killing fields around the Supernova music festival.
Like so many heroic Israelis who saw their fellow citizens in mortal danger that morning, Golan did not wait for orders. A former deputy IDF chief of staff, he took his sidearm and headed toward the fighting, repeatedly entering an area crawling with terrorists to rescue people and bring them to safety.
Yet Sara Netanyahu insinuated that Golan must somehow have had advance knowledge that something was about to happen, because he put on his uniform that morning – while her husband, the prime minister, had not been woken by the heads of the security establishment.
It was a disgusting accusation. It not only suggested some sort of conspiracy against Benjamin Netanyahu, but cast suspicion on a man who risked his own life to save others. To question the integrity, courage, and motives of Israelis who voluntarily entered a combat zone that morning is appalling.
While her comments were rightly condemned across the political spectrum, Sara Netanyahu is not really the story. She is the prime minister’s wife, not an elected official, and her comments should not consume too much of our attention.
The more important story is the coalition itself, which continues to do all it can to evade responsibility.
While Sara was in the headlines, Netanyahu was also pushing his new claim – had he been woken at 4 or 5 a.m. on October 7, he would have made decisions that could have prevented the Hamas invasion. Why wasn’t he woken? Because, he suggested, the security chiefs knew that he would force them to act, and they did not want him to.
There are several problems with this argument. The first is that it is highly unlikely Netanyahu would have done what he now claims.
Had he been woken, he would have heard from IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi, Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) director Ronen Bar, and Military Intelligence chief Aharon Haliva. All three would have given him essentially the same assessment they themselves mistakenly believed as they analyzed the little intelligence that was coming in that night: Hamas was probably not preparing for a major attack, and if something was going to happen, it would be limited in scope.
With every senior security official presenting essentially the same assessment, does anyone seriously believe Netanyahu would have ordered Israel to launch a war against Hamas at 4 or 5 in the morning?
Far more likely, he would have instructed them to remain vigilant, continue monitoring the situation, and reconvene a few hours later.
That, essentially, was the catastrophic mistake that Amir Bohbot and I describe in our book While Israel Slept. The warning signs were there, but they were interpreted through an intelligence framework that assumed Hamas did not want a major war.
But Netanyahu’s political objective now is to portray October 7 as exclusively their failure, a tactical intelligence breakdown that had nothing to do with him, his policies, or the strategy he pursued toward Hamas for years.
That strategy included containing Hamas, allowing Qatari money to flow into Gaza, and repeatedly deciding against using the IDF to remove Hamas from power.
Keeping the national debate focused narrowly on the intelligence and operational failures of the night of October 6 and the early hours of October 7 serves Netanyahu politically. It keeps attention away from the much larger question of strategy: how Israel reached a point where Hamas was able to build an army on the other side of the border, prepare an invasion for years, and convince Israeli leaders that it had no intention of using it.
The second problem with Netanyahu’s argument is even more fundamental.
It is a wrong illustration of leadership. Leadership is supposed to mean understanding that subordinates will sometimes make mistakes – even catastrophic ones – and that ultimate responsibility rests with the person at the top.
Sometimes I wonder what would have happened politically had Netanyahu chosen a different path after October 7. What if he had gone to the funerals of those murdered and visited their families during shiva? What if he had stood before the families and heard their yells and criticism, had appeared before the Israeli public and said something simple: I failed. What if he had publicly grieved for the 1,200 people massacred on his watch and accepted even a measure of responsibility for what happened?
Perhaps it would even have helped him politically. Perhaps showing compassion, humility, and accountability would have won back some of the Israelis who turned away from him after October 7.
It is an interesting thought experiment, but that is all it is. Because Netanyahu’s political doctrine has long been clear: never accept responsibility, never admit failure, and, above all, never say sorry.
The tragedy is that nearly three years after October 7, Israel is not only still fighting over who was responsible for the failures of that day. It is heading into an election in which those failures are being rewritten in real time.
And a country that cannot honestly confront how it reached October 7 will have a much harder time ensuring that another one can never happen.
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD Forum, a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His latest book (with Amir Bohbot), While Israel Slept, is a bestseller in the United States.

European states criticize Israel, but keep relying on its defense technology - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:11:44 UTC
19:11:44 KST

The gap between Israel’s diplomatic relations with several European countries and the security ties they continue to maintain with Jerusalem is widening. Even countries that have escalated their rhetoric, imposed sanctions, and limited political ties with Israel are not rushing to abandon Israeli weapons systems, technology, and defense equipment.
“Most countries maintain a certain degree of duality,” political officials familiar with the issue say.
Spain is the most prominent example. In September 2025, Madrid adopted a law intended to establish a broad embargo on weapons and defense equipment involving Israel, including restrictions on exports to Israel and imports from Israel. Israeli officials say that in practice, the embargo is not airtight, in part because the law allows the government to approve exceptions when it determines that the national interest requires it.
“There is nothing airtight, and they are not following it either,” Israeli officials say.
According to political officials, defense deals with Spain continued even after the law took effect, including activities permitted under the exemption mechanism.
The Spanish law includes an exception allowing the government to approve deals that would otherwise be prohibited if fully implementing the restrictions would harm “general national interests.” In some cases, therefore, defense activity is not taking place in violation of the embargo, but under the exemption clause that Madrid itself included in the legislation.
The Spanish government has already used the exception to allow Airbus to continue using Israeli technology in strategic projects after determining that completely halting its use could harm production capabilities, jobs and defense projects for which there is no immediate alternative.
Discussions held in Spain also highlighted the country’s continued dependence on Israeli technology, licenses and technical support for several defense systems. Fully replacing these components and systems is not possible in the immediate term and would entail high costs and the development of local or European alternatives.
Madrid has canceled deals with Israel, and Jerusalem does not claim that the embargo exists only on paper. Spain has halted certain purchases and projects and is working to reduce its defense dependence on Israel. However, the exemptions included in the law allow the Spanish government to continue defense cooperation with Israel when it determines that national interests require it.
The Netherlands is also advancing measures against trade with settlements
The Netherlands, for example, is advancing measures against trade with settlements, while its Defense Ministry continues to purchase Israeli systems when no available alternative exists. The Dutch government has publicly stated that, in certain fields, Israeli companies provide essential systems or components for which there is currently no suitable, available Dutch or European replacement.
In Finland, as public and political debate surrounding Israel intensified, Helsinki quietly extended its defense cooperation agreement with Israel until 2034. The agreement, which covers research and development and defense procurement, was renewed in 2024, after the war in Gaza had already begun.
The renewal was initiated by Finland and extended the agreement for 10 years, compared with five years under previous arrangements. The Finnish Defense Ministry did not announce the decision at the time.
The relationship with Israeli defense industries plays a significant role in Finnish defense procurement. Israel is Finland’s second-largest foreign defense supplier and provides systems such as the David’s Sling and Gabriel missiles. Finland has explained that maintaining the relationship is necessary to carry out existing deals, maintenance, and long-term cooperation.
In Germany, expanded defense cooperation with Israel continues even as Berlin has voiced criticism of Israeli policy on issues including E1 and settlements. The Arrow 3 deal and its expansion have made Germany one of the main customers of Israel’s defense industry and were among the factors that helped drive Israeli defense exports to a new record.
In Greece, another major deal with Israel was recorded on Monday, during a period in which criticism of the Gaza war has also been heard in Athens. The two countries signed the “Achilles Shield” deal worth approximately 3 billion euros, the largest defense export deal in the history of Israel-Greece relations and one of the largest in Israel’s history.
In the Baltic states, Jerusalem has identified an “upward trend” in demand for Israeli systems due to growing concerns over Russia. According to Israeli political officials, the Baltic states view themselves as being “on the front line” and fear they could be next if the Russian threat expands.
The war in Ukraine and the Russian threat have changed defense priorities across Europe. European countries are rapidly increasing their defense budgets and seeking systems that have already demonstrated operational capabilities. In several areas, there is no available European replacement for Israeli technology.
Finland, for example, has made it clear that the war in Ukraine has demonstrated the critical importance of air defense capabilities.
Defense exports at a record high
In Jerusalem, officials are seeking to separate, as much as possible, political disputes with European governments from security ties with them. Israel is not rushing to halt defense deals in response to political criticism.
“We are pragmatic,” political officials say.
From Israel’s perspective, stopping deals could harm domestic defense industries, hand market share to competitors, led by France, and reduce the influence created through long-standing ties between Israeli industries and European defense establishments.
The Israeli interest is also reflected in the numbers. In 2025, Israeli defense exports reached a record $19.2 billion, a jump of nearly 30% in one year and more than double the figure from five years earlier.
The Defense Ministry views expanding defense exports as a tool for strengthening industries, financing security needs and advancing diplomatic objectives.
Even in Israel, there is no complete separation between political and security considerations. A deal may be halted if there is concern about technology leakage, the transfer of a system to a hostile actor, or other security risks.
Political officials do not rule out the possibility that political considerations could affect a deal under certain circumstances. The diplomatic tensions with several European governments have not, for now, halted security cooperation.
European countries are increasing defense budgets and confronting the Russian threat, and in areas where no available alternative exists, they are finding it difficult to give up Israeli systems.
Spain is perhaps the most prominent example: even after enshrining a broad embargo on Israel into law, it left room for exceptions when its security needs and national interests require it.

Polish PM's 'right-hand man' gets nod from parliament for top court job
WARSAW, Sept 4 - Poland's parliament voted on Friday to make an ex-cabinet member known as Prime Minister Donald Tusk's "right-hand man" a leading judge, in a move critics, including within Tusk's coalition, said undermined government claims it is restoring checks and balances.
The appointment to the Constitutional Tribunal of Maciej Berek, who until August was Minister for Government Policy Implementation, created tension in the ruling coalition, which has vowed to reform a judicial system it says became politicised under the previous nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) administration.
Tusk says that Berek is "competent, brave (and) selfless", making him the best man for the job of fixing a court that has in effect ceased to function due to disputes over its composition between the government and PiS ally President Karol Nawrocki.
However, critics including members of left-wing and centre-right parties in government say the appointment displays hypocrisy, especially as this government itself tried to pass legislation in 2024 that would have stopped politicians moving directly into judicial posts.
"We were supposed to be different from PiS, we were supposed to do things differently, not exactly the same," Anna Maria Zukowska, a lawmaker from the Left party, said in August.
'REVOLVING DOOR'
Jakub Jaraczewski, Senior Research Coordinator at NGO Democracy Reporting International, called the appointment "a mistake".
"Politicians should not be entering the tribunal like it was a revolving door between politics and the judiciary," he told Reuters.
Berek has rejected such criticism.
"The actions taken by the... coalition are aimed at restoring everything to the way it is envisioned in the constitution," he told reporters on Thursday.
Prosecutors said on Thursday they wanted to question Nawrocki as a witness as part of an investigation into what they say is the unlawful prevention of judges appointed to the Constitutional Tribunal from taking up their posts.
In April, Nawrocki only agreed to hear two out of six judges nominated by parliament swear their oath of office, effectively blocking the remaining four.
He later heard a third take his oath, but the judge in question refused to start adjudicating at the Tribunal in protest at the treatment of the three remaining judges.
Nawrocki said on Thursday that he had doubts about Berek's candidacy and that "the last thing the Constitutional Tribunal needs right now is another politician". He added he had not made a final decision about the appointment. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Lebanon Amnesty Law: Who benefits and why is it controversial?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:10:20 UTC
19:10:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon abolished the death penalty, but its new amnesty law divides the country
Oneel Bou Saab keeps a photo of her father in his army uniform. Lieutenant George Bou Saab was killed serving in the Lebanese Armed Forces in 2013 during clashes with an extremist group in the southern city of Sidon, and for years his death sat inside a familiar civic story: a soldier who died defending "all of Lebanon," as his daughter puts it, not any one sect or faction.
That story cracked open again this August, when parliament passed a sweeping new law that automatically reduces the sentences of people convicted in cases like the one connected to her father's death, including a death sentence commuted almost overnight to a shortened prison term.
"If there are detainees who have been wronged, held for years without trial, of course we should stand with them and demand a fast, fair trial," says Oneel. "But we can't fix one injustice by committing a bigger one."
Her anger sits at the centre of a reckoning now playing out across Lebanon. On 11 August 2026, the country became only the second in the Arab League, after Djibouti, and the first in the Middle East, to fully abolish the death penalty, replacing it with life imprisonment and hard labour, applied retroactively to sentences already on the books.
Amnesty International welcomed the move as a landmark for human rights, noting that Lebanon had not actually executed anyone since January 2004, even as its courts kept handing down death sentences in the years since. Roughly 85 people were moved off death row as a result.
One day later, parliament approved a second, far more contentious measure: a general amnesty law that slashes sentences across a wide range of crimes and orders the release of anyone held in pretrial detention for more than the equivalent of 12 years, regardless of the offence.
A law written to ease a crisis, and the anger it unleashed
The amnesty law was framed by its backers as a response to a genuine humanitarian emergency.
Lebanon's prison directorate counted 6,268 detainees as of the end of March 2026, while the National Human Rights Commission and independent rights groups put the real figure closer to 8,500 — against a system built to hold barely a third of that number.
The overcrowding, exceeding 300 percent of capacity, has had lethal consequences: more than 48 prisoners died last year alone, a rate of roughly four deaths a month. Close to a third of the prison population is being held pretrial, with no verdict ever reached, and some 1,200 people are held on security tips alone, without a judicial warrant.
To relieve that pressure, the law converts abolished death sentences into 28 years of "prison years" (each counted as nine months rather than twelve), cuts life-with-hard-labour sentences to 17 prison years, reduces most other sentences by a third, and frees anyone held pretrial for more than 12 prison years no matter the charge.
Wadih Al Asmar, head of the Lebanese Center for Human Rights, draws a sharp line between the two laws.
He calls abolishing the death penalty "a historic and excellent step for Lebanon," pointing out that the country hadn't carried out an execution in over two decades and that the evidence shows capital punishment does little to deter crime — what actually lowers crime, he argues, is the certainty and speed of prosecution, not the severity of the sentence on paper.
But the amnesty law is a different matter. "Rights groups," he says, "generally oppose blanket amnesties unless they are part of a serious, deliberate transitional-justice process with real judicial reform behind it."
Lebanon has passed general amnesties before, in 1991, in the 1990s, and in 2005, and each time, Wadih argues, the tool has served politics more than justice.
This one, he says, was drafted without consulting rights experts or his own organisation, and it carries what he calls dangerous loopholes: someone convicted of rape and sentenced to six or seven years could walk free after serving only two, once the prison-year conversion and the one-third reduction are applied.
Wissam Lahham, a legal scholar with Legal Agenda, goes further, arguing that the law inverts a basic legal principle.
"Amnesty is meant to be a narrow, clearly defined exception, but instead this law is written so broadly that pardon becomes the default and prosecution becomes the exception," says Wissam.
He also points to who stands to benefit from that vagueness.
"The law's loose language could shield people accused of embezzlement, corruption, environmental violations, and financial engineering, cases usually associated with entrenched power rather than the pretrial detainees the law was publicly framed around," he adds.
The retroactive clause and the cases that test it
Nowhere is the law's reach more contested than in two specific files: the fate of militants convicted in past clashes with the army, and the long-running question of Lebanese who fled to Israel in 2000.
The clearest test case is Sheikh Ahmad Al Assir, sentenced to death over the 2013 Abra clashes that killed 18 army soldiers, among them Lieutenant Bou Saab, and 11 of his own fighters.
Under the new law, that death sentence automatically converts to 28 prison years, and once the nine-month prison-year calculation and the one-third reduction are applied, his release becomes a real possibility in the near term.
"Ahmad al-Assir is, for me, the clearest example of why we have a problem with this," says Oneel. "This isn't someone whose file is vague or unclear. His actions, his incitement, the weapons, the clashes, all of it is documented on video and in court records. So why, suddenly, because the political balance has shifted, are we supposed to start seeing him as the wronged party? If every sentence can be reversed a few years later depending on how politics shift, what rule of law are we even talking about?"
The law also reopens the door to roughly 4,000 people who left Lebanon alongside Israel's 2000 withdrawal, allowing their return if they renounce Israeli citizenship, are not members of the South Lebanon Army militia, and have no outstanding convictions.
Anwar Yassin, a former prisoner who spent 17 years in Israeli detention, objects to even calling this group "exiles."
"Those who surrendered to the Lebanese state after the withdrawal faced no punishment," says Yassin. "It was the ones who knew what they had done who fled."
A public that doesn't feel safe
The reform lands in a country where trust in both the justice system and basic public safety is already thin.
A recent European Union Agency for Asylum report described a surge in violent crime since Lebanon's economic collapse began, with rising homicides, attempted murders, kidnappings, and carjackings in Beirut and Tripoli straining an underfunded police force and army.
Lebanon's own Internal Security Forces dispute that picture, insisting that crime is actually falling, a contradiction that says as much about the widening gap between how the state and the public read the same streets as it does about the crime data itself.
Fouad Halabi, a 62-year-old retired civil engineer in Beirut, sees the amnesty law as "a symptom of a deeper structural problem: a political class that keeps reaching for backroom settlements instead of the rule of law," folding genuinely wronged detainees together with major drug traffickers and smugglers under the same sectarian power-sharing formula.
Whereas Gracia Zgheib, a 34-year-old bank employee from Jounieh, argues the fix belongs with the courts, not parliament.
"There's a real difference between young people pushed into prison by economic hardship or personal drug use and the networks profiting from addiction," says Gracie, and the law should not blur that line by offering criminal cover to traffickers who, in her words, are dismantling the country's social peace.
What comes next
Lebanon's president has limited constitutional power to block the amnesty law outright, but he can send it back to parliament with objections.
That is exactly what Oneel and other families of soldiers killed in the line of duty are now demanding — not a rejection of every provision, but a rewrite that separates genuinely wronged pretrial detainees from people already convicted of killing soldiers, committing sexual violence against children, or running organised crime.
"We know his powers are limited, and we know a returned law doesn't automatically fail," says Oneel of the president, a former army commander himself. "But sending it back at least gives the state a little of its dignity back."
For now, the law stands as passed: two reforms enacted a day apart, one hailed internationally as a human rights milestone, the other dividing the country that passed it.
Whether Lebanon treats this moment as a genuine reckoning with an overwhelmed justice system, or as one more chapter in a long pattern of amnesties that serve the powerful, is still being argued over — in parliament, in courtrooms, and in living rooms where families like the Bou Saabs are deciding what justice is supposed to mean.
Alaa Serhal is a freelance journalist with more than a decade of experience covering events and wars in Lebanon

Argentina is not a credible power able to threaten Falklands
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:10:17 BST
19:10:17 KST

Argentina has spent two years rebuilding an air force it let wither for a decade, and every new arrival brings back the question of what it means for the Falklands.
Argentina agreed in 2024 to buy 24 second-hand F-16AM/BMs from Denmark for around $300 million, a deal the Milei goverment called the most important military acquisition in fifty years. The first six arrived at Río Cuarto in Córdoba on 5 December 2025. Six more follow each December to 2028, and the fleet is working up with VI Air Brigade at Tandil.
Argentina retired it’s last supersonic fighters in 2015 and had no interceptor capability at all for nearly a decade after that. The F-16 closes the gap and brings Argentine aircrew onto Western avionics, weapons and logistics standards for the first time in a generation.
The first of a batch of American M1126 Strykers has also arrived, for an army still running TAM medium tanks and M113s, and there’s also a contract with Terma of Denmark for F-16 electronic warfare work covering software, mission planning and ground support. The 2026 budget carries a number of capital lines for hangars, ground support equipment and base protection at Tandil and Río Cuarto out to 2028.
The navy has had very little of this, as readers will know. The surface fleet is MEKO 360 destroyers and MEKO 140 corvettes, most of them needing maintenance or mid-life work that hasn’t been funded, the last S-2T Turbo Trackers are under evaluation for retirement, and there has been no submarine force since the ARA San Juan was lost in 2017.
Range, fuel, tankers
The nearest Argentine airfields are around 300 nautical miles from the islands. An F-16 flying that out, holding for any useful time and returning has very little margin left, and the tanker fleet that could support it is a small number of ageing KC-130Hs. That same geography shaped 1982, when Skyhawks and Daggers reached San Carlos with minutes of fuel and attacked at low level because they had no other option.
Defence spending is around 0.7 to 0.8 per cent of GDP. The 2026 budget aims to push defence and internal security together towards 2 per cent, though economic volatility has broken Argentine procurement timelines before and will probably do it again. There are about 72,000 active personnel and wages take the largest share of the budget, as they often do.
What’s on the islands
British Forces South Atlantic Islands is a permanent joint command, set up so that 1982, when the islands were held by a Royal Marines detachment and had to be retaken by a task force sailing 8,000 miles, cannot happen again.
Four Typhoon FGR4s of 1435 Flight hold QRA round the clock over the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, with A400M and Voyager providing transport and tanking. British fighters in the area have the refuelling Argentine ones lack.
Ground defence is a roulement infantry company, currently form 5th Battalion The Rifles, working with the locally recruited Falkland Islands Defence Force. Sky Sabre provides ground-based air defence, with radar coverage from Mount Byron among other sites. HMS Medway holds the South Atlantic Patrol Task and Mount Pleasant is hardened, able to take reinforcement direct from the UK. Cape Upholder in early July ran mortars, snipers and machine guns on the range with a section attack supported by simulated CAS from the Typhoons.
Taking an airfield defended by fast jets, modern GBAD and infantry, across 300 nautical miles, without air superiority, without tanking and without any way of supplying a lodgement, from a country that has fought for the islands once and now garrisons them permanently, is not a plan anybody in Buenos Aires is seriously working on. Not outside of the internet forums, anyway

India’s push to secure place in global chip supply has ‘secret weapon’: its people

But observers say the country should set its sights even higher upstream on the value chain by mobilising its “secret weapon” – a talent pool that could realise its dream to turn “Make in India” into “Engineer in India”.
New Delhi earlier this week launched the second phase of its mission with a budget of US$13 billion to build an industrial ecosystem spanning chip design to manufacturing. Building on the first phase, which focused heavily on foundational industrial set-up, the second expands support across the entire supply chain, including developing a large manpower pool.

Delhi has already approved 12 semiconductor manufacturing projects across six states. Three – Micron, Keynes Semicon and CG Semi – have started commercial production this year. They primarily handle assembly, testing and packaging rather than advanced wafer fabrication.

Spain proposes EU climate fund financed by taxes on oil, gas firms, private jets

2026-09-04
