====================================================================================================

Ruth Bar breaks silence on her 1993 affair with Netanyahu, his early political rise - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
07:26:13 UTC
16:26:13 KST

Dr. Ruth Bar is the most famous anonymous woman you have never heard of. On January 14, 1993, Benjamin Netanyahu, sweating and somber, burst into the studio of Israel's Channel 1 television to confess live on air that he had conducted an extramarital affair with the strategic adviser working for him in the race for the Likud leadership. That woman was Ruth Bar.
The primaries to succeed Yitzhak Shamir as Likud chairman were then in full swing, after Shamir's defeat by Yitzhak Rabin in the 1992 election. Netanyahu's rival, and the man standing in his way of winning the Likud leadership, was David Levy. Netanyahu, a scion of the Revisionist aristocracy and a member of Israel's old elite, was an outsider in Likud.
Only a few years earlier, he had returned to Israel from the UN, joined Likud, and decided to take the party by storm in an American style his rivals had never encountered.
The "Likud princes," including Bennie Begin, Ehud Olmert, Dan Meridor, Roni Milo, Limor Livnat and others, saw him as a threat. In their eyes, he was a phony opportunist, a foreign agent who had come to carry out a hostile takeover and was trying to exploit the defeat by Rabin to seize control of the party. To their astonishment, Netanyahu rapidly gained popularity and took the lead in the race. Even he had not expected his plans to materialize so quickly.
Then, in the middle of his ascent, someone called the Netanyahu family home and told his young wife, Sara, that her husband was having an affair with his strategic adviser at the primary campaign headquarters, and that unless he withdrew, a tape containing incriminating evidence of the affair would be made public.
Netanyahu decided not to give in to the blackmail. Instead, he chose to get ahead of the blackmailer and confess live on television. He arrived at the studio, where news anchor Ya'acov Ahimeir and police affairs reporter Uri Cohen-Aharonov were waiting for him, and told the nation that he had indeed cheated on his wife. It was a telenovela broadcast live. In the same breath, he accused a "senior Likud politician," meaning David Levy, of attempting to blackmail him, and said he was surrounded by "a gang of criminals," meaning Ya'acov Bardugo and the late Moti Mishani.
Israel had only one television channel at the time, with a 100% rating. The uproar was immediate. The entire country talked about the incident, after which Netanyahu was thrown out of his home by his wife Sara, with no intention of allowing him back. But, as usual, he returned. Crawling.
That tape was never published, for a simple reason: There was no tape. Someone had either played a prank or threatened Netanyahu with a cap gun. That was enough to send him racing to television to confess live on air that he had cheated on his wife.
Dr. Ruth Bar's name was indeed published at the time, but there were no social networks and there was no digital media. Bar managed to disappear back into anonymity, from which she never again emerged. She continued her work as a psychologist and strategic consultant specializing in branding and decision-making, working with senior politicians including Shlomo Lahat, known as Chich, former Ramat Gan mayor Zvi Bar, Ehud Barak, Ehud Olmert, Dan Meridor and Gabi Ashkenazi. Her past clients included brands such as Osem-Nestlé, Tivall, Sabra, Strauss, Jafora, Materna, Tara, Nirlat, Electra and others. In the financial sector, she worked with Bank Hapoalim, Bank Leumi, Clal, Psagot, Gazit Globe, the Tourism Ministry and others.
Bar conducted a very long series of scientific studies to substantiate the theses and theories she developed over the years. She never gave an interview, never appeared before a camera, microphone or reporter's notebook. Not off the record, not on the record. Very few political journalists, if any, know her.
Over the years, she focused on research, during which she cracked the formula that makes it possible to influence the brain and the decision-making mechanism. The same mechanism causes us to choose one particular product when we stand in front of a supermarket shelf, or one particular ballot slip at the polling station.
Now she is talking. For the first time ever.
This interview is not about politics, nor is it about the election. Bar is reluctantly giving up her anonymity. Her life's work, a book of more than 600 pages, is being published after years of work. That is the reason for the timing.
The book is called Brain Under the Influence, and it is due to reach stores around this time. It contains a great deal of professional material, but also a great deal of politics and a meticulous analysis of most of the election campaigns Israel has seen.
Bar's testimony has particular significance because she was part of the small team that shaped Netanyahu's political persona at the beginning of his career, when it was still in its infancy. As you will understand later, everything roiling our lives in these years was already sown and planted back then, in those days.
Holding on to life
Ruth Bar has been married all her life to the same husband, Dr. Shmuel Bar, who was also her husband during her affair with Netanyahu. He is an ophthalmology specialist who became known as an airborne physician with the 669 rescue unit and was the first to perform a full surgical tracheotomy on the battlefield.
Their marriage survived that trauma, "mainly thanks to my husband," she says, but that was only the preview. Later, two of their three children were killed, one in an accidental shooting and the other in a traffic accident. It is almost impossible to recover from a blow like that. They did. Ruth and Shmuel Bar somehow managed to pull themselves out of the abyss, overcome depression, cling to life and move forward.
This is the first interview she has ever given, 33 years after a single television broadcast turned her into the most famous woman in Israel, apart from Sara.
Is there really a mechanism that operates our decisions? One that makes us reach for a particular product rather than its competitor, or for a particular ballot?
"We have known for several decades that we have two decision-making systems. The first system is unconscious, intuitive, associative, simultaneous and very fast. It absorbs information and at the same time produces meaning from it. Then, what is in front of your eyes is what determines things. It isn't short-term memory, it is truly immediate. This system doesn't retrieve information from memory, only what is happening in front of your eyes, here and now. This system is very dominant. The second system thinks in a more logical, sequential, systematic way, and it is more critical. The first system is not critical. It is intuitive and unconscious. The second one is."
So what actually happens at the moment when we face a decision?
"There is an important model I developed called the 'survival layers model.' You have to understand, this model is backed by dozens of scientific studies I conducted over many years, with hundreds of respondents and hundreds of situations. According to this model, human perception is wired according to four survival layers. Nothing is accidental in the way we perceive events or brands. The first layer is impression, the second is the relations layer, the third is protection, and the fourth is emotions.
"Every experience, every event, everything receives a score in these four layers. Impression is how much this event impresses me. Relations is how much it relates or is connected to me. Protection includes values such as security and peace of mind. Emotions are the emotions the event generates in me: joy, hope, hatred, fear. This is where our processing begins, until the decision is made."
I assume we'll come back to that later. How did your professional relationship with Netanyahu begin?
"I started my career at the Warshavsky advertising agency as head of the marketing department, and from there I moved to Ariely Advertising, which sent me for professional training in Manhattan to entice me to join them. I arrived at a place that was the pinnacle of the advertising world. I studied under the greatest people in the field, and I had some nice successes in building brands. I worked with politicians. I came up with the phrase 'Lahat does Tel Aviv' for Shlomo Lahat, Chich, and Ariely loved it and turned it into a slogan.
"By 1989, I had already done my first political study. We didn't exactly know who it was being done for, but I assumed it was for Netanyahu, who had just returned to Israel and joined Likud. At one stage, we ran a campaign for Zvi Bar, who was then running against Ramat Gan mayor Uri Amit. Eyal Arad was on Bar's team, and they brought me in. Bar was trailing Amit by 20%, and in the end he won. On the day of the municipal election, Bibi Netanyahu unexpectedly arrived at the headquarters. That was our first meeting."
Was there chemistry?
"There were other people there. I was writing the numbers on the board, the results started coming in from the polling stations, and suddenly Bibi walked in. He started asking all kinds of questions, and I answered. A few days later, Arad approached me and asked whether I would be willing to meet Netanyahu. Of course I agreed."
What was the meeting like?
"We met in an apartment in Tel Aviv, I think at Eyal's place. They told me Bibi wanted me to watch his television appearances and analyze them, the advantages and disadvantages. They put in a tape and I watched. He was good, but there was a lot to correct. He listened to all my comments."
That's how it all began?
"Yes. After that I started doing political research for him. Intensive, in-depth research. At the time he had a 'submarine,' a close and secret group of advisers. Eyal Arad was there, Ivet Liberman was there, Ya'acov Akst was there, and others. One day Bibi and Ivet had an argument, and Bibi threw him out of the submarine. I was the one who convinced him to bring Liberman back. I told him: 'Ivet is very smart and very important to the campaign. Get over your anger.' And he got over it. Fortunately for him, because Ivet was a very important factor in Bibi's system."
Ignoring the affair, were your professional relations with Bibi good? Did he speak with you outside the political submarine meetings as well?
"Yes. Bibi would also call me privately and consult me. He asked me to come to his events in front of audiences and analyze those too. I did. At one of those events, in front of an audience of Likud members, he got a little lost. There was noise, the audience wasn't listening, they weren't impressed by him. We worked very hard on that. He wasn't the Bibi of today. He was at the beginning of his path. He was carving out his way. He needed help. He knew he intended to climb all the way to the top, to the highest floor."
How long did you work with Netanyahu?
"More than three years."
Were you paid, or, as is customary with him, did he manage to avoid that too?
"Of course I was paid. I have invoices. The payments went through the law office of Von Weisel, Fischer, Shimron."
Bar will not say a word about the affair between them. Contrary to what the public understood, the affair lasted almost as long as the professional relationship. It was not a momentary slip. It ended only with that televised uproar.
To the best of my knowledge, after the television uproar there were other scenes as well, including loud telephone conversations between the betrayed wife and the mistress. But Ruth Bar will not say a single word about that either. There is no point trying to persuade her. When asked why she is unwilling to talk about the affair itself, she answers dryly: "Ask him. After all, he's the one who ran to television to talk about it."
What was your impression of him as a politician, as a person?
"I was his adviser and pollster for three years, and the first thing I noticed about Bibi was his extreme sense of superiority. It was a sense of deep, almost frightening superiority. He was certain he was above everyone. He dismissively called everyone else 'clerks.' You could hear the contempt even in his tone of voice. All his rivals, in his eyes, were small, pathetic and insignificant. That was my first impression of him, and I remember it to this day. Not long ago, Yoav Horowitz, who was his chief of staff, called him an 'emperor.' I saw it even then, long before he became prime minister."
Didn't that make you think about leaving? What am I doing with this man?
"I had thoughts in that direction. But I have to admit that the professional temptation to work with him was enormous. Working with Netanyahu was an incredible school for me. I learned a great deal from working with him. It was the first time I had worked with someone who appeared on television with such high frequency, and that enabled me to build, implement and test all my models and theories. He was my training ground, and he was perfect for that purpose.
"I did a huge number of studies with him. We tested before an appearance, after an appearance, I wrote a great many theses and documents. He also asked me to come to his public appearances and analyze them, asked my opinion about the quality of the appearance, the messages, the body language, everything. I also conducted regular studies for him throughout that period on all his rivals in Likud. In those studies, you can see what position he starts from against them, and how he advances and overtakes them one by one as if they don't exist."
Whom did you examine?
"When you work on a brand, and Bibi was a brand, you need to examine the level of its brand equity. Where it is strong, where less so. And examine the rivals. I examined Bennie Begin, Olmert, Katsav, Meridor, and later, of course, Levy as well. We mainly surveyed the younger figures: who was most highly regarded, who was most popular, who was best suited to Likud. And you can see how Bennie Begin, for example, starts out highest and then declines, and how Bibi starts in the middle, but takes off and leaves all of them behind."
'Nationalism that conceals ultranationalism'
Bar has documentation and records. The studies she conducted for Netanyahu are laminated and arranged in order.
One examined the "authoritativeness" of the younger Likud candidates. In October 1989, Bennie Begin led the table with a score of 30.6, while Netanyahu had only 22.9. Moshe Katsav had 5, Olmert 6.9, and Meridor 13.3. Moving forward, Netanyahu steadily closed the gap. By the end of May 1991, Begin had fallen to 25.7, while Netanyahu had surged to 42.9. On charisma, Begin began with 32.8 and declined to 25.6. Netanyahu began at 32.4 and soared to 51.6. The same pattern appeared across all the other categories.
Bar also has documents she wrote for Netanyahu about the quality of his appearances and ways to improve them. One, for example, is titled "Ways to strengthen the image of the comprehensive expert." It stresses the need for clear and unequivocal messages, the need to sound forceful and in command of the material, and not to appear like a student being questioned by the interviewer. Instead, Netanyahu should seize the initiative and dictate the pace of the interview, so that the interviewer would be perceived as an "acolyte."
Another document, which may explain the beginning of the construction of Netanyahu's famous "base," on which he still relies, is titled "Ways to increase charisma." It contains the following jaw-dropping statements:
"Satisfying the need for self-admiration: Admiration of the leader causes the individual excitement and pleasure, since admiration of the leader satisfies the need for self-admiration (narcissism), through the mechanism of 'transference.' In order to strengthen the satisfaction of this need, beyond strengthening admiration for the leader, it is recommended to create a blurring between the leader's 'I' and the audience's 'I.' In this sense, it is important to emphasize the dimension of 'we'... In the realm of charisma, the emphasis is on emotional rather than rational content. Emphasizing the superiority of 'us,' or alternatively emphasizing the inferiority of the hated others."
Another subsection reads:
"Satisfying the need for forcefulness. This need is especially prominent among floating voters and Likud voters. Satisfying this need by demonstrating force and control definitely strengthens the leader's attractiveness. Emphasizing nationalism that conceals ultranationalism also serves this purpose. However, it should be remembered that the message must remain national, because then it serves both purposes: the need for nationalism, which carries a positive label, and the need for ultranationalism without the negative label."
The document later deals with "satisfying the need for national pride," as well as "satisfying the need for belonging," and "satisfying the need to remove inhibitions." This is done through the dimension of charisma, which operates mainly by stimulating the pleasure center. Part of creating pleasure comes from satisfying forbidden needs, or alternatively from removing inhibitions. "Therefore, the more correctly one works in this direction, under the protection of a positive label, the more one can increase the candidate's attractiveness."
When you look at him now, what do you think?
"It reminds me of something he said to me back then, in one of our meetings. He told me, 'I'm looking for someone with high verbal ability who can formulate a devastating verbal attack against my competitors.'"
How did you react to that?
"I didn't react. I probably repressed it. In retrospect, I understand that this idea, which entered Netanyahu's mind more than 30 years ago, is what lies at the foundation of what is now called the 'poison machine,' which floods life in the State of Israel with venom and poison. Now I understand the power of it. This machine activates the emotional layers so that the positive ones fall silent while the negative survival-emotion layers come to the fore.
"It floods people with negative thoughts and harms the target, undermining his spirit and also damaging his perceived brand equity, meaning his image, thereby harming his chances of defeating Netanyahu in an election. For example, everything they did at the time to Benny Gantz, with the alleged stutter, the 'Yoo-Yoo-Nit' interview, and the rumors. It is very important to expose the poison machine, explain how it works and how dangerous it is. They target someone and start crushing him. It looks instinctive and driven by impulse, but it is scientific. Completely scientific."
You spoke earlier about his sense of superiority, about everyone else being small, clerks. Whom does he actually mean?
"Everyone. Military people and chiefs of staff as well, of course journalists and media people, all his political rivals and colleagues, and the voters too, including his own voters. His superiority extends over the president of the United States as well. He is above everyone."
Isn't that going a little far? How did you reach those conclusions?
"He spoke about it explicitly. He said it in his own voice. The tone and manner every time other people were discussed. Who are they, anyway? They are all dwarfs. Clerks. And because he sees himself as above them, he can also influence them and control them, in his view. Look, I have worked with many politicians, brands, authors, professors, banks, and I have never encountered a person with such a sense of superiority. To his credit, he knows how to hide it."
It seems to me it's not so hidden anymore.
"Think about what that means. If he is above everyone, he can influence their minds, mold their personalities. The means is to have a dominant presence in the media. He understood that first. I didn't teach him that. He came to me with it. I learned it from him. That is why working with him fascinated me so much. Suddenly you see that you can give a client instructions according to your model and see how he implements them, how he corrects himself, in real time, like in a laboratory."
Do you agree that he is the best, by a wide margin, in this field?
"He understood how the media operates much better than others. What distinguished him from others and contributed significantly to his success from the very beginning was the enormous importance he attributed to prominence in the media. He understood that it had enormous significance, and he was the first and only one who understood it. That is where his advantage over everyone else begins. There is a precise Archimedean point at which he simply passed all the others, when he recognized how important media dominance is. He truly lives it."
Give me an example.
"At one of our working meetings, he was in a gloomy mood, when suddenly he noticed a photograph of himself in the newspaper. And suddenly, all at once, his face lit up. He was glowing with happiness. That reaction was purely emotional. It wasn't a pose. It was authentic. He was genuinely happy. It changed his mood. And I, as a psychologist, connect that reaction with his sense of superiority and his obsessive need to be above everyone. Rationally, he understood the enormous influence the media has on people's minds. He also understood it intuitively and acted accordingly."
And still, in the 1999 election, he was defeated.
"And that is why he said at the time that when he came back, he would come with 'my own media.' That is how his enormous motivation to control the media and suppress the free press was built. The Communications Law now is an expression of that."
What does it mean when people talk about the media's enormous influence?
"It is a dramatic influence that the media has in real time. At the very moment when things are published or broadcast before the public's eyes. What you see at that moment on television affects you immediately. We talked about this at the beginning of the interview, the intuitive, immediate, fast system. Bibi understood it first, and from that he understood that controlling the media means controlling people.
"I know, from conversations with him, that he doesn't get overly excited by something very bad or something very good. He understands that everything passes, everything is a matter of images, and in the end the only question that matters is how it is presented on television and in the media. He didn't understand the psychological mechanisms behind it, which I understand from the research. He grasped it intuitively. What you see now is what influences you. What you see later is what will influence you later. So there is no reason to panic over something bad, because it can be repaired afterward. When you control what people are shown, you control people."
He also has an amazing ability to control people himself, through demagoguery, charisma and other elements, doesn't he?
"Look, we once used to say that it doesn't matter what people say, what matters is what they do. People would say it doesn't matter what the gentiles say, what matters is what the Jews do. With him, it is the opposite. It was already the opposite 30 years ago. It doesn't matter what you do, what matters is what you say. He understood that words are the drug that acts on the brain, and that the story you tell through them is the most powerful drug."
So he is our drug supplier?
"Yes. Absolutely. For me, he was a school. Through him, I came to understand from the ground up the effect of the public sphere on the individual. That is why my book is called Brain Under the Influence."
'Bibi benefited from the missiles'
Do you remember the moment when he suddenly appeared on the Mabat television news that night?
"Of course."
Was it traumatic for you?
"I have more severe traumas. But it was very unpleasant. I received a warning that he was going to television. Someone from his circle told me it was happening."
Was it the right thing for him to do?
"It was a rash decision that came out of panic. Through that decision, you can understand his personality. How he activates his strategy in real time."
What does "activates" mean?
"Reactivates. From his perspective, in order to influence, he has to be the one dictating the pace and leading the story in the media. To lead, not to be led. At that moment, he was convinced there was a tape of him."
Of the two of you.
"Yes. So he has to take control of the event and lead it. True, on the one hand, it drew a lot of ridicule. People asked, why on earth are you running to television to confess that you cheated on your wife? On the other hand, it generated emotional involvement among a huge number of viewers."
So if we use for a moment the professional terms from your book, what is actually the source of Netanyahu's power? Within the four layers you described, where is he strong?
"Bibi's great asset is the survival layer of impression. The image of being big, successful, a leader, impressive, in a different league. That is what dictates everything. His weak layer is the relations layer. This is credibility, caring, compassion, personal connection. Especially credibility. I identified that back then, 30 years ago. Even today, go look at studies about him and you will see that credibility gets the lowest score.
"The relations layer is almost nonexistent for him. Everything is centered on the impression layer. In relations, he is simply disabled. And that is why he ran to television to babble about an extramarital affair, in order to take command of the event. That is impression. In the end, on the one hand, he got enormous ratings, and people were impressed that here was a man coming to confess. On the other hand, that is where his disability in the relations layer begins to emerge, and it continues to this day."
How does this business of the layers work?
"It's simple. When something happens, when an issue comes up in the public sphere, it belongs to one of the four layers. The candidate who is stronger in that layer is the one who benefits more from it. Take the haredi draft-evasion law. It belongs to the relations layer. That is why it hurts Netanyahu, who is weak in that layer."
Why is the draft-evasion law part of the relations layer?
"Because it deals with equality and fairness within society. By the same principle, every time we reached the issue of security or protection, Netanyahu led. That is the protection layer, where he is strong. And he has an advantage here because, as prime minister, he is responsible for these issues."
And what happened to that for him after October 7?
"Severe damage. He was hurt both in the protection layer and in the impression layer. Until then, he had a huge advantage in both. Now, no longer. It is still considered a strong point for him, but not like it used to be. The advantage is no longer unequivocal. Once, he played alone on that field."
Being prime minister essentially allows him to control the agenda and raise issues from the layers that are comfortable for him, right?
"Exactly. And that is critical. Control of the agenda is control of people, because you put on the agenda issues from the layers in which you have an advantage. That is one of the reasons there should be a two-term limit."
This thesis of yours is based on public opinion research. Is there also a biological basis for it?
"Of course. Each survival layer has a hormone that corresponds to it. It is all hormones. Because he has been badly damaged in all the survival layers, even when there is a war, which is entirely in the impression and protection layers, he cannot leverage it into an advantage. And you see that even at peaks of the war he did not manage to rise in public opinion for any sustained period, unlike in the past."
Incidentally, how do you create this situation in which you lead in the impression layer? Does it come naturally, or do you have to work at it?
"Of course you have to work at it. Netanyahu, for example, was not afraid to enter confrontations with almost every chief of staff he had. Maybe except Aviv Kohavi. He would enter confrontations with them, come out on top, and mark another target. That way, instead of them being Mr. Security, he became Mr. Security and Mr. Impression. It is a technique. I win, I dictate."
I'm trying to understand the division into survival layers and how dominant Netanyahu's strength in two of them, impression and protection, has been over the years.
"Take two examples. In the 2019 election, Gantz established Israel Resilience and released a video with a counter showing the number of terrorists killed while he was chief of staff. It was a security video par excellence. It was supposed to boost Gantz, but that did not happen. Because that is the impression and protection layer, and Netanyahu is strong in those layers. After the video, Gantz stayed at 13 seats and Netanyahu rose.
"Want another example? On March 25, 2019, Hamas fired missiles from Gaza toward central Israel, Gantz gave his famous 'Yoo-Yoo-Nit' interview, and Donald Trump recognized the Golan Heights. Bibi strengthened in the polls and widened the gap because all three of those events belong to his strong layers. And so, despite the missiles on central Israel, Bibi was not hurt. Missiles belong to the protection and impression layers, which are strong layers for Netanyahu."
Does that still hold true now?
"Less so. The fact is that he failed to rise even when there was a sense of victory over Iran and Hezbollah. Suddenly it didn't help him. He lost his excess dominance in those areas. It doesn't benefit him as it did in the past. Although, from his perspective, it is still better to raise those issues than, for example, the relations layer, such as the draft-evasion law."
'Peace disappeared from the campaigns'
We are less than two months from an election. In your view, is it still possible to move votes from one side to the other? The conventional wisdom is that people do not switch camps at the last minute.
"That is a mistake. I call them 'jumping votes,' and they are very significant. Some people call them the 'switchers.' Let's go back to Bibi for a moment. When I worked with him, during the period in which I examined all the young Likud leaders over a year and a half, he gave me completely free rein in the research. I did whatever I wanted, and among other things, I conducted repeated studies among the same respondents over a long period. I didn't change focus groups. I examined the same people over and over again.
"I discovered that even among regular respondents, people you return to again and again, between 10% and 15% can change their minds within a month. Move from supporting Bennie Begin to supporting Bibi Netanyahu. From one end to the other. At first I didn't believe it, and I focused on it, but it is a fact. I continued with it later in my doctorate as well. I did dozens of studies on it. I developed a model that can quantify what percentage of people's positions are stable, and what percentage can be influenced until the very last moment. I told Bibi about it, and he was pleased."
Instability in positions means the ability to influence more people. He was the underdog at the time and wanted the ability to influence.
"Later, I developed the model in my doctorate, and discovered that besides the fact that there is a scale for people's level of stability, and it depends on personality traits and several other things, there is a number of people who completely change their position as a result of external influence at any given moment, including at the very last moment. I called them the 'jumping votes' even during my time with Bibi. They exist in every layer and in every party. They are capable of changing their position not just along a continuum, but of actually jumping to the other side."
Most experts disagree with you and think it is impossible to move many people at the last minute.
"They are wrong. You remember that in 2015 all the polls showed a victory for Bougie, and in the end Netanyahu won by a large margin. There were jumping votes here. He brought them over through the statement that Arab voters were coming out to the polling stations in droves. That is the impression layer. The Arab enemy is charging at us. In the third election, in March 2020, he did the same thing to Gantz through Ahmad Tibi. He powerfully leveraged the impression layer and reactivated the message that without Tibi, Gantz has no government."
Now it's "without Mansour, Gadi has no government." Could that work for him again?
"It depends on Gadi and his strategists. Netanyahu is strong in the impression layer, but inferior in the relations layer. Even very weak. Recent events have weakened him even further in that area. The abandonment of the residents of the South and North, for example. The abandonment of reservists and fighters when it comes to enlistment.
"Gadi has a major advantage in the relations layer. Netanyahu whispered into Rabbi Kaduri's ear, told Orna Peretz, 'You're boring us.' Eisenkot let Gantz become chief of staff before him, he has a human and modest presence, the bereavement of his son. All those things built him a powerful image when it comes to relations. Therefore, Eisenkot needs to constantly raise issues from that layer. The classic one is haredi enlistment. When the relations layer is on the agenda, Gadi Eisenkot gets stronger. And he must not be dragged after issues from the impression layer, which play into Bibi's hands. Gadi is stronger in the relations layer than Bennett too, who is branded more as a strong right-winger and is trying to compete with Bibi in the impression layer."
But Bennett is also brotherhood, hugs, "together we'll fix it." I was sure he was strong in the relations layer too.
"It's hard to be both. It was clear to me that the connection with Lapid would hurt him in this respect. You cannot connect two opposite layers and hope it will work. Lapid is much more in the relations layer, Bennett in the impression layer, which is associated with the Right. When that is joined together, there is a collision. It creates terrible confusion.
"It was clear to me in advance that the connection with Lapid would hurt, and not for the reasons discussed in the media. You can't take two different layers at equal strength. One layer activates one set of associations, and the other layer activates another set, as well as different hormones. Lapid is positioned in the center and is much more in the relations layer. Bennett is positioned in the impression layer, which is characteristic of the Right. So it clashes. It creates terrible confusion."
What you're basically doing is expressing in professional language the idea that Bennett voters are afraid of Lapid, and Lapid voters are afraid of Bennett.
"I'm saying that there are deeper layers here than we are aware of. Impression and relations are different things."
So there is no leader who can hold two or three layers at once?
"There is, but it depends how. One layer has to be dominant, and the others complement it, but do not compete with it. Eisenkot is positioned in the relations layer, his party is called 'Yashar!,' and he was also chief of staff. That is completely opposite to Bibi. You can take values from another layer and put them alongside your dominant layer, add a shade, but not instead of it. Alongside. If, for example, Gadi now starts talking about security and mentioning that he was chief of staff and focuses on that, it would be a mistake. He would leave the layer where he has an advantage and enter the layer where Bibi has an advantage. And vice versa."
So what can he do?
"Say Gadi cares about people, Gadi will take care of security. The word 'cares' belongs to relations. That is how you bring security values into the relations layer. Gadi has to remain in the relations layer. All the parties in the bloc need to be there. And attack only Netanyahu. Eisenkot needs to focus only on him."
But if he attacks Netanyahu, doesn't that harm the relations layer?
"No. Netanyahu is an external body. The relations layer is within your own bloc."
Is this theory biological as well as psychological?
"Of course. We talked about the hormones. Each layer has the hormones identified with it. And I am talking to you about hundreds of studies in which this emerged. The impression layer is centered on sex hormones. In men, it is testosterone, and in women, two hormones, estrogen and estradiol. In the relations layer, it is the hormone oxytocin. When you caress your daughter, your oxytocin rises."
How do you explain the differences between polls?
"In the book, I analyze all the election campaigns here since 2019. There was an episode with Trump's Deal of the Century, when Gantz was ahead of Netanyahu in most of the polls, and with Shlomo Filber it was the opposite. What did I discover? Before Filber asked about voting, he asked two questions about Trump's Deal of the Century. Those questions brought the impression layer to the surface. He essentially primed the impression layer. It was a manipulation. One question was about the Trump plan, and a second question about applying sovereignty to the Jordan Valley and the Israeli communities. That raised Bibi."
Let's return to the jumping votes. Are they relevant in the current campaign?
"Very. The jumping votes, by definition, are the people easiest to influence, even at the last moment. When you see movement from small parties to large parties, those are the jumping votes. The atmosphere of victory, momentum, those are factors that influence them."
Who will they jump to this time?
"It depends what happens. If things happen in the impression layer, Bibi can get jumping votes. If things happen in the relations layer, Eisenkot will benefit."
So what is the best way to move jumping votes to your side before an election?
"Demonstrations, for example. They are very important for victory. I think that if people take to the streets ahead of the election, it will help. It focuses the media, gives expression to the things being said, to the leaders participating. The messages gain dominance. And who is influenced by that dominance? The jumping votes. It also strengthens and amplifies your 'home audience,' who will come out to vote, raising turnout on your side."
Are the jumping votes basically what we once called "floating voters"?
"Absolutely not. They do not say 'I don't know' or 'I haven't decided yet' in a poll. They identify as the audience of a particular side. But they can move to the other side. They have no inclination toward the other side. So when you move them from one side to the other, it has a double effect. Every bloc has potential jumping votes, between 5% and 15%. They belong to a brand's home audience, but are capable of leaping to the competing brand. Your job is to keep your own jumping votes with you and bring jumping votes from the other side over to you. That is what Netanyahu did in 2015. He transferred Herzog's jumping votes to himself."
Couldn't large demonstrations have the opposite effect? Frighten the jumping votes?
"They could, and therefore it depends on the messages. If you're talking about the change bloc, then the demonstrations need to be about enlistment, about a state commission of inquiry. Not about other issues. Control the messages, go for issues that are in the consensus. Large demonstrations mean major emotional involvement with a dramatic influence on the jumping votes, and they must contain the emotions layer. It is the strongest element that turns an 'exclusive preference' for a particular brand into a 'stable exclusive preference,' which is the strongest preference, the preference that influences actual behavior, meaning going to the polling station."
From the moment he ran to television and confessed to the affair with you, was your relationship with him completely severed?
"Yes, of course."
With his people too? Sara removed Eyal Arad from his surroundings almost immediately and blamed him for introducing the two of you.
"Yes. Everyone cut off contact with me. I haven't heard from them since."
Did you continue following him? Three years later he was already prime minister.
"I watched Peres make a mistake in the campaign with the slogan 'A strong Israel with Peres.' He went into the impression layer and played into Netanyahu's hands, where Netanyahu had an enormous lead over him. He entered Bibi's home field, while Bibi went after him with 'Peres will divide Jerusalem,' which also belongs to the impression layer, in the negative.
"Bibi also made a mistake with 'Making a secure peace,' which meant going into Peres's layer. Netanyahu's research showed that the word 'peace' drove voters away. Peace is the relations layer. They greatly reduced the use of the word 'peace' as the campaign progressed. The word 'peace' made Netanyahu voters uncomfortable, and strengthened Peres."
A double blow, with a birth in between
We've reached the truly difficult part. Tell me about the children.
"Shmuel and I lost two children. Two very heavy disasters came down on us. Shoham, our daughter, was killed on April 30, 2004, in a road accident in India. Two months earlier, in February, we came to visit her there, in India. She was 21 and a half, and had gone on a post-army trip with her boyfriend. We spoiled her. We bought her a car in Israel. We made her swear not to travel in anything, only in a car. They rented a motorcycle. He was driving, and she was killed. Eleven years later, in 2015, our son Omer was killed in a handgun accident. An accidental discharge. He was 37."
How do you recover from something like that? Is it even possible?
"After Shoham was killed, we were in a state of shock that is difficult to describe. It took us months just to digest it. But we chose life. And believe it or not, we had a son. Yes, after Shoham was killed. I was already 50. It was a very difficult pregnancy, and Matan was born. As impossible as it sounds, he filled the house with joy. The human brain is very focused on what is in front of it. The immediate experience. That is system number one we talked about. And the immediate experience with Matan was so powerful that it literally flooded us with happiness, which came within the endless bereavement we were living through."
You analyze even this as a psychologist, through an empirical research approach.
"That's right. In the brain too there is competition over which issue controls the agenda. As sophisticated and intelligent as the brain is, it is also stupid. What is present before its eyes is what activates and defines the experience. And because the experience of the new child was fresh and present, it gave us strength, both personally and as a family, to continue functioning for ourselves and for others."
And then, 11 years later, Omer was killed. A double blow.
"That's right. An extremely hard blow. But we had no choice. There was a small child at home. We clung to life. In bereavement, there is a phenomenon of clinging to pain. When you cling to the pain over the child who is gone, it is as though you bring him back to life. He is present. The pain keeps the loss alive. We decided to let go of that.
"For me, my children have a transcendent existence. Like transcendental meditation. Descartes explored this, that things have a spiritual existence even if they have no physical existence. They are present in the soul, in the mind, in the heart. I feel that my children, whom I adore and love so much, are here next to me all the time. And I never feel alone."
What is your advice to people going through experiences like that? Unfortunately, there have been quite a few of them recently.
"The main advice I can give is to give yourself permission to live. Give yourselves a break. Live. Love yourselves. Tell yourselves that you were excellent parents, that you did everything, that you gave everything. Don't sink into feelings of guilt. That is what the children would have wanted to happen."
Matan is 20 now, in the Academic Reserve program, about to begin serving in the IDF. I assume he was raised like a precious etrog.
"If it were up to me, he wouldn't leave the house and wouldn't move away from me for a minute. Thanks to my husband, he is allowed to do as he pleases. As he gets older, he is so charming, and we enjoy him so much. He radiates, he's handsome, excels in his studies, is in the Academic Reserve. Everyone loves him very much. We wish only one thing for him: a long life."
After a disaster like losing a child, is investing in and trying to have another child the right thing to do?
"Of course. Anyone who can should do it. Matan knows there is a lot of responsibility on him, he understands the situation, but he receives so much love, and it doesn't make him spoiled."
You've been married to the same husband since...
"That's right. Shmuel is a veteran and respected eye surgeon. We met when we were very young, 22 or 23. I knew from a very young age that I would go into academia and earn a doctorate. Education plays a leading role for me. I used to go on dates according to the man's education. I wasn't interested in money, only education. When I met Shmuel, he was already a doctor. We have something like 20,000 books at home. Shmuel has read all of them."
And then he found himself in the middle of the story of you and Bibi, and on television too. How does a marriage survive that?
"Usually it doesn't. Marriages don't survive something like that. We survived largely thanks to him. He has self-confidence, he is a successful and very handsome man, and he decided he wasn't prepared to lose me. And he doesn't regret it, I think."
Do you agree with the statement that the coming election is the most fateful in the country's history?
"Yes, very much."
Are you worried?
"Yes, very much. I once had a conversation with Netanyahu that shocked me deeply. He said there is no such thing as justice. And I was unwilling to accept that. As our acquaintance deepened, I understood that he doesn't aspire to justice either. The concept of justice is supposed to be protected at the core of the survival relations layer. When a person like Netanyahu, with an extreme sense of superiority, heads a country and does not believe in justice, it raises real concern. It is a very basic matter. It is enough to look now at the laws his government is passing in order to preserve its rule to understand that if he is elected once again, democracy in Israel will be in existential danger."
That serious?
"Yes. With a person whose survival relations layer is very weak, it is doubtful whether he will care for the citizens of the country more than he cares for himself. That means concern for the citizens' security is not in good hands either. With Netanyahu, he is always the victim. He is focused only on himself, on the aspiration to preserve power, on the deep conviction that the power belongs to him."
Did the fact that he managed to survive a full term after October 7 surprise you?
"No. I have an entire chapter in the book about what he did to make that happen. Once that is your supreme and almost only goal, and your entire system is subordinated to it, there is a chance you will reach the goal. He worked only on that. He dropped to 17 seats and managed to climb back up.
"He focused on dismantling all the other factors, placing responsibility on everyone else, preventing a commission of inquiry that could become an influential external factor, and clinging to the base. He understood that in order to survive, he had to divide the people into two polarized camps, and he did it. He bet on his base, and it was the right bet. Some of them are still with him. If he had spread his efforts elsewhere, he would have lost. He has no problem tearing the public into pieces, bringing us to the brink of civil war in order to survive. And that is frightening."

Air India capt. may have had psychoactive drugs in system during turbulence event, findings show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
07:25:18 UTC
16:25:18 KST

An Air India A320 flying from Phuket to New Delhi last month issued a stall warning when seatbelt signs were off, while a rapid pitch up and then down threw passengers and cabin crew against overhead bins and injured 24 people, Indian investigators said.
The Airbus plane, cruising at 36,000 feet, initially ascended 372 feet then fell to 292 feet below it, according to a preliminary report into the August 4 accident released on Friday.
The two-second stall warning came after the flight control system detected the loss of all three of the aircraft's hydraulic systems within four seconds, disengaging the autopilot and setting off a continuous cockpit alarm.
The hydraulic systems, which use pressurized fluid to power the flight controls and other equipment, began recovering about nine seconds after the first was lost, the report said.
The report from India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) did not say why the pressure loss was detected, which will require further investigation.
Flight's captain tested non-negative for marijuana
The event was updated to an "accident" from "serious incident" by investigators, and the report throws light on a chaotic few seconds on board the flight that had 137 passengers and eight crew.
The 32-year-old first officer was flying the plane at the time of the event, though the 34-year-old captain later took over the controls, it said. Both have been interviewed as part of the investigation.
The report adds to scrutiny of Air India, which has been under intense regulatory and public pressure since the June 2025 crash of one of its Boeing 787s in Ahmedabad killed 260 people.
The airline also faces separate questions after the report said the flight's captain returned a "non-negative" result in a confirmatory test for psychoactive substances.
The AAIB did not specify the substance for which the captain tested non-negative, but a source last month told Reuters it was marijuana.
Air India cooperating with probe, implementing mandatory substance testing
Air India said it was cooperating fully with the probe and giving investigators access to operational, maintenance, and technical records.
India's second-largest airline is implementing a one-time mandatory substance testing for all pilots after the accident, expanding checks beyond regulatory requirements.
The AAIB recommended the aviation regulator take appropriate action on priority to prevent abuse of psychoactive substances, calling the finding a "serious concern."
India is considering annual drug testing of all pilots after the accident, against the current requirement that 10% be tested each year.
The preliminary report did not make any recommendations to Airbus, which in a private report reviewed by Reuters told Air India the A320 aircraft registered losses in all three hydraulic systems in quick succession, briefly leaving key flight controls unresponsive.
For about four seconds, the pilots were unable to use the elevators and ailerons, which control the aircraft’s pitch and banking, Airbus' analysis showed.
Air India is controlled by the Tata Group, while Singapore Airlines owns a roughly 25% stake.

Congo’s Ebola response faces 5 critical gaps as outbreak spreads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
07:19:00 UTC
16:19:00 KST

Authorities in eastern Congo are shifting their Ebola response toward communities and villages as the virus continues to spread faster than health workers can track and contain it, Africa’s top public health agency said Thursday.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warned that the outbreak has likely not yet peaked. Since it was declared in mid-May, the virus has spread from three health zones to 60, infecting 6,250 people and killing 3,039, according to government data.
Insecurity, displacement and intense population movements have made it harder to detect cases, trace contacts and contain transmission.
The scale of the outbreak has already surpassed the devastating 2014-16 Ebola epidemic in West Africa, which killed more than 11,000 people and remains the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record.
The current outbreak has recorded six times as many confirmed cases and five times as many deaths, the Africa CDC said.
Despite efforts to contain the virus, significant gaps remain in Congo’s response, according to a U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report released this week.
Here are five areas where the response is falling short:
One of the biggest weaknesses is the limited use of community-based surveillance to quickly investigate alerts, identify infections and track transmission, the U.S. health agency said. Without faster detection at the community level, health workers risk losing valuable time as the virus spreads.
Delays in detection, reluctance to report cases and inadequate community engagement are contributing to preventable deaths. At least 63% of deaths recorded in the past week occurred outside Ebola treatment centers, Africa CDC data showed.
Authorities are now using a "village-centered approach," working with community leaders to build trust and improve collaboration with residents, said Yap Boum, head of emergency preparedness and response at Africa CDC.
Ituri province, where the outbreak is concentrated, is also at the center of the rebel conflict in eastern Congo, complicating efforts to gain residents' trust.
"Building that trust in the middle of an outbreak is quite complex," Boum said.
Quickly identifying and tracing people who have come in contact with Ebola patients remains challenging across the six provinces affected.
Although 81% of contacts have been followed up with by surveillance teams, that figure does not reflect the full reality because it refers only to listed contacts and does not include those who have yet to be traced.
Africa CDC estimates that cases confirmed in the last three weeks should have generated 97,600 contacts, based on an average of 60 contacts per confirmed case. Only 19% of the total expected contacts have been traced.
Health data shows that treatment centers had expanded capacity to more than 1,300 beds in late August, while their occupancy rate is currently 67%, with 869 patients.
However, experts have called for more treatment and isolation centers and beds in affected health zones to prepare for cases that have yet to be detected.
Many affected health zones are in areas where cases go undetected or unreported for several reasons, including distrust of health authorities.
Some health zones are also inaccessible to surveillance teams or health workers trying to treat patients, Boum said.
Experts also say laboratory testing capacity needs to be expanded to promptly identify cases and treat patients.
The World Health Organization said last month that several treatment and transit centers in Ituri, the outbreak's epicenter, were "saturated," while North Kivu, the second-most affected province, lacked sufficient options to refer patients to specialized facilities.
Health workers at existing treatment centers are also exhausted, said Jeannot Krikeija, who works at an Ebola treatment center in Bunia, Ituri's capital.
"Ebola is tiring us all the more because we don't know when this scourge will end. This ordeal is unbearable for me," Krikeija said.
Authorities have deployed safe and dignified burial teams for the more than 3,000 people who have died from Ebola, but gaps remain in how the burials are carried out, according to the U.S. health agency.
Ebola can spread between people through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of someone who is sick with or has died from Ebola. Experts have warned that the bodies of victims can still carry large amounts of active virus.
In Ituri and other affected areas, burial teams have been attacked on multiple occasions, often by families seeking to protect loved ones who died of Ebola. It is also common to see people surrounding the graves of Ebola victims during burials, sometimes within a few meters of the coffins.

Strongest El Nino in 40 years threatens global weather disruption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
07:18:00 UTC
16:18:00 KST

El Nino is forecast to become the strongest in four decades of comparable records, the United Nations' weather agency warned Thursday, as the U.N. chief said the world was entering the "danger zone of extreme weather."
The weather phenomenon is expected to strengthen to "very strong" levels in the coming months and is almost certain to persist through February, the World Meteorological Organization said.
"If this trajectory continues, it may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began," WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo told reporters in Geneva.
El Nino is expected to peak toward the end of this year, but its effects on global weather and climate could persist well into 2027, the WMO said.
The phenomenon occurs when surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, triggering widespread changes in atmospheric circulation, winds, pressure and rainfall patterns around the world.
Heat in the oceans is released more slowly into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures the year after El Nino develops.
The powerful 2023-24 El Nino contributed to 2024 being the warmest year on record, and "we should not be surprised if this record is broken," Saulo added.
"El Nino is firmly established and will intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, with big impacts on rainfall and temperature patterns and associated risks of floods, drought and extreme heat," the WMO said.
El Nino is a naturally occurring phenomenon and is not caused by climate change.
But scientists expect it to exacerbate the heat of a planet already warming because of the burning of fossil fuels, while amplifying weather extremes.
"El Nino is being supersized before our eyes," said U.N. chief Antonio Guterres.
"The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather."
WMO chief Saulo urged disaster management authorities and climate-sensitive sectors such as agriculture, fisheries, health, energy and water to prepare.
"This exceptional El Nino ... has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world," she said.
"We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to increase as El Nino intensifies."
El Nino typically occurs every two to seven years and lasts about nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Nino and its opposite, La Nina, with neutral conditions in between.
El Nino can reshape weather and climate patterns thousands of kilometers away from the tropical Pacific.
Wilfran Moufouma-Okia, the WMO's climate prediction chief, said some places would be affected before, some during and some after the peak later this year, though the strength of the peak is not an indicator of the severity of the impacts.
For September-November, WMO forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of above-normal temperatures "across almost all land areas."
The index that measures sea surface temperature anomalies in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific has strengthened from an average of 1.5 degrees Celsius above normal between May and July.
Weekly values between late July and mid-August ranged from about 2.2 to 2.6 degrees Celsius above average, indicating continued El Nino intensification.
The U.N. agency classifies El Nino events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong, meaning this one is set to reach the highest level of the four categories.
Moufouma-Okia said the classification meant a sea surface temperature anomaly of more than 2 degrees Celsius.
"That category is open: We know where it starts; we don't know where it ends," he told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
The average forecast points toward an anomaly peaking at 3.6 degrees Celsius, far higher than the last two very strong El Nino events in 1997-98 and 2015-16.
In some areas, subsurface ocean temperatures were more than 8 degrees Celsius above average during July and early August.
Saulo called this a huge reservoir of "very warm ocean waters that will fuel the intensity of El Nino."
The U.N.'s International Organization for Migration appealed Thursday for $110 million to protect 4.9 million people from the potentially severe impacts of the phenomenon.

====================================================================================================

Taiwan-developed automated repositioning mattress cuts nursing workload by 69%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
07:12:40 UTC
16:12:40 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Wellell Inc.’s automated repositioning mattress has entered clinical use at National Taiwan University Hospital after a joint study found that it reduced the workload required to reposition patients by 69%, CTEE reported.
In intensive care units, many critically ill patients need help repositioning every two to three hours. The task can be difficult when they are connected to multiple tubes and life-support equipment, often requiring two or three staff members, NTUH Department of Nursing’s Hsiao Wei-ling (蕭偉伶) said.
Frequent repositioning helps prevent pressure injuries in patients but can also increase the risk of lower back, shoulder, and neck injuries among nursing staff. The system was developed based on the needs of frontline clinicians and underwent multiple rounds of design improvements before clinical testing.
The study involved 424 critically ill patients and found that the mattress reduced overall nursing repositioning workloads by 69%. It cut the time required for each procedure by 53%, while the proportion of procedures that could be completed by a single nurse increased from 36.7% to 91.8%.
The findings suggest that the technology can not only ease the physical burden on nursing staff but also help protect critically ill patients from pressure injuries. The rate of new pressure injuries fell from 4.7% among patients who received conventional manual repositioning to 2.9% among those using the automated system.
Wellell announced Wednesday that it had donated 20 automated repositioning mattresses to NTUH, marking their introduction into the hospital’s intensive care units. NTUH Superintendent Yu Chong-jen (余忠仁) said similar equipment is already available overseas, but such products are expensive and may not fully suit Taiwan’s clinical needs.
Wellell said the system can adjust its repositioning angle, inflation level, and speed according to each patient’s weight and condition. Each procedure takes five to 10 minutes, or up to 15 minutes at the slowest setting. The company said gradual movement helps prevent patients from shifting or tubes from becoming dislodged.

2 workers pulled alive from Nepal tunnel 9 days after disaster

Two people were pulled alive from a tunnel Friday at a hydropower project on Nepal’s Trishuli River, nine days after an ice, rock and mudslide tore through the river valley, killing more than 1,200 people and displacing tens of thousands.
Officials and rescue workers believe the Aug. 26 collapse of a glacier in the upper reaches of the Trishuli River trapped at least 900 people inside tunnels serving six hydropower projects along the river.
At least 1,252 people were killed in Nepal after homes, roads and schools in towns and villages near the border with China’s Tibet region were swept away. More than 4,200 people remain missing, while thousands of others have been displaced.

A small group of workers had managed to escape from another tunnel in the hours after the disaster struck, but no others had been rescued from the hydropower sites until Friday.
The workers rescued Friday were Sanjay Sah, a mechanical foreman, and Kabir Maharjan, a mechanical supervisor, the office of Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said in a statement.
Videos and photos released by Nepali authorities showed Maharjan being pulled out of a hole in the ground amid cheers from bystanders and placed on a stretcher.
Sah was carried on the back of a worker to a rescue tent, his face covered in mud.
In one video, a team of army doctors attended to Sah at a tent near the tunnel before he was taken to a hospital. They fitted what appeared to be an oxygen mask around his mouth and checked his vital signs.
“His name is Sanjay Sah and he was working in mechanical control room. The vital parameters look normal,” an army official said.
Sah told rescuers he spent time reciting mantras, or verses from a prayer, while he was trapped, according to The Kathmandu Post. He said three or four more people could be alive in the tunnel, and possibly more deeper inside.
Maharjan cannot move his hands and legs, while Sah’s injuries are not critical, an aide to the energy minister told Reuters.
Amir Maharjan, Kabir’s brother, said he had not received any official news but had been told to go to the hospital.
“I have been hearing from the news that my brother has been found. The entire family is very happy,” Amir said.
Both survivors were in the intensive care unit, a source at the army hospital where they were taken told Reuters, adding that their vital signs were stable.
A team of experts in a WhatsApp group was guiding rescue workers in the search at the hydropower projects, which has become a valuable tool alongside helicopters and heavy machinery in the race to find survivors.
More search and rescue operations were underway around the Upper Trishuli 3A project, the Nepali army said. Rescue efforts were being led by the army and police, with assistance from experts from India, South Korea and China.
Dhan Bahadur Tamang, who earlier escaped from a tunnel linked to the Upper Trishuli 1 hydropower project upriver from where the two men were pulled out Friday, said their rescue was a miracle and raised hopes of finding more survivors.
Property, housing and infrastructure worth at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($2.56 billion) were lost in last week’s catastrophe, Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said Friday.
Nepal will need to rebuild around 20,000 houses in flood-ravaged areas, Upreti said Thursday, with at least 7,500 of those homes destroyed.
At least 583 foreign nationals were missing in the floods, Nepal said Thursday, many of them pilgrims and trekkers.
Australian disaster response specialists left for Nepal on Friday to join the search for survivors, as the government there expressed “serious concerns” about the welfare of its 36 missing citizens.

Estonian Defence Minister resigns after being defrauded by Indian company

Estonia’s Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur has resigned after a €70 million ($81.1 million) deal to buy artillery ammunition for Ukraine came under scrutiny over procurement failures.
Pevkur, who has served as defence minister since 2022, addressed the scandal while announcing his resignation on public broadcaster ETV on September 2.
“A leader must have the strength and courage to take responsibility,” Pevkur said in a Facebook post, adding that findings by the National Audit Office had raised questions over political responsibility.
The National Audit Office published a report on August 28 criticising defence procurements made by the Defence Ministry in recent years. The report warned that Estonia could ultimately have to cover the €70 million cost from its state budget.
According to Eesti Ekspress, an Estonian daily, Estonia signed the ammunition contract in 2024 with Datasel S.R.L., an Italian-registered company owned by Indian firm Neco Defense Munitions.
The contract was intended to supply artillery shells to Ukraine and was financed through the EU’s European Peace Facility.
Only some defective ammunition arrived
The Estonian Centre for Defence Investments (RKIK) made advance payments to Datasel, but shipments were repeatedly delayed and did not arrive for months.
A shipment eventually arrived in 2025, but Eesti Ekspress reported that the ammunition was defective and “useless”.
RKIK director-general Elmar Vaher, who oversaw the original contract, said the agreement should not have been signed because the supplier had no previous experience selling artillery shells.
“In my opinion, we should not have signed a contract with them,” Vaher said.
The deal was signed as Ukrainian forces faced severe ammunition shortages, worsened by delays in US military aid and the EU’s failure to meet its target of delivering one million rounds to Ukraine by March 2024.
The National Audit Office had repeatedly warned about risks surrounding defence spending, with its latest report raising concerns that the ammunition contract could ultimately burden Estonia’s budget.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal called a cabinet meeting for September 3 to discuss Pevkur’s resignation and the audit findings.
Estonia’s Prosecutor’s Office has also launched a criminal investigation into matters highlighted in the National Audit Office’s 2025 and 2026 reports.

NEW DELHI: So, who does Sonia Gandhi’s controversial memoir ‘Belonging’ belong to? The book will hit Indian shelves on November 10, 2026 — the same day as its international release.Billed as one of the most anticipated political memoirs in recent years, Belonging is described as a personal account of love, identity, duty and belonging, offering an insider's perspective on India's political journey through Gandhi's own eyes.

The company had earlier this year also halted distribution of cartoonist Joe Sacco's The Once and Future Riot, about the Muzaffarnagar riots — a decision critics have pointed to as part of a pattern.Adding a layer of intrigue to the row was the fact that Alfred A. Knopf, the memoir's American publisher, is itself a Penguin Random House imprint — raising the question, as Gehlot put it, of why a version cleared for global release would need alteration for Indian readers. "What is the reason, or what pressure is there that what is being published across the world cannot be published in India?" he asked.

Earle Meets World Is One Long ‘Get Ready With Me’ Video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
07:01:03 UTC
16:01:03 KST

“You’re gonna see everything on this show,” Alix Earle assures viewers in the voiceover that opens her Netflix reality series Earle Meets World. But if the show made a genuine effort to fulfill the 25-year-old social media star’s vow to reveal the rawest, most intimate aspects of her life, then the only reasonable conclusion to draw from it would be that there just isn’t much to see.
As her fans (she has 8.5 million on TikTok alone) will anticipate, “everything” refers specifically to ongoing drama around Earle’s parents’ divorce, her own breakup with NFL player Braxton Berrios, and her mysterious falling-out with fellow creator and former boss Alex Cooper. All of this does indeed come up in the eight-episode series, now streaming in full, which tries mightily to position the large, blended Earle family as the Kardashian-Jenners for a new generation. Yet the bombshells teased in months’ worth of promotional materials aren’t especially explosive. Nor is there a breakout personality among a cast that, understandably enough, seems either too chill or too concerned with appearing likable to really entertain. Earle Meets World plays less like a juicy docusoap than like a tediously extended version of the Get Ready With Me (GRWM) videos that made its subject famous—one that suggests less overlap than you might expect between the qualities of a successful influencer and those required for reality TV stardom.
Earle is one of those celebrities who are universally known to people under 30 but barely on the radar of anyone much older. (I’ll admit to having confused her with Cooper, another all-American blonde who parlayed internet fame into a Netflix series, and I know I’m not the only one.) Though I wouldn’t recommend making the show your first trip down the Alix Earle rabbit hole, here is a quick intro for the unfamiliar: Conventionally beautiful yet plagued by cystic acne, Earle grew her following as a University of Miami undergrad with mirror-facing GRWM TikToks, eventually going viral with a vulnerable post about her skin troubles. Then came the brand deals and new platforms. Cooper signed Earle, an obvious heir, to her podcast network; they abruptly parted ways in early 2025 and have been vaguely but publicly feuding ever since. Meanwhile, Earle has continued her ascent, launching a skincare brand, Reale Actives, and introducing herself to people elderly enough to watch network TV on Dancing With the Stars.
Synergistically positioned to bring her social media followers to a streaming platform that needs young subscribers to maintain its dominance while filling gaps in her own reach, Earle Meets World is a multigenerational family soap. Alix and 23-year-old Ashtin—a less-extroverted brunette whose TikTok audience still tops a million—are the It-girl sisters who constantly squabble but consider each other best friends. Their mom, Alisa, and dad, TJ, have been divorced for more than a decade, their split catalyzed by TJ’s affair with Ashley Dupré, a key character in the prostitution scandal that sank former New York governor Eliot Spitzer. Now Dupré is Ashley Earle, TJ’s wife and the mother of their three kids; the eldest, Izabel, is, at 13, already cranking out Outfit of the Day videos like the Gen Alpha Kylie Jenner she has the pedigree to become. A recent breast cancer survivor, Alisa has her own longtime partner, Todd. Her messy separation from TJ has evidently given way to a tenuous friendship between the couples, although it seems doubtful they spend as much time together off-camera as on. These relationships are further complicated by the role TJ, who made his fortune in construction, has assumed as Alix and Ashtin’s “dadager.”
All the raw material for an unscripted family drama is present. Somehow, though, the fireworks tend to fizzle as soon as they’re lit. With the divorce so far in the past, a season’s worth of halfhearted conflict among the parents is wrung out of TJ joking that Alisa could be a “young piece of ass” on The Golden Bachelor. Ashley’s friction with Alix is framed as fallout from the latter’s history of oversharing about the former but feels more like standard stepfamily tension, heightened by reality-TV producers' prodding and Alix’s hypervigilance about her stepmom’s sometimes-awkward social media presence. Ironically, we only really witness the self-centered, control-freak behavior relatives are always attributing to Alix when she’s struggling to manage her image and brand identity. As a result, the most intense moments of the series tend to involve cringey TikToks or premature glimpses of Reale Actives packaging. You probably have to be a diehard Earle girl to find this stuff compelling. And even if you are, you might be disappointed by how many climactic Earle Meets World scenes, from Ashtin kicking Alix out of her New York apartment to Cooper goading Alix to come at her, unfold in now-ancient vertical videos that already have millions of views.
It doesn’t help the show that the two people with whom Alix seems most preoccupied throughout the season—Cooper and Berrios—aren’t present. Instead, we get her side of these stories, conveyed in interviews and stiff conversations over cocktails at trendy, jewel-toned lounges, often so stripped of details that they come off as, respectively, a generic exploitative mentorship and your typical ambivalent breakup. A scene in the premiere that seems even more staged than the average docusoap grievance dump has Alix talking with TJ about Cooper in sentences that could’ve been scripted by a crisis-PR pro: “I definitely feel betrayed by Alex Cooper.” “She took advantage of my admiration for her.” Neither this storyline nor the Berrios one advances until the very end of the season, and even those late developments are anticlimactic. (Tabloid headlines linking Earle and Tom Brady, meanwhile, get coy winks but no substantive context.)
Much of the blame for Earle Meets World’s slightness and superficiality, as well as the shapelessness of episodes that drag despite running less than 40 minutes apiece, should fall on the show’s producers. Not only have they failed to identify entertaining narratives within this family’s daily life; they’ve also made their desperation to do so too apparent in the final product. To be fair, they had a difficult assignment. As eager as they look to be on screen together, the Earles are—or act—too calm and conciliatory to drive reality-soap plots. No one wants to look unhinged, least of all Alix, who talks about being unstable but can’t risk her credibility as an entrepreneur, pitchwoman, and parasocial companion to millions by getting truly ugly on camera. Which is precisely what natural born reality stars have always done. Compare Alix and Ashtin’s nights at the club to the sloppy-drunk violence and infidelity of the 20-somethings on Jersey Shore and Vanderpump Rules, or her parents’ relationships to chaotic Real Housewives marriages, and it all looks rather tame. No one here can quip like the best Bravo scrappers and Traitors debaters, either, so the show lacks the element of humor that suffuses every classic of the genre.
Influencers fall into a cultural gray area between entertainment and entrepreneurship; most excel at one more than the other. Both fields demand storytelling skills. But that doesn’t mean a person with a preternatural ability to sell people the products they watch her apply to her face as she scatters breadcrumbs about her personal life necessarily has the makings of an unscripted drama’s protagonist. Earle might be too shrewd a businesswoman to have unadulterated main character energy.

Another Chinese EV maker joins grid in Europe, with Xiaomi to launch sales next year
Xiaomi Auto says it has signed agreements with eight car dealer groups to build a sales and service network in Germany
Chinese tech firm Xiaomi will start selling electric cars in Europe next year, it announced at a consumer electronics trade show in Berlin on Thursday, adding to the growing list of Chinese carmakers expanding into the European market despite EU tariffs on China-made electric vehicles (EVs) and growing wariness across the bloc.
Xiaomi Auto, the group’s EV arm, said it would enter several European markets including Germany, where it had signed agreements with eight car dealer groups to build a sales and service network ahead of the launch.
The immediate obstacle would be Brussels’ countervailing duties on Chinese EVs. Since Xiaomi did not participate in an EU anti-subsidy investigation launched in 2023 – it only launched its first EV in China in March 2024 – it is likely to be hit with the highest duty of 35.3 per cent on the cars it exports to the EU, on top of the standard 10 per cent import duty.
Xiaomi declined to comment on whether it was in discussions with the European Commission on a price undertaking offer that would spare it the levy.
At the launch event at IFA Berlin, Xiaomi executives struck a positive tone on its expansion to Europe.
“Xiaomi Auto is committed to long-term investment in Europe,” said Yu Liguo, vice-president of Xiaomi Auto and head of its international business. Alongside its research and development centre in Munich, he said partnerships with local dealers would be key to its European expansion.
