Russian-linked vessels surveying Baltic infrastructure: Polish study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:27:26 UTC
15:27:26 KST

Jo Harper
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Russian-linked vessels are increasingly surveying critical infrastructure in the Baltic Sea region, according to a new report by Poland’s state-funded Center for Eastern Studies (OSW).
The report, Resilient Baltic, warned that protecting energy and telecommunications infrastructure and maritime and air navigation has become a major security challenge for Baltic Sea states.
It also highlighted the need to strengthen resilience against what it described as Russian hybrid operations.
Russia has rejected claims accusing Western governments of stoking "anti-Russian paranoia."
The OSW study said vessels linked to Russia have been used to map seabed infrastructure and gather information on ports, terminals and quays.
It warned that apparently civilian maritime activity could also serve intelligence purposes.
The center said six cases of damage to undersea cables and pipelines were documented between 2022 and 2025.
It said establishing responsibility for such incidents is particularly difficult outside territorial waters.
The report said Poland is particularly exposed because more than 40% of the value of its foreign trade passes through Baltic ports.
It said the ports of Gdansk and Gdynia handle more than 90% of Poland's container market.
The center said Baltic ports also play a growing military role, including handling equipment destined for Ukraine and facilitating the movement of allied forces along NATO's eastern flank.
The report called for closer cooperation between Baltic governments and port authorities, greater information-sharing on security incidents and increased EU funding for dual-use port infrastructure.
It also highlighted growing activity by Russia's so-called shadow fleet -- tankers used to transport Russian oil while circumventing Western sanctions.
The center said around 700 tankers are currently subject to sanctions imposed by the EU, UK, or US.
It said approximately half of Russia's seaborne oil and petroleum-product exports pass through Baltic ports.
According to the study, around 122,000 flights reported satellite-navigation interference over the Baltic between January and April 2025.

Artist of the month: Sangna Take
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:23:46 UTC
15:23:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — In an era obsessed with perfection, contemporary artist Sangna Take (桑拿大可) masters the art of effortless relaxation to soothe urban anxiety.
A favorite within fashion and pop-culture circles, Sangna Take brings an organic, self-generated momentum fueled by his signature "disillusioned boy" motif and unpretentious personal charm.
Returning to Eslite Gallery with his latest solo exhibition, “A Pair of Underwear, A Pair of Socks,” the artist presents urban dwellers with a soul-soothing invitation to slow down and embrace vulnerability.
Sangna Take’s appeal lies in his humor and willingness to embrace mistakes, coupled with a striking chromatic palette.
His use of color feels effortlessly intuitive, pairing saturated, contrasting hues, such as rich cobalt blue clashing against deep reddish-brown backgrounds, accented by golden hair and vibrant crimson hearts.
His layered brushwork creates a blurred, raw aesthetic suspended between figurative storytelling and abstraction. With a background in visual communication design, the artist candidly admits that "heartbreak is the best nutrient for creation."
Reflecting on his evolution over the past two years, he said "I have always wanted my work to feel more relaxed. As I grow older, I want the lines to be less sharp, gradually letting go to retain more traces of wiping and raw brushstrokes."
This approach echoes Pablo Picasso’s lifelong quest to "paint like a child."
True artistic maturity often means shedding rigid constraints rather than stacking techniques. By loosening his linework, Sangna Take strips away design precision to reclaim a pure and spontaneous freedom.
During the creation of his key visual piece, feeling unable to achieve his vision, he took a cloth and wiped the canvas clean. The resulting chaos and unpredictability yielded a surprising texture that far surpassed his original sketch.
"I was born wanting to rest and lie flat," he said, using humor and aesthetics to transform flaws into a singular artistic signature.
During his first solo show at Eslite Gallery two years ago, Sangna Take joked that his mind was "full of erotic thoughts." Meeting him again, he admited, "I still am!" Yet his visual language has matured into something richer and more layered.
The exhibition title, “A Pair of Underwear, A Pair of Socks,” evokes the uninhibited state of returning home and shedding societal identities.
Among the 34 new paintings and six ceramic sculptures on display, he integrates a long-standing fascination with Black figures. In his work, their deep skin tones and facial contours hold an intense visual allure, evoking a captivating, chocolate-sweet richness.
Meanwhile, socks subtly reference coded signals within queer and contemporary subcultures.
In his key series, “Lucky to Be Stepped On,” the lens zooms in on feet of diverse skin tones wearing various socks.
Through an intimate lens, erotic reverie and physical sensation are transformed into gentle and humorous visual symbols that capture the quiet moods of contemporary youth culture.
Sangna Take’s creative influence first bloomed on social media, reflecting a sharp intuition for pop culture. His moniker, "Sangna Take," stems from a playful Mandarin homophone of his passport name, "Sun Take."
Now based in Kaohsiung, his work is deeply shaped by southern Taiwan’s sunny climate and relaxed pace, offering viewers a comforting, sauna-like respite from daily anxiety.
A key highlight, “Fickle Flower,” originated as a casual Instagram story doodle drawn with a phone brush tool, which he then translated onto physical canvas while preserving its digital granularity.
The exhibition also unveils his very first self-portrait, capturing his early days as a painter — a complex mix of uncertainty, fear, and persistence. Moving away from the cool, detached faces rendered for fashion collaborations, this self-portrait delivers an authentic moment of self-gaze.
Everyday ephemera abound throughout the gallery, ranging from paintings executed on convenience store microwave heat-insulating cardboard to subtle homages to Nara Yoshitomo, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Umi Kumnano.
Exhibition Information
Dates: Aug. 15 – Oct. 10
Venue: Eslite Gallery (B1, Eslite Spectrum Songyan, Songshan Cultural and Creative Park, Xinyi District, Taipei)
Hours: Tuesday to Saturday, 11 a.m. – 7 p.m. (closed Sunday and Monday)
Admission: Free

Ukrainian Kate Koval says she left Louisiana State University's basketball programme because of the team's decision to sign a Russian player.

Koval said Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine was why she stepped away.
"My father serves in the Ukrainian military and takes tremendous pride in defending his country against Russian aggression," she wrote on Instagram.
"For me, this war is not distant or abstract. People close to me have been killed and wounded in Russian attacks, and places where I grew up and first began playing basketball have been destroyed by missile strikes.

Koval, who was expected to be LSU's starting centre this year, has two years of collegiate eligibility remaining.
The transfer portal has closed, but she said she hopes the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) "recognises the circumstances surrounding my situation and understands the seriousness and deep nature of this matter" and allows her to join a different university for the upcoming season.
Koval said: "I felt I had found a home at LSU, and I am incredibly grateful for my team-mates who became family, as well as my coaches, staff, professors and the entire LSU community.
"I will always cherish the relationships, experiences, and memories I made there."

Nepal’s Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina said officials remain hopeful that more workers will be rescued.
“We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,” Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page.

About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities.

El Niño is already wreaking havoc around the world — and it's only getting started
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:10:15 UTC
15:10:15 KST

In brief
- While El Niño is expected to peak later this year, some countries are already struggling through extreme weather linked to the phenomenon.
- Parts of Central America are suffering severe drought, and in Indonesia, El Niño is exacerbating widespread wildfires.
The strengthening El Niño is already disrupting lives around the world, as the United Nations warns the "surging" climate pattern is raising the risk of months of heatwaves, floods, drought and extreme weather.
On Thursday, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said there was a likelihood of "nearly 100 per cent" that El Niño will persist through to February, noting that this was the first time that an El Niño update had been so unequivocal.
The WMO's secretary-general, Celeste Saulo, said the climate driver, which was officially declared underway in June, has already dealt a blow to communities worldwide.
"We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies," she said.
The phenomenon is expected to peak at very high intensity towards the end of the year — potentially at a record-breaking level — with lasting effects on the climate well into 2027 and the prospect of unprecedented global heat.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
UN secretary-general António Guterres warned that El Niño is "being supersized before our eyes" by climate change.
"The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," Guterres said in response to the WMO update.
El Niño is associated with higher global temperatures and can bring drought and extreme heat to some regions while increasing rainfall and flood risks in others.
In Australia, El Niño typically increases the likelihood of hotter, drier conditions in the east and south-east, though its influence varies, and other climate factors also shape rainfall and temperatures.
Warmer-than-usual weather is expected across most of Australia through the spring.
Here's how El Niño is already affecting some parts of the world:
Southeast Asia
More than a million students are learning remotely this week as toxic wildfire haze blankets parts of Indonesia, with officials warning that efforts to extinguish the blazes are entering a critical phase.
"Our problems are not over. September is the peak of El Niño," Indonesia's forestry minister Raja Juli Antoni told reporters this week.
El Niño is driving hotter, drier conditions in the region, intensifying a dry season that has seen thousands of hectares burnt.
Almost 95,000 hectares were burnt in July alone.
Indonesian forest fire forensics expert Bambang Hero Saharjo told the BBC this year's El Niño-fuelled blazes could burn an area as large as 11 million hectares.
The haze has spread across parts of Southeast Asia, triggering health warnings and hospitalisations.
The health ministry in neighbouring Malaysia has reported rising cases of asthma and conjunctivitis nationwide as air quality worsens.
Six districts in the state of Sarawak recorded hazardous Air Pollutant Index (API) readings, including the state capital, Kuching, where the API hit 407.
Under national guidelines, levels above 300 are classed as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 could prompt consideration of a local emergency.
Local resident Ivana Mason said the conditions are affecting her health and preventing her from going outside.
"If I do, I can literally taste the smoke in my mouth," she said.
Latin America
Multiple Central and South American countries, some of which are particularly susceptible to El Niño's influences, are on high alert as they brace for impact.
Panama, Ecuador, Honduras, Colombia and El Salvador have declared emergencies in response to the El Niño episode, activating agencies to prepare for imminent risks.
More than 70,000 corn-farming households in Central America's Dry Corridor — a drought-prone region spanning parts of Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador — have reported devastating crop losses, according to a recent report by Oxfam.
Further south, Peru has declared a state of emergency in a third of its cities due to El Niño, warning that intense heat and rain could leave people without enough to eat.
Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, and parts of North, Central and South America are among the regions more consistently impacted by El Niño events, according to associate professor Andrea Taschetto, a climate researcher at the University of New South Wales.
"The last El Niño had a really big impact in the Amazon Basin, and that affects all the communities that are along the Amazon River," she told SBS News.
The river network is a vital transport route for the region, she noted, meaning low water levels can disrupt access to food, healthcare and other essential supplies.
The World Food Programme has warned that El Niño is a massive threat to food security for millions of people, with the largest impacts expected in parts of Central America.
Its modelling showed more than 16 million people could be affected in Latin America and the Caribbean, with an 81 per cent increase in food insecurity projected.
El Niño could also disrupt global trade.
Starting Friday, the Panama Canal, an important shipping route connecting the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, will restrict the number of vessels that can transit for only the second time in its history.
It's a bid to conserve water amid drought that may last until next year.
Five per cent of global trade passes through the man-made canal, which relies on water from reservoirs including Lake Gatun to operate locks that raise and lower ships in the waterway.
South Asia
Sri Lanka is among the South Asian countries badly affected by weather disruptions this year, with some key farming districts recording rainfall deficits of 85 per cent to 100 per cent below long-term averages.
Soaring temperatures have left large swathes of Sri Lanka's north, east and southern regions parched, with small tanks, rivers and lakes that usually feed crops and provide drinking water drying out.
The Sri Lankan government has said the impact this year could be the worst in decades and that water levels at hundreds of such tanks in the country have dropped to about 10 per cent.
Sri Lanka's current dry conditions are forecast to give way to heavy rains from late September until December, but those rains are expected to be followed by a prolonged drought early next year.
The government has set up a ministerial panel to deal with the fallout from what its environment minister has said would be the island's "worst" El Niño.
— With additional reporting by Agence France-Presse and Reuters.

hissy cooling jacket pairs CO₂ cartridges with technical apparel for extreme urban heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:05:30 UTC
15:05:30 KST

Hissy brings a cooling system into lightweight technical apparel
Hissy is a wearable cooling system developed for increasingly high urban temperatures. The garment uses a dedicated CO₂ cartridge in place of the heavy batteries and fan-based ventilation commonly found in portable cooling devices. Once the cartridge is docked, high-pressure liquid carbon dioxide vaporizes within the system, absorbing surrounding heat and producing a cooling airflow of approximately -30°C.
The concept responds to the limitations of conventional cooling technologies in extreme heat. As global temperatures rise and summer outdoor activities become increasingly affected by heat, portable fans become less effective at temperatures above 35°C. Battery-powered cooling devices also become heavier and less efficient, while exposure to high temperatures can further affect battery performance and safety. Hissy addresses these constraints through a lightweight garment-based system that integrates the cooling hardware directly into the apparel.
The garment is organized around an internal tubular Air Path that distributes cooling through the body of the garment. Its pattern and construction are determined by the route of this internal system, with the fabric cut and sewn to accommodate the tubing. The Air Path follows an ergonomic spiral based on the natural curves of the body, helping prevent bending or kinking that could obstruct the high-pressure cooling spray. Micro-perforations along the Air Path direct the airflow toward the body’s major heat-generating areas. Their dimensions and distribution were established through thermal mapping and heat-distribution experiments, allowing the cooling pressure to remain consistent from the hardware connector through to the end of the tube. This localized distribution avoids dispersing airflow indiscriminately while supporting controlled thermal comfort.
Hissy system extends from cooling apparel To lifestyle products
The CO₂ cartridge is integrated into the sleeve through a magnetic docking structure. Instead of screw threads, the system uses magnetic attraction to draw the cartridge into position, where locking protrusions engage with the internal hardware. The connection prevents vertical extraction and keeps the cartridge secured against the recoil generated by the high-pressure cooling spray. Removal follows the same magnetic mechanism. A slight rotation switches the poles of the internal dual-magnetized structure to repulsion. A groove within the hardware guides the cartridge through the required release angle, allowing the empty cartridge to be removed with a simple twist.
Additional details address the garment’s use during outdoor activity. An internal strap and external sleeve zipper secure the hardware according to the wearer’s wrist size and limit movement during use. A dedicated chest pocket provides storage for spare cartridges, keeping replacements accessible while maintaining the garment’s integrated appearance. The cooling system designed by Dongheon Kang, Minseo Jung, Yuha Ko, Juhyeon Jeon, and Woohi Park for Samsung Design Membershipalso incorporates a circular approach to CO₂ use. The carbon dioxide is captured from industrial processes that would otherwise release it into the atmosphere and repurposed as the cooling medium. After use, the cartridges are collected, inspected, refilled, and recirculated. The system is designed to keep both the products and the CO₂ resource in circulation without adding net carbon to the atmosphere.
Hissy’s apparel features a function-driven design, cut and sewn to mirror the optimal path of the cooling airflow
Hissy is conceived as a broader cooling platform beyond the initial garment. Its proposed expansion is structured across three phases. The first extends the CO₂ cooling technology to other wearable formats, including footwear, to distribute thermal management across the body. The second applies the system to lifestyle products such as outdoor can coolers for keeping food and beverages cold. The third moves into industrial applications, positioning the technology as a B2B thermal-management system for machines operating in high-temperature outdoor environments, including delivery robots and drones.
Through this approach, Hissy combines wearable design, airflow engineering, material construction, magnetic interaction, and CO₂ recirculation into a cooling system intended to operate across personal, lifestyle, and industrial applications.

Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:04:06 UTC
15:04:06 KST

Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
Scientists have revealed that the human brain’s earliest stem cells use both nutrients and physical signals to decide what kinds of brain cells to build.
- Date:
- September 4, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Los Angeles Health Sciences
- Summary:
- UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. Those signals can alter which types of neurons are produced, including upper-layer neurons that are especially prominent in humans.
- Share:
Before birth, the human brain is assembled through an enormous series of cellular choices. At the center of this process are radial glia, a special type of stem cell that helps create many of the features that distinguish the human brain.
These cells produce large numbers of the neurons and support cells that make up the cerebral cortex, the brain region involved in thought, memory, and language. Radial glia are also believed to contribute to the unusually large expansion of the human cortex compared with that of other species. Although most disappear before birth, similar cells can later appear again in brain cancers for reasons scientists still do not fully understand.
"Radial glia are the coolest cells that have ever existed," said Aparna Bhaduri, an assistant professor of biological chemistry at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. "They're really key to making us human. But they're also at the center of many neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders, as well as cancer -- so understanding how they make their decisions is one way to start understanding how those conditions arise."
Two new studies published in Cell and Science now provide a closer look at how radial glia make those developmental choices. Bhaduri and her colleagues found that the cells respond to two very different kinds of information: the way they process nutrients and direct physical signals from another part of the developing brain. Together, these findings offer new insight into how the human cortex produces its remarkable variety of cell types.
Metabolism helps direct brain stem cells
In the Cell study, researchers built a detailed map of metabolism in the developing human cortex. The project was a collaboration between Bhaduri's lab and Heather Christofk's lab and was led by co-first authors Jessenya Mil and Jose Soto.
To create the atlas, the team analyzed donated human tissue along with brain organoids grown from stem cells. Their results pointed to an unexpected conclusion: metabolism does not simply support brain development in the background. It can actively influence which kinds of cells are produced.
The researchers found that radial glia depend heavily on the pentose phosphate pathway, a metabolic process that uses glucose to make materials needed by cells that are dividing rapidly.
When the scientists lowered the amount of available glucose or interfered with this pathway, the stem cells changed what they produced. They began generating more inhibitory neurons and other cell types that normally appear later in development.
"What was surprising is that metabolism isn't just a passive thing that happens in the background," said Bhaduri, a member of both the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center and the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center. "It can really control how stem cells make decisions."
The results could help scientists investigate how maternal nutrition, metabolic disorders, and other environmental influences affect the developing brain. The metabolic atlas also provides one of the most detailed resources yet for researchers studying metabolism during human brain development.
A signal arrives early from the thalamus
The second study, published in Science and led by first author Claudia Nguyen, examined a completely different source of developmental information. This time, the researchers focused on signals coming from the thalamus, a structure deep inside the brain that helps relay information throughout the nervous system.
Scientists have known for years that neurons in the thalamus send long projections toward the cortex. These wire-like fibers eventually form connections with specific cortical neurons. However, anatomical studies have shown that in humans, the projections reach the cortex long before those final connections are established.
That raised an important question: Why do the fibers arrive so early?
Using human stem cell-derived brain "assembloids," the UCLA researchers found part of the answer. The thalamic projections physically touch radial glia while the brain is still developing.
That contact changed the behavior of the stem cells. It caused them to produce more excitatory neurons, the primary signal-carrying neurons in the cortex. The effect was especially strong for upper-layer neurons, which are particularly expanded in the human brain.
"We already knew that these projections influence how the cortex develops," Bhaduri said. "What we specifically found is that this influence comes through an actual physical connection between the projections and the radial glia -- a point of contact that just hasn't been identified before, and one that very likely does not exist in rodents."
A gene linked to autism enters the picture
The researchers connected this physical interaction to NRXN1, a gene already known for helping neurons form connections with one another. Mutations in NRXN1 have previously been associated with autism spectrum disorder.
To investigate its role, the team created assembloids from patient-derived cells carrying an NRXN1 mutation. In these models, the altered thalamic signals behaved differently from signals made by unaffected cells.
Those changes shifted the balance between the number of stem cells and the neurons they generated. The result offers researchers a possible way to study how disturbances early in brain development could influence the formation of the cortex.
The developing brain is in constant communication
Although the two studies focused on very different mechanisms, they point toward the same broader idea. One examined metabolism, while the other explored neural connections, yet both showed that radial glia do not make their decisions in isolation. Their behavior is continuously shaped by signals from the environment around them.
The studies also demonstrate how dramatically organoid technology has changed the study of human brain development. About a decade ago, scientists had few practical ways to directly investigate how uniquely human neural stem cells behave.
Today, brain organoids and related models allow researchers to recreate important features of human brain development in the laboratory. These systems also make it possible to test questions that cannot be addressed through animal models alone.
Bhaduri hopes the findings will encourage scientists to view metabolism and physical cellular connections as active drivers of development rather than as background processes.
"Ultimately, these studies give us a glimpse under the hood of how these cells make decisions," she said. "Understanding those decisions is a first step toward understanding normal brain development, disease vulnerability and, potentially, how similar stem-cell programs operate in brain cancer."
This research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation, the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation, the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, the Rose Hills Foundation, the Esther A. & Joseph Klingenstein Fund, the Simons Foundation, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, the NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, the International Foundation for Ethical Research, the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center's Stem Cell Research Training Program, and the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center and UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center Ablon Scholars Program.

In a post on X on Thursday, Ghalibaf directly addressed Bessent, saying, “Short harder, champ. Like your career depends on it (because it does). Or drain below the danger zone and watch your caverns collapse (along with your career). Or pray to the salt gods of Bryan Mound. The world's already got its popcorn :)”
Accoridng to Press TV, Ghalibaf’s remarks came amid growing pressure on the US administration over the performance of the Treasury and energy markets.
Bessent has pursued buyback operations in the US Treasury market, particularly involving 10-year bonds, in an effort to bring down long-term yields and reduce borrowing costs ahead of the midterm elections.
However, the bond market has largely resisted the intervention, with yields remaining elevated or even increasing. Critics, including veteran Wall Street figures such as Stanley Druckenmiller, have questioned the effectiveness of the measures and warned of growing market risks.
The United States has also drawn heavily on its Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) amid the war with Iran and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
The SPR, which is stored in vast underground salt caverns in Texas and Louisiana, has fallen to its lowest level since the early 1980s. Bryan Mound, near the Texas coast, is among the reserve’s major storage sites.
Concerns have also been raised over the structural risks associated with excessive withdrawals from salt caverns, including pressure changes, salt-wall stability, well integrity and potential damage to long-term storage capacity.
Some oil traders have interpreted Bessent’s signals as an indication that US efforts could push futures prices lower. However, Oman and UAE oil futures, which are being closely watched as indicators of market expectations surrounding oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, have risen above $100 in recent days.
Washington had been counting on psychological pressure and assurances about the reopening of the southern shipping route through Hormuz to bring down futures prices.
The combination of elevated bond yields, sharply reduced strategic oil reserves and rising oil futures prices has created mounting pressure on Bessent and the Trump administration.
According to Ghalibaf, Washington is attempting to mask the situation through rhetoric over Iran, while market indicators are providing a clearer picture of the underlying pressures.

Fancy cars and hanging with mum, the paradox of Aussie's EPL teen dream
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:00:25 UTC
15:00:25 KST

Fancy cars and hanging with mum, the paradox of Lucas Herrington's EPL teen dream
Lucas Herrington has gone to number one with a bullet in 2026, at a speed so dizzying it would leave many teenagers' heads spinning.
Turning 19 this weekend, he is fresh off a breakthrough World Cup, has a multi-million-dollar contract in the best football league in the world, and has fans fawning over him.
But true to his persona on the pitch, the central defender is calm, level-headed and capable of tackling any challenge.
"My parents have always instilled that factor of humility in my life and having that humbleness to stay grounded and just to keep working hard," he told Australian media on a call from Hull.
"I'm always trying to get better. So I think it's always having that positive mindset that I've still got a lot of things to work on. And I'm not the finished product."
Herrington made his bolt-from-the-blue Socceroos debut in March, which turned into a maiden World Cup appearance a few months later.
His impressive efforts in North America captured interest from some of the biggest clubs in the world including Barcelona and Liverpool.
But he settled on Hull City, newly promoted in the English Premier League, and a five-year deal for a transfer fee reportedly worth $33 million with add-ons, to become the most expensive Australian player ever.
Alessandro Circati recently joined that rich list with his transfer from Parma to Benfica.
The money is astronomical for an Australian footballer, and despite his down-to-earth nature, even Herrington was lured in by the EPL stereotype of fancy, fast cars.
"It's a nice car park. I do have a car right now; it's nice. I'm enjoying it," he laughed, almost sheepishly.
But when he speaks about his off-field highlights in his few weeks in England, the teenager goes back to keeping it real.
"Mum's here at the moment. She leaves soon, so I've just been exploring around with her," he said.
"So that's been really nice, some great quality time with her."
Advice from a legend
Herrington made his debut for the Tigers off the bench in their upset win over Manchester United.
"It was only a week and a couple of days from when I landed to that game against Man United," he said.
"Great moment for the city and for me personally, with my mum and my agent in the stands, it was a super proud moment for me.
"And it was a great match, very grateful for the opportunity to be there."
He was again used as a substitute in a win over Coventry, while he started the EFL Cup penalty shootout win against Stoke.
A strong show of confidence for the youngster, who is the only Australian in England's top flight.
"It's probably the best league in the world. So to be here at 18 is super special," he said.
"I've always wanted to play in the Premier League, so I'm very grateful for the opportunity from the coaching staff and the club to do so. And I've loved my first three or so weeks here.
"It's a league with the best players in the world, so to be up against them every week is really special and a great challenge for me as a young defender.
"It's just about trying to learn as much as possible from the older boys in the team and just try and take every game as a lesson."
And don't mistake his modesty for meekness; he knows he belongs.
A message reinforced by former Sweden international Zlatan Ibrahimović, who publicly supported Herrington after missing a penalty in the Socceroos' World Cup round of 32 shootout loss to Egypt.
“This is just the beginning of your career," Ibrahimović said on Fox Sports USA's post-game analysis.
"You stepping up there, you show a lot of courage. Not everybody would do that. My friend, you're the best. Don't listen to the rest. Listen, Herrington, if you want to reach out, I'm here."
Ibrahimović made good on his promise and ended up calling the Queensland product himself.
"He just said, really don't fear anyone. I'm here for a reason, so just go enjoy," Herrington said.
Dreams do come true
Herrington's meteoric rise means he has not yet played for Australia in his home state.
Something the former Roar product hopes to do in the Socceroos' friendlies against Brazil later this month, in Townsville and Brisbane.
"It'd be a dream come true to play for the Socceroos in Brisbane," he said.
"Something that I've always wanted to do, and to play in front of hopefully a packed-out Suncorp would be a dream, and in front of my family and friends would be awesome."
And he is happy to be a role model for others.
"Just trying to be an inspiration for all the young Australians that there is really a pathway to the Premier League," he said.
"I think a lot of young footballers in Australia like me wake up at all hours in the morning to watch the Premier League.
"So hopefully I can make them proud, make Australia proud.
"Just to keep working hard, enjoy the process, and to have big dreams because dreams do come true."

Australia Should Work With China, Not Try to Contain It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Greg Sheridan has always been provocative. The foreign editor of The Australian is well known for his strident view that Australia should fully embrace American military power. One recent sermon focused on the need to support the U.S. Navy base at HMAS Stirling. “Frankly,” he writes, “I’d much rather entrust Australia’s security to the U.S. Navy than to the Albanese government.”
Sheridan then moves to flattery for Labor’s resident Kentucky Colonel, aka the minister for AUKUS, Richard Marles. Marles, he says, has “done quite well on the critical question of U.S. alliance management.” Despite his distaste for most things Labor, Sheridan concludes that Marles is a good fit for the job at hand: kowtowing to the U.S. military and its boss, the belligerent Pete Hegseth. He claims we don’t need to pretend that Stirling is an Australian military base because “we actively and happily shelter under the U.S. extended nuclear umbrella.” Sheridan proposes that the U.S. and Australia should now draw up “common battle plans” to prepare for conflict with “the only candidate for adversary – China”
There is no doubt China has developed its People’s Liberation Army (PLA) land, navy, air force, marines, rocket force, and cyber warfare capabilities to now claim military ascendancy in the South China Sea and beyond. In June, the Lowy Institute in Sydney released a well-researched analysis of the PLA’s military strength entitled “Understanding the Chinese military threat to Australia.”
Authored by Sam Roggeveen and David Vallance, the study is good work. It explains China’s rise and President Xi Jinping’s aim to complete China’s “great rejuvenation” by 2049, the 100th anniversary of Mao’s revolutionary victory. By then, the authors assert, China will be a prosperous, technologically advanced and a global military superpower – “a world class force.” Many would say this has already been achieved.
The Chinese submarine-launched ballistic missile test conducted on July 6 in the Pacific confirmed that the Chinese Navy now has the capability to reach the Australian mainland. Despite the complaints voiced by Penny Wong about “destabilization of the region” and the Prime Minister’s accusation of “a provocative act,” no criticism is ever made by Australia of comparable practices by U.S. forces.
On the day of the Chinese test, The New York Times reported that “the United States routinely carries out test launches of ballistic missiles from land or sea, including one fired from California at a target in the Marshall Islands this March.” They say the U.S. conducts five to 10 tests of its Minuteman and Trident missiles over the Pacific every year. Australia’s hypocrisy is breathtaking.
While analysis of China’s growing military capabilities – as distinct from its threat – is relevant to understanding our legitimate defense needs, it should be understood that China already has the capability to interdict Australia’s trade routes and undersea communications technology – as well as to conduct cyber operations against our critical communications and energy infrastructure. None of this requires missiles to be fired in anger, but there is no reason to conclude that China intends any such interdiction or military threat to Australia.
Contrast this with the fact that China is, by far, Australia’s largest trading partner, taking one-third of our exports, providing 570,000 direct jobs in Australia, and driving two-way trade worth $200 billion per annum. The conclusion is surely that China already has the ability to subdue Australia economically without firing a shot. China also has the ability to continue making Australia rich.
Currently Australia is engaged in what the Canberra press gallery is calling “a diplomatic knife fight” with China over the security preferences of small Pacific nations. There are now calls for a region-wide security network that The Australian says “will further marginalize Beijing.” Former Australian ambassador to China, Dr. Geoff Raby, says the AUKUS deal sends a “very clear signal to the leadership in China that Australia now sees China as an enemy.” Raby and other experienced diplomats have consistently warned us that Australia needs to rely more on diplomacy and statecraft rather than national security rhetoric and military posturing.
Whereas there are good reasons for Australia to invest more in Pacific nations to counter climate change and support infrastructure development, the recent move to convert those relationships into military alliances is wrong-headed and provocative. This policy may also complicate collaborative work with our neighbors in Southeast Asia. Engaging in cooperative regional diplomacy with ASEAN nations and engaging respectfully with China is far preferable to stoking hostility and inciting a conflict that Australia cannot win.
China is asserting its right to exercise power and influence in our region. Some of its actions are open to strong criticism and challenge. But the question we should consider is this: are we more likely to influence China’s behavior as a great power through military containment and confrontation – or by engaging proactively through middle-power statecraft?
A reasonable conclusion is that the rise of China to superpower status is a reality that Australian foreign policy must embrace. The U.S., despite its war-mongering in other theaters, is pulling back from its position as overlord in the Asia-Pacific. Beijing reads this as tacit U.S. recognition of China’s emergence as a strategic and military equal. While Washington prods Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Australia to spend more on weapons and develop Sheridan’s relished “battle plans,” Uncle Sam is leaving the front line for its proxies to defend. That is a fool’s errand in any language.
Japan has its own East Asia security preoccupations, South Korea wants détente with North Korea and China, and Taiwan wants the status quo. Only the weak and brash military of the Philippines think a fight with China is advisable. Meanwhile, Australia dithers with AUKUS and a confused diplomacy of “strategic equilibrium” – all while striving to conjure a Pacific alliance of microstates to confront and contain China.
After Suez in 1956, Great Britain, the motherland, finally revealed its impotence as a world power. By then, Australia had already switched horses to pay tribute to Washington. Now, after Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan and Iran, the ability of the U.S. to project power across the globe is manifestly waning. Like all empires in decline, America has degenerated into a rogue state engaged in endless conflicts. For Australia, the new geopolitical reality presents a historic opportunity to recalibrate our defense and foreign policy.
Perhaps we should embrace our new ally Papua New Guinea’s dictum: “a friend to all – an enemy to none.” It would surely work better than the current policy of barely concealed hostility toward China. The decline of American power in the Pacific is irreversible because China’s economic, diplomatic, and military rise is inexorable. There is no chance that Australia can resist that power by trying to contain it. It would be, to borrow Paul Keating’s famous metaphor, “like throwing a handful of toothpicks at the mountain.” Our wisest course is to embrace China’s rise and influence it through good neighbor statecraft and the strengthening of existing economic ties.
The irony of our time is that China’s rise, including the military power that Sheridan and Marles so fear, may well prevent war in our region. America’s growing reluctance to confront that power may save us from a toxic alliance that serves only to stimulate endless strife.
This article was originally published by the website Pearls and Irritations and is reprinted with permission.

'Will always face consequences': Yogi Adityanath warns 'anti-national' forces

Anti-national forces harming India's unity will face consequences: Adityanath
NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Friday warned that anti-national and anti-social forces seeking to spread hatred or undermine India's unity would face consequences, invoking Lord Krishna's message on the occasion of Janmashtami.Addressing a gathering in Mathura, the birthplace of Lord Krishna, on the second day of his visit, Adityanath emphasised that His teachings and message remained equally relevant today.
"Wherever the forces of goodness exist, they will be protected under all circumstances. But wherever anti-national and anti-social forces raise their heads, create hatred in society or attempt to harm India's unity, integrity and faith, Lord Krishna had already said 5,000 years ago what their fate would be," PTI quoted the chief minister as saying.Yogi Adityanath also cited the Bhagavad Gita's teaching, "Paritranaya sadhunam, vinashaya cha dushkritam" (for the protection of the righteous and destruction of evil), stressing that it continued to guide society.The chief minister highlighted the Braj region's role in preserving its religious heritage and the memories of Lord Krishna despite repeated invasions and attempts by various groups to impose their faith on India.
"Many invasions took place and many people tried to impose their faith on India, but no one could erase the Sanatan faith," Yogi Adityanath said."Those who dared to erase Sanatan faith themselves disappeared into the dust, but the memories of Shri Krishna and Radha Rani, not only in Braj but across India, continue to inspire us today and provide an encouraging environment for future generations," he added.The chief minister welcomed devotees arriving in Mathura for Janmashtami and extended his greetings to the people of Uttar Pradesh on the festival marking the birth of Lord Krishna.Yogi Adityanath has been in Mathura since Thursday for Janmashtami celebrations and has been attending programmes ahead of the festival.

Interview: Customer-oriented approach vital in AI-driven economy, says Sberbank CFO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:58:59 CST
14:58:59 KST

by Xinhua writers Vladislava Chugueva, Zhang Chaoqun
MOSCOW, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Only companies that prioritize their customers' interests will survive and thrive amid the fundamental changes artificial intelligence (AI) has brought to the global economy, Sberbank Deputy Chairman and CFO Taras Skvortsov has said.
Over one billion people worldwide still lack access to formal bank accounts, and AI can effectively lower banks' service thresholds to reach these underserved groups, Skvortsov told Xinhua ahead of the ongoing Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.
As Russia's largest bank, Sberbank plays a leading role in the country's AI research and application, translating its advances in AI into more accessible everyday services for customers, he said.
In Russia, social tax deductions for education, fitness and medical expenses have long been underused because of cumbersome procedures. Sberbank has simplified the process with one-click processing, allowing customers to have the bank apply for deductions on their behalf.
"Within the framework of our human-centric strategy, we asked ourselves whether we could streamline the entire process for users, allowing them to simply tick a box to authorize Sberbank to apply for tax deductions on their behalf," Skvortsov said, noting that the bank expects the service to attract 60 million to 70 million users annually.
The bank itself is also among the biggest beneficiaries of AI, he noted, saying that the technology is transforming the traditional financial cycle of data collection, reporting, analysis and decision-making by generating analysis and actionable solutions as soon as data is acquired.
Sberbank has stepped up AI investment, Skvortsov said, spending about 100 billion rubles (1.15 billion U.S. dollars) on AI research and development in 2024 and planning to invest 350 billion rubles by 2026, with a focus on its GigaChat model and applications in personalized financial services, credit risk assessment and operational cost reduction.
Earlier this year, Sberbank unveiled Russia's first optical computing processor for AI applications, designed to speed up AI model training and deployment while improving energy efficiency, helping address rising power demands from AI data centers, he added.
In an era of global economic uncertainty, institutional resilience hinges on adaptability and a human-centric philosophy, Skvortsov said. "We believe that in a decade, only enterprises embracing this people-oriented mindset will survive and thrive."
"Companies that fail to prioritize user interests will gradually lose competitiveness and fade from the market," he said. ■

Japan's household spending falls 3.6 pct in July
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:58:44 CST
14:58:44 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Japan's household spending dropped 3.6 percent in inflation-adjusted real terms in July from a year earlier, the eighth straight monthly decline, government data showed Friday.
The reading marked the steepest fall since a 6.3 percent slide in January 2024, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications said.
Households of two or more people spent an average of 301,245 yen (around 1,926 U.S. dollars) in the reporting month.
By category, food and beverage spending declined 1.3 percent as inflation weighed on purchases, while cooler weather than the previous year also curbed beverage demand.
Consumers gravitated toward cheaper prepared food, a shift a ministry official described as a "trend towards tighter spending."
Outlays for energy and water bills tumbled 9.2 percent, a drop an official attributed largely to reduced air-conditioning use amid lower temperatures than the same month last year.
The household spending data serves as a key indicator of private consumption, which accounts for more than half of Japan's gross domestic product.
The average monthly income of salaried households of at least two individuals fell by a real 3.8 percent to 689,476 yen, according to the ministry. ■

New Zealand records 3rd-warmest winter on record
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:58:33 CST
14:58:33 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand recorded its third-warmest winter on record in 2026, with a nationwide average temperature of 9.7 degrees Celsius, Earth Sciences New Zealand said Friday.
The temperature was 1.1 degrees Celsius above the 1991-2020 winter average, making it the third-warmest winter since the country's seven-station temperature series began in 1909, the agency said in a statement.
Exceptional warmth in June and a relatively warm winter throughout the South Island were the dominant features of the country's overall seasonal temperature, while temperatures were near average in parts of Northland, Auckland, Waikato, eastern Bay of Plenty and Gisborne on the North Island, it said.
Winter rainfall was above or well above normal in Southland, Otago, southern and inland Canterbury and the West Coast on the South Island, while large parts of the North Island recorded below-normal rainfall, the agency said.
Impactful heavy rainfall from July 5 to July 9 affected eastern parts of the country, with three local states of emergency declared, it noted.
The highest winter temperature was 26 degrees Celsius on June 20 at Bromley in Christchurch, the South Island's largest city. It was the country's second-highest winter temperature on record. The lowest was minus 13.5 degrees Celsius at Lake Tekapo on July 12.
El Niño conditions in the tropical Pacific strengthened considerably from mid-winter onward, the agency said, adding that sea surface temperatures around New Zealand were mostly near or above average, with marine heatwave conditions experienced around much of the South Island and Tasman Sea during July and August.
Scientists said El Niño typically brings stronger, more frequent southwesterly to northwesterly winds, resulting in drier conditions in eastern and northern areas of both islands and wetter conditions in the western and lower South Island. ■

2 trapped Nepal workers rescued from buried tunnel 9 days after devastating floods, and more voices heard
Kathmandu, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal pulled two hydropower workers from a tunnel Friday as emergency teams raced to find more survivors, spurred on by the dramatic rescues more than a week after the devastating flash floods that killed more than 1,200 people.
CBS News' Ramy Inocencio said there was hope more survivors could emerge from the tunnel — possibly dozens more — as rescuers heard voices coming from deep inside the structure that the was covered by mud and filled with flood water during last week's catastrophe.
The two men were rescued from the Trishuli 3A tunnel nine days after floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, devastated towns and swept away villages in Nepal.
Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane posted about the second rescue on his Facebook page shortly after army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet confirmed the first trapped worker's rescue.
Nepal Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told Inocencio in a text message that he was "thrilled" about the two rescues and "hoping to see more survivors." He said it was unclear how many survivors might still be inside the tunnel, but with voices heard, he said the clock was ticking to find and rescue everyone still alive.
Rescuers first heard voices from inside the tunnel Friday morning, enabling them to locate the two men, Neupane said.
Local television news channels showed images of the first rescued worker, covered in mud, being carried from the site on a rescuer's shoulder. Officials said both men were in stable condition and were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu.
Mechanical foreman Sanjay Shah said "thank you" when he was pulled out, but he was then advised not to speak due to his weakened condition, Inocencio reported.
Amir Maharjan, brother of the other rescued worker, mechanical supervisor Kabir Maharjan, told The Associated Press he "can't explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to God." He said the family were on their way to the hospital to see him.
"We couldn't properly eat or drink for 10 days," Kabir Maharjan's wife, Hirashova, told CBS News partner network BBC News. "We were very scared. Now we are all happy. We are even crying."
At least 557 workers from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project along the Trishuli River remain missing, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.
A Nepali energy adviser told Inocencio it was not just a tunnel that goes into the ground next to the Trishuli River, but a system of rooms and chambers that snake up and down, where the workers are apparently stuck.
The adviser also told Inocencio the trapped workers were some of the smartest engineers in Nepal, and they probably have been trying to figure their own way out, and how to get oxygen so they don't run out of air — the biggest risk.
At least 1,287 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the country's disaster management agency. China, as of late Wednesday, said 21 people were killed and 541 were missing on the Tibet side of the border.
About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities.

Air India Phuket-Delhi incident: All 3 hydraulic systems failed; pilot tested positive for psychoactive substance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:57:23 UTC
14:57:23 KST

The hydraulic failure itself, the more immediate cause of the injuries onboard, unfolded within a five-second window. VT-EXO, an eight-year-old A320neo carrying 145 people, had just been cleared to climb from FL340 to FL360 after entering Kolkata Flight Information Region.
MUMBAI: The preliminary investigation into the August 4 Air India Phuket-Delhi accident has found that the aircraft's three hydraulic systems, green, blue and yellow, lost pressure within seconds while the A320 was cruising at 36,000 feet, triggering an autopilot disengagement, stall warning and an altitude upset. Alongside the technical findings, the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has recommended that the DGCA take action against the Pilot-in-Command, who tested non-negative for psychoactive substance use following the flight."The confirmation of use of psycho-active substance is a serious concern, and AAIB recommends appropriate actions by DGCA on priority," the report said. The interim safety recommendation asked the regulator to "take appropriate actions as deemed fit to prevent abuse of psycho-active substance." Post-flight, both pilots underwent a breath analyser test, which came back satisfactory. But the subsequent psychoactive substance detection test returned a non-negative result for the PIC, a finding confirmed by a follow-up laboratory blood test. The co-pilot tested negative on both counts.The hydraulic failure itself, the more immediate cause of the injuries onboard, unfolded within a five-second window.
VT-EXO, an eight-year-old A320neo carrying 145 people, had just been cleared to climb from FL340 to FL360 after entering Kolkata Flight Information Region. At 04:02:43 UTC, the flight control system "detected loss of green hydraulic system." Four seconds later, the flight control (F/CTL) system detected loss of Blue and Yellow hydraulic systems. With all three systems compromised simultaneously, the autopilot disengaged, a continuous repetitive chime sounded, and the stall warning triggered for two seconds. The aircraft "encountered altitude upset," gaining 372 feet before falling 292 feet from its assigned level, the report said.The co-pilot, who was Pilot Flying, responded first to the upset before the captain took over the controls. Recovery was swift. "At around 04:02:52 UTC, the Blue hydraulic system was recovered, and a few seconds later, the Yellow hydraulic and the Green hydraulic systems were also recovered," the report said. It restored normal flight control surfaces within seconds of the failure.But with seatbelt signs off during cruise, the sudden upset threw passengers and crew around the cabin. Twenty-four people, including four cabin crew, needed medical attention on landing; four were hospitalised with serious injuries. The cabin damage was extensive: cracked ceiling panels across multiple rows, dislodged overhead bins, a broken emergency exit handle, a lavatory commode "uprooted from its original location," and a bent crew seat. Despite the injuries, the flight crew chose not to divert, opting instead to continue to Delhi while requesting medical priority from ATC. The aircraft landed safely on runway 11L at 05:30 UTC, around ninety minutes after the failure.Investigators have already flagged one detail for closer scrutiny: the aircraft was dispatched from Phuket under an active Minimum Equipment List item for the Power Transfer Unit, invoked a week earlier on July 28. The PTU serves as an auxiliary hydraulic source shared between the green and yellow systems, and its status at the time of the failure is expected to be a focus of the ongoing probe. Flight recorder data has been downloaded and is under analysis, and a technical team from Airbus and France's BEA inspected the aircraft in Delhi in mid-August, after which hydraulic components and fluid samples were removed for further testing.“The Airbus A320 aircraft has three hydraulic systems. They are identified as the green, blue and yellow systems. Together they supply hydraulic power at 3000 psi (206 bar) to the main power users. Services which are not used during flight are isolated from the main supply. Hydraulic fluid cannot be transferred from one system to another. Each system has its own hydraulic reservoir,” the report said, explaining the hydraulics on the aircraft.
On the green system, the normal source of pressure is the Engine Driven Pump (EDP) located on the left engine and, as an auxiliary source, the Power Transfer Unit (PTU). On the blue system, the normal source of pressure is the electrical pump (E-Pump) and, as an auxiliary source, the Ram Air Turbine (RAT). On the yellow system, the normal source of pressure is the EDP located on the right engine and as auxiliary sources the PTU and the electric pump (E-Pump). “Each hydraulic system pressurisation information is available for the aircraft systems through one pressure transmitter (numerical value of the pressure), two pressure switches (discrete value indicating if there is a loss of pressure). Relevant Hydraulic components were removed from the aircraft for further analysis,” the report said. The PTU is an auxiliary pressure supply for either the green or yellow systems without transfer of fluid between the two systems. It operates automatically if there is a delta pressure of 500 psi between the green/yellow or yellow/green hydraulic systems, it addedThe said report is preliminary, and a detailed technical investigation is still underway.

This virus has evolved. Australia doesn't have a new vaccine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:55:36 UTC
14:55:36 KST

IN BRIEF
- Pfizer's latest COVID vaccine targets the XFG subvariant, but it has not yet been registered for use in Australia.
- Experts say Australia's vaccine update process could be streamlined as new COVID variants continue to emerge.
Australians can't yet access a COVID-19 vaccine tailored for new variants, highlighting how Australia's system tends to lag behind, as a major manufacturer confirms it has no plans to push into Australia's market.
Pfizer and BioNTech's latest COVID-19 vaccine, adapted to target the XFG subvariant, has been approved in the United States for the 2026-27 season, following international guidance to more closely match vaccines with contemporary circulating variants.
Australia does not yet have that formulation registered.
But experts say the lag is not necessarily cause for alarm, with Australia continuing to monitor circulating variants and having access to relatively recent updated vaccines.
Pfizer and BioNTech's LP.8.1-adapted COVID-19 vaccine was registered on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods in late 2025 and became available in Australia in December.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Moderna's LP.8.1 formulation has also been registered in Australia.
Australia has updated vaccines — just not the latest formulation
The issue is therefore less about Australia going without updated COVID-19 vaccines, and more about how quickly newer formulations can be made available as the virus continues to evolve.
Professor Paul Griffin, an infectious diseases physician and clinical microbiologist, said Australia tended to lag behind some countries in updating COVID-19 vaccines.
"I think it's just some of the way we're managing those updates just means it's not quite happening as streamlined a way as we might like," he said.
"We know that some countries are able to do that a bit more quickly."
Griffin said countries with more established frameworks could update vaccines closer to real time.
"We tend to lag behind a little bit," he said.
While he said faster access would be preferable, he also stressed the importance of continuing to update vaccines as the virus changes.
Several reasons for the delay
But Sarah McGuinness, a senior research fellow at Monash University, told SBS News there was no single explanation for why a new formulation might become available overseas before it does in Australia.
She said one factor is the decisions vaccine manufacturers make about which countries to seek regulatory approval in, and when, with vaccine sponsors responsible for deciding whether to seek regulatory approval in different countries.
McGuinness also said Australia is a relatively small market compared with areas such as the US and Europe, meaning new formulations are not always brought here first.
Peter Markey, a GP and public health physician who chairs the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners' public health special interest group, said Australian authorities were continuing to monitor the virus internationally.
He said governments, researchers and the World Health Organization would be watching circulating strains and sub-strains and "looking out for vaccines to match them".
There is also an established international process for determining which variants vaccines should target.
Pfizer and BioNTech say their latest XFG-adapted vaccine follows guidance to more closely match contemporary circulating variants.
Along with Pfizer-BioNTech's XFG-adapted vaccine, updated vaccines from Moderna and Novavax-Sanofi have been approved in the US for the 2026-27 season.
AstraZeneca has confirmed to SBS News that it has no plans to release a COVID-19 vaccine for the 2026-27 season.
It withdrew its vaccine from the global market in 2024, and it hadn't been available in Australia since 2023.
What does the lag mean for Australians?
For Australians, the emergence of newer formulations overseas does not mean the vaccines currently available are ineffective.
The challenge is keeping vaccine formulations aligned with a virus that continues to evolve.
Pfizer confirmed to SBS News that its LP.8.1-adapted vaccine is registered in Australia and available to people aged six months and older.
The company has not provided a timeframe for when its newer XFG-adapted vaccine could be submitted for Australian registration.
Griffin said Australia could nevertheless look for ways to streamline the updating process.
"I think that's just where we need to consider a really streamlined way of getting those updated vaccines here and available in Australia as quickly as possible," he said.
For now, experts say Australia's vaccine system is continuing to monitor the changing virus, while manufacturers decide which updated formulations to bring to the Australian market.

Xiaomi plans to bring electric vehicles to the European market in 2027
Kyiv • UNN
Xiaomi plans to sell electric vehicles in Europe starting in 2027 and is creating a dealership network. In China, the company has already delivered more than 700 thousand vehicles.
Chinese electronics giant Xiaomi plans to launch its electric vehicles on the European market starting in 2027. The company announced this at the IFA technology exhibition in Berlin on September 3, UNN reports, citing dpa.
Details
The company has signed letters of intent with groups of car dealers to create a network of workshops and showrooms.
"Xiaomi Auto is committed to long-term investment in Europe," Xiaomi Auto Vice President and Head of International Business Yu Liguo said on Thursday.
He said that, alongside the company's existing research center in Munich, local dealership partners are key to a reliable market entry.
What is known about Xiaomi vehicles
In China, Xiaomi has delivered more than 700,000 vehicles since launching its SU7 electric sedan in spring 2024, according to company data. Until recently, the group had refrained from entering the European market, claiming that its production capacity was fully absorbed by domestic demand.
However, observers recently noted that Xiaomi has been actively demonstrating the performance of its vehicles in Germany. At the Nürburgring Nordschleife, the manufacturer has set several lap records: the production SU7 Ultra set a lap record for luxury electric vehicles, while the YU7 SUV recently completed a fully autonomous lap of the track without a driver.
In China, the world's largest automotive market, Xiaomi achieved in record time what many technology companies have failed to do: successfully transform itself into a credible carmaker. Since the debut of the SU7 sports sedan in spring 2024, the company reached the top spot among Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers in just over two years.
Unlike competitors seeking to gain market share through budget electric vehicles, Xiaomi has positioned itself in the premium and technology segments with higher margins.
The SU7 lineup became China's best-selling sedan priced above 200,000 yuan (approximately €24,000 or US$30,000), while the recently unveiled YU7 SUV recorded more than 240,000 binding orders in just 18 hours. As a result, the automotive division has become the group's strongest growth driver alongside its smartphone business.
What does Xiaomi do
Xiaomi is the world's third-largest smartphone manufacturer, after Apple and Samsung. Its entry into the automotive market is part of the group's "Human x Car x Home" strategy, through which Xiaomi seeks to unite cars, smartphones, and connected home electronics using its own operating system and AI applications. Alongside this, the company announced at IFA that it will also expand the European offering of its Mijia home-appliance brand and its own XRING semiconductor line.

Volkswagen board approves plan to cut another 50,000 jobs
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:33:14 BST
14:33:14 KST

Volkswagen board approves plan to cut another 50,000 jobs
- Published
The board of German car giant Volkswagen has approved a plan to cut another 50,000 jobs as part of the biggest restructuring in the group's almost nine-decade history.
It brings the total number of roles the carmaker plans to shed by 2030 to 100,000, after announcing in March that it would cut 50,000 roles.
The group - which includes Audi, Porsche, Skoda as well as the VW brand - is also considering the future of four of its German plants.
The move is a "strong signal" for the future of the firm, which is "taking responsibility for our entire workforce", VW's chief executive Oliver Blume said in a statement on Thursday.
Blume said in July that the firm was looking to make the additional cuts.
Shares in the company were up by around 7% in Frankfurt on Friday morning.
The Golf-maker has been hit by a drop in profits due to falling sales and fierce competition, especially from Chinese brands.
The firm also said that by 2035 it would cut the number of models it produces by 50% and reduce the complexity of its offering by 75%.
VW will also prioritise the "most compelling vehicles" and make more of each model, which will help lower costs, it said.
A "fundamental adjustment of the global workforce capability is necessary" to safeguard the competitiveness of the company, which faces shifting demand and technological change.
It added "a group-wide workforce adjustment of approximately 50,000 positions - including management roles - will be necessary."
The company is also weighing options for operations in Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and Neckarsulm, where it has said production capacity exceeds demand.
"Alternative uses for these plants are being assessed," it said.
As of 2025, VW employed more than 660,000 people worldwide. Its brands also include Seat, Bentley and Lamborghini.
Christianne Benner - the president of Europe's largest industrial union IG Metall and deputy chair of VW's Supervisory Board - said the carmaker had "fought hard for good solutions" to address a "crisis situation".
VW's profits have fallen sharply in recent years, hit by falling sales in China, which was once one of its biggest markets.
Sales have also fallen in the US, partly due to the impact of tariffs on car imports that were introduced by President Donald Trump's administration.
Chinese carmakers have been expanding aggressively as they roll out new technologies while benefiting from lower production costs than their rivals.
In recent years, firms such as BYD have seen their sales rise sharply in markets including the UK, European Union and South East Asia.

First Look at the Completed Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, Opening September 22, 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art has confirmed that it will open to the public on September 22, 2026, releasing new images of its completed building. The date aligns with the announcement made by the institution nearly a year ago. The museum is housed in a building with a sculptural, curved silhouette designed by Ma Yansong of MAD Architects, with landscape architecture by Mia Lehrer of Studio-MLA and Stantec serving as executive architect. The project was approved in 2017, with construction beginning the following year; the opening was originally planned for 2025. The museum sits within an 11-acre (4.5-hectare) site in Los Angeles's Exposition Park and comprises a 300,000-square-foot (27,900-square-meter) structure featuring galleries, two theaters, a retail store, a library, a café, a restaurant, and event spaces.
Founded by George Lucas and Mellody Hobson, the museum is dedicated to narrative art, defined as the art of telling stories through images, and traces visual storytelling across cultures and centuries, from prehistoric cave paintings to illustration, comics, film and murals. Its collection is built around the idea of engaging audiences with the stories embedded in photography, magazine and book illustration, film, and digital media, work the institution describes as giving new form to the myths and stories that "shape beliefs, communicate values, spark the imagination, and create communities." The collection's more than 40,000 works were gathered over five decades by filmmaker and producer George Lucas.
 The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art was created to honor humanity's stories and the artists who illustrate them. The artists in this collection didn't just create images; they connected our modern imaginations with our ancient emotions—with common beliefs creating community. Their work spans genres, media, and time. They deserve to be in a museum. — George Lucas
Related Article
MAD Completes Shenzhen Bay Culture Square, a Coastal Design Museum and Public Park in China
Ma Yansong's design conceives the museum as an organic, sculptural form set within a park. The building is lifted off the ground, a move intended to preserve views, keep the street-level scale human, and free up ground-level space for public use. Central arched steel beams spanning 185 feet (56 meters) form a lifted public plaza that functions as a canopy. The plaza provides access to north and south lobbies with tall ceilings and abundant natural light, and a central elliptical oculus opens a sightline from the plaza to the sky four stories above. Principal public spaces on the lower floors include two theaters seating 299 each, a horseshoe-shaped library and learning space with floor-to-ceiling windows facing the park, ten studio and classroom spaces, a shop, a café, and roughly 100,000 square feet (9,300 square meters) of gallery space. Three of the building's five public elevators on the north side are cylindrical and enclosed in glass shafts, carrying visitors from the north lobby to the fourth-floor galleries, which span approximately 82,000 square feet (7,600 square meters) and are organized around a continuous circulation path. The fifth floor adds nearly 8,000 square feet (750 square meters) of gallery space beneath a sculpted ceiling, along with an event space and a restaurant with indoor seating and an outdoor terrace, the Skywalker Grill.
The building's form is designed to cantilever well beyond its points of ground support, an effect meant to give the impression of floating above the park. Its exterior is clad in more than 1,271 uniquely shaped panels of fiberglass-reinforced polymer (FRP), a material chosen for its ability to form smooth, curved surfaces at relatively low weight; the curved panels measure approximately 8 by 32 feet (2.4 by 9.8 meters) on average. Each panel was produced through a combined digital and robotic fabrication process, finished by hand to maintain consistent smoothness and color, with joint lines between panels varied in width and orientation to follow the building's geometry. An architectural ribbon of glass fiber-reinforced concrete (GFRC) runs along the edges of the park. The building's broader material palette also includes concrete, steel, glass, and plaster, and the design and construction process involved a team of more than 150 architects, engineers, and designers working through a cloud-based modeling and collaboration system.
The museum building sits within a larger 13-acre (5.3-hectare) campus that includes new park and gardens designed by Mia Lehrer of Studio-MLA, conceived as a community resource for learning, art, and public engagement in the heart of Exposition Park. Replacing what was previously an asphalt parking lot, the park draws on the diversity of Southern California's native and drought-tolerant vegetation, with more than 300 newly planted trees, including jacarandas, oaks and pines, alongside meadows, grasses, shrubs and flowering plants. Additional features include a hanging garden, an amphitheater, a fountain conceived as a waterfall, and ten monumental outdoor sculptures installed along the campus walkways, serving as a free extension of the museum's galleries. The museum also includes a research library featuring high ceilings, floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, and glass windows offering views of the Museum's park and gardens.
The inaugural exhibitions trace the history of narrative art through around 1,300 works from the museum's collection. The first floor houses The History of Narrative Art: Heroes • Myths • The Sacred, which pairs signature collection pieces with reproductions of immovable artworks, architecture and archaeological sites produced in collaboration with institutions including the Vatican Museums, the Louvre, and Mexico's Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia. On the fourth and fifth floors, thematic galleries are organized around subjects such as love, family and community, alongside dedicated spaces for narrative genres including fantasy, romance and adventure, and further galleries devoted to specific artistic mediums such as comic books, manga, graphic novels, photography and murals. Several galleries on these floors honor individual twentieth-century illustrators, and a Cinema gallery will present the inaugural installation Star Wars in Motion, drawing on the Lucas Archives. The museum will also include an installation dedicated to Ma Yansong's work for MAD, and a fifth-floor gallery focused on large-scale public murals.
The film program is housed in two dedicated theaters, the Robert Flaherty Theater and the Slavko Vorkapich Theater, both designed as continuous, drop-in gallery experiences that allow visitors to enter and exit programming at will, with films ranging from a few minutes to 90 minutes. The Robert Flaherty Theater is named for the documentary filmmaking pioneer (1884–1951) and centers on cinema's capacity to capture reality, screening films connected to the museum's inaugural exhibitions and to the creative processes of the artists featured within them. The Slavko Vorkapich Theater takes its name from the experimental filmmaker and montage pioneer, who chaired the University of Southern California's Department of Film from 1948 to 1950, the same school George Lucas later attended, and is dedicated to the formal mechanics of film: light, motion, sound, color, and editing.
Elsewhere, several cultural institutions are approaching milestones of their own. In Boston, construction is nearing completion on the William and Charlotte Bloomberg Public Science Common, a new venue at the Museum of Science designed by William Rawn Associates. In Sydney, Powerhouse Parramatta, a new museum and cultural institution on the banks of the Parramatta River, is set to open on November 7, 2026, with exhibitions designed by OMA/AMO and Open Architecture. In San Salvador de Jujuy, Pelli Clarke & Partners has completed the Lola Mora Cultural Center, dedicated to the life and work of Argentine sculptor Lola Mora (1866–1936). In Suzhou, BIG's first completed art museum has officially opened on the shores of Jinji Lake.

Taiwan and Lithuania sign agreement on advanced semiconductor packaging
