The Stakes of America’s 2026 Midterm Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:30:02 UTC
04:30:02 KST

Five years ago, in the wake of the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, America’s civic institutions pledged to do more to defend our system of fair and free elections. Major philanthropies increased their investments in programs that defend democracy. Law firms expanded their pro bono election-protection work. University presidents publicly condemned the effort to thwart the will of American voters. Many of the country’s largest businesses pledged to stop donating to candidates who had tried to overturn an election.
Today, our elections are again under attack. But while some institutions have maintained their commitment to defending democracy, far too many have retreated.
There are fewer than 100 days until the 2026 nationwide elections. Now is the time for everyone to protect the system of fair and free elections upon which our society and prosperity ultimately depend.
Together, the two of us have spent considerable time in all the major sectors of American society: philanthropy, business, academia, and the law. We understand that leaders in these sectors fear government retribution, and understandably so. But with the integrity of our elections under enormous strain—and with government officials signaling that more aggressive attacks may follow—it is time for all institutions to reaffirm their role as defenders of the free and fair elections at the heart of American democracy.
Defending our democracy begins with a clear-eyed assessment of the threats to it. Over the past 18 months, the Justice Department has disbanded government agencies meant to protect elections from foreign interference and to help states administer them smoothly. President Donald Trump has repeatedly made false claims that the 2020 election was fraudulent and made new ones—without evidence—about the midterms. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin recently threatened to jail local election officials his department finds were insufficiently responsive to the federal government’s unproven claims of fraud. Overall, the federal government has tried to wrest control of elections from the states, with courts repeatedly finding such efforts illegal.
Now, experts across the country are deeply concerned about what might occur in the coming months, whether it’s false allegations that cast doubt on individual races, state officials refusing to certify election results as required by law, or baseless efforts to block House members from taking their seats in January.
The good news is the success of these efforts to undermine the midterms is not inevitable. To the contrary, enormous work has already been done to protect the integrity of November’s election from those who would undermine it.
Now, it is time for leaders who haven’t yet joined that effort to get off the sidelines no matter what their politics are. Losing our system of fair and free elections would not just affect one element of American life. It would affect all elements of American life.
There are many ways for institutions to meet the moment and keep our country’s elections free and fair. First, many leaders, particularly those from the business community, meet regularly with members of the executive branch and Congress. They should use these relationships to remind elected officials of the need to respect election results no matter who wins or loses.
These nonpartisan principles are the basic preconditions for a functioning democracy and should be respected by all.
Second, many institutional leaders have strong ties to state and local officials. Now is the time to remind state legislators that attempting to disenfranchise eligible voters via last-minute changes to election rules, baseless claims of fraud, or partisan attempts to deny certification harm our democracy and create the kind of turmoil that negatively affects a state’s reputation and business climate.
Third, leaders should forcefully support the local election administrators who run our elections. These are not professional politicians. They are our neighbors, co-workers, and friends—and recently, they have far too often been subject to threats and harassment by those who wish to undermine their nonpartisan mission. Institutional leaders can help elections run smoothly by encouraging their employees to become poll workers, and by supporting nonpartisan civic organizations that defend election officials in performing their duties, or that bring Americans from across the political spectrum together to support the right of all Americans to have their vote counted.
Standing up for fair and free elections is not without risk. But with the foundation of our democracy under unprecedented assault and our basic rights on the line, the far greater risk is ignoring the threat to our country until it is too late.
One day, leaders of America’s institutions will face the same profound question as every other citizen who loves this country. Future generations will ask, “Where were you when the stakes were highest?”
What will you tell them?

AI agents aren’t ready to replace humans in behavioral research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:30:00 UTC
04:30:00 KST

AI agents aren’t ready to replace humans in behavioral research
A new study shows that digital twins don’t respond like the individuals they were modeled after
Replacing human subjects with AI surrogates, or digital twins, is on some social scientists’ wish lists. Human subjects are expensive, tire easily and can suffer psychological distress from some studies.
But those wishes may take more time to be realized, a study appearing September 2 in Science Advances suggests. AI twins designed to mimic a given individual’s behavior instead seem to distort their surrogate’s views, creating a “funhouse mirror” effect, the researchers note.
“There’s some promise,” says Olivier Toubia, a computational social scientist at Columbia Business School in New York City. “But [the twins’ performance] was overall a bit disappointing.”
In work reported last year in Marketing Science, Toubia and colleagues recruited more than 2,000 individuals from across the United States. Those respondents answered 500-plus questions about characteristics including age, ethnicity, income, education, religious practices, political preferences, personality traits, spending habits, mathematical abilities and vocabulary skills. Many of the questions come from scales that are used commonly in psychology, economic and business research. Respondents also completed various online tests designed to assess thought patterns and biases.
Because research testing the value of digital twins remains limited, the goal of that project was to create an open-source dataset for others to use, Toubia says. “I think it’s been downloaded like 25,000 times at this point.”
To develop the twins in the newly published study, the researchers fed all the information for each individual into a large language model and prompted the LLM to respond as if it were that person. Across 19 social science experiments, the team evaluated everything from how individuals and their twins respond to people who donate to both Republican and Democratic party candidates to what they “think” about algorithmic hiring.
These digital twins performed better than chance, the team found, but they were wrong on average about a quarter of the time. They performed roughly on par with chatbots that received demographic information alone.
The digital twins did, however, better capture real variation in people’s responses compared with the LLMs that knew only demographic info. For example, one person may rate themselves as a 2 on a scale of self-control while another rates themselves as a 4. The LLM with more limited info might report a 3 for each person, washing out any differences. But the digital twin might report a 3 and 5. Though still wrong, the predictions give a better sense of potential differences across the group.
Toubia and colleagues attribute the digital twins’ poor performance overall to several key distortions: Twins’ responses tended to be more homogenous than people’s responses and often skewed to demographic stereotypes. And their accuracy increased with more affluent and educated participants. They also displayed certain biases, such as expressing more trust in others and showing less concern about technological threats. Compared with their human surrogates, the twins also appeared more rational.
AI researcher and economist Hadi Hosseini of Penn State University has seen a similar effect in his own research into how AI agents make health care decisions when resources are scarce: “LLMs distort human judgment in a very specific direction toward something that is very rational [and] more reasonable than actually what people are.”
But he says there are ways that the digital twins could be improved. The researchers used “a very static set of questions,” he says. Adding more dynamic approaches, such as having a chatbot shadow an individual across the day or converse regularly with a person, as is already common, could make for a better dataset, he says.
Toubia wants to try more complex training methods. Still, he says, there are cases where even digital twins of the type tested in this study would be useful. For instance, sometimes researchers need a detailed response to a question. Tired humans might provide single-sentence answers while indefatigable digital twins churn out essays. Similarly, pretesting an experiment with digital twins could help researchers ensure their design is working before sapping their human respondents’ limited bandwidth.
But Toubia also urges humility. Social scientists tend to think that scales and surveys capture the full range of human experience, he says. But it’s incredibly hard to predict human behavior with a machine. “We need to be realistic in terms of the expectations we have from synthetic data.”

Economy won't improve until Australia climbs productivity mountain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03

analysis
Jim Chalmers is positive on growth but Australia's productivity problem persists
Treasurer Jim Chalmers would have sighed with relief at this week's economic growth figures. Despite some preview talk of possible stagnation, we saw modest growth of 2.1 per cent in the year to the end of June.
But every economic number these days seems to bring a negative. Economists immediately strengthened their predictions of another interest rate rise.
For the average Australian, just where we are economically is, at best, confusing; at worst, alarming. For years, people have been under cost-of-living pressure. Real wages fell by more than 5 per cent over the five years from 2021.
This year's extended Middle East conflict has added to the strain. The housing market is disoriented after the budget's tax changes.
In this week's Essential poll, nearly six in 10 people thought the country was headed in the wrong direction.
The government tries to empathise with people's circumstances while claiming it's pulling the right levers, an assertion strongly contested by the opposition, which, in particular, flails at high government spending.
The public no longer trusts the messaging from either side. Many frustrated voters are combining their economic and political grievances into support for One Nation.
Loading...
In light of the often baffling picture, this column asked two independent economists, Chris Richardson and Saul Eslake, for their snapshots of our economic health — or lack of it.
Richardson points to growth easing as interest rates have risen.
He says, over the longer term, "Australia's economy has been getting bigger mostly because we have more people."
On a per-hour-worked basis, the economy is only 1 per cent bigger today than it was a decade ago, which is "depressingly weak".
Inflation "has been frustratingly slow to come to heel" and the job isn't finished, Richardson says.
"Even more frustratingly, we still have inflation at around 3.5 per cent [well above the 2.5 per cent target for it] even though Australia's economy has already slowed a lot."
A combination of weak growth and lingering inflation is happening "because the engine of the economy — productivity — has been stalled for a long time".
"With a weak engine behind it, the Australian economy doesn't need to be travelling fast at all before it starts to blow black smoke in the form of inflation."
Given we've had multiple interest rate rises, and the budget's tax changes have taken some heat out of housing prices, Richardson predicts we'll probably see only one more rate rise (either this month or in November).
Loading
That could be followed, on his assessment, by one or two rate cuts next year, driven by low growth.
"But not more than that: higher interest rates look set to be the new normal," Richardson says.
Higher interest rates and the budget's tax changes are driving down housing prices — the question is, how far?
Richardson says: "There's momentum in that fall — having dropped by around 4 per cent already, they could fall another 6 per cent before stabilising."
But, he says, taxes and interest rates alone "can't fix Australia's broken housing market. Doing that would require local councils saying 'yes' to much more building than they've done in decades".
Eslake says that in an "underlying" sense the economy is growing at about 2 per cent a year — roughly in line with the Reserve Bank's assessed "speed limit" (how fast the economy can grow without triggering unacceptably high inflation).
"Of this, a bit under 1.5 per cent is coming from population growth, and a little over 0.5 per cent is coming from per capita real GDP growth, that is, improving material living standards."
Australia's inflation rate has only been inside the Reserve Bank's 2–3 per cent target on two occasions in the past almost five years, Eslake says.
He says the most recent inflation numbers (3.5 per cent annual in July) have increased the odds of a rate increase at the RBA's September meeting, taking the cash rate to its highest level since late 2011.
"The RBA can't afford to repeat the mistake, which [with the benefit of hindsight] it made last year, in cutting rates before inflation was sustainably back within its target band. That means the RBA is probably going to want to see at least two quarters with the annual 'underlying' inflation rate being 2-point-something — which on its own forecasts won't be until the first half of 2028."
Eslake says a key reason for this combination of weak economic growth and persistent inflation is the economy's "abysmal productivity growth performance".
Wednesday's national accounts show "overall labour productivity growth over the year to the June quarter of –0.2 per cent, the worst performance since the year ended March 2025".
"And it isn't solely because of the growth in the so-called care economy," Eslake says.
"Labour productivity in the 'non-market' sectors of the economy declined by 0.3 per cent over the year to the June quarter, but 'market sector' productivity also declined by 0.2 per cent. Big declines in productivity in the mining and construction sectors are a large part of this story.
"Weak productivity growth means that the 'speed limit' is also very low by historical standards. In effect, we can't sustain economic growth of more than about 2 per cent per annum and have inflation at around 2.5 per cent."
Both Richardson and Eslake highlight that Australia is in a very bad place when it comes to productivity. Chalmers's rhetoric since the election has put much focus on productivity, but so far the government's talk has outpaced the walk.
Unsurprisingly, the government is pinning hopes on artificial intelligence.
This week, Chalmers released a Treasury analysis of the economic implications of AI. Although hedged with qualifications and uncertainties, the paper argued AI could help Australia reach Treasury's long-term target of an annual growth of 1.2 per cent in productivity, although it emphasises it will only provide some of this growth.
AI is not a "substitute for domestic structural reforms".
The government is currently preparing legislation setting out conditions for data centres. That's necessary not only to encourage investment but to maintain the social licence for data centres which, if the US experience is anything to go by, are likely to become more unpopular as time goes on.
But Productivity Commission chair Danielle Wood stresses it's not all about data centres.
"What matters much more for productivity is how quickly businesses are adopting AI and embedding it into their processes. At the moment we are lagging nations like the United States, the United Kingdom and Germany when it comes to business take-up.
"There isn't a single policy answer for this, but regulatory clarity, skills and training support, and government's own adoption can play a role," Wood says.
The productivity mountain is a steep one to climb.
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

The Federal Reserve should cut interest rates to make homes more affordable, Vice President JD Vance said Thursday, adding to the pressure President Donald Trump has placed on the central bank to cut borrowing costs.
The remarks came days after Trump's handpicked Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, hinted at the possibility of doing the opposite: addressing persistently high inflation by hiking rates.

Vance added, "We're doing a lot of things to try to keep those interest rates down, but it would be nice to have some help from the Federal Reserve."
Vance's remarks may add to concerns about the erosion of the Fed's independence under Trump, who aggressively pushed Warsh's predecessor to slash rates and is trying to fire Governor Lisa Cook.
Less than a week earlier, Warsh said he is committed to bringing the inflation rate back down to the Fed's 2% target, and sees interest rates as the key tool to rein it in.
"Short-term interest rates are the predominant tool to achieve the dual mandate," he said at a speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.
Vance's remarks came less than two weeks before the Federal Open Market Committee is set to convene and decide whether or not to adjust rates.
The outcome of that meeting is far from certain: Traders are about evenly split on the odds of a rate hike at the Sept. 15-16 meeting, according to CME Group's FedWatch gauge.
On Tuesday, Fed Governor Michael Barr said he would be prepared to back a rate increase if inflation stays elevated.
But on Thursday morning, Governor Christopher Waller said he is more likely to keep rates steady.

B-52s Deploy for Bomber Task Force to Australia’s New BUFF Base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:17:49 UTC
04:17:49 KST

U.S. Air Force B-52 Stratofortress bombers landed at a northern Australian air base this week, a major display of the U.S. military’s ability to project force in the Pacific.
Multiple B-52s landed at Royal Australian Air Force Base Tindal in the country’s Northern Territory on Sept. 1, according to official Air Force imagery released Sept. 3 and service officials.
The joint military-civilian airfield near the town of Katherine, which the Pentagon plans to use as a launching pad for operations in the Pacific, has undergone a $1.1 billion upgrade in recent years.
That work enables it to support the deployment of a half-dozen B-52s, giving the U.S. more locations to stage bombers in the region amid China’s growing military might.
The base also houses Australian F-35A Lightning stealth fighter jets and MQ-4C Triton remotely piloted surveillance aircraft.
Australia is south of the U.S. territory of Guam, where Andersen Air Force Base serves as America’s current bomber hub in the Western Pacific. RAAF Base Tindal would give the U.S. Air Force more basing options for long-range missions in the region.
“Operating from RAAF Base Tindal marks our ability to project, sustain, and regenerate decisive airpower across an expanding extended network,” states one photo caption released by Pacific Air Forces. The deployment from the base “deepens our partnership and interoperability” and “highlights our shared commitment to regional stability, ensuring our forces remain agile and responsive in support of a Free and Open Indo-Pacific,” PACAF added in other captions.
It is unclear how long the bombers will be deployed to the region and how many aircraft are operating from Australia. The bombers hail from the 2nd Bomb Wing at Barksdale Air Force Base, La. Air Force Global Strike Command and the Eighth Air Force, which oversees the nation’s bomber fleet, referred questions about the deployment to Pacific Air Forces.
“These missions demonstrate seamless interoperability with our partners and bolster regional security across the region,” a PACAF spokesperson said in a short statement confirming the B-52 deployment to Australia. The spokesperson declined to provide further details, citing operational security concerns.
Multiple wargames on potential conflicts with China have highlighted the strategic and operational value of Australia’s airbases and naval facilities, said retired Col. Mark Gunzinger, a former B-52 pilot and deputy assistant secretary of defense for forces transformation and resources.
“That has been a constant in our wargames: using Australia’s multiple airfields—and not just in northern Australia but in the south too—to generate long-range bomber strikes and tanker sorties to support bomber and fighter operations,” said Gunzinger, the Director of Future Concepts and Capability Assessments at AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.
“China has a limited number of very long-range ballistic missiles that can reach U.S. air forces stationed at Diego Garcia, in Australia, and other air bases that are not located along the First Island Chain.” Bombers’ longer ranges would allow them to be stationed at airfields even further from China if necessary, Gunzinger added.
Washington and Canberra are increasingly aligned under the AUKUS security pact, which also includes the United Kingdom. The agreement will give U.S. nuclear-powered subs to Australia and allow the U.S. to stage subs out of Australia starting next year. Conceived under the Biden administration, AUKUS has also been embraced by the second Trump administration.
Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Richard Marles met with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Sept. 2 to commemorate the 75th anniversary of the ANZUS Treaty, a mutual defense pact, during which the two defense chiefs “discussed how both nations will continue to advance the alliance and strengthen deterrence in the Pacific.”
“The Secretary noted the alignment between U.S. and Australian National Defense Strategies and also acknowledged that Canberra recognizes the gravity of maintaining a favorable balance of power in the region to ensure that both countries remain safe and prosperous,” the Pentagon said in a readout provided from the meeting. “Both leaders agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises.”
The U.S. has operated fighters and bombers from other Royal Australian Air Force bases, such as RAAF Base Amberley, and the two countries conduct the biennial Talisman Saber, one of the largest and most complex military training exercises held. By 2030, the U.S. Navy expects some 2,300 Americans to be based in Western Australia.
“What we’re seeing is a real increase in U.S. posture in Australia,” said Zack Cooper, an expert on U.S. strategy in Asia and a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. “Sometimes it can take a really long time to build out the infrastructure, but in this case, we’re seeing the U.S. and Australia move pretty quickly on both the air and the naval side. I think it’s emblematic of the step-up in effort we’re seeing from both Canberra and Washington.”
“The U.S. needs to diversify the locations from which it can operate air and naval assets. Australia’s northern bases do that on the air side and the naval facilities in Perth are critical on the nuclear submarine side,” he added.
Equipping a base to handle large bombers with heavy payloads is no small task: runways must be long, sturdy, and adequate, with ramp space, fuel infrastructure, and safe weapons storage facilities.
“That can all drive some considerable investment in airfields, which Australia has made and continues to invest in to bolster regional deterrence,” Gunzinger said.

'Sometimes things happen': Vance defends US as Iran wedding strike sparks outrage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:16:42 UTC
04:16:42 KST

US Vice President JD Vance has said that Washington is investigating reports that a US air strike struck a wedding gathering in southern Iran, while insisting that American forces do not deliberately target civilians.
“I’m extremely sceptical of this,” Vance said of Iranian state media reports alleging that the strike hit a wedding celebration, saying he had been briefed on the investigation but did not yet have information establishing whether US forces were responsible.
“What I can say with 100 percent confidence is that, unlike the IRGC, the United States never targets civilians in combat,” Vance said on Thursday.
“We never will do that. We never have done that.”
Vance said civilian casualties can occur during military operations, adding, “Unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen.”
He added that when US forces make mistakes, the military investigates them and seeks to learn from them. The US military has separately said it is reviewing the reports.
Iran reports 18 killed, 142 wounded
Iranian Health Ministry spokesperson Hossein Kermanpour said at least 18 people were killed and 142 wounded in US strikes between August 30 and September 2.
He said the casualties included four people in Sirik, seven in Khuzestan, four members of the IRGC Aerospace Force in Kermanshah and three Basij members on Lavan Island.
Kermanpour also said at least 50 people were wounded at a wedding gathering in Sirik. Other Iranian officials have reported four people killed and dozens wounded in the strike on the gathering.
The reports have drawn international concern, with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres saying he was “deeply alarmed” by reports of civilian casualties, including the strike that allegedly hit the wedding.
No talks until Iran stops targeting ships
Vance also said Washington is not currently negotiating with Tehran and would not resume talks unless Iran stops attacking commercial shipping.
“The message to the Iranians is simple,” he said. “You’ve got to stop shooting at commercial shipping.”
He rejected calls for a fixed timetable, arguing that a deadline could allow Iran to continue attacks while making US strategy predictable.
Vance said the administration was using military, economic, diplomatic and other forms of pressure to protect commercial vessels and keep oil and gas moving through the Strait of Hormuz.
He said about 15 million barrels of oil had passed through the strategic waterway despite the conflict.
Vance said the broader US objectives were to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and avoid a global energy crisis, arguing that US military operations had limited the impact of the conflict on global energy markets.

Dozens die from toxic fumes during oil pipeline theft in Nigeria: NGO

2026-09-03
19:15:54 UTC
04:15:54 KST

At least 37 people died early on Thursday in Nigeria's oil-rich southern Niger Delta after inhaling fumes during the theft of fuel from a pipeline, a local NGO has said.
Illegal oil-siphoning is a major problem in Nigeria - an OPEC member and one of Africa's largest petroleum producers - causing serious pollution.
Accidents are common in swamps in the Niger Delta, where smugglers tap into pipelines to steal crude and refine it into fuel for sale.
The Youths and Environmental Advocacy Centre (YEAC-Nigeria) said it had "received and confirmed a report from its network of youth volunteers and human rights defenders in the Niger Delta in the Okrika Local Government Area of Rivers State that some persons, not fewer than 37 have been confirmed dead after inhaling 'Indorama fuel'."
It said in a statement that those killed are "suspected to be oil thieves", adding: "Many others are still missing."
It said "youths had connected a pipe to a tapping point on a pipeline that normally transports" crude from producer Indorama Eleme Petrochemical through the Port Harcourt Refinery to vessels loading for export.
The men tapped into the pipeline and were loading oil into their own boats, it said.
"Many are still missing, and some corpses have been seen floating on the river but have not yet been recovered," the organisation said.
Oil pollution
Rivers State police confirmed the incident in a statement saying the victims were allegedly attempting to steal oil, but it did not give a toll.
The Niger Delta is home to Nigeria's multi-billion-dollar oil and gas resources, but residents of the region live in poverty due to decades of oil exploration, neglect and pollution.
YEAC-Nigeria called "on the government to provide alternative livelihood opportunities", including "the legalisation of artisanal refining".

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday underscored the importance of the quality of teachers, who play a vital role in shaping the future of the country, and held National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE) can seek annual performance appraisal report (PAR) from teacher education institutions (TEIs).
A bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said the role of NCTE in ensuring quality education for children is immense and teacher education has assumed greater importance since right to education has been recognised as a fundamental right under Right to Education Act.
The bench stressed that it is necessary for the council and its bodies to ensure accountability of educational institutions. It quashed the HC order which had found fault with the council's decision to seek PAR from TEIs. "We fail to understand how a regulatory measure of a statutory body, empowered to achieve planned and coordinated development of teacher education system in the country, could be restrained from calling upon TEIs to file PAR. ...it is but natural and incidental that NCTE would require the stakeholders to provide the necessary PAR," it said.

Microsoft to impose time limits on Xbox cloud gaming subscribers as costs continue to climb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:03:56 UTC
04:03:56 KST

Microsoft's Xbox unit said Thursday that it will impose monthly cloud gaming time limits for Game Pass subscribers after years of unlimited access, as the company seeks to find a better balance between usage and costs.
Players will be able to pay for additional hours beyond the caps, which go into effect in November.
Across product organizations, Microsoft executives have been devising ways to charge customers based on usage to better reflect rising costs. Demand is climbing for the software company's finite amount of computing power — not unlike its technology peers — and clients of artificial intelligence products such as GitHub Copilot and the Microsoft 365 Copilot increasingly pay based on how much they use.
"We're introducing this model because the cost of providing cloud gaming grows as more people use it and play for longer," Xbox said in a blog post. "Moving to monthly limits allows us to keep offering the service while continuing to invest in its reliability and performance. We understand that for some players the practical result is a higher cost."
Users with high-end Game Pass Ultimate subscriptions, which cost $22.99 per month, will have access to 15 hours of cloud gaming. Game Pass Premium account holders, who pay $14.99 per month, will have 10 hours of cloud-based playtime, while Game Pass Essential, which costs $9.99 a month, includes five hours, according to the blog post.
Inside Xbox, new CEO Asha Sharma has been busy evaluating business model changes to return the division to growth and boost profitability. In July, Xbox said it would test ad-supported game streaming.
Just 4% of Game Pass subscribers spend more time each month streaming games through the cloud, Microsoft said. The company did not specify fees for extra hours.
Those who don't subscribe to Game Pass will be able to buy cloud gaming time to stream games they already own, Xbox said.

John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell Are Pure Delight in Martin McDonagh's Wild Horse Nine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:01:16 UTC
04:01:16 KST

Where's the line between shtick and style? If a filmmaker returns to similar themes over and over again but folds them into entertaining shapes each time, is that consistency or a lack of imagination? Writer-director Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine—playing in competition here at the Venice Film Festival—might prompt you to ask those questions, though it doesn’t fully answer them. Like In Bruges and The Banshees of Inisherin, Wild Horse Nine—in which John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell play 1970s CIA agents stationed in Santiago, Chile, sent to Easter Island on a special mission—deals with fractious male friendships. There are some beautiful four-legged animals—in this case, horses—but one of them must die; it’s as if McDonagh feels he needs to toughen us up to the realities of nature, rather than just allow us to enjoy an animal’s spirit and beauty. And there are ways in which McDonagh gets tripped up by his own excessive cleverness: the screenplay is so packed with quirky quips that you might long for a little breathing room.
But if the writing sometimes comes off as winking and belabored, the acting is not. Malkovich and Rockwell are a joy to watch, and that, after all, is what we continue to go to the movies for: to see actors at play, even as they work. Malkovich’s Chris and Rockwell’s Lee are an odd-couple duo who have been working together long enough to intuit one another’s thoughts and moods. They also bicker, a lot. Lee seems annoyed by his elder partner’s tendency to tootle down trails of fanciful thought. In an early scene, Chris complains that his apartment in Santiago is riddled with moths, and he doesn’t want them to ruin his clothes. But he also doesn’t want to kill them. Instead, he says, “I’ve been escorting them outside.” It’s 1973, not long before socialist president Salvador Allende will be overthrown in a military coup—Chris and Lee know that’s going to happen, given that their job is to destabilize democratic governments here and there around the world. In one of his many pensive moments, Chris muses, “Sometimes I think I care about the moths in Chile more than I care about the people in Chile.”
Yet somehow Chris does care, despite having secretively killed some 68 people in his long career, and possibly, as one of the movie’s running gags suggests, having had a hand in some grassy-knoll shenanigans in November 1963. He falls asleep listening to one of the saddest ballads ever written, Hank Williams’ “I’m So Lonesome I Could Cry.” He not-so-secretly hates his boss, MJ (a delightfully ruthless Steve Buscemi) and joyfully spreads lies—or are they?—that he’s a junkie. But Chris himself does heroin, not for pleasure, but because cancer is killing him. He’s happy to have been dispatched to Easter Island—he has long wanted to see what he calls “the big heads”—and he claims that he’s going to get some work done on his long-planned memoir. Lee reminds him that his memory is like a sieve; Chris asserts that working on the memoir will bring it back. He wants his book to begin with a surprise opening, not a boring one, so he decides he’s going to open by talking about dinosaurs. “Did they have souls?" he wonders aloud. Lee scoffs at this idea, but by this point, we’ve already seen the affection, mingled with annoyance, between these men. Chris considers Lee his only friend.
That basic framework sets the stage for lots of acerbic CIA jokes, some flirtation with a duo of pretty student tourists (played by Ailín Salas and Mariana Di Girólamo), and a truly fantastic gag about how the “gay” countries produce the best cheeses. (Chris’ definition of what makes a country gay or not is far from sound, but even so, he may be onto something.) Chris delights in the wild horses that roam Easter Island, forming a kind of soul communion with one in particular, a striking, sensitive beast who nods his head perceptively whenever Chris asks him a question. McDonagh never wants our emotions to get too squishy—remember the donkey in The Banshees of Inisherin?—and thus this noble creature meets an unexplained, albeit gentle, end. But there’s still a degree of warmth here, perhaps more so than in most of McDonagh’s films. This one, at least, has none of the smug superiority of Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, a film ringing with condescension toward small-town America.
McDonagh may often be excessively arch, but he does know how to write for actors. Rockwell’s Lee is essentially the straight man here, absorbing the vibrations of his friend and colleague’s meandering thoughts on mortality and other subjects. That doesn’t make it a minor role; Lee is Chris’ mirror and sounding board, the trustworthy compatriot who both protects his friend and gives it to him straight. This is a generous performance, one that favors listening over mere line delivery. And Malkovich is simply wonderful. Chris, nearing not just the end of his CIA career but his life, has blown out his filter; now he just blurts the truth. When one of the young, earnestly leftist tourists speaks, with sparkling eyes, about the power of organized protests, Chris gives it to her straight: “Marches are just the places we can get the clearest photos of you without your knowing.” Malkovich doesn’t make the line sound cruel or demeaning. He launches it with a kind of bounce, the way you’d serve a tennis ball. He’s having fun here, and his pleasure becomes our delight. He makes you believe in a guy who would send an invasive, wool-munching insect out into the night air without crushing it. No one can deliver a moth soliloquy like he can.

The Ethics of Slopaganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Slopaganda
On February 28, 2026, the U.S. and Israel initiated an armed conflict against Iran. Widely discussed as the first AI-fueled war, the war has engendered many debates on the moral complexity of modern warfare and AI’s role. One of the most interesting progressions is the use of AI to generate propaganda called slopaganda. Throughout the war, both the United States and Iran have used slopaganda to exchange political jabs. Iran, in particular, has created numerous high-quality, AI-animated LEGO videos that have gone viral and gained international popularity. Even though both AI-generated content and propaganda aren’t new, the way that the U.S. and Iran have used slopaganda to achieve military objectives is distinctive. Ultimately, its success makes it clear that this new form of non-lethal, militarized AI is here to stay. That is why I believe policymakers should include it in discussions of AI ethics.
To understand why this matters, take for example the development and use of AI in lethal forms, like Autonomous Weapon Systems (AWS). AWS have to follow the principles of jus in bello, which regulate the conduct of parties during armed conflict. In contrast, we don’t have ethical guidelines for institutions using slopaganda in their official capacities, despite the overt military themes. Furthermore, the way the U.S. and Iran are using slopaganda is important because it shows a pivot from traditional warfare that has increasingly included the digital realm, but mostly relied on gains achieved on the ground. Now, the gains achieved online are part of an online military objective (e.g., undermining the adversary’s authority and the trust its people have in its institutions) as well. Consequently, the meme war between the two countries provides a real-world example of what that pivot looks like ethically.
The Costs of Shitposting Diplomacy
The use of slopaganda in the U.S./Israel war in Iran demonstrates that countries will conduct war online and with social media algorithms. Denise Garcia notes in her new book, The AI Military Race: Common Good Governance in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, that militarized AI disincentivizes countries equipped with AI capabilities to use diplomatic means to solve global conflicts or to reinvest in social justice issues. Instead, she worries that countries will resort, at whatever cost, to their AI systems or programs.
Furthermore, she notes that the use of militarized AI can shift societal norms, undermine global stability, and make wars more frequent and perpetual. Because this is the first AI-fueled war, I believe we are seeing this shift unexpectedly with slopaganda. For example, the United States popularized shitposting as a new form of diplomatic communication. However, this has come at an ethical cost of trivializing the loss of human life and undermining the significant negative impact armed conflict has on democratic values and human dignity globally.
In addition, the U.S. and Iran engaging in this meme war is only further instilling distrust in government institutions, exacerbating political polarization, and amplifying and creating new frustrations with government. It isn’t just chronically online people who are viewing content about the war and growing increasingly frustrated as algorithms feed them more (dis/mis)information about it. Robust research shows that dis/misinformation and social media both play a significant role in polarization and increase the likelihood of provoking offline violence. The use of slopaganda is not an exception.
While Garcia focuses on weaponized AI, particularly lethal AI, I extend her account. I apply it to the pervasive use of slopaganda in this U.S./Israel war against Iran, as it has become a new form of weaponized AI. My concern is that other enterprising countries may see the success of this use of AI and rely on slopaganda and memetic forms to wage their wars. Consequently, they may feel less obligated to engage in traditional diplomatic approaches to address global issues and tensions. This may result in more countries prioritizing short-term online influence over establishing more stable international relationships.
Although the slopaganda videos and memes are persuasive and highly shareable, they can conceal the true costs of armed conflict. For example, the public may be more familiar with the AI-generated videos than they are with any formal or sanctioned talks or actions taken during the conflict. Additionally, both the United States and Iran have had diplomats or official government social media accounts share different forms of memes and slopaganda instead of informational text for the public. Furthermore, official government accounts and diplomats using slopaganda normalize shitposting as a political and military tool. They also shift expectations about the role of government social media accounts. Instead of communicating important, fact-based information, these accounts are increasingly posting informal, meme-based content and slopaganda. This changes the public’s standards of institutions and the types of communications expected of them.
Thus, we must expand our conceptions of militarized AI to include this new frontier and establish ethical guidelines of its use. The U.S., Israel, and Iran will not be the last and only countries to substantively use AI in the digital battleground or through slopaganda. However, policymakers can develop ethical standards and guidelines, so that memes do not overshadow human values. Consequently, if we want our governments to use AI for the common good, as Garcia does, then we need to restore diplomatic communication and refocus our intention on social justice issues. This requires establishing clear ethical guidelines and accountability mechanisms for the institutions posting slopaganda on official accounts. This starts with recognizing that slopaganda is a new form of non-lethal militarized AI.
The post The Ethics of Slopaganda first appeared on Blog of the APA.

Taiwan FM to 'Post': The UN cannot defend freedom without Taiwan's participation - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

The rules-based international order is under growing strain as authoritarian states seek to weaken its safeguards and reshape international rule to serve their own interests. Even the fundamental principles of peaceful settlement of disputes and prohibition against the threat or use of force, which are enshrined in the United Nations charter, have been openly challenged and flagrantly flaunted.
Today, the international community stands at a critical juncture. Either we act together to uphold justice, defend the rule of law, and maintain peace and security, or we watch the world order steadily crumble away, taking freedom, self-determination, and democracy with it.
There are few places where this choice is more starkly presented than in the first island chain of the Indo-Pacific. The region’s security has come under growing pressure from China, which continues to deploy gray-zone tactics – including military intimidation, cyber intrusions, and economic coercion – in an attempt to unilaterally reshape the existing rules and norms.
Standing on the front line of defense of freedom and democracy, Taiwan will continue to firmly uphold the status quo. However, preserving peace and stability in the region is not just in Taiwan’s interests. It is a shared concern of the international community.
The Taiwan Strait is one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes and a major artery for international supply chains. Its significance to global security and prosperity is reflected in statements from the G7 and other summits and ministerial-level meetings between Japan, the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, and other countries. They make up a growing chorus of voices worldwide that underline the importance of cross-strait peace and stability.
The integrity of the rules-based order is also being undermined by China’s deliberate misrepresentation of UN General Assembly Resolution 2758. Adopted in 1971, the resolution covers the question of China’s representation at the UN. The text does not mention Taiwan, determine its political status, or address its participation in the UN system. Yet China has conspired to conflate UNGA 2758 with the so-called “one China principle” and use the resolution to block Taiwan’s participation in the UN and other international organizations. If left unchecked, this distortion could set a dangerous legal precedent and serve as a pretext for future military action across the Taiwan Strait.
Taiwan as a force for good
Despite its exclusion from the UN, Taiwan is determined to act as a force for good. The strengths that Taiwan possesses in advanced manufacturing, disaster preparedness, and public health could contribute to the international community in many ways.
Taiwan has pursued an integrated and value-added foreign policy based on strengthening democratic alliances, promoting collective security, and building economic resilience. Working with like-minded partners, Taiwan advances democracy, human rights, and freedom worldwide. As a leader in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and technology, Taiwan is committed to building supply chains that are secure, resilient, and free from dependence on authoritarian regimes.
Through its Diplomatic Allies Prosperity Project, Taiwan fosters coprosperity with its partners. Taiwan contributes its expertise and resources to technology-driven projects in cooperation with its diplomatic allies to address development challenges and enhance local capacities. Concrete examples include collaboration on an integrated healthcare information system with Paraguay, the construction of a strategic oil reserve facility in Eswatini, and collaboration with Palau National Hospital on smart healthcare. These initiatives have strengthened data management and efficiency, bolstered energy security, fostered industrial growth, and advanced sustainable development.
Khalilur Rahman, president-elect of the upcoming 81st UN General Assembly, has made restoring trust and managing institutional transformation the overarching themes of his presidency. Taiwan shares these objectives and stands ready to help realize them.
Restoring confidence in the UN must begin with treating every member of the international community in a fair and just way. Transformation cannot be complete while a constructive and trustworthy member remains unjustly excluded.
We are calling on the international community to uphold the principles of inclusiveness, leaving no one behind, settling disputes peacefully, and neither threatening nor using force. These imperatives underpin the rules-based international order and should be applied consistently and without exception.
The free world needs Taiwan – and a stronger, more credible United Nations needs Taiwan’s meaningful participation. Working hand in hand with Taiwan will strengthen collective security, enhance economic and technological resilience, and build our shared capacity to withstand authoritarian pressure. Ensuring Taiwan’s meaningful participation in the United Nations is therefore essential to building a more inclusive, secure, resilient, and rules-based international order.
The writer is the Taiwanese foreign minister.

The occupiers shelled civilian infrastructure located within the UNESCO World Heritage Site—the "Ensemble of the Historic Centre of Lviv." According to the case materials, the enemy launched two Kinzhal hypersonic aeroballistic missiles and one Kh-101 cruise missile.
The attack on civilian targets was assigned to units of Russia's 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division, commanded by Major General Mykola Varpakhovych. He then ordered Colonel Oleh Skytskyi, commander of the 121st Heavy Bomber Regiment of the russian Federation, to carry out a missile strike on Lviv.

====================================================================================================

States fume over private health changes 'robbing Peter to pay Paul'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
18:40:34 UTC
03:40:34 KST

Commonwealth stares down states on controversial private health changes
In short:
Some states are calling on the Commonwealth to ditch its proposal to cut the extra private health insurance rebate for Australians aged 65 and over.
States and territories have also launched a coordinated attack after new figures showing more than 3,700 aged care patients are stranded in public hospitals.
What's next?
The federal government is pushing ahead with its private health insurance changes, banking $3 billion to be spent elsewhere in the aged care system.
The federal government has vowed to push ahead with its controversial private health insurance rebate changes despite some states demanding the plan be ditched over fears it will worsen the strain on public hospitals.
State and territory health ministers entered a meeting this morning in Sydney armed with a list of concerns, including the Commonwealth's planned changes to the private health insurance rebate for older Australians and the rapidly growing number of stranded aged care patients in public hospitals across the nation.
The government is proposing to wind back the rebate those aged 65 and over receive on their private health cover, banking $3 billion to spend elsewhere in the aged care system.
Ditching the Howard-era policy would mean more than 3 million older Australians would have to pay hundreds of dollars more for their private health insurance each year from next April.
New South Wales, South Australia, Victoria and the Northern Territory are among those who have raised concerns over the proposed changes, while the Queensland LNP and Tasmanian Liberal governments have gone further, calling for the plan to be ditched.
Speaking after the meeting, federal Health Minister Mark Butler said he recognised the changes would be a cost-of-living hit for older Australians, but the state of the budget bottom line meant there was little money available for new spending.
"This is not a decision I particularly would like to have made in ordinary circumstances, but this is one of those difficult choices we have to make," he said.
"For those who are opposed to it, including my state minister colleagues, I say, where else are we going to get that $3 billion to invest in the beds that they've just been arguing for here? You know, these are about choices."
The federal government's modelling has indicated that about 44,000 Australians would dump their private health insurance as a result.
Those figures have been backed by independent modelling from health economists at the University of Melbourne, who said the impact on hospitals would likely be small.
However, NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said his health department's modelling showed the proposed changes would have a much more significant impact on the public health system.
The upper end of the modelling estimates that in NSW alone, 80,000 residents aged 65 and over may either cancel or downgrade their private health insurance as a result.
It also estimates that public hospitals in NSW could pick up more than 23,000 additional surgeries a year.
"The Commonwealth's proposed changes to private health insurance rebates will place additional pressure onto NSW's public hospitals at a time when health services are already experiencing significant demand," Mr Park said ahead of the meeting.
Victorian Health Minister Ingrid Stitt also raised concerns, saying "any change that would leave older Victorians worse off" and put additional pressure on the states's public hospitals was "unacceptable", while Queensland's Tim Nicholls said he did not believe the Commonwealth understood the impact of the changes.
"This is, I think, robbing Peter to pay Paul, and Paul hasn't been paid yet," he told the ABC.
"If we see more people dropping out of private health insurance, then we'll see more people turning up in our public health institutions, including our public hospitals."
The issue has become increasingly political, with Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston vowing the Coalition would block the legislation in the Senate because it was "nothing more than a cost shift onto older Australians to the public hospital system."
That means the federal government will need the support of the Greens to get the legislation through parliament, with the party yet to land on a formal position.
There is also a Senate inquiry into the issue, which is due to report its findings in October.
3,700 aged care patients stranded in public hospitals
The health ministers also mobilised to launch another coordinated attack against the Commonwealth over the number of stranded aged care patients.
New figures collated by the states and territories reveal more than 3,700 aged care patients are now languishing in public hospitals across the country.
That is compared to about 2,500 last September, an increase of about 50 per cent in 12 months.
Those patients have been medically cleared for discharge but remain in hospital because there is nowhere suitable for them to go.
"I think it is the singular biggest issue that the South Australian health system faces today," South Australian Health Minister Blair Boyer told the ABC.
"They are beds that we don't have available to us today for people who might be presenting at an emergency department or arriving by ambulance, in some cases for elective surgery that is planned."
While states run public hospitals, the Commonwealth funds and regulates aged care services.
Tensions flared in the lead-up to the latest public hospital funding agreement cinched in January, with state governments of different political stripes abandoning party allegiances to unite on the issue.
As well as occupying beds and placing increased pressure on hospitals, long stays in hospitals also strip elderly patients of independence and put them at a greater risk of illness and infection.
Tim Nicholls this week revealed a patient had been stranded in a Queensland public hospital for more than 1,000 days, with more than a dozen other patients stranded for more than 700 days.
He said long-stay patients accounted for more than 11 per cent of the state's acute hospital capacity.
"This is an enormous issue for all states," he said.
"Every bed that is taken up by someone who could be out of a hospital means that we can't move people out of our emergency departments and that means we can't transfer people from the back of an ambulance into an emergency department to receive treatment."
WA Health Minister Meredith Hammat said the issue had reached "worrying new heights".
"It is having an impact on people's ability to access care in our hospitals where they've got acute care needs," she told the ABC.
Australian Medical Association president Danielle McMullen said without urgent action, the number of aged care patients stranded in public hospitals would likely continue to rise.
"Unless we change how our system flows, we will continue to see growing pressure on our public hospitals and on our care system more broadly," she said.
The Commonwealth has pledged an additional 5,000 aged care beds a year by 2029 as part of a $3.7 billion package, alongside funding for specialist dementia care units and a joint taskforce examining long-stay hospital patients.
Mr Butler said there was "no easy fix" to the challenge of demand.
"The numbers are simply unprecedented," he said.
"We increased the number of home care packages last year by 25 per cent. Even with that increase, there's still more and more demand.
"There are some natural constraints on what we can do, how quickly we can build new facilities. We are leaning in as much as we can."

China Focus: China unveils five-year plan to promote SME development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:33:51 CST
03:33:51 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- China has issued a plan to promote high-quality development of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) during the 2026-2030 period, setting targets for business growth, innovation and the development environment.
By 2030, China's SMEs are expected to achieve growth in both quality and scale, with per capita operating revenue of major SMEs posting cumulative growth of around 15 percent over the five-year period, according to the plan, which was jointly issued by 10 government departments, including the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT).
The plan describes SMEs as an important force in driving innovation, creating jobs and improving people's livelihoods. It calls for efforts to improve systems for cultivating high-quality enterprises and providing public services, strengthen the legal and policy framework, and ensure better access to factors of production and a more supportive development environment.
SMEs contribute roughly 70 percent of China's technological innovation, 60 percent of its gross domestic product, and 80 percent of its urban employment, according to an OECD report on SME financing.
SMEs' innovation capacity will be notably enhanced, with average annual growth in internal research and development expenditure by major industrial SMEs targeted at over 8 percent and the number of "little giant" firms expected to reach 22,000 by 2030, according to the plan.
"Little giant" firms refer to the novel elites of SMEs that are engaged in manufacturing, specialize in a niche market and boast cutting-edge technologies.
The plan calls for continued improvements to the SME service system and an increase in the number of cooperation zones for Chinese and foreign SMEs to 50 by 2030.
By then, the development environment for SMEs is expected to improve further, with a sound long-term mechanism for resolving payment arrears owed to SMEs largely in place and access to diversified financing further broadened.
The plan sets out seven key tasks, including keeping businesses and employment stable, strengthening enterprise cultivation, accelerating digital, intelligent and green development, promoting coordinated and integrated development, improving the supply of production factors, strengthening the SME service system, and enhancing legal and policy safeguards.
It further specifies measures that include helping SMEs develop trademark and brand strategies, and launching the second phase of a national SME development fund, among others.
"SMEs face strategic opportunities, as well as risks and challenges, as a new round of sci-tech revolution and industrial transformation gathers pace and competition among major countries grows more complex and intense," said an MIIT official.
The official said that, in response to new circumstances, China needs to step up policy support, strengthen reform and innovation measures, boost SMEs' internal drivers of growth, and reinforce the foundations of the real economy.
The plan is expected to open up more pathways for SME transformation and upgrading, said Ma Yuan, deputy director of the Institute for Enterprise Research under the Development Research Center of the State Council.
Supporting SME development is among the priorities of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), which calls for promoting the growth of SMEs that use specialized and sophisticated technologies to produce novel and unique products, reducing computing costs for SMEs, and strengthening services to support their digital and intelligent transformation.
This year's government work report also pledged stronger support for SMEs undergoing digital and intelligent transformation.
China made notable progress in SME development during the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), with more than 63 million SMEs operating nationwide by the end of 2025, accounting for over 95 percent of all business entities. ■

China Focus: China commemorates 81st anniversary of victory against Japanese aggression
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:33:27 CST
03:33:27 KST

Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, attends a symposium to commemorate the 81st anniversary of the victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Ye)
BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- People across China held commemorative activities on Thursday to mark the 81st anniversary of the victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War.
The Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-1945) was the first to break out and lasted the longest in the World Anti-Fascist War. Over 14 years, some 35 million Chinese were killed or wounded. Japan officially surrendered on Sept. 2, 1945, by signing the Instrument of Surrender.
The war marked China's first complete victory against foreign aggression in modern times. Through immense sacrifice, the Chinese people made a major contribution to the salvation of human civilization and the defense of world peace.
In 2014, China's national legislature designated Sept. 3 as Victory Day of its War of Resistance. Last year, China held grand commemorative events in Beijing on Sept. 3 to mark the 80th anniversary of the victory, including a military parade in Tian'anmen Square.
On Thursday, a symposium was held in Beijing to commemorate the 81st anniversary. Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, attended the event.
About 200 people took part in the symposium, including veterans of the war, relatives of wartime commanders and fallen soldiers, and international friends who contributed to China's victory, as well as representatives of their families.
Officials, young military personnel, and student representatives spoke at the event, vowing to remember history, honor fallen heroes, cherish peace, and build a better future.
In Harbin, capital of northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, a series of activities commemorating the hard-won victory 81 years ago was held at the Northeast China Revolutionary Martyrs' Memorial Hall.
Representatives from government agencies, businesses, military units, schools and social organizations attended a memorial event and paid silent tribute to those who fell in the War of Resistance.
They also visited an exhibition featuring wartime relics to learn more about the historical significance and contemporary relevance of the spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army (NAJUA).
For 14 years, the soldiers of NAJUA fought in extreme conditions, suffering severe food and clothing shortages while facing overwhelming enemy superiority. Yet they still inflicted heavy losses on Japanese forces, making an indelible contribution to the World Anti-Fascist War.
"We commemorate the victory so that we do not forget history," said Tong Guobo, head of the memorial hall. "The NAJUA spirit -- of unwavering faith, deep patriotism, and dauntless courage -- has taken deep root in northeast China, inspiring generations to forge ahead."
At the Memorial Hall of the Victims of the Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders in east China's Jiangsu Province, people took part in poetry readings and historical reenactments, bringing to life the harrowing stories of that dark chapter for the audience.
"Both my parents were survivors of the Nanjing Massacre, and we lost six family members to the Japanese forces in 1937," said Cao Yuli, who was participating in the event.
"We should always remember the past and value the peace we enjoy today," said Zhang Xinjue, a student choir member during the commemorations.
In east China's Shandong Province, more than 3,000 artifacts that bear witness to the Japanese atrocities are exhibited at a private museum in Pingyin County. Among them are military postcards and letters and soldiers' diaries, as well as photographs, combat maps, and other items such as swords, helmets, and gas masks.
Han Guangyou, the 65-year-old curator of the museum, has spent more than four decades amassing these artifacts from across China. "These exhibits stand as undeniable proof of the war crimes committed by imperial Japan," he said.
The museum now receives more than 20,000 visitors annually. Han is currently collaborating with several universities to catalog, digitize and research the collection. "These stark exhibits serve as a sobering reminder for young people to remember the lessons of history and strive to build a stronger China," Han said.
"Today's world is far from peaceful," said Zhang Shaoduo, an associate researcher at Shanghai International Studies University. "These commemorative events remind people across the globe that a stronger China remains a pillar of world peace."
Also on Thursday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun urged Japanese right-wing forces to adhere to the path of peaceful development, in response to Japan's record-high defense budget request for the 2027 fiscal year.
"Our solemn message to Japanese right-wing forces: the right way forward for Japan is to fulfill its international obligations, fully remove the pernicious influence of militarism, and keep to peaceful development," Guo told a regular press briefing in Beijing. ■

Portuguese researchers develop new approach to treating Machado-Joseph disease
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:33:13 CST
03:33:13 KST

COIMBRA, Portugal, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- A new approach to treating Machado-Joseph disease has been developed by Portuguese researchers, it was announced this week.
Machado-Joseph disease is a hereditary neurodegenerative disorder with a high prevalence in parts of Portugal. Also known as spinocerebellar ataxia type 3, the disease causes progressive problems with movement, speech and swallowing. There is currently no cure for the disease.
The study, conducted by researchers at the University of Coimbra and the GeneT Center of Excellence in Gene Therapy and published in the scientific journal Biomaterials, could contribute to new treatments for the disease.
The researchers used tiny particles naturally released by cells to carry the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool, allowing them to target the mutated gene responsible for the disease.
"We wanted to understand whether it was possible to use extracellular vesicles to achieve transient exposure to the gene-editing machinery and minimize unwanted edits," said Kevin Leandro, first author of the study.
According to the researchers, the method could overcome some limitations of conventional gene therapies by reducing immune reactions and limiting the time gene-editing tools remain active in cells.
The researchers also developed a light-controlled system to improve the efficiency of the gene-editing process.
The University of Coimbra said the study is among the first internationally to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in Machado-Joseph disease, and could contribute to the development of safer treatments for the disease and other rare genetic disorders. ■

Update: Africa CDC says too early to declare DR Congo Ebola outbreak under control
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:33:11 CST
03:33:11 KST

KINSHASA, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said Thursday it remains too early to say that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is under control, despite signs of stabilization in recent weeks.
"We're still early to say that we're controlling the whole outbreak," Africa CDC official Wessam Mankoula told an online press briefing, noting that the outbreak "is still evolving."
According to the latest government situation report published Thursday, the DRC had recorded 6,250 confirmed cases and 3,039 deaths as of Sept. 1, with a case fatality rate of 48.6 percent. A total of 1,439 patients have recovered. The outbreak has affected 60 health zones across six provinces.
Four health zones have interrupted transmission after reporting no new cases for more than 42 days, while another five are in "control phase", which have gone between 21 and 42 days without a new case. Transmission, however, remains active in 51 health zones, Mankoula said.
"For the last two weeks, we are seeing a decline in the number of cases; we are almost at the plateau phase," Mankoula said, cautioning that "it's very early to say we have sustained decline in this outbreak."
Mankoula said the plateau could reflect stronger surveillance, earlier case detection, active case finding, infection prevention and control measures, and improved case management. "Hopefully, when we're following now the third week, we continue with this plateau, then we start seeing a decrease," he said.
But he cautioned against drawing conclusions too soon. "We saw this plateau previously in June, then later on it's followed by an increase. This is why we are cautiously interpreting those data," Mankoula said.
The current outbreak, declared in May, has since become the country's largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic on record and the second-largest globally, behind the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa.
Mankoula also noted that while Uganda recently declared its own Ebola outbreak over, the continued active transmission in DRC's eastern provinces bordering Uganda poses a persistent cross-border risk.
He stressed that strong surveillance systems must remain in place at points of entry and along border communities to detect any potential spillover cases early and prevent a new wave of cross-border transmission.
"This outbreak is still evolving," Mankoula said. "Incremental measures are no longer effective. This is the time for scaling up all different responses to control the situation on the ground."
Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya said Wednesday that Ebola in the DRC "remains extremely serious and continues to spread." "Despite the considerable efforts of the (DRC) government and partners, we are not yet where we need to be," said Kaseya.
With no approved vaccine or treatment specifically targeting Bundibugyo virus, the cause of the current outbreak, the international community is turning to experimental and repurposed medical tools.
As for vaccines, the Ervebo vaccine, the licensed shot against the Zaire ebolavirus, is currently being evaluated for cross-protection against the current Bundibugyo strain through an effectiveness study in the field.
Meanwhile, under protocol-governed compassionate use, which allows the use of unapproved or partially studied vaccines in an outbreak setting, vaccinations for frontline healthcare workers and at-risk populations began on Aug. 27.
As of Sept. 1, a total of 1,124 healthcare workers and frontline workers had been vaccinated, said Mankoula.
"So we think that very soon we'll be able to provide more detail and a precise answer regarding the level of cross-protection using the Ervebo vaccine," said Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC's director for research, clinical trials and innovation at the briefing, noting that Ervebo's efficacy against the Bundibugyo ebolavirus has not been demonstrated yet. ■

Researchers observes gravity's predicted quantum phase
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
02:33:10 CST
03:33:10 KST

JERUSALEM, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- An international team of researchers has observed a long-predicted effect of gravity on a falling quantum object, showing a key principle behind Einstein's theory of gravity remains valid even in the quantum world, Israel's Ben-Gurion University of the Negev said in a statement on Thursday.
Einstein's equivalence principle is the idea that gravity affects all objects equally, regardless of mass. According to this principle, a freely falling observer should locally experience no gravitational force. However, quantum objects can behave as waves and effectively travel along more than one path, raising the question of whether the principle remains valid when "the object" does not follow a single definite classical path.
In the new study published in the journal Science Advances, the researchers tested the principle on microscopic objects governed by quantum mechanics and found that gravity behaved exactly as Einstein predicted.
The team used extremely cold atoms placed in a quantum state that allowed them to follow two paths simultaneously.
They used the Quantum Galileo Interferometer, in honor of Galileo's work on gravity. It allowed them to split the quantum wave associated with an atom into two paths, one in place (stationary relative to the laboratory and Earth) and the other for free fall, and then reunite them to see how gravity had changed the falling wave.
When the two paths were brought back together, the researchers measured a tiny change in the atoms' quantum state, and the result was the same as that predicted when Einstein's principle is applied to such a quantum wave.
The researchers said their experiment provided insight into one of the most fundamental questions in physics: how gravity, described by Einstein's theory of relativity and quantum theory, can be unified into one understanding of the universe.
The researchers noted that their finding did not prove that gravity itself is quantum, but showed that Einstein's equivalence principle still holds with quantum mechanics in the regime tested.
They added that their technique could enable future experiments with heavier objects, such as nanodiamonds, to test whether quantum mechanics could break down under extreme conditions. ■

Global aircraft engine lessor makes direct leasing move in China

TIANJIN, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Major global aircraft engine lessor Rolls-Royce & Partners Finance (RRPF) on Thursday announced to set up a direct aero engine leasing entity in China as it seeks to cash in on the world's second-largest aviation market.
RRPF, a joint venture between British aircraft engine giant Rolls-Royce and U.S. firm GATX, signed a deal for its new China subsidiary with the Dongjiang Comprehensive Bonded Zone in north China's Tianjin Municipality on Thursday.
The direct leasing business, the first of its kind in China by leading global aircraft engine makers, marks a shift in how overseas aviation assets are managed in the country.
The new entity, backed by more than 2.3 billion yuan (about 339 million U.S. dollars) in total investment, will own and base engines domestically, breaking with the industry norm of keeping assets offshore while leasing them into China.
The new business can sharply reduce intermediate procedures and lower airlines' foreign exchange management and leasing costs, providing domestic aviation firms with more stable, predictable and high-quality engine leasing services.
"China is currently the world's second-largest aviation market. For the next 10 years, it's gonna grow," said Ben Hughes, RRPF's chief strategy officer. He added that the new entity would help lower customer expenses and that hiring local talent would support more efficient operations.
The Tianjin Dongjiang Comprehensive Bonded Zone is known as a hub for leasing activities and is the world's second-largest cluster for aircraft leasing. By the end of August, it had facilitated the leasing of more than 2,600 aircraft and over 300 aircraft engines, according to local officials. ■
