A new study explains why stress makes us both cooperative and defensive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
18:00:03 UTC
03:00:03 KST

People under acute stress may cooperate with potential allies while becoming more defensive toward the people responsible for the stressful situation, according to research published in Psychoneuroendocrinology. The findings suggest that stress does not have one universal effect on social behavior; whom a person is dealing with may shape the response.
Two theories have traditionally offered different predictions about behavior under pressure. The “tend-and-befriend” account proposes that people seek affiliation and cooperate with others who could provide support. The “fight-or-flight” account proposes that threats can instead encourage withdrawal, aggression or protection of one’s own resources. Previous studies have found evidence for both patterns, prompting researchers to examine whether features of the situation can explain the inconsistency.
Laura Oswald of the University of Freiburg led a team that investigated whether the social role of an interaction partner changes behavior following acute stress. The researchers expected people to treat another, unstressed participant as a possible ally but respond more defensively to an evaluator who had helped create the stressful experience.
The final sample contained 121 healthy young adults (62 women, average age of 23.64 years). Participants first completed the Trier Social Stress Test for Groups. After five minutes of preparation, they gave a 12-minute speech and completed an eight-minute mental-arithmetic task before a jury wearing white coats that provided no encouraging feedback. Saliva samples, heart-rate recordings and subjective ratings confirmed whether the procedure produced a stress response.
Participants then made decisions involving real money in four established games measuring trust, trustworthiness, sharing and punishment. They completed decisions involving another participant who had not been subjected to the stress test and decisions involving a jury member who had been part of the stress test. This allowed the researchers to compare how the same stressed person treated a peer and a source of stress.
The stress hormone cortisol, heart rate and perceived stress all increased substantially during the procedure. Participants made an average of 2.52 trusting choices toward peers, compared with 2.02 toward jury members. They also made more trustworthy choices toward peers, 3.06 compared with 2.40, and more sharing choices, 2.83 compared with 2.27. Conversely, punishment was more frequent toward jury members than peers, averaging 0.74 compared with 0.54. Each difference was statistically significant.
The behavioral pattern did not differ significantly between men and women. The size of participants’ cortisol, heart-rate or perceived-stress response also did not clearly predict how differently they treated peers and jury members. The findings therefore point more strongly to the interaction partner’s role than to the measured intensity of an individual’s stress response.
As the researchers explained, “individuals adapt their behavior toward others depending on the social role of their interaction partner.” Cooperating with a peer may increase the possibility of receiving reciprocal help, while withholding cooperation from an evaluator may protect resources or help restore a sense of control.
Important caveats remain. Everyone completed the stress procedure, so the study cannot show whether stress increased cooperation with peers, decreased cooperation with jury members or produced both changes. Also, participants always dealt with peers before jury members, leaving possible order and comparison effects. Studies including a non-stress control group, friendlier evaluators and more natural interactions are needed.
The study, “Tend-and-befriend toward peers, fight-or-flight toward stressors: A dual response to stress,” was authored by Laura Oswald, Fabian Dvorak, Jeremy P. Jamieson, Markus Heinrichs and Bastian Schiller.

The Freedom Flotilla Coalition has announced a new international maritime mission to Gaza, with vessels making stops at European ports before a planned attempt to reach the besieged enclave in October.
“We are sailing again because Israel hasn’t stopped its genocide and because Palestine is still not free,” the coalition said in an appeal for international support.
The mission seeks to challenge Israel’s blockade of Gaza and mobilise public pressure across Europe, the coalition said in a statement published on Wednesday.
The voyage is already under way, with the coalition’s Handala II vessel having visited ports in Norway, Sweden and Denmark during June and July.
Another vessel, the Kate, departed from the British city of Bristol in August and subsequently made stops in Ireland, Germany and France, according to the statement.
The vessels are expected to visit ports in Spain, Portugal and Italy before continuing toward Gaza, where the coalition plans to arrive in October.
The mission brings together human rights advocates, trade union activists, elected representatives, journalists, medical professionals and other supporters of Palestinian rights, the coalition said.
‘Serious risks’
The coalition said it would work with local communities to pressure governments to block weapons and energy shipments to Israel, end diplomatic and military cooperation with it and impose sanctions.
“The Freedom Flotilla sails again because our governments continue to fail to uphold their obligations,” said Zohar Chamberlain Regev, a member of the coalition’s steering committee.
“At every port, we will carry the demand that Palestinians be free to live with dignity,” she added.
“In October, we intend to carry that demand and the solidarity of people around the world to Gaza’s shores.”
The coalition urged governments to demand safe and unobstructed passage for the flotilla and to make clear that any attack, seizure or detention of its participants would have consequences.
It also called for immediate and unrestricted access to Gaza and an end to Israeli restrictions on the entry of food, water, medicine and other essential supplies.
Governments should defend freedom of navigation and use diplomatic, economic and legal measures to end the blockade, it added.
“We know that sailing toward Gaza carries serious risks,” said Edward Digilio, an engineer from the US state of Maryland participating in the initiative.
“But silence and inaction carry a much greater cost for Palestinians and the world,” he said, describing the mission as “an expression of shared humanity and a refusal to accept the destruction of an entire people as normal.”
The coalition said Israeli forces had attacked and illegally detained hundreds of flotilla participants during an earlier mission in the spring of 2026. It said volunteers reported severe beatings, broken bones, gunshot wounds, repeated tasering and sexual assault while in Israeli custody.
It also recalled Israel’s May 2010 raid on the Gaza-bound Mavi Marmara, during which 10 activists were killed.

EU to help cities clamp down on tourist rentals

EU to help cities clamp down on tourist rentals
- The EU plans to introduce rules allowing cities to restrict short-term tourist rentals like Airbnb to address rising housing prices and protect residents.
- The new law will define when areas are "under housing stress" based on house prices and income, permitting restrictions on rentals and property purchases for short-term letting.
- The legislation excludes landlords renting their primary residence and aims to balance housing supply issues while addressing pressures from short-term lets, amid a 60% rise in property prices over ten years.
AI generated
BRUSSELS - The EU is set to lay out rules helping European cities to curb short-term rentals such as Airbnb in a bid to tackle rising house prices, according to plans seen by AFP on Sept 4.
The European Commission is expected to unveil next week a legal proposal setting out the conditions under which authorities can restrict the provision of short-term tourist lets.
Such rentals have increasingly come into the crosshairs of local authorities in tourist hotspots such as Florence and Barcelona, as residents complain about being priced out by visitors.
But curbs have often been followed by court challenges from rental providers and tourism operators, resulting in legal uncertainty.
The commission’s Affordable Housing Act aims to clarify when authorities can take action without falling foul of EU single market rules.
Cities, regions and other relevant authorities would be allowed to restrict access to, or the provision of short-term rentals as well as the purchase of property for short-term letting in areas “under housing stress”, according a draft seen by AFP.
The document lays out a series of parameters that need to be met for an area to be defined as under stress, such as the difference between house prices and incomes there.
The legislation will not affect landlords that rent out their own primary residence for short periods of time.
Housing affordability has become a growing issue across the 27-nation bloc in recent years.
Property prices have surged by 60 per cent, while rents have climbed by 20 per cent over the past decade, leaving millions struggling to find a home they can afford, according to Brussels.
The EU says this is mainly driven by insufficient housing supply but short-term lets add extra pressure in certain areas, further reducing supply and driving up prices – something rental providers dispute.
“Europe’s housing crisis needs structural solutions, and the implementation of this Act should focus on increasing the supply of homes,” said an Airbnb spokesperson. AFP

Ukraine adopts two-tier air raid alert system as Russia’s mass drone attacks become the new normal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
17:53:24 UTC
02:53:24 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine adopted a decision to introduce two levels of air alerts, with yellow for drone attacks and red for a heightened threat of missile or combined strikes, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on 3 September. Under the yellow level, designated businesses can operate if they meet safety requirements, while a red alert will require work to stop and people to move to shelters.
Russia continues to attack Ukrainian cities with drones and other long-range weapons, repeatedly disrupting civilian and economic activity. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia is using mass drone attacks to wear down civilian life and economic activity, while the existing system of signaling all aerial threats in the same way no longer fits Russia's tactics.
How it will work
Businesses cleared to operate under a yellow alert must ensure staff and visitors can reach shelters. Where that access is missing, the Cabinet is giving businesses three months to provide it.
The General Staff, the Air Force, the government, the Defense Ministry, the Interior Ministry, and the State Emergency Service will set the specific indicators for declaring each level weekly, Zelenskyy said.
What still has to be worked out
Zelenskyy also directed officials to develop geographic targeting for alerts, so warnings can be limited to areas facing an actual threat. The measure is still being worked out and is not yet part of the new system.
The new approach is intended to allow economic activity to continue during drone threats while preserving stricter measures for more serious attacks. The government has not yet finalized which businesses will qualify to remain open under a yellow alert or all of the criteria for applying the two levels.

Yemen’s army says recaptured key territory as clashes with Houthis continue

Yemen’s army say they have recaptured strategically important territory, as heavy clashes with Houthi rebels continue in the southwest of the country.
Yemeni government forces recaptured al-Khazan and al-Makahna hills in Jabal Habashi district west of Taiz city, according to a statement on Friday.

The clashes between government forces and Houthi fighters continued for the second day in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah, two governorates along the Red Sea coast, after the rebel group launched a broad offensive along front lines on the coast.

Australian tennis player Nick Kyrgios accepted a one-month suspension Friday after testing positive for cocaine and is now eligible to return to competition.

He warned that further escalation could have “devastating political, economic, and security ramifications for Yemen and all of its people.”
“The parties must prioritize dialogue and engage constructively with the United Nations-led efforts towards a negotiated political settlement,” he added.
On Lebanon, Dujarric said UN Humanitarian Coordinator Imran Riza visited Nabatieh in southern Lebanon, where he met communities receiving people returning to their homes as well as displaced residents.
Authorities highlighted damage to vital infrastructure, including water and sanitation systems, he said.
In the village of Mayfadoun, damage to a water well station, including solar panels and pumping equipment, has affected water supplies, according to Dujarric.
He stressed the importance of “early recovery efforts to restore these essential services” and support municipalities and communities seeking to recover.
Dujarric said the UN’s 2026 Lebanon flash appeal ended last month after receiving less than 52% of the requested funding, with $330 million received.
Despite the funding shortfall, humanitarian partners have reached more than 1.2 million people with at least one form of critical assistance since the latest escalation began, including more than 900,000 people who received cash assistance.
“Yet, as Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher stressed, the needs continue, access remains constrained, and many families in Lebanon still cannot return home safely,” he said.
Regarding the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Dujarric said the UN remains “very concerned about the safety of civilians both in the Gaza Strip and in the West Bank.”
He said UN agencies and humanitarian partners in Gaza were helping communities prepare for the rainy season, but “more funding and access are urgently needed.”
Citing World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Dujarric warned that public health risks are growing as winter approaches, with many people still displaced in overcrowded tented sites.
“Gaza’s already overwhelmed health system cannot withstand additional surges in diseases and illness,” Tedros said, according to Dujarric.
In the West Bank, UN humanitarian colleagues reported that more than 6,400 Palestinians have been displaced from 130 communities by occupiers' violence since 2023. More than 2,500 were displaced this year alone, over half of them children.
Dujarric said the UN’s humanitarian concerns were being compounded by repeated attacks, damage to homes and infrastructure and restrictions on access to land and essential services.
